In particular, the ECB broadened the base of acceptable collateral data for the main refinancing operations, proceeded to carry out more longer-term refinancing operations, expanded the number of eligible counterparties for the normalisation of short-term liquidity fluctuations, and finally provided liquidity in dollars and Swiss francs, in cooperation with the Federal Reserve and the Swiss National Bank of Greece; respectively. These actions prevented the deterioration of the situation in the financial system in the euro area and internationally. Last week, on 4 December, the Governing Council of the ECB cut its key interest rate by 75 bps, to 2.5%. In connection with the previous two recent declines of 50 bps, on 8 October and 6 November, some analysts have raised the question of whether the room for further monetary expansion by the Governing Council is now more limited. Similar questions arise for other central banks, for example the Federal Reserve, where the official interest rate is now at 1%, and for the Swiss National Bank, which decided today to lower the three-month interbank reference rate (Libor) by 50 bps to the level between 0 - 1%. Reference is made to the fact that very short-term nominal interest rates, for example, the daily interest rate in the interbank market, has a lower limit of zero. Therefore, the argument is that there is a limitation on the resources that monetary policy has in its arsenal when the short-term interest rate reaches very low levels. I would like to clarify that the view that monetary policy becomes ineffective and cannot provide a further expansionary impetus when the short-term interest rate reaches zero or a very low level is wrong. Zero levels of short-term interest rates are not a temporary obstacle to further monetary expansion if necessary. This is because a central bank, as an issuing authority, has no restriction on the possibility of issuing money through the expansion of its balance sheet. In this way, the central bank continues to have a positive impact on denominations and to influence longer-term interest rates, even when the daily rate remains unchanged. Of course, monetary policy is more complex and difficult in cases where short-term interest rates are already too low. This, however, does not limit the effectiveness of monetary policy. Inevitably, the effects of the economic turmoil on the euro area and global real economy have already started to be more pronounced and for this reason international organisations are dramatically revising downwards their forecasts for the outlook for the global economy. Specifically, according to the IMF's forecast last November, GDP in 2009 is expected to contract by 0.7% in the US and 1.3% in the UK. For the euro area, according to forecasts published last week by the ECB, GDP is expected to contract by 0.5% (a change in growth between -1% and 0%) compared to the September forecast that predicted an increase of around 1.2%. As regards inflation, the ECB expects the euro area to hover around 1.4% in 2009 compared to the September forecast of around 2.4%. The significant slowdown in inflation projected for 2009 is mainly due to the decline in oil prices that began in July 2008. Indeed, as a result of this decline, it is possible to observe for some months of 2009 the phenomenon of deflation in the euro area. If this phenomenon is observed, it will be transient and will be solely due to the fluctuation of the prices of oil and other basic goods. Moreover, it is extremely important that the long-term expectations for the inflation in the euro area (as calculated by relevant perception surveys) is still close to 2% and is in line with the ECB's quantitative definition of price stability (inflation just below 2%). This is also reflected in the fact that core inflation, which excludes imponderable exogenous factors such as oil prices, has remained and is projected to remain relatively stable in 2009 as well. As far as the economy of our country is concerned, the degree of deterioration of the negative developments and the extension of the effects of the crisis to various sectors, such as tourism and construction, will depend on the continuation or not of the international financial crisis, the degree of impact of the real economy in the euro area, the degree of efficiency of the coordinated measures taken at European level and worldwide and the preventive shielding of our own economy with the appropriate measures. But we must bear in mind that, in the age of globalisation, it is impossible for the economy of any country to remain unscathed by turbulence of the extent that we are experiencing today. In particular, if we take into account the fact that Cypriot economic activity relies heavily on foreign demand. On the other hand, of course, we should not lose sight of the fact that any negative effects on Cyprus will be extremely milder than the effects we would have had with the small and open economy if we had not joined the euro area. Let me remind you that in many EU countries that do not belong to the euro area and have been hit hard by the crisis, a public debate has begun on the need to join the euro area. In some of these countries lending rates are currently much higher than those prevailing in Cyprus and other euro area countries. In several countries the value of the national currency has come under considerable pressure and some currencies have lost a significant part of their value against the euro. A similar debate on the adoption of the euro has begun in Iceland, which has been hit hard by the crisis and which now wants to join the EU in order to be able to join the euro area as well. Taking into account the data so far, the estimates of the CBC are that a significant slowdown in the real GDP of our country will be recorded in 2009, with the growth rate hovering around 2%. I stress, however, that, in the current situation, the degree of uncertainty is very high and that is why various analysts are making different growth scenarios. More optimistic growth scenarios are not excluded. However, we must also bear in mind possible scenarios below 2% in case the international recession intensifies and the construction sector and tourism in Cyprus are affected even more significantly. The recovery in economic activity is projected, under the central scenario, to start in 2010, without ruling out a prolongation of the recession in the event of a stronger than currently expected global economic slowdown. Of course, although the slowdown of the Cypriot economy today reflects to some extent the effects of negative international economic developments, however, the overheating observed in the last one to two years and the consequent economic imbalances that have arisen, such as excessive borrowing, overconsumption, high inflation, the widening of the current account deficit and the excessive activity in construction, they could not be sustainable, even without the negative impact of international financial deterioration. Let me remind you, for example, at this point that the Central Bank has been sounding the alarm, at least since July 2007, about the excessively high growth rate of borrowing. This was because we were concerned that this unsustainable growth rate would also lead to an increase in the new units available for sale, which would ultimately create a dangerous surplus that could not, if any, be absorbed by existing internal and external demand. Especially today, with the recession observed in the economies of the United Kingdom and other countries, foreign demand seems to have fallen significantly. In fact, the decrease at the moment may be greater than the one the Central Bank warned about. I repeat, however, that even without the international recession, the rate of construction of new properties, as well as the rapid increases in their prices, was not sustainable and inevitably at some stage we should expect a correction of the imbalances created in this market. Against this background, a mild corrective slowdown in economic activity with a consequent reduction in the aforementioned imbalances should not be seen as negative for our economy. With prudent measures, we will maintain sustainable development by limiting inflationary pressures and unsustainable deficit situations that burden the younger generations and the weaker strata of the people. At the same time, however, I would like to stress that in the event of a deterioration in the economic situation due to the international recession, the implementation of specific and carefully designed measures to mitigate the effects of the crisis is legitimate. At this point, I would like to stress that emphasis should be placed on development projects that will bring the greatest added value to the economy and that will increase the productivity of Cypriot businesses. Let us not forget that the negative consequences of the chronic structural problems that Cypriot businesses are facing and which have hitherto been disguised to some extent by the high rates of GDP growth are beginning to emerge more strongly on the surface. At a time of reduced demand, increased competition and more difficult borrowing, low competitiveness can deal a blow to Cypriot businesses, which rely on international demand, show high resistance to the introduction of new technologies and generally have sclerotic structures. It is characteristic that the labor costs of businesses in Cyprus in the first half of 2008 increased by 5.9%, surpassing the corresponding increase in labor costs in the eurozone (3.1%) by 2.8 percentage points. Productivity growth, while still above the corresponding growth in the euro area, is not enough to close the gap in labour costs. In summary, the competitiveness of the domestic economy has fallen over the last year and this should be paid particular attention now in view of the fact that our currency is now shared with all the other countries of the euro area. Measures that increase productivity, such as the adoption of innovations and new technology, must be a priority for the business world and the government. Further progress can also be achieved by simplifying public procedures relating to businesses and reducing red tape. Any measures taken to deal with the crisis must be carefully planned because wrong reactions may worsen the long-term prospects of the economy and further erode the competitiveness of Cypriot businesses. All stakeholders must present our reality and assessments without embellishment or scaremongering. What is important is to understand the effects of the crisis and to rally everyone to overcome it. As far as our banking sector is concerned, despite the turmoil that has hit this sector to its core internationally and in contrast to the problems that have arisen in several other countries, including countries in the euro area, I still see that it remains healthy and strong. The good state of the banking system primarily reflects the correctness over time of the CBC's supervisory policy. The fact that Cypriot banks have not been exposed to either risks of lack of liquidity or excessive investment risks is due to the supervisory framework of the CBC, which although at times considered strict, nevertheless acted as a shield to protect our banking system. However, the international turmoil, especially after its peak in September and October, has inevitably affected borrowing conditions in Cyprus as well. As in many other countries, deposit and lending rates have increased significantly, along with the Euribor interbank rate, which is a reference rate on many loans and deposits. These interest rate increases, however, are projected to be gradually reversed, as is already evident from the continued reduction in Euribor interest rates. The drastic and decisive moves of the central banks mentioned above have contributed decisively to this course of normalization. I think needless to say that in the Governing Council of the ECB we are closely monitoring macroeconomic developments and we are always ready to take further measures whenever this is deemed legitimate. In conclusion, I would say that the great financial crisis has given an important lesson to the actors and governments involved: that without coordination and without close cooperation, no country alone can cope with the consequences of such an international crisis. The governments of the euro area countries have understood this reality and, in close cooperation with the ECB, have taken and are taking appropriate measures to get out of economic instability as quickly as possible. A particular lesson for Cyprus is the fact that due to the adoption of the euro, the worse for our country, in terms of the international economic crisis, have been avoided. Of course, the shocks of such turmoil cannot leave us completely untouched. However, with prudence and proper planning, as well as with a clear definition of priorities, our country has the capabilities to find the appropriate solutions for a return to economic normality.

Title: Speech at the session of the Parliamentary Committee on Institutions, Values, and Commissioner of Administration
text: The international financial turmoil and the economy Speech by Athanasios Orphanides, Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus, at a dinner of the Institute of Certified Public Accountants Limassol, 28 January 2009 It is a great pleasure for me to be here this evening and I would like to thank the Limassol-Paphos Coordinating Committee of the Institute of Certified Public Accountants for the kind invitation. I will use this opportunity to share with you some thoughts on the international financial turmoil, its mounting global impact on the real economy and the concomitant policy response, particularly from a central bank perspective. In this context, I will also review the outlook for the Cyprus economy. I note that the views I express are my own and do not necessarily reflect the views of my colleagues on the Governing Council of the European Central Bank. The financial system is the heart of the modern capitalist economy. When it functions properly, it efficiently allocates scarce financial resources to the most productive use, allowing a seamless transfer of funds from lenders to borrowers through banking institutions, capital and money markets. If this key role is disrupted, the real economy may suffer. Depending on the magnitude of the disruption, the implications for the real economy could be dire, especially if policy measures do not succeed in isolating and correcting the problem sufficiently quickly. In that case, a negative feedback loop may materialise with a financial disturbance and a worsening real economy reinforcing each other in a downward spiral for a time. Today the world is facing such an extraordinary disturbance of the international financial system. How bad is it? We need to go back many decades---to the 1930s---to identify a disturbance to the international financial system of a similar magnitude. Over the past several months, we have experienced the collapse of major international financial institutions and a systemic breakdown of key financial markets which have led to a severe and synchronised economic downturn in the worldd5s advanced economies. How did it happen? Briefly, the trigger for the turmoil is associated with the end of the most recent housing cycle and the related rise in defaults on subprime mortgages in the United States. The cause of the crisis, however, must be traced to an accumulation of imbalances in the world economy that built up over a number a years and gaps in the regulatory framework that permitted excessive risk taking by a number of systemically important financial institutions around the world. In the years leading to the outbreak of the financial turmoil in August 2007, consumers, firms and investors, especially in the United States and Europe, were encouraged by a benign macroeconomic environment of low interest rates, low inflation and sustained economic growth to expect continued prosperity. More specifically, the success of economic policies during this period to dampen significantly macroeconomic fluctuations as well as the low cost of borrowing contributed to an underestimation of the risk and its under pricing by economic agents. This in turn resulted in excessive risk taking and a proliferation of complex financial instruments. Prices of real estate and other assets as well as leverage rose significantly. Regulators did not sufficiently appreciate the accumulating dangers to the financial system and were not fully aware of their seriousness. When house prices started to fall in the United States and subprime-mortgage-related defaults increased by more than was expected, it became evident that the risk in securities related to subprime mortgages was mispriced. This raised questions about valuations of complex securities that contained elements backed by subprime mortgages and about possible solvency problems of banking institutions holding these securities. From the subprime-related market segment, tensions spilled over to other markets, including the money markets in the US and in Europe. Following the outbreak of the turmoil in August 2007, tensions remained elevated for over a year only to become vastly worse following the failure of the American investment bank Lehman Brothers in September 2008. Money markets essentially froze in September d0 October 2008 due to a collapse in confidence that made banks unwilling to engage in unsecured transactions with each other. These developments also hastened the deleveraging process that was already under way and prompted an abrupt tightening of credit conditions and a sharp deterioration in the global economy during the fourth quarter of 2008 that appears to be continuing in 2009. It drastically changed the outlook for inflation, reversing the upward pressure exhibited during the first half of 2008, but also vastly raised the uncertainty about the outlook for the economy worldwide. The policy response to the turmoil in September 2008 was also massive, reflecting the magnitude of the problem. Governments and central banks took a multitude of measures in a concerted fashion with a view to alleviating the impact of the financial crisis on the real economy, restoring confidence and the efficient functioning of financial markets. These included coordinated liquidity provision operations and interest rate reductions by major central banks, measures to enhance the liquidity in the banking system and government programs to buy toxic assets, recapitalise financial institutions and set up deposit protection schemes. At the same time, regulatory and supervisory frameworks have been scrutinised so as to identify how they may be strengthened. Against this background, it is of particular interest to focus on the way central banks have reacted to the crisis since the collapse of Lehman Brothers. In addition to operations designed to alleviate worsening liquidity problems, and in light of the deterioration in the real economy and dampening of inflation pressures, all major central banks in the industrialised world have reduced their policy rates. In an unprecedented coordinated interest rate move on 8 October, six major central banks, including the ECB, reduced their policy rates by as much as 50 basis points. With a continued deterioration in the financial system and a related worsening of the real economy and dampening of inflation pressures, policy rates around the world were subsequently reduced even more drastically to record low levels. On December 11, the Swiss National Bank lowered its three.month Libor target range all the way down to 0.0d01.0% and on December 16 2008 the Federal Reserve reduced its target further, to a range of 0 to 25 basis points for the target federal funds rate. Likewise, the Bank of England reduced its rate by a total of 3. percentage points in only four months to 1.% in January 2009, its lowest ever level. Against diminishing inflationary pressures and downward prospects for the euro area, the ECB substantially reduced the main refinancing rate to 2% in January 2009, matching the lowest rate ever. I note that the Bank of Japan, which had maintained very low rates for a decade, also reduced the target for its policy interest rate from 0,5% to 0,3% at the end of October 2008 and further reduced it to 0,1% in December 2008. Since short-term nominal interest rates cannot be reduced below zero, the fact that policy rates set by some central banks, such as the Bank of Japan, the Federal Reserve and the Swiss National Bank are already extremely close to zero, and that policy rates of other central banks, including the ECB and the Bank of England, are at historical lows, has rekindled interest in questions regarding possible complications for monetary policy operating at very low interest rates. It is sometimes stated, for instance, that monetary policy becomes ineffective once the short-term interest rate gets close to zero, in the sense that monetary policy cannot be eased any further, even though the central bank may wish to do so. As I have stated before, this idea of such policy ineffectiveness is a fallacy. I should add that the fallacy that monetary policy is ineffective when short-term interest rates are close to zero is dangerous because it may promote inaction. A central bank that has already reduced its policy rate to zero could be incorrectly advised to stop pursuing expansionary measures because these are thought to be ineffective. And a central bank with a policy rate that is positive but rather low, might be incorrectly advised to d2save its ammunitiond3 so that it may still be in a position to ease policy later on. One flaw in the policy ineffectiveness argument and related policy advice is that it focuses too narrowly on the short-term nominal interest rate as the instrument for monetary policy. While this focus is convenient and appropriate under normal circumstances -that is when rates are not close to zero -it is insufficient for describing changes in the stance of monetary policy when short-term interest rates touch zero. Under such circumstances, attention should shift to the quantity of money and reserves, the size of a central bankd5s balance sheet, and interest rates at longer maturities that do not touch zero. Ultimately, a money issuing central bank does not face limitations in increasing the quantity of money by expanding its balance sheet and can continue to do so even if short-term interest rates cannot be reduced further, for example when the overnight interest rate equals zero. By doing so, a central bank can have a positive effect on nominal asset prices and influence longer-term interest rates even if the overnight rate is unaffected. That said, it should be recognised that conducting and communicating additional monetary policy easing is far more challenging when it is not accompanied by a reduction in the policy rate. Because the historical experience with the conduct of monetary policy at very low rates is very limited, calibrating the correct size of a non-conventional policy easing conducted through expanding a central bankd5s balance sheet is far harder than the equivalent determination of how much to reduce the short-term interest rate under ordinary circumstances. Precisely because of these challenges, it may be desirable for central banks to take forceful and pre-emptive interest rate action aiming to minimise the probability that they may later find themselves in a situation where they will be forced to resort to unconventional policy easing. Perhaps paradoxically, the greater the concern about conducting monetary policy with zero interest rates, the more aggressive should be the interest rate cuts that are pursued beforehand in response to adverse economic shocks that threaten to bring inflation significantly below the central bankd5s price stability objective. With interest rates at or very close to the zero bound, central banks inevitably have to deploy beyond the key interest rate some other facilities, in their operational frameworks. These measures essentially constituted quantitative expansion in that they all make use of the asset side of the central banksd5 balance sheet. A multitude of tools have been used to that end which comprise the provision of liquidity, the purchase of commercial paper, asset-backed securities and bonds. The mounting importance of the use of these operations, especially after the intensification of the crisis in September d0 October 2008, can be illuminated with a cursory look at the evolution of the balance sheets of some major central banks. For the Federal Reserve, the size of the balance sheet more than doubled between July and December 2008. This expansion includes numerous credit easing measures but also bail-outs as well as some of the government measures already taken. This also holds for the total assets in Bank of Englandd5s balance sheet. The Eurosystemd5s total assets also increased by around 40% between July and December 2008. It is interesting to note however, that the expansion of the Eurosystemd5s balance sheet did not require any legislative or related efforts, reflecting the flexibility inherent in its framework. In the case of the Bank of England and the Federal Reserve, some of the measures taken needed to be approved or coordinated by the respective ministries of finance before they were applied. Focusing briefly on the Federal Reserve, its policy toolkit now can be thought of as having three sets of tools. The first set, involves the provision of short-term liquidity to sound financial institutions through the creation of new facilities for auctioning credit and making primary securities dealers, as well as banks, eligible to borrow at the Fed's discount window. The Federal Reserved5s second set of policy tools involves the provision of liquidity directly to borrowers and investors in key credit markets. An example is the introduction of facilities to purchase highly rated commercial paper at a term of three months and to provide backup liquidity for money market mutual funds. In addition, the Federal Reserve and the Treasury jointly announced a facility that will lend against AAA-rated asset-backed securities collateralised by student loans, auto loans, credit card loans, and loans guaranteed by the Small Business Administration. The Federal Reserve's third set of policy tools for supporting the functioning of credit markets involves the purchase of longer-term securities for the Fed's portfolio. Comparable tools that can facilitate further policy easing, as needed, are also part of the Bank of Englandd5s toolkit. The Bank of England is prepared to purchase a range of financial assets in order to expand the amount of reserves held by commercial banks and to increase the availability of credit to companies. Further, as was announced earlier this month, the Bank will be authorised by the Treasury to purchase high quality private sector assets. This should encourage the banking system to expand the supply of broad money by lending to the private sector and also help companies to raise finance from capital markets. The Bank of England will also use asset purchases for monetary policy purposes should the Monetary Policy Committee conclude that this would be a useful additional tool for meeting the inflation target. The Bank of Japan, which about a decade ago was the first central bank in modern times to embark on quantitative easing, has also introduced additional tools. A new operation has been announced through which financial institutions can borrow low-interest funds from the Bank against corporate debt. The ECB has also stepped up its efforts to ensure access to central bank liquidity by solvent banks. To that end, the ECB adopted new measures in its monetary policy implementation framework. Among others, it proceeded with the enlargement of the basis of eligible collateral for the conduct of its main refinancing operations. Further, it proceeded with the provision of liquidity in dollars and Swiss francs, in cooperation with the US Federal Reserve Bank and the Swiss National Bank, respectively. It also increased the number and duration of longer-term refinancing operations. By adopting a fixed-rate tender procedure with full allotment in all refinancing operations the ECB essentially made available unlimited liquidity to banks for up to six months, upon presentation of appropriate collateral. These measures have contributed towards averting a devastating collapse of the financial system, both in the euro area and internationally. However, despite their benign impact on the functioning of financial markets, the global economic outlook has continued to deteriorate in the past few months. As new data were coming in, all international organisations revised their forecasts for the next couple of years. The European Commission in its interim forecasts, released on 19 January 2009, anticipates a broad-based economic downturn during 2009, with forecast GDP growth at -1,9% for the euro area, -1,6% for the USA, -2,4% for Japan and -2,8% for the UK. This represents a substantial downward revision from the Commissiond5s earlier projection that was released in November of last year. The corresponding European Commission forecasts for 2009 GDP growth released just three months ago were considerably more optimistic, specifically, by 2% for the euro area, by 1.1% for the USA, by 2 percent for Japan and by 1.8 percent for the UK. Inescapably, Cyprus could not be exempted from such an across the board deterioration of the economic outlook. According to the Commission Cyprus GDP growth for 2009 is expected to average just 1,1%, compared to the 2,9% forecast presented in the autumn. Our economy could not of course remain unaffected from the global economic downswing I described above. However, we cannot overlook the fact that any negative repercussions will be substantially milder as a result of our accession to the euro area and the adoption of the euro which acts as a shield against an exchange rate crisis. In addition, the stability of the single currency has been a significant factor in preserving the attractiveness of our banking system for foreign deposits in Cyprus. The biggest risk factor facing the banking system has been avoided and so far no serious problems have been experienced. To sum up, the euro adoption in combination with the banking supervision by the Central Bank and the conservative lending policies of the commercial banks have contributed to the shield against the crisis. Of course, the fact that the UK, one of our major trading partners is one of the countries most affected by the financial crisis continues to be a source of concern. We will have to wait and see whether the expected decline in UK tourist arrivals and British purchases of houses will be as bad as is anticipated. In any event, our economy is doing relatively better than most other economies in the European Union. While our economy compares well with other economies in the euro area, it must be recognized that it is slowing down. The construction and tourism industries are facing a downturn and overall consumer confidence has fallen. More important, the degree of uncertainty regarding the outlook of the global economy is so substantial at the moment that the country should be prepared with an emergency recovery plan in case a worst case growth scenario materializes owing to a worse than expected deterioration in the euro area, the UK, and the economies of out other major trading partners. It is essential to plan in advance of the need to implement measures that might be deemed appropriate for limiting the repercussions of the crisis in Cyprus. In light of the well known lags associated with the implementation of government initiatives, it is imperative that the preparatory work needed to implement specific and carefully planned measures is done well in advance. As always, attention should be given to those development projects from which our economy would derive a higher value added and a larger productivity gain. The issue of productivity is extremely important in the current situation of slowing foreign demand, increased competition and tougher borrowing conditions as a reduction in competitiveness can undermine the performance of Cypriot enterprises compete overseas. The increase in productivity that our economy has achieved so far, even if it continues to be above the corresponding increase in the euro area, is not sufficient to eliminate the differences in labour costs that still prevail. Productivity boosting measures, such as the adoption of innovations and new technologies, should constitute a high priority for the business world and the government. Further progress can also be achieved with more simplified administrative procedures dealing with businesses and a reduction of bureaucracy. Whatever expansionary measures may be contemplated, they should also be targeted and temporary, with an expiration date. It would be undesirable to risk a long-term deterioration in the countryd5s public finances, in an effort to provide a temporary boost to consumption. Undoing the hard-earned gains of fiscal consolidation of the past several years would be ill advised and would undermine public confidence in the sustainability of public finances. With regard to our banking sector, and contrary to the problems appearing in several other countries including some in the euro area, I continue to believe that it remains healthy and strong. Nevertheless, the international turmoil has inevitably affected the lending conditions in Cyprus. As in many other countries, deposit and lending interest rates have increased considerably, along with the interbank rate Euribor, which constitutes a reference rate for lending and deposit rates. However, these interest rates increases are gradually being reversed, as can already be seen from the continuing decrease in Euribor interest rates. The drastic and decisive action taken by the ECB and other central banks, has contributed decisively to this process of normalisation. Our government could also contribute to the enhancement of credit availability in the private sector by taking measures similar to those that have already been implemented in a number of other euro area countries in line with the Common European Action Plan agreed to by the EU and national authorities in October. Such measures could include the issuance of special government bonds which could be lent to banks, which in turn, would use them as collateral to access cheap funding from the Eurosystem, as well as the provision of government guarantees to banks wishing to access the international capital markets through bond issuance. The implementation of such measures may facilitate credit at lower cost. Because such measures have already been implemented in other euro area countries including Greece, it may be particularly important for our government to consider them also in order to promote a level playing field between local and foreign banks and thus avoiding putting our banks in a competitive disadvantage. I would like to conclude with an observation and a wish. The observation is that we live in interesting times. Since last September, in particular, we are experiencing a financial crisis, the magnitude of which we hope not to experience again in our life time. The policy response was swift and massive. The measures taken so far appear to have succeeded in averting the worst that could have otherwise materialised. Unfortunately the financial crisis has spilled over to the real economy and, compared to 2008, 2009 is set to be a difficult year. I wish that it proves to be less interesting.

Title: Address on "Osteoporosis and Musculoskeletal Disorders"
text: Reflections on the international economic crisis and the Cypriot economy Introductory speech by Athanasios Orphanides, Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus, in the context of the public discussion on "The International Economic Crisis and its Impact on the Cyprus Economy" organized by the CUT and OPEC Limassol, 10 March 2009 I would like to thank the Cyprus University of Technology and the Reflection Group for the Modernization of Society for their kind invitation to participate in this discussion concerning the international economic crisis and its impact on the Cypriot economy. I would also like to mention that the views that I will express this evening, both in this brief introductory speech and in the debate that will follow, do not necessarily reflect the views of my colleagues on the Governing Council of the European Central Bank. The issue that will concern us does not only concern economists, central banks and the wider banking and business sector, but is of direct interest to the whole of society and to each individual citizen. The international economic crisis that has plagued the world for about a year and a half has worsened since last September, ultimately hitting the real economy of many countries hard. Our country has been affected, so far at least, to a lesser extent than other developed countries by the consequences of the crisis. This is due both to our timely and successful integration into the euro area before the outbreak of the crisis, as well as to the strong long-term supervision of our banking system by the Central Bank of Cyprus. Nevertheless, the great dependence of the Cypriot economy on foreign demand and tourism cannot leave us unaffected by such a widespread and deep international economic recession. Before referring to the impact of the crisis on the Cypriot economy, I would like briefly to talk about the impact on the euro area more broadly. Based on the ECB's most recent forecasts, the growth outlook has clearly deteriorated further, while inflation forecasts have fallen significantly below the ECB's proclaimed definition of price stability, i.e. inflation below but close to 2%. More specifically, on the basis of the latest ECB forecasts announced on 5 March, euro area GDP for 2009 is expected to contract by 2.7% (between 3.2% and 2.2%) compared to last December's forecast of around 0.5%. This reflects, among other things, reduced consumer confidence but also reduced investment and exports. Contrary to previous forecasts, the euro area economy is not expected to recover significantly in 2010 either. Specifically, the growth rate is expected to be limited to around 0% (between -0.7 and 0.7%), significantly below the 1% forecast last December. As regards inflation, a significant slowdown in prices is expected to occur in 2009, reflecting both low oil prices and reduced demand, with inflation limited to 0.4% (between 0.1% and 0.7%) compared with 1.4% in the December 2008 forecast. Finally, regarding 2010, inflation is expected to hover around 1% (between 0.6 and 1.4%) compared to a forecast of around 1.8% last December. The dramatic downward revision, both for the growth rate of economic activity in the euro area and for inflation for 2009 and 2010, which is now expected to fall significantly below 2%, are factors in the light of which decisions were taken at the last meeting of the Governing Council of the ECB on 5 March to further ease monetary policy. In particular, the ECB cut interest rates by 50 basis points by limiting the key interest rate to an all-time low of 1.5% and the interest rate on the deposit facility to just 0.5%. With this reduction in the base rate, the overall reduction in interest rates in the euro area has risen to 275 basis points since last October. The reduction in interest rates was accompanied by further decisions to extend the non-standard measures that the ECB had already adopted. As you know, an unconventional measure in the ECB's arsenal is the provision of unlimited liquidity with a guarantee of up to six months at the base rate. On 5 March, the ECB decided to continue to provide liquidity in this way, for as long as necessary and in any event beyond the end of 2009. This decision in practice means that a bank can, if necessary, obtain as much liquidity as it needs from the Eurosystem at a very low interest rate beyond the end of this year. The above ECB decisions contribute to the consolidation of inflation expectations in line with the ECB's Governing Council's aim of keeping inflation below, but close to, 2% over the medium term. Divergences in inflation significantly below 2% for an extended period of time should, in general, be avoided in order to prevent any destabilisation of inflation expectations. The commitment to price stability supports sustainable economic growth and employment and promotes financial stability. Turning now to our own economy, I believe that the good state of our banking sector has contributed to the fact that the Cypriot economy is in a better situation than the other countries of the euro area. The sound situation of the banking sector in Cyprus is certainly due to a significant extent to the prudent supervision over time exercised and exercised by the Central Bank of Cyprus. An important element of this strict supervision, which in the past has been unjustly criticized as too strict and conservative, is the pre-existing and existing instructions for keeping liquidity in domestic and foreign currency. Based on our guidelines, banks should adhere to a minimum cash ratio of 70% of total foreign currency deposits and the definition of liquid assets is restrictive and does not include the various complex products that before the financial crisis were considered internationally directly liquid. Therefore, Cypriot banks had no room to invest in these products since their liquidity would be burdened, resulting in their substantial protection from the causes that led other banking institutions abroad to the verge of collapse. Another measure to protect the banking system, which we took and for which we were wrongly and strongly criticised, was the stricter regulations to limit excessive housing lending and, in particular, the reduction of the bank financing rate of the real estate market (excluding the primary residence) from 70% to 60% from July 2007 to May 2008. Today it is widely recognized that the above restrictions have contributed decisively to the protection of the banking sector and the economy in general. The good situation of the banking sector can, by adopting appropriate measures, help to prevent a possible further deterioration of the economic situation in Cyprus. Similar measures to those that have long been adopted in a number of other euro area countries in accordance with the Joint European Action Plan agreed by the Heads of State of the European Union in October 2008, could, through the financial sector, contribute to stimulating the financing of the economy at low cost. In particular, I would like to refer to two specific measures to which I have referred in the past in order to achieve the above objective. The first measure concerns the issuance of special government bonds with a maturity of up to three years with a view to their assignment to credit institutions against collateral, which in turn will be able to use these securities to raise liquidity from the ECB. For the granting of securities, a commission is paid by the credit institutions to the State as well as sufficient collateral. Such collateral could include, in addition to securities of other bonds, up-to-date loans to natural persons (e.g. housing loans) as well as up-to-date claims against businesses. The second measure concerns the granting of business loans by the domestic financial system through risk-sharing agreements between credit institutions and the state. This measure is important because the current increased uncertainty in the economy discourages banks from taking on the entire risk of financing projects. The apportionment of the risk could stimulate investment and support small and medium-sized enterprises by ensuring improved employment prospects. In conclusion, I would say that the great financial crisis and the deep international recession that accompanies it have highlighted the need for drastic monetary measures that are certainly unusual in times of normal macroeconomic development. In our own country, the effects of the crisis seem to be relatively limited and our banking sector remains healthy. However, the uncertainty is very high and we cannot rule out a further significant deterioration in domestic economic activity. It would therefore be legitimate to be prepared for any eventuality.

Title: Speech at the session of the Parliamentary Committee on Economic and Budgetary Affairs
text: What the current crisis teaches us about the future of the architecture of supervision of the financial system Introduction by Athanasios Orphanides, Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus, at the speech of the Governor of the Bank of Greece, Mr. George A. Provopoulos, at the CCCI event Nicosia, 9 April 2009 I would like to thank the Cyprus Chamber of Commerce and Industry and in particular, the President, Mr. Manthos Mavrommatis, for the invitation to preface the speech of the Governor of the Bank of Greece, Mr. George Provopoulos, on the subject of "What the current crisis teaches us about the future of the architecture of the supervision of the financial system". Current developments in international financial markets strongly demonstrate the need for more effective regulation and supervision. Although it is not easy to determine the ideal level of regulation and supervision, nevertheless, the events that we have all been experiencing since the start of the global financial turmoil in August 2007 suggest that the supervision of the financial system applied to date contained serious gaps. The experience not only of the current financial crisis but also the historical economic development of recent centuries show that it is impossible to completely prevent future crises. We can, however, make an effort to limit their size and frequency. Given this, the aim of all those involved should be to reflect on the future of the architecture of supervision of the financial system, based on the recent lessons learned and ongoing experiences that we experience every day. But what is the main lesson of the current financial crisis in relation to the supervisory and regulatory role that the competent authorities exercised or should exercise? Was there, in fact, a failure on the part of the authorities in the implementation of the existing supervisory and regulatory framework which, in general, was considered sufficient? If so, then the most rational approach to dealing with possible future crises may be to apply the existing framework more strictly. But has the crisis shown the inadequacy of the regulatory system itself? In this case, we must first identify and then focus on the fundamental weaknesses of the system. Therefore, we will have to reshape the international supervisory framework accordingly. Without wishing to pre-empt the views and positions of Mr Provopoulos, allow me to raise the following concern about the whole issue. During the 90s, up to and including the summer of 2007, there was a trend around the world towards the removal of supervisory powers from Central Banks and its assignment to other supervisory bodies. An example is the supervisory model that was in place in the Uk when we experienced the "banking run", that is, the abrupt withdrawal of deposits due to a collapse in confidence in Northern Rock and the consequent collapse of the bank itself in September 2007. In my view, the above model has proved to be insufficient during the current crisis. But what could be the alternative approach? In the context of the overall reflection on the future of the architecture of the supervision of the financial system, I feel the need to stress the importance of two key factors which are, I believe, particularly important. The first factor is the exercise of banking supervision by the Central Banks. The financial crisis has shown that those countries whose Central Banks had direct access and thorough knowledge of the supervisory data of the entire banking sector, both at the macroeconomic and micro-economic level, were better placed to deal with the effects of the crisis successfully. The reason goes back to the fact that the Central Banks exercised both micro-prudential and macro-prudential supervision. This allowed timely and comprehensive decisions to be taken in matters of enhancing the liquidity and solvency of each bank separately and of the entire banking system. The need for closer cooperation in the exchange of financial and supervisory information between the Central Bank and the Supervisory Body is also highlighted at a pan-European level in jacques de Larosiere's recent report which, among other things, proposes the creation of a European Systemic Risk Board, under the auspices of the European Central Bank, thus giving a supervisory role to the Eurosystem. The second factor is that the exercise of banking supervision must be governed by technocratic and rational criteria, completely independent and free from any temporary political expediency and influence. The experience of recent months indicates that countries and sectors where the responsibility for supervision was not exercised by virtually independent bodies and were prone to political influences and interference have reinforced the current crisis. Ladies and Gentlemen, It is with great pleasure that I welcome close collaborator George Provopoulos to today's event. Although Georgios Provopoulos does not need any special introductions, allow me to refer briefly to his extensive academic and professional experience in the banking sector of Greece. Georgios Provopoulos is a graduate of the Department of Economics of the Law School of the University of Athens. After obtaining his PhD in economics from the University of Essex in the United Kingdom, he served for many years as an academic at the Department of Economics of the University of Athens. Between October 1990 and November 1993 he served as Deputy Governor of the Bank of Greece and between January 1994 and May 2008 he served in senior positions in major credit institutions in Greece. I would like to make a special reference, in view of his presentation today, to his award, on December 30, 2003, by the Academy of Athens with the Class Award of Moral and Political Sciences for his book entitled "The Dynamics of the Financial System" (jointly with P. Kapopoulos). Since June 20, 2008, Georgios Provopoulos has been Governor of the Bank of Greece, a position that gives me the opportunity and the special honor to meet him almost every two weeks in the context of the meetings of the European Central Bank. As you know, we sit on the Governing Council of the ECB in our personal capacity to formulate the best possible policy for the euro area and not as representatives of our countries. That is why we sit at the round meeting table in alphabetical order. Therefore, from the day George Provopoulos began to participate, he always sits right on my left. You understand how much this strengthens the constant communication between us that is anyway imposed by the well-known cross-border connection of the banking systems of our countries.

Title: Opening Statement by the Governor at the meeting of the Parliamentary Committee on Institutions, Values, and Commissioner of Administration
text: Annual Report of the Central Bank of Cyprus for 2008 Speech by Athanasios Orphanides, Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus, at the press conference for the presentation of the Bank's Annual Report for the year 2008 Nicosia, 5 May 2009 2008 was a year of significant developments, achievements and challenges for the Cypriot economy with two important and historical, I would say, events: the adoption of the euro in Cyprus and the intensification of the international financial turmoil with its unprecedented extension to other sectors of economic activity in many countries and with the inevitable consequence of influencing our own economy. With the accession of our country to the euro area and the adoption of the single currency as of January 1, 2008, both the Cypriot economy and the Central Bank of Cyprus are now operating in a modern European economic environment that promotes and supports macroeconomic stability and economic growth. It is with great satisfaction and pride that I recall that the introduction of the euro in our country was a great success and the participation and contribution of our institution in the whole multidimensional preparation and painstaking effort contributed decisively to this. 2008 was the first year of operation of the Central Bank of Cyprus in the euro area which, of course, has brought about significant changes in its operation and role. The Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus participates in the Governing Council of the European Central Bank as an equal member in decision-making on many issues, including monetary policy in the euro area, the primary objective of which is to protect price stability over time for the benefit of all its citizens. A consequence of the Extended Obligations of the Governor due to our participation in the Eurosystem is the increased obligations of the executives of the Central Bank of Cyprus in relation to work stemming from our upgraded participation in the operations of the European System of Central Banks and other competent European bodies. I would mention, for example, that the staff of the Central Bank participates in some 80 committees, working groups and ad hoc groups that support the work of the Governing Council of the European Central Bank and the European Union, in general. A more detailed description of the large volume of work successfully carried out by the staff of the Central Bank of Cyprus can be found in the Annual Report presented today. I would like to take this opportunity to thank my colleagues for their contributions to the successful conduct of the Bank's operations both in the context of the requirements of the Eurosystem and in the context of domestic requirements. The Governor's participation in the Governing Council of the European Central Bank implies the closer monitoring and analysis of economic developments in the euro area by the Central Bank of Cyprus. Our responsibility to monitor, analyse and evaluate developments in the euro area gives us the opportunity to have a better picture and broader representations of how they affect the course of our own economy. So we have better information in order to be even more meticulous observers and analysts of the main macroeconomic figures of our country, such as economic activity, inflationary developments, the fiscal situation and the competitiveness of our country. I believe that this also increases our responsibilities for independent constructive interventions in matters of economic policy, where we consider that these are necessary. Our information and responsibility in relation to the supervision of our banking system and the maintenance of financial stability in our country are also increased, given our closer cooperation, especially with the other central banks of the euro area member countries that have a supervisory role. This cooperation is all the more useful and urgent because of the second important event that characterised 2008, to which I referred earlier, namely the international financial crisis which has spread to other economic sectors in many countries and continues to this day. The Annual Report for 2008 that you have in your hands today, analyzes the economic developments of an unusual year for the financial years. A year marked strongly by a widespread international financial turmoil whose first signs began to be recorded in the summer of 2007, that is, only a few weeks after the political decision to join the euro area of Cyprus, and have since had a decisive impact on global and Cypriot economic activity. The underestimation of the investment risks to which various foreign financial institutions had been exposed due, mainly, to the absence of a strong and effective supervisory framework was the most substantial cause of the crisis that finally peaked in September-October 2008 with the immediate result of the most severe global economic recession in decades. Large foreign banks and other financial institutions collapsed or reached the verge of bankruptcy, which led to government interventions to rescue them. Without these interventions, the financial crisis would lead the entire global financial system to its disintegration, with all that this would mean for the economies and the standard of living of all the countries of the world. This severe turmoil also had a significant impact on Europe's banking system with a substantial negative impact on the euro area real economy. The vicious circle that has, unfortunately, been created between the negative developments in the global financial system and the decline in real economic activity is not easy, nor is it simple to overturn without the drastic conventional and unconventional measures adopted and continue to be adopted by the various governments and central banks. At the same time, a long-term strategic plan is underway to restore normality to the severely shaken global financial system, a fact that is being set in the light of forecasts about the course of the international economy that in recent months have become systematically more pessimistic. On the basis of the european Commission's most recent forecasts announced yesterday, on 4 May 2009, the growth outlook as well as the inflation forecasts for the euro area have been significantly revised downwards for 2009 and 2010. In particular, euro area GDP is expected to record a contraction of 4.0% in 2009 and a further marginal contraction in 2010 compared to the forecasts for growth rates of 0.1% for 2009 and 0.9% in 2010 projected in November 2008. As regards inflation, the European Commission expects it to be around 0.4% for 2009 and 1.2% for 2010, which is below the ECB's proclaimed definition of price stability. These negative data in the euro area and internationally, as I mentioned, have forced governments, central banks and international organisations to intervene immediately to avoid further slippage in real economic indicators. Among other things, I mention the coordinated drastic interest rate cuts that are already at historically low levels and the measures to enhance bank liquidity by the ECB and other important central banks, as well as the announcements of measures by various governments. As regards the ECB in particular, its Governing Council has made six successive reductions in the base rate by 300 basis points since October 2008. These reductions, as well as the strengthening of liquidity by the Eurosystem, have been instrumental in contributing to the gradual normalisation of the turmoil in the financial system and to the maintenance of the stability of long-term inflation expectations. Alongside the interest rate cuts and the unconventional measures taken by the central banks, fiscal support measures for demand are also being taken by the various governments. Within the euro area, of course, this is more easily applied in those countries where fiscal consolidation has preceded it to such an extent that there is now room for a more comfortable fiscal expansion. However, these decisions must be taken within a strictly planned and well-thought-out framework. Crisis response measures must be temporary and well targeted so as not to jeopardise countries' long-term fiscal balance. Because a situation of fiscal deficit imbalance that remains and is widening can never lead to healthy and sustainable long-term growth without first having substantial fiscal consolidation. Our economy is experiencing, it seems so far, the effects of the international crisis to a relatively smaller extent, compared to other economies inside and outside the euro area. The strong and strictly independent supervisory framework implemented over time by the Central Bank as well as our timely integration into the euro area have largely protected our economy from the shocking economic shocks that have been observed in other countries. Of course, it is natural that the great dependence of important and large sectors of our economy (and in particular tourism, services and construction) on foreign demand as well as the current degree of globalization of economies, inevitably led to a significant slowdown in the Cypriot economy. According to the latest forecasts of the European Commission for Cyprus, real GDP growth will be significantly limited to 0.3% in 2009 and 0.7% in 2010, in contrast, of course, to the negative rates expected for the euro area. The Central Bank's forecasts that are now being prepared and will be published next month are not expected to deviate significantly from the above estimates. Apart, of course, from the aforementioned effects of the international recession on our economy in general, the fact remains extremely important and encouraging that the situation of the banking sector in Cyprus continues to remain healthy. This, of course, is largely due to the timelessly prudent and, above all, independent and fair supervision exercised and exercised by the Central Bank of Cyprus. This supervision, which in the past has been unfairly criticised by some as being too strict, contains, among other things, rules concerning the maintenance of a satisfactory and secure level of liquidity, both in domestic currency and in foreign currencies. In particular, based on our instructions, banks should adhere to a minimum cash ratio of 70% of total foreign currency deposits and the definition of cash is restrictive and does not include various complex financial products whose excessive use has led to the financial crisis in other countries. Therefore, Cypriot banks had no room to invest in these products, resulting in their substantial protection from the causes that led other banking institutions abroad to the verge of collapse. Another measure to protect the banking system, which we have taken and for which we have been unfairly and strongly criticised, has been the stricter regulations to limit excessive housing lending, namely the reduction in the bank financing rate of the real estate market from 70% to 60% from July 2007 to May 2008. Today it is widely recognized that the above restrictions, but also in general, the existing supervisory framework and the practices that were successfully followed for many years, have contributed decisively to the protection of the banking sector and the economy in general in the current crisis. For this reason, as Governor of the Central Bank, I am concerned that unnecessary challenges to the existing framework governing independent decision-making in supervisory matters undermine the healthy state of our banking system and, by extension, the very well-being of our country and its citizens. You know that I believe in the potential and prospects of this place, its institutions and its people. We have achieved, as a society, a lot and we can achieve even more. The contribution of the Central Bank of Cyprus over time to the achievement of our strategic goals was also decisive in 2008. It is generally accepted that the technocratically capable and independent exercise of policy by the Central Bank of Cyprus, far from political or other expediencies, played an important role in the difficult but successful course of our country. In the unprecedented situation we are now facing, as Governor I expect that the Central Bank of Cyprus will continue its contribution for the common good unhindered.

Title: Introduction at the Seminar of the Central Bank of Cyprus for Law Students and Graduates
text: Recent policy challenges through the lens of economic forecasts Speech by Athanasios Orphanides, Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus, at the CFA Society of Cyprus annual forecast event 2009 Nicosia, 14 May 2009 It is a great pleasure for me to be here this evening and I would like to thank the CFA Society of Cyprus for the kind invitation to address this gathering. This being the annual forecast event of the Society, I thought it might be of interest to share with you some thoughts about the policy challenges we have experienced over the past two or so years through the lens of economic forecasts. More specifically, I will trace recent events and policy by looking at the evolution of recent forecasts of the euro area economy prepared by euro area professional forecasters and collected and published quarterly by the European Central Bank. Before I proceed, I should note that the views I express are my own and do not necessarily reflect the views of my colleagues on the Governing Council of the ECB. Earlier this month, I completed the first two years of my term as Governor at the Central Bank of Cyprus. Having spent my professional career in central banking, and having studied the history of central banking along the way, I was keenly aware that monetary policymakers must always be ready to face difficult challenges, and that sometimes we need to quickly map an appropriate response even when precise guidance from historical experience may be lacking. As Cyprus was preparing to adopt the euro when I joined the Central Bank, it was clear to me that possible challenges would pertain not only to our economy and banking system, but also relate to the economy and monetary policymaking of all the euro area. However, I never imagined that I would be confronted with challenges such as the ones recently encountered. In broad terms, the euro area macro economy has faced two very different challenges over the past two or so years. The first was an inflationary threat, an adverse supply shock, associated to a large extent with a sharp increase in energy costs and the prices of other key commodities. The acceleration of oil prices from the beginning of 2007 until the summer of 2008 was so dramatic as to bring back bad memories from the 1970s, specifically the painful experience we associate with the oil shocks of 1973 and 1979. Subsequently, though, this inflationary threat subsided and indeed we have experienced a reversal of much of the earlier increase in energy costs during the past several months. But it was the second challenge that proved more vexing and more threatening for the worldwide economy. This second challenge initially manifested itself as a financial turbulence that erupted suddenly in August 2007, and continues to this day. Although it threatened our financial system, prompt policy action initially contained the impact of this turbulence on the real economy until last September. Unfortunately, following the collapse of Lehman Brothers in the United States last September, this turbulence evolved into a full blown international crisis, one so severe that it eludes comparison with anything experienced worldwide in the post-World War II era. This crisis had a severe adverse effect on confidence worldwide, and evolved into a synchronized severe economic downturn, causing an unprecedented collapse in industrial production and world trade. For several months following last September, there were concerns about a developing adverse feedback loop with the financial disturbance and a worsening real economy reinforcing each other in a downward spiral for a time. The second major policy challenge I focus on is precisely this financial crisis we have experienced since September. The rollercoaster ride of the past two or so years can be described in numerous ways and is evident in many financial indicators and data. The macroeconomic environment has been associated with extreme uncertainty and poor visibility, a most unfriendly environment for anyone daring to forecast the future. I note as a pertinent illustration the wild swings we have experienced in inflation over the past two years in the euro area, with HICP inflation registering both its highest and its lowest readings recorded in the 10-year history of the euro area (Figure 1). Following several years of relative stability, when HICP inflation fluctuated within just a few tenths of a percentage point around 2 percent, we have experienced over the past year a new peak exceeding 4 percent last July and a new low at 0.6 percent in the past two months, and cannot exclude negative readings in the months ahead. Comparing the path of actual inflation shown in Figure 1 against the one year-ahead forecasts shows how difficult it has been of recent to forecast inflation, even by professional forecasters. Just how difficult has it been to forecast inflation during these times? The last year-ahead forecast that can be evaluated with available data is the forecast made in the 2008Q2 survey for the 12-month period ending in March 2009. The mean forecast was 2.1 percent while the actual inflation reported was 0.6 percent, a difference of 1.5 percentage points. Figure 1 also presents the evolution of longer-term inflation expectations from the survey, specifically the expected rate of inflation 5 years ahead. I note that despite the unprecedented challenges in the economic environment and unusually violent swings in inflation over the past two years, long-term expectations have remained remarkably stable and in line with the ECB objective of keeping HICP inflation close to but below 2 percent over time. I present this evidence as confirmation of the credibility of the ECB in achieving its mandate even under the challenging circumstances experienced over the past year or two. Well-anchored inflation expectations are of the essence not only to facilitate attainment of the ECBd5s primary objective to maintain price stability but also to allow the flexibility that monetary policymakers can have to alleviate the adverse effects of financial disturbances as well as shocks to the real economy. Economists sometimes find it useful to decompose economic disturbances into "aggregate demand" and "aggregate supply" shocks. This decomposition is also useful for understanding differences in how policy might respond to different challenges. Recognizing the risk of oversimplification, it may nonetheless be instructive to categorize the two challenges mentioned above in this manner. The first challenge, as I already mentioned, could be seen as an adverse supply shock. Adverse supply shocks tend to put upward pressures on inflation while also dampening aggregate demand. The policy response is not straightforward and depends on a number of factors. If inflation expectations are well-anchored and there is no threat that second round effects on inflation could potentially materialize, then monetary policy could ease slightly, thus dampening the drop in economic activity. But if threats of second round effects on inflation appear on the horizon, then a tightening of policy is appropriate to ensure that inflation expectations will not become unmoored. In this manner, monetary policy secures price stability over time and the sustainable growth in economic activity that comes with it. The experience with the evolution of short-term forecasts of the euro area during the second half of 2007 and the period prior to the Lehman collapse in 2008, suggests the pattern of an adverse supply shock. As can be seen in the top two panels of Figure 2, in successive quarters from 2007Q4 to 2008Q3, the outlook for inflation deteriorated, with inflation projected to exceed significantly 2 percent, while at the same time growth prospects also deteriorated somewhat in successive forecast rounds. But expectations beyond the very short-term horizon remained well-anchored and the ECB Governing Council decided it was appropriate to adjust monetary policy only very slightly during this period, a 25 basis points increase in its policy rate on 3 July 2008. As shown in Figure 1, for the longer-term forecasts, and confirmed by the pattern of convergence towards the ECBd5s definition of price stability shown in the forecasts in the upper left panel of Figure 2, this slight policy adjustment succeeded in maintaining inflation expectations in the medium and longer-term well anchored. The effects of the second challenge on the economy, that is developments associated with the financial crisis since the collapse of Lehman last September, could be seen as an aggregate demand shock---indeed, a massive demand shock of unprecedented size in the post-World War II era. Adverse demand shocks tend to put downward pressures on inflation, while also dampening aggregate demand which tends to reinforce further downward pressures on inflation. Unlike the case of adverse supply shocks, in this case the policy response is quite a bit clearer. Policy easing is required so as to avoid a severe depression in economic activity since such an outcome could threaten price stability by increasing the risk of deflation. The experience with the evolution of short-term forecasts of the euro area since the second half of 2008, suggests this pattern of an adverse demand shock. As can be seen in the two bottom panels of Figure 2, forecasts for both inflation and growth prospects have been revised significantly downwards as the crisis evolved. The sharpest downward revisions could be seen in the forecasts from the survey for the first quarter of this year, when the sharpness of the downturn started to become more clearly evident. Some further downward revisions can be seen in the most recent survey, but these revisions are not as large as those recorded in the previous quarter. The deterioration in the forecasts over the past two quarters has been unprecedended in the history of the survey. I note that the pattern of forecasts in the Survey of Professional Forecasters is not significantly different from that of forecasts by other organisations. Looking more closely at the most recent survey results from the 2008Q2 survey, it should be noted that although the inflation forecast for 2009 is well below the ECBd5s price stability objective, forecasters expect a sizeable pick-up in inflation for next year. In addition, inflation expectations five-years ahead remain at 1.9 percent, which is in line with the ECBd5s definition of price stability. I consider it important to monitor closely inflation expectations going forward. A protracted period of inflation below our definition of price stability could risk unmooring inflation expectations on the downside, with all the associated adverse consequences. Seen in the light of the deterioration in the economic outlook experienced over the past several months, it is easy to understand why the Governing Council of the ECB thought it was appropriate to proceed with a series of decisive monetary policy easings. Since October 2008, the main policy rate has been cut drastically, with last weekd5s decision bringing it down to an all-time low level of 1 percent. Similarly, the interest rate on the deposit facility is at a historic low 0.25 percent. We should keep in mind that when policy rates are close to the zero lower bound, they may no longer suffice as the best indicators of the monetary policy stance and of how expansionary monetary policy may be. In these circumstances, non-standard policy measures acquire an elevated role. To evaluate policy, it is important to look at the complete policy package, accounting both for standard and non-standard policy easing. In this light, it should be recalled that the Governing Council has implemented a series of non-standard policy easings since October 2008, and further expanded upon those at the policy meeting last week. All in all, the present level of monetary accommodation should be considered appropriate, taking into account the information and analysis available at the last policy meeting. In closing these brief reflections, I cannot avoid but reiterate the extreme uncertainty we still face at the moment and the need to remain alert and ready to react appropriately to incoming information. Needless to say, in addition to data releases it would remain of interest to keep monitoring the evolution of forecasts and I can safely predict that you may wish to continue this tradition of your annual forecast event.
