Title: The Evolution of the Cyprus Banking System: A Reform Story and its Challenges
text: Central bank exit policies Panel remarks by Athanasios Orphanides, Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus, at the Shadow Open Market Committee Meeting on "Exit Policies for Sound Central Banking" Washington, DC, 30 September 2009 A few years ago, when I was on the official staff of the Federal Reserve Board, I was asked to participate in an ECB Watchers meeting in Frankfurt. One reason why I was invited, and a reason I found it attractive, was that I could offer an outsiderd5s view from within the central banking community, complementing the perspectives of ECB insiders at that meeting. I did not realise at the time that I was also setting up myself for this meeting of the Shadow Open Market Committee (SOMC). I was familiar with the long history of SOMC meetings and knew that they did not involve Fed insiders at all. So when my friend and former Fed colleague Gregory Hess told me that a Fed insider would participate for the first time and then invited me to offer an outsiderd5s view, it was hard not to accept the invitation. After all, it would be only fair to return the favour from the other side of the Atlantic. So it is with great pleasure that I address this meeting of the Shadow Open Market Committee on exit policies for sound central banking. Since last September, we have experienced the most severe global financial crisis in the last 60 years. Central banks have reacted promptly and decisively, thus minimising the risk of a protracted economic slump similar to that experienced during the 1930s. In doing so, some central banks have found it appropriate to resort to unconventional measures to supplement their traditional interest rate policy responses. And for this reason, the exit from these unconventional policy measures for monetary policy is of considerable interest. I should clarify, however, that talking about this topic should not be misinterpreted as suggesting that now is the appropriate time to exit from unconventional monetary policy measures. In the euro area, following the sharp economic decline in the fourth quarter of last year and the first quarter of this year, there are increasing signs of stabilisation but the outlook remains uncertain. Now is not the appropriate time to exit. Nonetheless, it is important to communicate that an exit strategy exists and that it can and will be implemented when the time is appropriate. With this in mind, in my brief intervention I will address some of the questions posed by the organisers of this panel discussion. Before proceeding, I would like to note that the views I express are my own and do not necessarily reflect the views of my colleagues on the Governing Council of the European Central Bank. By definition, unconventional policies are termed d4unconventionald5 because they are not frequently encountered and implemented. There are a number of different and not mutually exclusive ways to think about unconventional policies depending on their economic impact and the reasoning behind their adoption. Some unconventional policies may be introduced to improve market functioning. Others, may be introduced primarily to supplement traditional monetary policy easing. Differences in the structure of the economy and institutional arrangements may make different unconventional measures more appropriate and/or more successful in different economic areas. For example, if banks are the most important source of financing in an economy, as is the case in the euro area, unconventional measures focusing on enhancing credit may be the most effective. For other economies, alternative interventions, such as support for the commercial paper market and money market mutual funds, may be more appropriate. ECB President Trichet has described the ECBd5s unconventional policies as "enhanced credit support" since these policies enhance the flow of credit in the economy over and above what could be achieved through policy rate reductions alone in the face of the financial turmoil (Trichet, 2009). As Trichet states, the ECBd5s enhanced credit support comprises five elements: the full allotment of banksd5 demand for liquidity at fixed rates the provision of liquidity in foreign currencies the expansion of the list of assets accepted as collateral the lengthening of the maturity of liquidity provision the direct purchase of covered bank bonds. The first two of these measures were introduced initially to address the seizing up of the money market and malfunctioning of the international swap market, which was important in light of the currency mismatch in banksd5 balance sheets. The expansion of the list of assets accepted as collateral provided additional assurance to banks that they could refinance assets that had become less liquid during the turmoil. The lengthening of the maturity of liquidity provision facilitated better liquidity planning by banks over longer horizons and served to depress term-premia in money market rates. And finally, the purchase of covered bank bonds was a direct action in financial markets that improved market functioning in the covered bond market leading to smaller spreads over comparable government securities. The unconventional policies that have been implemented as a result of the financial turmoil can, as already mentioned, be thought of as serving one or both of the following two related functions. First, to facilitate liquidity provision and improve market functioning, in other words to restore the transmission mechanism thus contributing to financial stability. And second, to influence the stance of monetary policy beyond what is normally reflected in the setting of the very short-term nominal interest rate, which serves as the traditional monetary policy tool. Conceptual separation of these two functions may be useful for understanding the timing and circumstances for the adoption or the exit of any particular unconventional measure. A measure adopted to improve the functioning of a particular market may become unnecessary when that market improves, in which case exit from that unconventional measure would be warranted. On the other hand, the traditional considerations determining the appropriateness of an easing or tightening of monetary policy under normal circumstances would be pivotal for the adoption and exit from a measure adopted primarily to influence the stance of monetary policy. When short-term nominal interest rates are not close to the zero lower bound, the first consideration is the more important determinant. For example, the primary function of the full allotment of banksd5 liquidity demand by the ECB in October 2008 was to address the dysfunction of money markets. In other words, the primary purpose was not to engineer a monetary policy easing, although it did obviously contain the deterioration in monetary conditions arising from market difficulties. In the light of the deterioration of economic conditions, monetary policy was also eased by aggressively reducing the ECBd5s main policy rates in the months since October 2008. In contrast, when short-term nominal interest rates are close to zero, unconventional policy measures can be employed with the primary purpose being to engineer additional monetary policy easing. Such measures could include increasing the size or changing the composition of a central bankd5s balance sheet by, for example, purchasing assets such as covered bank bonds. They also include engaging in operations that have a bearing on interest rates with maturities beyond the very short term, for example the provision of long-term liquidity, such as 6-and 12-month maturities at the same interest rate offered for shorter maturities. These measures induce additional monetary policy easing by reducing credit and term spreads. Indeed, as policy rates get close to the zero lower bound, they may no longer suffice as the best indicators of the monetary policy stance. Movements in interest rates at longer maturities that are not as close to the zero bound, for example money market rates at maturities of 3-, 6-or 12-months, may become more informative regarding the stance of monetary policy. As already mentioned, the utilisation and exit from an unconventional policy measure adopted primarily to influence the stance of monetary policy near the zero lower bound will be determined by similar considerations to those determining a conventional policy easing or tightening. In the case of the ECB, the clarity of our price stability mandate is pivotal for these decisions. Our mandate has not changed in light of the crisis. First and foremost, our goal is to ensure a continuing environment of price stability in the euro area, by which we mean a stable rate of inflation close but below 2 percent a year. Price stability is the best way to ensure maximum sustainable growth in the long run. High inflation as well as deflation are undesirable and inconsistent with our mandate. In light of the lags associated with the monetary transmission mechanism, policy must be forward looking. This is the reason why the monitoring of inflation projections and inflation expectations over various horizons are critically important. If inflation projections and expectations suggest that inflation is likely to remain subdued and significantly below 2 percent for a considerable time, then it would be appropriate to ensure sufficient monetary policy accommodation is in place to minimise the threat of deflation and to restore price stability. If, on the other hand, inflation threatens to rise above our definition of price stability, the appropriate tightening would be warranted to ensure price stability. The high degree of anchoring of long-term inflation expectations we have observed in the euro area in the light of the financial crisis has been reassuring. However, partly due to the large swing in energy prices over the past two or so years, actual inflation as well as inflation expectations at the policy relevant horizon have been more volatile than usual and are currently below our definition of price stability. Going forward, continued monitoring of inflation expectations is of the essence. A final issue I wish to mention is that of the increased uncertainty facing policymakers in the current environment. Over the past several decades, our experience with very low policy rates and unconventional policies is rather limited, and for some policies non-existent. As a result, we face greater than usual uncertainty about the multipliers and transmission lags of our policy measures. In such an environment, the risks that one may misjudge the appropriate timing and force of policy action become greater. One risk is that of removing policy accommodation too late. If so, inflation would rise above our price stability objective. This is particularly the case when the money multiplier rises from a historical low and thus excess liquidity starts being converted into credit. A second risk is that of removing policy accommodation too early. History suggests that this latter error may be extremely costly in an environment with inflation below a central bankd5s definition of price stability. Two well-studied historical examples of apparently (1) premature tightening by exiting from unconventional policy measures are those of the Federal Reserve in 1937 and the Bank of Japan in 2000 . The risks of removing policy too early and too late have to be appropriately balanced for policy to be successful. In conclusion, talking about an exit strategy should not be confused with its implementation. Now is not the appropriate time to exit. But the process would begin when there are clear signs that markets are functioning properly, the economic recovery is firmly under way and, therefore, upside pressures on inflation appear. As with all monetary policy decisions, safeguarding the central bankd5s primary objective of price stability will be the determining factor regarding the exit from unconventional monetary policy measures. ENDNOTES: (1) Friedman and Schwartz (1963) and Meltzer (2002) examine the 1937 Federal Reserve error in detail. Orphanides (2004) compares the Federal Reserve policies leading to 1937 with those of the Bank of Japan in 2000. REFERENCES: Friedman, Milton, and Anna Schwartz (1963) A Monetary History of the United States, 1867-1960, Princeton: Princeton University Press. Meltzer, Allan H. (2003) A History of the Federal Reserve, Volume 1, 1913-1951, Chicago: University of Chicago Press. Orphanides, Athanasios (2004) "Monetary policy in deflation: the liquidity trap in history and practice", The North American Journal of Economics and Finance, 15(1): 101-124. Trichet, Jean-Claude (2009) "The ECBd5s exit strategy", ECB Watchers Conference, Frankfurt, 4 September.

Title: Introduction at the event organized by the Union of Cypriot Economists on Financial Illiteracy
text: Preventing deflation: the role of policy research Remarks by Athanasios Orphanides, Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus, at the International Research Forum on Monetary Policy conference, Federal Reserve Board Washington, DC, 27 March 2010 Policy research at central banks -judiciously employed to distil the implications of theoretical knowledge, historical experience and empirical evidence for policy challenges -is a crucial component of good policy practice. By providing a solid analytical foundation for reaching and explaining policy decisions, policy research can be helpful even in ordinary times. Policy research proves particularly invaluable when it anticipates issues before they become too pressing, providing for better informed decisions when time for reflection may become short. And the payoff can be huge during crisis management episodes -better policy research means better odds against major policy mistakes. Over the past two to three years, the global economy has experienced an episode as intense and as demanding for policy as any in the history of central banking. What appeared at first, in August 2007, to be a manageable turbulence in money and financial markets, evolved over a number of months into a global financial crisis reaching its climax in September 2008. By the end of 2008, the financial headwinds, coupled with a collapse in confidence, culminated in a dramatic drop in aggregate demand and world trade. The threat of a protracted deflationary slump loomed large, evoking comparisons with the Great Depression of the 1930s. Prompt and decisive policy action, including by the Federal Reserve (Fed) and the European Central Bank (ECB), was instrumental in averting the worst outcome. Although uncertainty remains, the world economy today seems to be on its way to recovery. The conventional monetary policy response to a fall in aggregate demand is a reduction in nominal and real interest rates. But zero is effectively a lower bound on policy rates. Does this present a constraint on the conduct of monetary policy? Prior to the present episode, practical experience with near-zero policy rates had been quite limited in the central banking world and debates about the "liquidity trap" seemed too old-fashioned to occupy centre stage in modern-day academic research. And yet, in the course of a few months following the climax of the crisis in September 2008, most major central banks around the world had driven overnight rates to near zero. Overnight rates remain at historic lows for a number of currencies, including the dollar and the euro. A key policy challenge during this episode has been the conduct of monetary policy when short-term interest rates are driven very close to zero. Fortunately, on this occasion, pertinent policy research conducted at policy institutions well in advance of this episode, provided a foundation that proved crucial in guiding monetary policy towards preventing a protracted deflationary slump. I would like to take this opportunity to address the International Research Forum on Monetary Policy to revisit some of the pertinent work on the zero lower bound and relate it to the monetary policy response to the recent crisis. I will focus my attention on policy research and the policy environment at the Fed and the ECB, the two central banks that co-sponsor the Forum, as well as central banks about which I believe I have a comparative familiarity advantage. Before proceeding, I would like to note that the views I express are my own and do not necessarily reflect the views of my colleagues on the Governing Council of the European Central Bank. *** Paradoxically, characterising very low interest rates as a challenge is also a reflection of the very success that central banks around the industrialised world have had in achieving and maintaining an environment of price stability. Preserving price stability is the best contribution monetary policy can make to enhancing welfare. During the last few decades of the twentieth century, inflation was a constant challenge for many central banks around the world. The inflationary disease was gradually overcome by the end of the century. In the United States, CPI inflation fell from 5.6 percent per year in the 1980s to 3 percent in the 1990s, and to just 2.6 percent in the 2000s. Similarly in the euro area, HICP inflation fell from 5.3 percent in the 1980s to 2.6 percent in the 1990s and just 2.1 percent in the 2000s. In an environment of price stability, with inflation being very low and, correspondingly, interest rates being low as well, reducing policy rates as a response to a slowdown in aggregate demand may bring them close to zero. This situation may lead to two logical mistakes, either one of which could potentially induce a policy error. The first potential error can occur if an observer erroneously associates the level of nominal interest rates with the degree of policy ease. Certainly, in an economy with a steady and unchanging rate of inflation, higher nominal interest rates ought to reflect tighter monetary conditions, and lower ones easier conditions. Furthermore, in an environment where policy rates are usually considerably above zero, bringing short-term interest rates close to zero may be deemed extremely expansionary. And this could well be the case if the economy did not experience a deflationary impetus. But, of course, the degree of monetary policy ease should be associated with the level of real interest rates, not nominal interest rates. Near-zero policy rates that may be considerably expansionary in an economy with high inflation could be contractionary when inflation is too close to zero, or worse, when deflation has set it. In a deflationary economy, even zero rates can be contractionary. The error is one of misdiagnosis of the need for further policy easing. The second potential error can occur if an observer erroneously associates the level of short-term interest rates alone with the degree of monetary policy ease. This error can occur, for example, if an overnight interest rate, such as the federal funds rate in the United States, or the eonia in the euro area, is viewed as a sufficient indicator of the monetary policy stance. When overnight rates approach zero it may appear that a central bank has "run out of ammunition": that is, it may appear that the central bank is powerless to stimulate the economy further with additional monetary policy easing. This error is one of misdiagnosis of the power for further policy ease. An observer who mistakenly views overnight rates as sufficient indicators of monetary policy, and is therefore convinced that the central bank may "run out of ammunition" if it reduces overnight rates to zero in response to an adverse shock in aggregate demand, may suggest that policymakers should not reduce policy rates as much as needed when rates are already low in order not to exhaust their ammunition. This advice to policymakers, to "keep their powder dry", would only compound the error. Insufficient policy easing under the circumstances would risk a further deterioration in aggregate demand, and thus increase the risk of deflation. But of course, overnight rates are not sufficient indicators of monetary policy. Monetary policy is also about the supply of money and the assets a central bank purchases when it injects high-powered money into the economy. Quantities do matter. Monetary policy decisions that change the size or composition of the central bank's balance sheet can potentially influence various asset prices and the yield curve of government and private paper, even when the overnight interest rate does not move. This quantitative easing is the essence of unconventional monetary policy action central banks need to resort to, when short-term nominal interest rates approach zero. Thus, even if the zero bound on nominal interest rates short-circuits the conventional mechanism for inducing a monetary policy ease, it does not imply that monetary policy is ineffective when overnight rates reach zero and cannot be reduced further. Indeed, unconventional measures could be effectively introduced even while keeping overnight rates somewhat above zero. Monetary policy has the power to influence various asset prices and other interest rates even in an environment when the overnight interest rate remains unchanged. However, typical models employed for the study of monetary policy, including many models commonly used by central banks, rely on such a stylised abstraction of the financial sector of the economy that one short-term interest suffices to determine all other interest rates and asset prices in the model economy, independent of other monetary policy actions. Even when longer-term interest rates appear in such models, they are determined from the expectations of short-term rates without any role for monetary quantitative easing to influence term or risk premia. In these models, absolute and relative quantities of money, reserves and central bank assets are, by assumption, irrelevant for determining the stance of monetary policy. To be sure, under ordinary circumstances, when interest rates are not close to zero, this abstraction may be sensible. The independent role of quantitative policy effects -beyond their influence on the policy rate -may be inconsequential when short rates are not close to zero and allowed to adjust with policy changes. Furthermore, in estimated policy models, it may be very difficult to separately identify the role of conventional and unconventional monetary policies, especially if the sample over which a model is estimated does not contain a sufficiently informative period near the zero bound. Under these circumstances, Occam's razor would guide the modeller to focus on conventional monetary policy. No wonder that central bank modellers often feel uneasy about assessing the quantitative impact of unconventional policies in their models! The logical error of ruling out the power for further policy easing by unconventional means, stems either from the need for analytical oversimplification (in theoretical models) or the need for empirical oversimplification (in estimated models). Either way, once the limits of these simplifications are recognised, this logical error can be avoided. Crucially, the considerable uncertainty regarding the precise degree of policy effectiveness associated with unconventional measures should not be misinterpreted as ineffectiveness. *** The Federal Reserve reached the zero bound on 16 December 2008, when it reduced its policy rate establishing a target range for the federal funds rate of 0 to 1/4 percent. According to the minutes of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), a part of that meetingd5s discussion related to the zero lower bound on nominal interest rates. This was not the first time such a discussion took place, however. Indeed, according to the FOMCd5s records, related discussions took place at its June 2003 meeting, before that at its January 2002 meeting, and even earlier at its June/July 1998 meeting. On each occasion, the discussion benefited from briefings on the topic drawing on prior policy research. Indeed, work on this topic at the Federal Reserve started as early as 1993 with a pair of working papers: A quantitative exercise by Jeff Fuhrer and Brian Madigan (1994) that illustrated how constraining the zero bound could prove to be for conventional policy easing during a recession and a paper by David Lebow (1993) examining the unconventional policies that the Fed could pursue once the policy rate were driven to zero(1). A large number of research projects followed. Some focused on quantitative investigations, based on estimated models of the US economy, assessing the deterioration in economic performance corresponding to different steady state rates of inflation associated with the zero bound, and the effectiveness of alternative interest rate policy strategies when only conventional monetary policy was considered. Other studies examined how unconventional policies could be employed and the role of uncertainty associated with the effectiveness of unconventional policies. The range of unconventional policies available to the Fed when considering the legal and institutional framework in place was also studied. This range was very broad, varying from the use of derivative instruments to topics of research involving pertinent historical experience on policies, including that of the United States during the 1930s and Japan during the 1990s. Yet another topic was the potential implications of very low rates on specific financial markets and instruments(2). On 30 June 1998, when the initial FOMC discussion took place, the zero bound was not a pressing issue. The federal funds target rate was 5 1/2 percent. There were two motivating factors. The first was the desire to focus attention on how low inflation should be for the FOMC to consider that it had reached price stability. The second was the realisation that monetary policy in Japan during the 1990s appeared to have been influenced, perhaps adversely, by the zero bound. Together with the adverse outcomes experienced in the United States during the 1930s -when the Fed had faced near zero rates -it appeared pertinent to study the issue. This was an occasion of policy research anticipating an issue before it became too pressing. Don Kohn, who at the time was the Director of the Monetary Affairs Division at the Board, briefed the Committee. After explaining the difficulty with conventional monetary policy easing at the zero bound, he summarised the role of unconventional policies: "Unorthodox monetary policy may work, but it obviously would have to be through channels other than reducing short-term interest rates since they are already at zero. Those channels might include reducing expected short-term rates by tilting down long-term rates, or reducing term or risk premiums in long-term rates. The latter also would tend to reduce long-term rates and exchange rates as well" (Federal Reserve Board, 1998, p.90). Finally, he drew lessons from the historical experience on how the problem might likely arise: "I think one of the lessons from the United States in the 1930s and Japan in the 1990s is that problems have tended to follow sharp breaks in asset prices coupled with sluggish monetary responses because the authorities were concerned about re-igniting asset price increases or inflation and with destabilizing fiscal policy because the fiscal authorities were focused on budget balance or long-term surplus" (pp. 90-91). *** The euro had yet to be introduced in 1998, when the first FOMC discussion on the zero lower bound took place. But the implications of the zero bound were contemplated when in one of its first meetings, on 13 October 1998, the Governing Council discussed how it should interpret price stability, the primary mandate of the ECB. On the one hand, the Governing Council wished to delineate the limit of increases in the measured level of prices deemed consistent with price stability. On the other, it wished to protect against the risk of deflation. The Governing Council adopted the following definition: "Price stability shall be defined as a year-on-year increase in the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP) for the euro area of below 2%" (European Central Bank, 1998). As Otmar Issing explained shortly after: "In this way, the definition takes into account the threats posed by ongoing deflation in combination with nominal rigidities in the real economy. While periodic and transitory falls in the price level may be quite normal, and should not give rise to major concerns, a prolonged deflation is clearly inconsistent with any meaningful definition of price stability. Moreover, since nominal interest rates cannot fall below zero, the private expectation of a sustained fall in the price level may render the interest rate policy of the central bank rather ineffective. All that remains is outright purchases of assets -both foreign and domestic" (Issing, 1998). Issues pertaining to the zero bound on nominal interest rates were subsequently discussed at the "First ECB Central Banking Conference in November 2000" (see in particular the paper by Jose Vinals, 2000, and the related discussion). And a number of research projects were completed and published in the ECB's working paper series, including quantitative investigations based estimated models of the euro area(3). *** The pertinent policy research was influential during the thorough evaluation of the ECB's monetary policy strategy in 2003. With regard to price stability, the Governing Council decided to clarify its definition. While it confirmed its definition of price stability as year-on-year increases in the HICP for the euro area of below 2 percent, it noted that: "in the pursuit of price stability it will aim to maintain inflation rates close to 2% over the medium term." The Governing Council proceeded to explain: "This clarification underlines the ECB's commitment to provide a sufficient safety margin to guard against the risks of deflation" (European Central Bank, 2003). In a press seminar on the evaluation of the ECB's monetary policy strategy that followed the announcement, Otmar Issing explained that without this safety margin, the zero lower bound on nominal interest rates posed greater deflation risks (Issing, 2003a). Later, he explained: "The major concern is the fact that monetary policy may become less effective, if interest rate management by the central bank is constrained by a liquidity trap or a 'zero bound' problem" (Issing, 2003b). The ECB's clarification was important in robustifying the protection against deflation for two reasons. First, it clarified the size of the safety margin sought for HICP inflation, close to 2 percent. This was an important preventive measure. Prior to this clarification, lower margins, for example . percent or 1 percent, could not be ruled out as they were not inconsistent with the definition of price stability without the clarification offered in 2003. Second, the clarification presented a more precise focal point for anchoring inflation expectations by households and businesses. This was a measure that enhanced the effectiveness of the response of monetary policy, should a deflationary shock to aggregate demand materialise. The layer of protection against deflation offered by the clarification of the definition of price stability became evident during the recent crisis. Medium-to-long-term inflation expectations remained remarkably well-anchored during the episode. The value of a clear focal point for the formation of inflation expectations was also appreciated by the Fed, leading to FOMC discussions regarding the establishment of an explicit numerical objective for inflation. The FOMC discussed the pertinent issues during a conference call on 16 January 2009. The minutes note that: "Some indicated that the establishment of a numerical inflation objective could be particularly helpful under present circumstances in forestalling an unwelcome decline in longer-run inflation expectations and hence in contributing to economic recovery while also assuring the public that actions taken to counter economic weakness will not lead to high inflation over the longer-run" (Federal Reserve Board, 2009, p.16). While the FOMC decided against establishing such an explicit numerical objective, it proceeded to supplement its members' projections, including on inflation, with projections for the "longer term," thereby providing a helpful indication of members' interpretations of price stability. The central tendency of the responses was just below or equal to 2 percent. Overall, the policy research on the zero bound at the Fed and the ECB reached similar conclusions. This reflected, in part, the close cooperation between researchers from the two institutions. First, focusing on conventional monetary policy, the research confirmed that the zero bound could raise the odds of adverse deflationary slumps, if central banks aimed to achieve average inflation rates that were too low. Aiming to achieve a measured inflation rate close to 2 percent would yield better macroeconomic stability overall. Second, unconventional policy could be employed to engineer additional monetary policy ease, when this was necessary. Third, policy communication acquired an elevated role during turbulent times. In the face of a deflationary shock, explaining the central bankd5s commitment to price stability could influence policy expectations in a stabilising manner. Communication became more important when short-term interest rates could no longer adequately reflect additional policy easing. Fourth, the research reaffirmed the stabilising role of well-anchored inflation expectations. Fifth, to better mitigate deflationary risks, aggressive conventional policy easing in advance of zero was advisable. Arguments for "keeping your powder dry" or for "saving your ammunition," were not supported by the research. *** The decisive policy easing by the Fed and the ECB during the crisis and the adoption of unconventional measures by the two central banks were crucial in countering the threat of deflation in the current episode. Differences in the institutional structure of the two central banks as well as differences in the relative role of banks and non-banking institutions in the US and euro area, has meant that the unconventional policy measures adopted differed. Nonetheless, the end result was appropriate and effective policy easing on both sides of the Atlantic. A pertinent question is how this response compares to the handling of earlier episodes when policymakers faced a similar challenge. Such a comparison is not available for the euro area, since this was the first such episode in its history. A historical comparison could be attempted for the Fed that also faced the zero bound during the 1930s, and research results have already emerged. (See, for example, Bordo and James, 2009, Reinhart and Reinhart, 2009, and Wheelock, 2010). A comparative analysis of the Federal Reserved5s policy responses to the current episode relative to that following the October 1929 stock market crash, reveals striking differences. With respect to conventional easing, the Fed reduced interest rates more slowly and in a rather erratic manner following the 1929 crash, which in the face of declining prices, implied significant increases in real interest rates. Most striking, however, is the difference in the Fedd5s policy response in the use of unconventional monetary measures. In the current episode, the Fed promptly expanded the monetary base and the size the Fedd5s balance sheet. By contrast, in the early 1930s quantitative easing was not pursued. Indeed, the record suggests that a lack of understanding regarding the power of quantitative easing misled the Fed into inaction. Perceptions that the economy was in a "liquidity trap" that made monetary policy ineffective were, unfortunately, not uncommon. However, the evidence could not support the view that the economy was in a liquidity trap (Brunner and Meltzer, 1968). A spectrum of longer-term interest rates remained well above zero throughout the 1930s and Federal Reserve actions did eventually bring these longer rates down, when quantitative easing began. The real problem was not that Fed policy didnd5t work, but rather that the Fed was unwilling to use the tools that it had to conduct expansionary monetary policy because it feared a resurgence of asset market speculation and inflation. The Federal Reserve in the early 1930s misdiagnosed both the need for additional policy easing as well as the power of the Fed to engineer it. These mistakes were not repeated. In the current episode, aggressive unconventional policies, including the provision of massive lending to distressed financial institutions, allowed for a rapid expansion in the monetary base. This unprecedented expansion was reflected in a large increase in the Fedd5s balance sheet. The size of the Fedd5s balance sheet more than doubled. By contrast, the Fedd5s balance sheet contracted in the crucial period following the stock market crash in October 1929. Indeed, it took around three years for the absolute level of the Fed balance sheet to return to its October 1929 level. Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz (1963) had already recounted the Fedd5s errors during the Great Depression, greatly influencing a generation of subsequent research. At a conference honouring Milton Friedmand5s ninetieth birthday, on 8 November 2002, then Governor Ben Bernanke remarked "I would like to say to Milton and Anna: Regarding the Great Depression. Youd5re right we did it. Wed5re sorry. But thanks to you, we wond5t do it again". With the benefit of pertinent policy research, the Fed kept this promise. *** I would like to conclude by recalling Otmar Issingd5s (2004) editorial introduction of the first ECB Research Bulletin. Issing highlighted the value of policy research in providing a sound conceptual and empirical basis for policy-making, particularly for ensuring the central banksd5 ability to deliver price stability. He argued that trust, confidence and credibility in a central bank can never be taken for granted and that they must be continuously defended by sound analysis and communication of the rationale of the central bankd5s actions. The recent experience affirms, I believe, how valuable policy research can be towards fulfilling this task, especially during challenging times. text: Supervision of the financial sector: reflections and conclusions from the crisis Speech by Athanasios Orphanides, Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus, at the 3rd Banking Forum of the Cyprus Business Administration Development Company and the Cyprus Bank Association Nicosia, 27 April 2010 The financial crisis has put the stability of the international financial system to a serious test and has shown significant weaknesses in the architecture and implementation to date of the regulation and supervision of the financial sector. It has also highlighted noticeable gaps in the quiver of available tools of the competent authorities for crisis prevention, management and resolution. Although even timid signs of international recovery from the crisis have already begun to appear, complacency is not allowed. Now is the time to prepare intensively to avoid and deal with future crises. The experience not only of the recent financial crisis but also of the historical economic development of recent centuries show that it is practically impossible to completely prevent future crises. But we can make an effort to limit their size and frequency. Given this, the aim should be to reflect on the future of the architecture of supervision of the financial system and on the further fundamental changes needed in the regulatory and supervisory framework in the light of recent lessons learned and experiences. To this end, a wide-ranging debate on the most effective ways of improving regulation and surveillance and of dealing with possible future crises has long since begun in international for a(1). It has been understood that an integrated approach is needed to prevent, manage and resolve crises with a view to ensuring financial stability. In my speech today at the 3rd Banking Forum I will first refer to some weaknesses of the international framework for the regulation and supervision of the financial sector that have emerged from the recent crisis and the resulting conclusions. Next, I will examine some implications of the lessons learned from the international experience on Cyprus. I will refer to desirable changes in the existing regulatory and supervisory framework in Cyprus, with particular reference to the role of the Central Bank of Cyprus. *** As I mentioned, discussions are under way in various for a aimed at improving the architecture of supervision of the financial system at international and European level. These initiatives are based on two pillars: microprudential and macro-prudential supervision. The main objective of financial supervision is to prevent financial crises or mitigate their negative effects. Micro-prudential supervision aims to reduce the problems that individual financial institutions may face. This is done through the monitoring and analysis of information concerning each institution separately in order to assess, among other things, the risks they face, the adequacy of the systems and their management as well as their compliance with the regulations. On the other hand, macroprudential supervision focuses on risks to the stability of the financial system as a whole, stemming from the collective behaviour of financial institutions, the interconnections between financial intermediaries and markets as well as from the macroeconomic environment. It aims to identify, monitor and assess potential risks and weaknesses that threaten the financial system as a whole. These two components of supervision are inextricably intertwined in both substantive and operational terms and both contribute to ensuring financial stability. The recent financial crisis has highlighted shortcomings and inefficiencies in the global regulatory and supervisory framework. The financial turmoil has demonstrated the lack of coordination and harmonisation reflected in different regulatory and supervisory frameworks even within single economic regions such as the US and the EU. It is inescapable of concluding that these gaps and shortcomings have contributed to the severity of the crisis, which demonstrates the urgent need to strengthen cross-border cooperation to establish uniform rules and, in general, to adopt homogeneous regulatory frameworks. The greater the heterogeneity of the regulatory and supervisory frameworks between the various countries, the greater the problem. The lack of a stable set of rules necessarily leads to distortions in competition between financial institutions and encourages arbitrage in matters of regulation. The absence of a harmonised set of rules, at the global level, for example in the definition of capital is obvious. Heterogeneities in the regulatory framework exist even in the case of single financial markets, such as the EU, which create problems. As noted in the de Larosiere report (2009), the existing regulatory framework in Europe lacks coherence mainly due to the different options provided to EU Member States in the implementation of Eu Directives. These choices lead to a great diversity in terms of the transposition of directives into national law depending on the local conditions, legislation and practices followed. Achieving a greater degree of regulatory homogeneity within the EU can be an important component of a wider effort to strengthen the economic governance of the single European economy, with the aim of strengthening and functioning as smoothly as possible. In addition to the need to harmonise regulatory and supervisory frameworks, a key lesson from the recent financial crisis is the need to strengthen the macro-prudential orientation of the regulation and supervision of the financial sector as well as to ensure a close and effective link between macroprudential supervision and the supervision of individual financial institutions. The crisis has admittedly highlighted the issue of the underestimation of systemic risk in the exercise of micro-prudential supervision. This has led to a broad consensus on the need to better understand how the different components of today's complex financial system interact and the distribution of risk within the financial system. Such an understanding helps to identify gaps and strengthen macroprudential supervision with a view to ensuring the stability of the financial system as a whole. The result of this understanding was the clarification of the role of the authorities involved in the effort to strengthen the macro-prudential orientation of the regulation and supervision of the financial sector and the common understanding to strengthen the participation of central banks in this effort. By definition, micro-prudential supervision focuses on individual institutions and cannot effectively assess the broader macroeconomic risks that threaten the financial system as a whole. This work and role is best suited to central banks since they are anyway focused on analysing macroeconomic and financial conditions. In order for a central bank to successfully exercise macro-prudential supervision, it should be provided with the appropriate means to take meaningful action at the level of micro-prudential regulation and supervision. In its effort to ensure financial stability, a central bank is not only responsible for identifying and assessing risks and issuing early warnings, but should also have the power to impose corrective measures. There are significant information synergies between micro-prudential and macro-prudential supervision, which makes it particularly attractive to arrange for both supervisors to be carried out by the same organisation. Central banks can benefit from and rely on their extensive access to supervisory data and information, in particular with regard to systemically important institutions, in order to assess the risks that threaten the financial system as a whole. Moreover, in the area of crisis management and resolution, the financial crisis has shown the importance of close interaction between the responsibilities of central banks and supervisors, in particular when the need arises to provide liquidity in exceptional cases. Indeed, many central banks considered that the exercise of financial supervision by themselves and in particular banking supervision and the resulting ease of the flow of information within the same organisation were extremely helpful in the way they dealt with the recent crisis, even in terms of prudential measures. This further strengthened the arguments in favour of the exercise of central bank responsibilities and supervisory responsibilities by the same organisation. In recent years, countries such as the Netherlands, Slovakia, the Czech Republic and Finland have delegated to their central banks exclusive responsibility for micro-prudential financial supervision or have established a single financial supervisory body within the central bank. The responsibilities of banking supervision (on-the-spot checks and analyses based on statements submitted) previously exercised by the country's single financial supervisory authority have also been transferred to Austria. In Germany, suggestions are under discussion which will enable the central bank to control all supervision of the financial system. A very recent example of a country where the central bank has been entrusted with supervisory powers is Belgium. In particular, a "Committee on Systemic Risks and Systemically Important Financial Institutions" has recently been set up in this country. This Committee, which is responsible for the micro-prudential supervision of these institutions, is part of the central bank, which will be responsible for monitoring and evaluating strategic developments as well as the risk profile of each systemically important financial institution separately. Transferring micro-prudential supervision under the umbrella of central banks can also be the most effective way to maintain the institutional independence of supervision  an important form of defence against political pressures or pressure from individuals or influence groups with their own interests. Central banks are always among the most independent institutions in democratic societies, as a high degree of central bank independence is required to ensure monetary stability. The experience of the recent crisis has shown that countries and sectors where the responsibility for supervision was not exercised by substantially independent bodies and were prone to political influence and interference contributed to the worsening of the situation. Tangible cases of how the lack of supervision by the independent central bank caused major problems during the recent financial economic crisis can be found, for example, in the USA, where the crisis began. An example is that of the financial institutions Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, which were involved in financing residential loans guaranteed by the US government. Although the systemic risks posed by these two institutions had been promptly highlighted by the Federal Reserve, these were not addressed. These two institutions were not supervised by the Federal Reserve, which is the main supervisory authority of the banking sector in the United States. Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, however, were able to expand their portfolios almost without limit and with a tacit guarantee from the government. The result is well known. Apart from the fact that these institutions collapsed, their involvement and contribution to the development of the whole financial crisis was decisive. Unfortunately, in the above case, despite the early warnings, the problem was left unchecked. The expansion of these two institutions has helped to facilitate the expansion of credit to households with a rather poor credit rating. Many analysts see political influence as playing a key role in easing supervision and excessively increasing risks. In this particular case, the political pressure on these institutions was aimed at 'affordable housing'. The result, however, was the creation of financial instability in the real estate market. Unfortunately, and no matter how well-intentioned the political interventions were, the results proved disastrous even for households that were supposed to be helped by the lax provision of credit. The consequent increase in the number of seizures in the United States underlines the truth of the matter. Another example that highlights the importance of central bank supervision is that of investment banks in the US. Institutions such as Bear Sterns, Lehman Brothers and Goldman Sachs were not under the supervision of the central bank before the crisis. As is well known, Lehman Brothers and Bear Sterns took excessive systemic risks, as a result of which they needed state support to avoid collapse. And as you know Goldman Sachs is now facing accusations of crisis-related fraud. A third example of an organisation that took excessive risks that not only led to its bankruptcy but was also crucial to the crisis, is the case of the insurance company AIG. In this case, the Federal Reserve was not responsible for supervision either. In retrospect, I would say that if the Federal Reserve had a broader supervisory role it could have handled systemic risks better in the above cases. This might have prevented what eventually became the root cause of the global financial crisis. In Europe, a typical example of a malfunctioning of the supervisory framework where the central bank did not have a meaningful role is the case of the United Kingdom. Despite the existence of a single supervisory authority for the entire financial sector, the well-known FSA, the disengagement of the Bank of England from supervision had, I would say, unpleasant results which led, for example, to the collapse of Northern Rock. *** I would now like to focus on the situation in Cyprus in terms of improving the supervisory and regulatory framework with a view to ensuring financial stability. I believe that there are enough conclusions that can be drawn from the international crisis for our own system as well. In Cyprus, in the aftermath of the crisis, it is particularly important to stress that the prudential regulations of the Central Bank of Cyprus (CBC) on bank liquidity, which have long been applied by commercial banks, as well as the prudential liquidity management practices adopted by the banks themselves, have protected the domestic banking system from the serious liquidity problems that have occurred in the banking sectors of other countries during the financial crisis. The effectiveness of these prudential liquidity regulations has been recognised in the recent report on the stability of the Financial System of Cyprus by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), in the context of the Financial Sector Assessment Programme published in November 2009. Indeed, current international initiatives to strengthen prudential liquidity regulations around the world are in line with those that the CBC has followed for years. Regarding the need for central banks to have a strong macroprudential orientation in the exercise of their supervisory responsibilities, I mention that in Cyprus the legislation entrusts the responsibility of ensuring the stability of the financial system to the CBC. As mentioned earlier, in order for a central bank to be successful in macro-prudential supervision, it should be provided with the appropriate means to take meaningful action at the level of micro-prudential regulation and supervision. Unfortunately, in Cyprus there is some anomaly in this aspect since the micro-prudential supervision of credit institutions is the responsibility of two different supervisory authorities: commercial banks are supervised by the CBC, while the Service for the Supervision and Development of Co-operative Societies is responsible for the supervision of Co-operative Credit Institutions (MFA). Such an arrangement has obvious drawbacks since it can lead to heterogeneous application of the rules of operation of credit institutions, which implies unequal operating rules within the same sector of the financial system. The arguments in favour of consolidating the micro-prudential supervision of banks and MFA were also highlighted in the recent IMF's assessment report on the stability of the Financial System of Cyprus (2009), which noted that both categories of institutions take deposits, have similar activities, face similar risks and perhaps most importantly, theoretically operate under the same regulatory framework. Although in theory commercial banks and MFA have the same regulatory framework, it seems in practice that at critical moments the lack of a single regulatory framework creates risks. A concrete example of the problems arising from the separation of the exercise of micro-prudential supervision, which inevitably hinders the proper adoption of a macroprudential orientation in supervision, is a relevant recent experience of Cyprus: During the excessive euphoria that prevailed in the real estate sector in Cyprus in the period 2006-2007, the CBC, in the context of the monitoring and supervision of its banks, it identified an increasing concentration of risk due to the rapid expansion of bank lending to the real estate sector. He considered that in order to ensure the stability of our financial system, this risk needed to be reduced. As a result, in July 2007, the CBC reduced the maximum funding ratio as a percentage of the value of real estate for the purchase of a second home from 70% to 60%. For the first house the indicator remained unchanged at 80%. I would remind you that the decision of the CBC, although considered correct in retrospect, received harsh criticisms at the time of implementation and pressure was also exerted for revocation by affected bodies and political forces. I would like to point out that a similar concentration of loans in the real estate sector at the same time in Cyprus was recorded in the MFA, which, however, as I mentioned, are not subject to the supervision of the Central Bank but of the Service for the Supervision and Development of Co-operative Societies. It is noted that the percentage of loans from MFA corresponded to ; approximately the total loans of domestic banks and MFA. The MFA supervisor did not take the appropriate action, despite being aware of the risks and of the CBC's circulars issued to commercial banks. Thus, the maximum funding ratio as a percentage of the value of real estate for the purchase of a second home for MFA remained unchanged around 70%, thus exacerbating distortions in the financial sector and reducing the effectiveness of the CBC's efforts aimed at ensuring financial stability in our economy. In addition to consolidating the supervision of banking and co-operative institutions, I believe that considerations can also be given to a broader integration of the supervision of the financial sector in Cyprus as is done in other countries. There are potentially significant benefits and synergies in the case of a single organisation exercising supervision and regulation of all sectors of the country's financial system, such as savings and improved efficiency and effectiveness of supervision. The aforementioned recent IMF report on Cyprus agrees with this in mind. In addition to proposing an immediate consolidation of the supervision of banks and MFA under one roof, in the medium term the IMF recommends consolidating the regulation and supervision of all areas of the financial system. The IMF report also underlines that integrating the supervision of all sectors of the financial system under one principle will enhance efficiency and bring significant savings through the achievement of economies of scale, e.g. in supporting functions such as IT, human resource management services and legal services. In the spirit of what I said earlier about the tendencies to upgrade the supervisory role of central banks in other countries of the European Union, where the central bank has supervised the banking sector, there are thoughts of transferring other supervisory responsibilities to the central bank. For example, the Bank of France and the Bank of Greece are planning to transfer the supervision of insurance services together with banking supervision. Moreover, in these countries, as well as in other European countries, including Cyprus, banking groups are also involved in insurance operations. I stress that an important reason for making it legitimate to upgrade the supervisory role of central banks is the fact that this ensures that the institutional independence of supervision is maintained. In the EU in particular, the independence of the central banks was guaranteed by the Maastricht Treaty. In Cyprus it should be noted that the full independence of the other supervisory authorities is not guaranteed. Unlike the CBC, they do not have financial independence since they depend on state sponsorship for their operation. In addition, when they need reinforcement in personnel, the approval of the Ministry of Finance and the Parliament is required. *** Based on the recent experiences and trends I have mentioned above, the supervisory framework of Cyprus needs to be strengthened and, above all, modernised. A practical way of strengthening the supervisory framework that avoids radical, time-consuming and complex procedures would be to link the other supervisory authorities to the CBC, thereby ensuring their independence. This will also be in line with the existing international trends mentioned above and will contribute to the success of the objective of ensuring financial stability. In the aftermath of the crisis, changes are being made to improve the supervision of the financial sector around the world. I think it is important that we also make improvements to the regulatory and supervisory framework in Cyprus. These changes must be adopted in good time to further strengthen the safeguarding of financial stability in the future. ------------------------------------------------------------- FOOTNOTE: (1) ,  , Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (2009), European Commission (2009)  International Monetary Fund (2010). text: Annual Report of the Central Bank of Cyprus for 2009 Speech by Athanasios Orphanides, Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus, at the press conference for the presentation of the Bank's Annual Report for the year 2009 Nicosia, 3 May 2010 I welcome you to the presentation of the Annual Report of the Central Bank of Cyprus for the year 2009. The Report reviews the economic developments which occurred during the year in question and the bank's operations. Before proceeding with my short speech, I would like to express warm thanks to all the staff without exception for the dedication, hard work and support of our efforts to achieve the goals and achieve the goals and aspirations of the Central Bank and the economy in general. 2009 was a year of two major negative developments for the Cypriot economy. The first negative development concerns the decline observed in the country's real GDP of 1.7%, which was the most significant contraction since 1974-75 and is partly due to the effects of the international financial turmoil and the ensuing economic downturn. The second negative development was the serious widening of the budget deficit beyond the extent that it could be explained as a result of the economic downturn. During 2009, at international level, the various governments and central banks intensified the exceptional measures to support the financial sector and the real economy that were severely affected by the financial crisis that preceded it. As a result, the international economy began to recover. In the euro area, for example, real GDP growth in the second half of 2009 was positive following the sharp decline observed at the end of 2008 and the first half of 2009. As far as our own economy is concerned, the deterioration of the economic climate was confirmed by the decline recorded by the real Gross Domestic Product ("GDP") during 2009, but also by many other economic indicators. In particular, real GDP growth recorded a decline of 1.7% in 2009. Also, during the year under review, the Harmonized Index of Consumer Prices recorded a significant slowdown, reflecting the general climate of recession and the fall in fuel prices, reaching 0.2% compared to 4.4% in 2008. However, it is with particular concern that I would like to note that domestic inflationary pressures continue to lurk and are stronger compared to the rest of the euro area, thus further affecting the competitiveness of Cypriot products. In particular, core inflation, i.e. harmonised inflation excluding energy and food prices, although decelerated to 1.7% in 2009 compared to 2.5% in 2008, nevertheless remained at higher levels than the euro area average (1.3%). Another particularly negative development is the significant deterioration of public finances in Cyprus by ten percentage points in the last two years, about 1.7 billion euros. As I have said in the past, compared to the other countries in the euro area, the budget deficit is not one of the highest, but there is a significant difference. In most euro area countries, the economic recession was more pronounced than the recession we had in Cyprus, which is why their budget deficit was most strongly affected by the recession. In our country, the fiscal deterioration of 2009 compared to 2007 and 2008 is of a structural nature and is largely due to the large expansion of public expenditure of a non-developmental nature. It should be noted that in recent years total public expenditure as a percentage of GDP has ranged from 42-43%. However, according to the recently published Stability Programme, public expenditure as a percentage of GDP reached an all-time high of 46.4% in 2009, while a further increase to 47.6% is projected in 2010. Of course, this trend cannot continue without particularly negative effects on the economy of the place. What is important, then, is the aim of fiscal policy to restore public finances to a sustainable basis without undermining the country's growth background. Unfortunately, the difficulty in taking substantial corrective measures has already negatively affected the development course of the place. It is imperative to immediately draw up a rational and long-term planned handling as well as to avoid fictitious reforms in order to temporarily and only beautify the situation. I would also remind you that budgetary reflection efforts must also take into account the acute and long-standing problem of finding resources to finance pension funds, a problem which is also further exacerbated by the ageing of the population. This challenge must also necessarily be part of the long-term planning of fiscal policy. Despite the negative developments in the real economy, our banking system still remains in very good shape. Our banks are healthy, robust and have a strong capital base with a capital ratio of 11.9% as at 21 December 2009, which is well above the minimum requirement of 8%. The non-performing loans ratio, which has steadily declined over time, has increased in 2009 but is at acceptable levels. It is noted that satisfactory provisions for doubtful debts have been made for these loans. As regards the profitability of banks, this was satisfactory in 2009. In the year in question, which was a difficult year, the banks remained profitable but with a profitability lower than that of 2008. The financial crisis also significantly affected the results of the Central Bank. Specifically, the Bank's net profit for 2009 reached a historically high level of 115.4m. In this regard, I note that the Annual Profits of the Bank during the period 2004  2008, i.e. the period after the accession of Cyprus to the European Union, on average were 9.8 million. The exceptionally high profit made by the Bank in 2009 was mainly the result of the investment policy implemented during this very difficult period. In particular, we assessed in good time and correctly, at the end of 2007, the investment options that our accession to the euro area would create. The investment policy we have implemented since 2008, combined with the special conditions due to the financial crisis, has brought about these very significant gains. Concluding this brief statement and returning to the negative developments that have occurred in the real economy of the country, I would like once again to emphasize that I consider it imperative to accelerate the procedures for the immediate adoption of measures to contain public expenditure in such a way as to return our economy to a path of sustainable growth. The slower the structural changes needed to restore public finances to a sound basis are made, the more painful for the country's economy will be the inevitable corrective course. This reality is now recognized by almost all the political, economic and social actors of the country. We therefore have the choice either to proceed boldly with the adjustment of budgetary policy on a rational basis, or to remain inactive and trapped in counterproductive confrontations. We all know that the wrong choices seriously affect the development prospects of our country. I hope that political boldness and the effort for consensus will prevail for the good of our country.

Title: Introduction at the award ceremony for green public contracts
text: The role of central banks and social dialogue in the light of the financial crisis Speech by Athanasios Orphanides, Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus, at the XII Conference of the Committee of Trade Unions of Central Banks of Europe (SCECBU) Nicosia, 12 May 2010 It is with great pleasure that I attend the XII Conference of the Committee of Trade Unions of Central Banks of Europe that is taking place this year in Cyprus. I would like to thank the Cyprus Bank Employees Association (ETYK) for the invitation to address a short greeting. A decade has already passed since the establishment of the Social Dialogue of the European System of Central Banks (ESCB). The purpose of this institution is to provide information and discuss issues that may significantly affect labour relations in the central banks of the ESCB and the European Central Bank (ECB). The ESCB Social Dialogue ensures that employee representatives from the 27 national central banks and the ECB can express their views before taking decisions that may have a significant impact on labour relations within the ESCB. In its capacity as a special forum for consultation, the Social Dialogue normally deals with a multitude of banking issues. It includes issues of banknotes and payment systems up to issues of labour mobility, training and cooperation within the ESCB. Inevitably, the agenda of the Social Dialogue could not fail to include the issue of reforming the regulatory and supervisory framework of the financial system, a need strongly demonstrated by the global economic and financial crisis. Ongoing efforts to restructure the regulatory and supervisory framework of the financial sector are dramatically diversifying the landscape, with significant implications for the role of central banks in the stability of the financial system. The financial crisis has undoubtedly taught important lessons to decision-makers around the world, and has fuelled dialogue in various international for a. Globally, the G20 has taken a leading role in international cooperation to reform the international regulatory and supervisory framework. Specific areas of joint action were identified to improve the global framework for prudential regulation and supervision, such as enhancing transparency and cross-border coordination, strengthening with complementary measures of the New Basel Pact, as well as reforming international financial institutions such as the IMF. The response to the crisis was also coordinated at European level, with important initiatives by EU heads of state and the adoption by the Council of EU Finance Ministers (ECOFIN) of a roadmap for financial supervision, stability and regulation. A key lesson from the recent financial crisis is the need to strengthen the macro-prudential orientation of the regulation and supervision of the financial sector. At the same time, a close and effective link between macro-prudential supervision and the supervision of individual financial institutions, i.e. micro-prudential supervision, must also be ensured. On this need, there was a general consensus at global level and this is also reflected in the reform of the EU supervisory framework. On the basis of the recommendations of the de Larosiere report, a new supervisory framework is being set up in the EU consisting of the European System of Financial Supervisors focusing on micro-prudential supervision and the European Systemic Risk Board, which will be responsible for macroprudential supervision. Let me focus on the European Systemic Risk Board, since this is the new body that highlights and upgrades the role of the national central banks in promoting financial stability in the European Union. Its main task is to identify, monitor and assess risks to the stability of the entire financial system with a view to providing warnings and recommendations on risks where necessary. The European Systemic Risk Board will bring together central bankers, the heads of the three supervisors operating under the European System of Financial Supervisors, the European Commission and the supervisors of EU Member States to discuss and assess financial stability conditions in the EU. The ECB will support the European Systemic Risk Board in its analytical, statistical, administrative and logistical work, building on the knowledge and analytical potential of the EU's national central banks. In general, central banks are in a better position to assess macroeconomic risks to financial stability through the macroeconomic analysis they are tasked with carrying out on a permanent basis. Furthermore, in my view, the recent crisis has also shown that the required close and effective link between macroprudential and micro-prudential aspects of financial supervision is best achieved when central banks also shoulder micro-prudential supervision. In other words, they are involved in the supervision of individual financial institutions, which deals with vital issues such as liquidity, capital adequacy and risk management. There are significant information synergies between micro-prudential and macro-prudential supervision, which makes it particularly attractive for them both to be managed by the same organisation. Central banks can benefit from and rely on their extensive access to supervisory data and information, in particular with regard to systemically important institutions, to assess the risks threatening the financial system as a whole. Moreover, in the area of crisis management and resolution, the financial crisis has shown the importance of close interaction between the responsibilities of central banks and supervisors, in particular when the need arises to provide liquidity in exceptional cases. Indeed, many central banks considered that the exercise of financial supervision, and in particular banking supervision, by them, and the resulting ease of the flow of information within the same organisation, acted as extremely helpful factors in the way they dealt with the recent crisis. This further strengthened the arguments in favour of the exercise of central bank responsibilities and supervisory responsibilities by the same organisation. In view of these new realities, central banks should seize the opportunity and successfully play their new upgraded role that puts them at the heart of the new European financial landscape. To this end, the demonstration of responsibility on the part of central banks towards the whole of society, both at the level of decision-making and at the level of employees, is of the utmost importance. Social responsibility must be a key feature of labour relations between central banks and their staff. Central banks need to continue to invest in knowledge and skills to broaden the skills and analytical capabilities of their staff so that they can better carry out their work. They must also continue to contribute to an unhindered and, above all, productive dialogue with the representatives of their workers. On the other hand, central bank workers must recognise how privileged they are towards their colleagues in the private sector. Their social responsibility lies in the need to adopt an exemplary attitude for other employees, especially during these difficult times that we are going through. Within the framework of EMU, the social partners play a very important role in boosting economic growth and improving employment prospects and the social face of the EU. And this role is achieved, the better the process of setting wages is linked to the employment conditions prevailing in the sector. Increases in nominal wages in euro area states should be, overall, consistent with the objective of price stability, while increases in real wages should take into account productivity developments. In relation to Cyprus, by examining the issue of the responsibility of the social partners from a broader perspective, the existence of the code of industrial relations has contributed substantially to the timeless safeguarding and maintenance of conditions of workers' peace. At the same time, the consensus of the social partners at critical moments for the country has contributed greatly to the maintenance of conditions of macroeconomic stability. However, as has been the case in other euro area countries, the deterioration of the economy in the midst of the global economic crisis has highlighted even more some structural weaknesses of the Cypriot economy, which can only be of concern. For example, it is with particular concern that I would like to refer to the problem of domestic inflationary pressures. Unfortunately, upward trends in domestic inflation continue to lurk and are stronger than in the rest of the euro area, further affecting the competitiveness of our economy. In particular, core inflation, i.e. harmonised inflation excluding energy and food prices, although decelerated to 1.9% in 2009 compared to 2.5% in 2008, nevertheless remained at higher levels than the euro area average (1.3%). In order to highlight the importance of inflation developments for the competitiveness of the Cypriot economy, it is worth looking at the differences in some relatively fundamental figures, such as earnings and productivity between Cyprus and the euro area, from the accession of Cyprus to the euro area to the present day. Specifically, according to Eurostat data in 2009, earnings per employee in Cyprus increased by 2.9% compared to 1.4% in the euro area. Productivity declined by 1.1% in Cyprus, while in the euro area it decreased by 2.2%. As a result, unit labour costs increased in Cyprus by 4.0% compared to 3.7% in the euro area. In particular, in the financial intermediaries, real estate and business, which is an important service sector, earnings per employee in Cyprus increased by 5.7% compared to 1.3% in the euro area. Corresponding productivity increased by 0.4% in both Cyprus and the euro area, resulting in unit labour costs increasing by 5.2% in Cyprus compared to 0.9% in the euro area. The above figures show divergences in inflation, which are also reflected in earnings, which are not explained by differences in productivity and tend to undermine the competitiveness of our economy. This can be seen in the increased unit labour costs relative to that of the euro area. Following our joining the euro area, ongoing divergences affecting competitiveness in relation to our other euro area partners are not sustainable. Therefore, I would like once again to stress the importance of social responsibility. Requests from the social partners must always reflect developments in the productivity and competitiveness of our economy. Economic realities and the knock-on effects they will have on the economy and on the interest of the country in the long term must be taken into account. In conclusion, I would like to underline that the dramatic developments in Europe have highlighted the importance of cooperation at European, collective level. First and foremost in a united Europe, the common good of the citizens of the European Union comes first. With these few words I wish you a productive and successful conference.
