In the end, it was forced, due to the well-known problems and the crisis created in 2010, to make drastic reductions in salaries and pensions. These reductions were unfair in my opinion but necessary, since for years the warnings about the problems emerging in the pension and public finances were ignored and, unfortunately, the necessary measures were not taken in time. Today, of course, the sustainability of the pension system in Greece has improved, because the Greek Government has been forced to move in the right direction. Unfortunately, the Greek people did not previously have the right information in their hands to demand the right decisions from their governments in good time. Here I come back to the importance of our role as economists and as teachers to give the right information, because in this way we can push decision-makers, help them, if you like, especially when they are struggling, to make those decisions that promote the common good. The economy is facing an extremely critical juncture. Economic policy-making should take into account future income constraints and reflect the areas necessary for fiscal consolidation. Structural changes in the public sector can be an important starting point for a long-term balanced budget and stability in the development and prosperity of the country. The correct information and teaching that you offer are key factors for making better decisions, those that are required to put our country back on a path of rapid and sustainable development.

Title: Speech in the Parliamentary Committee on Economic and Budgetary Affairs on the Budget for 2022
text: Annual Report of the Central Bank of Cyprus for 2010 Speech by Athanasios Orphanides, Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus, at the press conference for the presentation of the Bank's Annual Report for the year 2010 Nicosia, 27 April 2011 During 2010 our economy found itself in critical condition. As a result, today we are at a crossroads with critical choices before us. Following the recession recorded in 2009, there was a recovery in 2010 with real GDP increasing by 1% compared to a decrease of 1.7% in 2009. However, this recovery has not been uniform and many sectors of the economy are still experiencing problems. GDP growth in 2010 came almost exclusively from the financial sector, at the center of which is our banking system. With many sectors lagging behind, GDP growth in 2010 was subdued, far from the pre-crisis rate of 3% to 4%, which no longer seems feasible. The weak recovery of 2010 resulted in unemployment rising to historically high levels. According to Eurostat data, the unemployment rate reached an average of 6.5% in 2010. In fact, in the last months of the year unemployment worsened and the upward trend in the unemployment rate continues in 2011, reaching 7.2% in February. Unemployment is particularly high among young people under the age of 29, as the percentage of registered unemployed in this category exceeded 25% in 2010 and still remains at particularly high levels. Alongside high unemployment, there was also an increase in inflation in the year under review. The Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices recorded a significant increase to 2.5% in 2010 from 0.2% in 2009 while inflationary pressures continue to exist in 2011. Specifically, during the period January-March 2011, harmonized inflation reached 3.1% in Cyprus. Of particular concern is the fact that the inflation gap between Cyprus and the euro area has once again begun to widen, undermining the competitiveness of the Cypriot economy and further widening the current account balance. The deterioration in the current account balance is indicative of the imbalances created by the ongoing negative path of government figures. More generally, in 2010, the economic crisis mutated into a fiscal crisis in some countries in the euro area and the markets have become particularly sensitive and demanding in terms of fiscal problems in specific eurozone countries with a large financial system such as Cyprus, driving the corresponding interest rates for financing public debt to very high levels. Unfortunately, one of those euro area countries where public finances present significant problems is Cyprus. The structural problems in Cyprus have been known for a long time, but the high growth rates that prevailed overshadowed the need for their immediate treatment. However, with the crisis that erupted internationally and the recession that arose in the Cypriot economy, these growth rates ceased to exist without the immediate prospect of their complete recovery, while the excessive increase in public spending continued. Indicatively, I recall that, while the growth of nominal GDP in the period 2008-2010 was about 10%, the corresponding increase in public expenditure exceeded 20%. This course is not sustainable and must be reversed. As a result of the fiscal deterioration, our country in 2010 was included by the EU in the excessive deficit surveillance process. This negative development was followed by a cycle of downgrades of our economy by international rating agencies, from which we have not yet escaped. Coupled with concerns about the general fiscal problem in the euro area, these developments deserve particular attention in countries with a large financial sector such as Cyprus. It is therefore imperative that we shield our economy. It is my view that we must move along two interdependent axes: the first axis is about ensuring the stability of the financial sector. The second concerns the adoption of measures to reverse the negative course of fiscal aggregates in recent years. With regard to strengthening the stability of our financial sector, I would remind you that the Central Bank is implementing a strict system of supervision, which has worked effectively even in the unprecedented difficult circumstances of the international crisis of recent years, with the result that it remains healthy. I would mention, for example, our instructions for maintaining high levels of liquidity and imposing a maximum funding rate in the real estate sector (loan to value ratio), which in the past were considered by some to be excessively strict, but with the resulting crisis they are recognized as prudent practices that are also adopted by other supervisory authorities. To further strengthen the banking system, the Central Bank has urged our banks to strengthen their capital base beyond the minimum funds deemed necessary. I note that the large banks during 2010 strengthened their capital base while, in 2011, they are proceeding with further increases. In addition, the CBC is proceeding with the establishment of a Hellenic Financial Stability Fund with the resources of the banks. Such a Fund can act as a cushion of protection against the pressures exerted due to the deterioration of the state. For this reason, the Central Bank of Cyprus welcomes the adoption by the House of Representatives of its proposal for the creation of a Hellenic Financial Stability Fund. In addition to the above actions to strengthen our banking system, we also took important measures to strengthen the Central Bank against the new risks that arose in the international financial environment due to the international financial turmoil. The global financial crisis that erupted in 2008 resulted in additional risks being taken by the Eurosystem. These increased risks also necessitated a review of the capital adequacy of the Eurosystem's central banks. For example, the European Central Bank has doubled its capital and is building further reserves. Acting in the same direction, the Central Bank of Cyprus increased its provision against risks in 2010. It also doubled its capital from 30m. to 60 mil. However, these actions to strengthen the financial sector alone are not enough to ensure the smooth running of the economy. With the government under surveillance for an excessive deficit and the multiple downgrades of the credibility of the State, the continued postponement of corrective measures puts our economy at serious risk. To end the dangerous cycle of downgrades, a reversal of the course of public finances is required. I consider it positive that the government and all the political and social actors of the country have recognized the need for long-term fiscal consolidation. For example, it is good that the need to contain public spending and to restructure the pension system has been recognised. The recognition of the need for fiscal consolidation was also reflected in the targets set in 2010 in the budget for 2011, which provides for a reduction in the budget deficit to 4%. However, there are concerns that these objectives do not seem to be being realised. In particular, the fiscal data for the first quarter of 2011 are disappointing and make doubtful, among other things, the implementation of the targets set out in the new Stability Programme that the government will submit very soon to the EU. What is even more worrying, however, is that we have not yet taken measures to reverse the long-term budgetary imbalances that we are facing. Therefore, radical changes are needed in the course taken so that we can achieve the complete reversal of the course that it has brought us to the current unpleasant situation. Who doubts that the increases in expenditure are not sustainable and that the pension scheme with the current parameters is unsustainable? The economy is still facing an extremely difficult time. Corrective decisions are urgent and imperative. Wrong choices are seriously affecting our country. The timeframe for changing course is dangerously tight. Tidying up public finances is essential. Continuing to postpone decisions will confront us with even more difficult situations, such as those experienced by other countries in Europe. That is unfortunately the reality. I hope that the competent bodies will rise to the occasion and work without delay towards the imposed path of fiscal consolidation. Because the economy is a national matter.

Title: Speech at the 12th Limassol Economic Forum
text: Perspectives on the ongoing crisis Remarks by Athanasios Orphanides, Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus, at a panel discussion on "Financial Crisis: Global and Local Perspectives" organised by the University of Cyprus Nicosia, 12 September 2011 It is a pleasure to participate in this discussion on global and local perspectives of the crisis and I would like to thank the organisers for the kind invitation to be part of this distinguished panel. In my brief intervention, I will focus on the sovereign debt crisis that has engulfed the euro area.the global perspective.and say a few words about how this is affecting us in Cyprus.the local angle. Back in 2007, when the financial turbulence we associate with the ongoing crisis first became evident, few could have anticipated how the crisis would morph into the various stages we have been through. By the end of 2008, what was originally seen as a difficulty with subprime lending confined to the United States had become a full-blown global banking crisis. The sharp recession that followed exposed additional weaknesses in some regions of the global economy. In the euro area, in particular, over the past year or so the crisis has evolved into a sovereign debt crisis which has challenged the economies of a number of member states where the soundness of fiscal balances were not deemed entirely credible. As a result, the creditworthiness of the sovereigns has been brought into question. These difficulties are reflected in the widening of sovereign spreads for a number of euro area sovereigns and the spillover into banks, especially those operating in member states where the sovereigns are most challenged. What is the underlying cause of these difficulties in the euro area? In short, it is shortcomings in the economic governance of the euro area that has failed to live up to the original design of the common currency area. More precisely, contrary to the original design, economic governance arrangements in the euro area have failed to discipline member states to undertake sound fiscal policies and accountability for and penalisation of bad policies by member states has been grossly deficient. The importance of sound fiscal policies for preserving the stability of the euro was recognised in the original Stability and Growth Pact (SGP). The SGP was meant to provide a mechanism that would prevent excessive deficits from emerging and quickly correct them if they materialised so that government debt would remain at manageably low levels. However, the Pact has in the main failed as member states have demonstrated little ownership of the fiscal targets to which they were committed. Euro area governments failed to exhibit sufficient discipline to stay within the bounds of the original SGP. Peer pressure within the euro group failed to impose restraint on members pursuing untoward policies. Unfortunately, peer protection rather than peer pressure prevailed. There has been a failure in budgetary reporting and surveillance. In this regard, particularly damaging to the euro area as a whole has been the revelation of the enormous size of the fiscal imbalances and government debt in the Greek economy that was hidden until the situation became critical. There has also been a failure of enforcement of commonly agreed fiscal rules. Without proper incentives to ensure that it is respected, no framework, however well designed, can be effective. The development of a credible enforcement mechanism is an indispensable element of improved governance. Fiscal frameworks and rules must be binding. Recognition of these difficulties has been the first step towards strengthening euro area governance to ensure stability of the framework going forward. A number of important steps are in process. Based on the recommendations of the final report of the Van Rompuy task force for reinforcing economic governance in the Union (Van Rompuy, 2010), six legislative proposals have been put forward by the Commission. These include proposals aimed at improving fiscal surveillance and the implementation of the SGP as well as revamping national budgetary frameworks and strengthening fiscal discipline by member states. Following deliberations by the European Parliament and an agreement by the heads of state of the European Union on 21 July, this legislation is very close to being enacted. However, there have been serious delays in moving ahead, which has been extremely costly for the euro area. These delays associated both with the handling of the ongoing crisis as well as with effectively putting into practice strengthened economic governance arrangements, have exacerbated the sovereign debt crisis. Let me now briefly turn to the situation in Cyprus. Although Cyprus was in a quite solid fiscal position at the beginning of the global crisis, its public finances have deteriorated rapidly since the beginning of the crisis, becoming engulfed in the euro area sovereign crisis. Following the deterioration of its fiscal finances, the credibility of our government was severely challenged in the first half of this year, and the creditworthiness of our sovereign put into question. Continuation of the downward spiral of deteriorating public finances in the broader context of the euro area sovereign crisis poses an extreme danger for the health of our economy, and especially our financial services sector where confidence is a prerequisite. It is of the essence to reverse this trend as rapidly as possible. It is critical to restore the credibility of our governmentd5s fiscal affairs and its creditworthiness. In this light, I would like to support the positive and encouraging developments observed over the past several weeks. Having recognised the problem, it is reassuring to observe the efforts of the Minister of Finance, Mr Kikis Kazamias, aimed at putting the fiscal affairs of our country back in order. I believe it is important for all involved, including political parties and social partners, to help in this effort. To be sure, there is always some disappointment when overindulgent government spending based on unrealistic expectations needs to be curtailed. The short-term pain experienced during the adjustment is unfortunate but it is unavoidable in order to ensure a restoration of the countryd5s fiscal credibility and solid long-term growth prospects. The more the adjustment is delayed, the greater the accumulated cost to the Cypriot economy and its citizens. A convincing fiscal consolidation is necessary to restore confidence in Cyprus. But our job will not be completed with this. As already mentioned, going forward Cyprus will be called to implement European legislation that will require revamping our national budgetary frameworks and strengthening fiscal discipline. Some other euro area member states have already moved towards the adoption of fiscal rules and constitutional amendments ensuring balanced budgets. As a financial centre, Cyprus should be a leader in reforming economic governance and should adopt the best fiscal practices at an early juncture. Striving to be ahead of the curve may be the best defense against the next sequence of events that we may subsequently call a crisis. REFERENCES: Van Rompuy, H (2010) Strengthening Economic Governance in the EU: Report of the Task Force to the European Council, Brussels, 21 October

Title: Introduction in the Cyprus Economic Society Seminar
text: Policy challenges in the euro area Wrap-up panel discussion by Athanasios Orphanides, Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus, at the BIS Research Conference on "Central Bank Balance Sheets in Asia and the Pacific: The Policy Challenges Ahead" organised by the Bank of Thailand Chiang Mai, 13 December 2011 When I arrived in this beautiful setting, for which I want to thank the organizers, some people suggested that this must be a respite from thinking about the euro area. There was a point to that, perhaps. But it was then suggested to me that maybe we should talk a little more about the present difficulties in the euro area at this conference, so why dond5t I focus my comments on that. With respect to the broader topic of the conference, it should be noted that in the euro area we have been pursuing balance sheet policies at the ECB which are not qualitatively different from those pursued by the Federal Reserve and the Bank of England. As elsewhere, these policies have succeeded in significantly lowering interest rates, as reflected, for instance, in government yields perceived to be nearly risk free. But that is not the issue. The issue is that the major problem we are facing right now and that is having an impact on the rest of the world, is that the euro area is not a single country and the government debt of a number of member states is no longer perceived to be nearly risk free. Following the creation of the ECB and the single monetary policy in 1999, the euro area did indeed behave as a common currency area where the single monetary policy was transmitted in pretty much the same way in all member states. As of 2009, however, this, increasingly, no longer works. This can be easily seen by plotting the two-year government yields for different countries in the euro area. By plotting the two year yield, we can focus on a rate that is closely associated with the transmission of monetary policy in macro models. The chart plots the yields of the six largest member states of the euro area that make up almost 90% of the economy. What can be observed in the last couple of years is a divergence in yields suggesting increasing problems with the ability of the single monetary policy to function properly. Note that Greece, Portugal and Ireland are not included in this chart. That is, the chart does not include the countries that have experienced such severe difficulties that they have had to ask for assistance from the IMF and their European Union partners. Let me briefly provide you with my take on the problem and the steps towards a solution. Let's start with some fundamentals. For a currency union to function properly, some minimal fiscal policy coordination is necessary. This can occur with a fiscal union, which in the European Union, we decided not to have. The European Union treaty prohibits member states from assuming the debts of other member states and prohibits monetary financing by any central bank in all member states. The alternative approach that was adopted is to try to have strict limits on debts and deficits. This was the idea behind the Stability and Growth Pact. The idea was to have such a tight control of fiscal policy in each individual member state, that no member state would run into trouble. Indeed, in order to avoid any moral hazard issues, no crisis management mechanism was set up at the beginning. It was assumed that the strict fiscal rules and the absence of any crisis management mechanism would be sufficient to avoid any country getting into trouble. Unfortunately, the fiscal framework was not properly enforced. In addition, the market discipline that might have worked to help limit large deficits in countries with a large debt did not work, because prior to the crisis every member state was able to finance their deficits at virtually the same rate.there was no differentiation. During the crisis in 2009, it became clear that some member statesd0Greece is the most important exampled0had been running deficits that were too large and were not limiting the size of their debt. So the question was: once this was observed in 2009, how could the problem be solved? It was no longer feasible to say we could not have a crisis mechanism in place.one now had to be created in a hurry. Then two things happened in the spring of 2010. First, a makeshift mechanism to help Greece by providing it with loans was set up. The second was to create the EFSF as the temporary crisis management mechanism. But the problem was how to provide help in a way that would avoid moral hazard in the future. Here I want to focus on two choices. The first choice would have been to focus on strengthening prevention and credible enforcement. Specifically, introduce even stricter fiscal rules or constitutional amendments for balanced budgets and consider limiting the sovereignty of member states that misbehave to ensure compliance. The second choice was to raise the cost a country would face during a crisis. The first approach was not chosen in 2010 because some of the decision-making countries did not want to tighten the rules and did not want to limit their own sovereignty. So the second approach was chosen.raise significantly the costs of handling a crisis, including the present one. This was a very critical decision. Throughout 2010, and since then, there have been discussions about whether one way to enforce better discipline would be to introduce the concept of private sector involvement (PSI) in euro area debt. The concept was that an investor buying euro area sovereign debt would have to worry that if the country misbehaved, then a haircut on the debt would be implied, even if there was no issue regarding the sustainability of the debt. Following its adoption in October 2010, this approach proved quite effective in raising the cost of financing of any country that was perceived as facing a potential difficulty. Unfortunately, it was quite damaging and it was probably a key factor behind the difficulties faced by Ireland and Portugal in the few months after its introduction. Surely, the idea of introducing PSI in euro area sovereign debt markets was to raise the cost of a crisis for the country involved and serve as a deterrent, helping countries avoid getting into trouble. However, it wasnd5t such a good idea to introduce PSI during the current crisis. Even worse were two decisions taken this year, the first on 21 July and the second on 26 October, to impose haircuts on Greek debt. I will not dwell on whether Greek debt was sustainable or not. As discussed in an earlier presentation, this assessment is sensitive to the underlying assumptions and is subject to great uncertainty. What is certain is that creating the precedent that a member of the euro area would be forced to impose a haircut on the holders of its debt reinforced to investors how the PSI concept would be applied in the euro area. This is very costly. As can be seen in the chart, following the first decision on 21 July that suggested a small haircut the spreads of Spain and Italy rose. Following the second decision on 26 October that raised the size of the Greek haircut, the spreads of Belgium and France rose. The chart shows clearly the resulting problem. Once the political decision was taken to impose haircuts on one country, international investors had to allow for the possibility that sometime in the future, haircuts would be imposed on other countries. As a result, a large number of the euro area member states are now considered much less trustworthy than before the PSI decisions and face higher costs of financing. So where do we go from here? First, a positive note. The damage created by the PSI decisions seems to have been understood. A major U-turn was observed in last weekd5s meeting of the European heads of state. The notion that private sector involvement should be expected with higher frequency for those who purchased euro area debt is now recognized as damaging and there is an effort to remove it from the framework that is being built for the future. There is essentially an effort to go back to the alternative choice I mentioned earlier that was not made in 2010. Instead of raising the costs of solving a liquidity crisis when that occurs, this backpedaling is taking us to the other alternative, that of prevention and credible enforcement. A very important step that was agreed last week is the agreement that, going forward, all euro area governments will impose stricter rules on themselves by adopting balanced budget amendments in their constitutions. And there is a discussion on limiting sovereignty as an enforcement device. We are going to see in the coming weeks how this will be implemented. With this in place, and if this indeed goes on as projected in the coming weeks, then the second element could be discussed perhaps by the next meeting of the heads of state. And that would be to find more reasonable ways to provide liquidity, helping a country that is under market threat. This is something that we havend5t touched upon yet. Here I want to note that although the EFSF was created last year and a permanent stabilization fund is planned, by limiting the size of resources that can be made available during a crisis we have failed to convince the markets that sufficient resources would be available in case countries such as Italy or Spain face difficulties. Since the decisions that improve the governance framework and protect against moral hazard have been taken, we now need to improve the crisis management framework so that potentially unlimited backing is available from governments to other governments, if needed. I leave you with a question. A lot of analysts around the world are looking at the EFSF and saying to the ECB, isnd5t that your job? And the answer is no: the ECB is the lender of last resort to the banking system, it cannot serve as a lender of last resort to governments. What we have here is a fiscal governance issue that our governments need to solve. Once the political solutions are provided, once we have the appropriate framework at the political level, then and only then can we solve this problem convincingly.

Title: Fintech Evolution in the Banking System and Managing Consequent Risks
text: Annual Report of the Central Bank of Cyprus for the year 2011 Speech by Athanasios Orphanides, Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus, at the press conference for the presentation of the Bank's Annual Report for the year 2011 Nicosia, 02 May 2012 Before proceeding with the presentation of the Annual Report for 2011, I would like to thank the staff of the Central Bank of Cyprus for the hard work and professionalism they have shown during my five-year term as Governor of the Central Bank and to express my satisfaction with the important work we have done together. Based on the economic developments and the data analyzed in the Report, the recovery path presented by the Cypriot economy in the first half of 2011 was interrupted in the second half of the year mainly due to the destruction of the power plant in Vasilikos in July 2011 and its consequences. In addition, the international economic and financial developments were negative for our country, especially in Greece, as well as the effects on Cypriot banks from the impairment of Greek debt. Overall, in 2011 the domestic economy recorded marginal growth of 0.5% compared to an increase of 1.1% in 2010, and unemployment continued to show an alarming upward trend and until December of the year, seasonally adjusted harmonized unemployment reached historically unprecedented levels of 9.4% while it continues to increase in the first months of 2012. At the same time, during this period, the consequences of the enlarged budget deficit increased significantly, while the cycle of downgrades in which the Cypriot economy has fallen, unfortunately, creates new risks for domestic growth and the prospects for recovery of our country. But how did we get to this difficult point for our economy? The answer is obvious: despite the apparent serious deterioration of the budgetary situation in the period 2008-2010, the necessary measures were not taken in time as they should have been. Unfortunately, while it was known that the situation was critical, the necessary measures were not taken even in the first months of 2011, with the result that in May the Republic was excluded from the international markets. Since then our economy has been in a borderline state. The exclusion from international markets has created and continues to create multiple problems: It has raised lending rates in the domestic market, hurting growth and increasing unemployment. In addition, it exerted tremendous pressure on the banking sector, having significantly increased the cost of financing and raising capital, placing the banking sector at unprecedented risk and making it prone to negative external developments. Following the reshuffle of the Council of Ministers in August 2011, the government's economic policy changed direction, with the result that by the end of the year substantial fiscal consolidation measures were taken. However, the measures were not enough to restore the confidence of the markets in the government, with the result that to date Cyprus is still excluded. As far as the banking sector is concerned, the government's inability since May 2011 to refinance its debt has raised international doubts about its ability to support banks in case of need. Thus, when European leaders decided to write down Greek debt on July 21 and October 26, 2011, which hit the capital of banks in Europe, both banks and the government entered the negative vicious circle we find ourselves in to this day. As far as the results of the CBC are concerned, over the last five years we have strengthened the Bank in many ways, on the model of other central banks of the Eurosystem and also of the ECB. We have thus made the CBC a more powerful organization in the midst of the unprecedented economic crisis with strong fortifications and financial cushions. The financial strengthening of the CBC was deemed necessary in view of the increased risks stemming from the crisis, from counterparty credit risk and from the larger volume of eurosystem monetary policy operations. This is despite the fact that the national central banks of the Eurosystem are particularly cautious and conservative about the items they buy or even accept as collateral for monetary policy operations. More specifically, the Bank's profitability before the strengthening of provisions and transfers to reserves was EUR 66.6 million. euro. In 2011, we increased our forecasts for general risks by EUR 25 million. bringing the total forecast to EUR 100 million. We have also increased the Bank's capital by EUR 30 million. eur 90 million. euro. In total, over the last five years, the Bank's capital has increased by 250% (from EUR 25.6 million to EUR 90 million), the reserves by 71% (from EUR 34 million to EUR 58 million) and we have established provisions for dealing with general risks which, from non-existent at the end of 2006, amounted, by the end of 2011, to EUR 100 million. euro. In other words, the total capital, reserves and provisions have increased more than four times, to EUR 248.1 million. from 59.6 million euro. The total profit for the five-year period amounted to EUR 260 million. with an average of EUR 52 million. euro. The bank's total financial cushions stood at 800 million at the end of the five-year period. compared to EUR 350 million. at the beginning of 2007, after, of course, the distribution of EUR 133.8 million. euros to the government. I would like to point out that with our accession to the Eurosystem, the Bank's obligations have increased significantly, with the result that more working hours are required. Nevertheless, not only have we not increased human resources, but today there is a slight decrease compared to five years ago, which indicates an increase in productivity. Specifically, at the end of my term of office the staff numbers 333 people, of whom 325 are officials. The staff of the CBC is scientifically trained and admittedly of a high level. This is due to the faithful implementation of an enviable meritocratic recruitment system that we have consolidated and are faithfully implementing. The independence of the system and the evaluation of recruitment on the basis of purely technocratic training should be preserved as the pupil of an eye. The reduction of staff is also in line with the general effort that must be made to the wider public service to limit its size. I repeat that our country is today facing unprecedented challenges. The negative vicious circle created by the negative interaction between public finances and banks must be broken. For the banks in particular, I am optimistic that, if the fine-tuned handling carried out over the last few months by the Ministry of Finance and the CBC continues in the right way, this challenge will be successfully addressed. With regard to the deeper problem of public finances and the necessary structural reforms, these need to be strengthened and intensified. I wish the Minister of Finance every success in his efforts, which are being carried out under adverse circumstances. I stress that what we have achieved in recent decades as a country is unfortunately in question. If we fail this time to make the right moves, then Cyprus will inevitably be led into adventures with very significant economic consequences for our future and the future of our children. In closing, I would like once again to thank the staff of the CBC, their cooperation was valuable to me. I also thank the social partners with whom, during my term of office, I have worked closely together. Finally, I would like to thank you, the press officers, regardless of whether I did not always agree with you. I believed and believe that your role is crucial for the functioning of a Democracy.

Title: Recent policy challenges through the lens of economic forecasts
text: Statement by Mrs Chrystalla Georghadji on taking over as Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus Nicosia, 10 April 2014 Today, I am assuming the duties of the Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus. The honour is great but the responsibility is even greater. I am fully conscious of the expectations for financial stability and overcoming the problems in the economy. I have served in various posts in the past and I have dealt with difficulties and challenges in a technocratic manner, always respecting the constitution, the laws and the citizens of the Republic of Cyprus. I shall work in the same way and I will do my best from the high office entrusted to me by the President of the Republic. In the same manner, I will work to meet the requirements of the Statute of the ESCB and the European Central Bank. I acknowledge, like everyone else, the extremely difficult economic conditions our country is experiencing. I share the sense of insecurity and distrust households and businesses feel on a daily basis. I am also aware that labour and capital are flowing out of Cyprus. The challenges we are facing are great. Cyprus, our country, needs all of our help. I undertake the responsibility to ensure that everything possible is done to counter the difficulties in a substantive and decisive manner. Any bitterness in the past must stay there. However, we should learn from the past and move forward. There is no other choice. Everyone expects and demands us to lead the way. I am fully aware of this. All the major issues regarding the financial sector will be examined in depth, and always in the context of the law pertaining to the functioning of the Central Bank of Cyprus and the Eurosystem. I feel assured and secure by the wealth of experience of the people working in the Central Bank, who as of today are my colleagues. I invite you to work together harmoniously and conscientiously in order to achieve our goals of restoring confidence in the Central Bank and the financial sector, and this will be achieved through the proper functioning of the Bank itself. My door will always be open to colleagues. We must communicate freely with honesty in a professional, impartial and selfless manner. In these difficult times, we need to enhance cohesion and solidarity between us, creating those conditions which will enable us to act promptly and effectively. Our primary strategic goal is to restore confidence in the banking system. This is inextricably linked to a number of other issues of high priority such as adequate liquidity in the economy, the management of non-performing loans and the strengthening of corporate governance in the banking sector. I consider the close working relationship with the Bankd5s board of directors to be of major importance and I warmly thank all of the board members for giving me their support ever since the announcement of my appointment. Our cooperation is unquestionable. I also wish to thank the outgoing Governor. Thank you dear Panicos Demetriades for your support during these last days, which assisted in the smooth transition. My dear colleagues, all of you are part of the Central Bank of Cyprus. Together we have the responsibility to make the difference. We owe it to our country.

Title: Drawing lessons from banking and financial history for the current crisis
text: Presentation of the Bank's Annual Report for the year 2013 Speech by the Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus, Mrs. Chrystallas Yiorkadji at the press conference for the presentation of the Bank's Annual Report for the year 2013 Nicosia, 25 June 2014 Distinguished guests, friends, representatives of the Mass Media, dear colleagues, It is with great pleasure and honor that I welcome you to today's press conference for the presentation of the Annual Report of the Central Bank of Cyprus for 2013, during which Mr. Panicos Dimitriadis was at the head of the Bank. Today, as the new Governor of the Bank, I will briefly present the activities of the previous year but, at the same time, I will refer to the present and the significant challenges we have to face in the future. 2013 was a year in which our country was faced with unprecedented situations, a year whose consequences we would all like to quickly overcome. Our banking system was shaken to the core, public confidence in it was eroded, we experienced the large decrease in incomes, the shrinking of small businesses, the significant increase in non-performing loans, as well as the increase in unemployment to unprecedented levels for Cyprus. Since March 2013, the Cypriot economy has been in an economic adjustment program within the framework of the Memorandum of Understanding concluded with the European Commission, the European Central Bank and the International Monetary Fund. On the basis of the adjustment programme, several measures have already been implemented concerning fiscal policy, the restructuring and consolidation of the banking system, as well as the structure of the Cypriot economy. So far, the course of implementation of the program is considered quite successful, with four consecutive evaluations being very positive and prescribing an auspicious course for the economy and the Cypriot banking system. At the same time, however, it should be stressed that the road is long, many challenges still exist and there is no room for complacency. Starting with macroeconomic developments in 2013, it is noted that the deterioration in real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) was lower than initially estimated by the Troika. Specifically, while initially a decrease in GDP of 8.7% was expected in real terms, the decrease was eventually limited to 5.4%. At the same time, a particularly positive development is the fact that the fiscal targets set for 2013 have not only been achieved, but have been exceeded, reflecting, among other things, the prudent implementation of the state budget. Inflation based on the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices decreased in 2013 to 0.4%, while unemployment reached an unprecedented level of 15.9% of the labour force. Of particular concern are the higher unemployment rates among young people under the age of 25, which recorded an increase of 40% in 2013 compared to 2012, as well as the share of the long-term unemployed, which reached 10.2% of the labour force in the fourth quarter of 2013. Turning now to the outlook for economic developments for 2014, I note that the decline in GDP in the first quarter amounted, on an annual basis, to 4.1%, as opposed to a 5% decrease recorded in the fourth quarter of 2013. Based on this development, the Troika's forecast made in the context of the fourth review, for an overall decline in GDP of 4.2% during 2014, seems to be rather pessimistic. Inflation based on the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices remains in negative territory in 2014, while prices are declining with a slowdown. More specifically, inflation hovered at -0.1% in May 2014, compared to -0.4% in April, and deflation risks for the year as a whole remain. Unemployment continues to be at an all-time high, but there are some signs of stabilisation. Specifically, in the first quarter of 2014 unemployment reached 16% of the labor force, compared to 16.2% in the fourth quarter of 2013. The fiscal balance in the first quarter of 2014 recorded a deficit of 0.2% of GDP, and remains within the fiscal targets of the adjustment programme. It is also noted that the 2014 budget aims at a faster implementation of part of the additional fiscal adjustment required in the years 2015-2018 in accordance with the Memorandum of Understanding. The aim is to achieve and maintain in the long term a primary surplus of 4% of GDP, so that public debt is driven on a steadily downward and sustainable path. As far as the financial sector is concerned, the progress achieved is significant and seems to have already begun to bear fruit. The Decisions of the Eurogroup of 25 March 2013 included a number of resolution measures that have been implemented by the Central Bank of Cyprus, in its capacity as Resolution Authority. Laiki Bank's activities and assets in Cyprus (with the exception of its investments in foreign subsidiaries), its insured deposits, as well as its liabilities from the provision of emergency liquidity, have been transferred to the Bank of Cyprus. The Bank of Cyprus, upon completion of the independent valuation of its balance sheet items, was recapitalized through the conversion of a significant part of the unsecured deposits into shares and the essentially full contribution of shareholders and securities holders. The report of the Independent Commission on the Banking System, appointed by the Central Bank, analyses in sufficient detail the reasons that led to the banking crisis. The Central Bank of Cyprus has already taken drastic measures to address the causes that led to the crisis and restore the viability of the banking system. Following the recapitalisation of the Bank of Cyprus and despite the unfavourable economic conditions that prevailed, the Hellenic Bank Group has succeeded in strengthening its capital base by raising private capital, while the Cooperative Central Bank has been recapitalised by the state, through financial support received under the adjustment programme. In addition, a number of important steps have been taken to strengthen the supervisory and regulatory framework in order to lay the foundations for a healthy and stable banking sector in both the medium and long term. For example, I would like to mention the Directive of the Central Bank on the capital requirements of banks, the amendments to the Business of Credit Institutions Law concerning the President and the members of the Boards of Directors and the restrictions on the credit facilities of the directors and independent consultants of the banks, as well as the Directive of the Central Bank in relation to the procedures for the evaluation of customers for the granting of new credit facilities. In addition, I note that the restrictive measures taken in March 2013, regarding the movement of capital to protect the liquidity of banks and safeguard financial stability, have already been abolished in relation to the movement of capital within the Republic of Cyprus. The removal of the remaining restrictions on transfers of capital abroad is expected to be achieved by restoring confidence in the banking sector, as provided for in the relevant roadmap agreed in the adjustment programme. At euro area level, I could not fail to mention developments concerning the role of the European Central Bank in the prudential supervision of credit institutions. The decision to establish the Single Supervisory Mechanism is a milestone in european Union banking supervision. The implementation of the new supervisory framework is already underway with the Assumption by the European Central Bank, as of 4 November 2014, of direct supervision of banks considered significant, as well as indirect supervision of other banks. In the case of Cyprus, significant banks, based on the criteria set, are the Bank of Cyprus, the Cooperative Central Bank, Hellenic Bank and RCB. The establishment of the Single Supervisory Mechanism aims to supervise banks in a coordinated manner, while ensuring equal treatment for all banks. This should strengthen the confidence of depositors - and the public at large - in the banking sector. A Supervisory Board has been established for the operation of the Single Supervisory Mechanism, bringing together representatives of the competent supervisory authorities, as well as representatives of the central banks of each member country. The European Central Bank will take over the supervision of significant banks, after which they will be thoroughly assessed, to ensure that they are adequately capitalised. This assessment is known as the Comprehensive Assessment and includes: First, a valuation of the balance sheet value of each significant bank with a reference date of 31 December 2013, with a view to identifying distressed assets. This process is called Asset Quality Review (AQR). It is essentially an X-ray on banks' balance sheets as at 31 December 2013 and the main objective is to determine whether, on that date, banks' provisions for riskiness were sufficient. Second, the Comprehensive Assessment includes the Stress Test. They are the well-known stress tests and which will be carried out on the basis of two scenarios. The first is the baseline and the second is the adverse scenario with a reference date again of 31 December 2013. This is an exercise that will assess banks' capital adequacy for the next three years, i.e. for the period 2014 to 2016 inclusive, initially on the basis of defined macroeconomic conditions (baseline) and second, on the assumption of a severe deterioration of these macroeconomic conditions (adverse scenario). At the end of the three-year period, banks should have a minimum baseline capital ratio (CET1) in the baseline of 8% and in the adverse scenario of 5.5%. Any additional capital needs arising from this Comprehensive Assessment exercise should be covered in the baseline scenario within six months of the announcement of the results and in the adverse scenario within nine months. As far as the Stress Test is concerned, the exercise is conducted in cooperation with the European Banking Authority. The results of the Bank Asset Quality Review and the Stress Test are expected to be announced around the end of October 2014. Next, I will refer to the significant challenges presented to the euro area economy that led to the very recent decision of the Governing Council of the European Central Bank to take a series of measures to further easing the Eurosystem's single monetary policy. Despite signs that the euro area economy is undergoing a gradual recovery, economic activity remains subdued, unemployment is at particularly high levels, and the number of increases in credit to the private sector continues to be negative. Moreover, the required deleveraging of the public and private sectors is expected to continue to have a negative impact on economic growth. The European Central Bank's decision is aimed primarily at supporting and recovering the economy, and, moreover, at addressing the risk of deflation by gradually restoring inflation rates to levels very close to, but below, 2%, as the European Central Bank's target. In particular, the Governing Council of the European Central Bank decided on 5 June 2014 on the following five main measures: 1. The key interest rates of the European Central Bank, since 11 June 2014, have stood at historically low levels. The interest rate for main refinancing operations was set at 0.15%, while the deposit facility rate was set negative at d0 0.10%. For the first time since the introduction of the euro in 1999, the deposit facility rate has become negative, that is, a negative interest rate will be levied on deposits held by financial institutions with the National Central Banks and, among other things, on reserves held in excess of the mandatory reserves. It is noted that the negative interest rate does not directly affect the deposits of bank customers. In addition, a negative interest rate will also be imposed on deposits, in addition to an amount, maintained by the Government with the Central Bank. 2. Carrying out a series of targeted longer-term refinancing operations (known as TLTROs) with a maturity until September 2018, with a view to strengthening bank lending to the euro area's non-financial private sector. This measure will enable banks to provide as additional loans, at a low interest rate, a percentage (7%) of all their loan portfolios. The initially potential amount of loans from these operations is estimated at euro area level at around EUR 400 billion. euro. The use of this measure is up to each financial institution, on the basis of its own data and depending, of course, on the demand for loans from the private sector, to finance new sustainable projects and activities. 3. The intensification of the preparatory work for the conduct of final purchases of Asset-Backed Securities (ABS) relating to loans to the private sector, with the aim of facilitating new credit flows to the economy. Such a programme should help both the secondary market and the primary market in the euro area. The presence of the Eurosystem as a new large investor in the market is expected to act as an incentive to boost bank lending to specific sectors of the economy, as banks will be able to securitise these loans and then raise liquidity from the Eurosystem by collateralising these securities. 4. The continuation of refinancing operations as fixed rate tender procedures with full allotment for as long as necessary and at least until December 2016. This means that banks ensure that there is a stable and cheap source of funding for at least the next two and a half years, which is expected to have a positive impact on the funding plan of credit institutions. Credit institutions will be able to borrow from the Eurosystem any amount they wish at the applicable interest rate for main refinancing operations. This interest rate currently stands at 0.15%. 5. The suspension of the absorption of liquidity provided under the Securities Markets Programme (SMP), given that the risk currently facing the euro area is deflationary and not inflation. This measure brings about an increase in excess liquidity by EUR 163 billion. it is therefore expected to be an additional incentive for the affected banks to find alternative ways of making use of this amount. Dear friends, I would now like to briefly turn to the audited financial results of the Central Bank of Cyprus for 2013, which are part of the Annual Report. As a consequence of the global financial crisis and the expansionary monetary policy pursued by the Eurosystem, the balance sheet of the Central Bank of Cyprus, like that of the other National Central Banks of the euro area, appears to be generally inflated compared to the years before the crisis. Typically, at 31 December 2013, total assets amounted to EUR 14.3 billion. euro approximately. The Bank's profit and loss account shows a net surplus of ECU 226.7 million. in 2013, compared to a net surplus of EUR 111.6 million. in 2012. The big difference between the two years is due to the fact that in 2012, an amount of 185.0 million euros. the euro was transferred to the provisions account for risks stemming, in the main, from the provision of emergency liquidity assistance. As provided by the Central Bank of Cyprus Laws, 80% of the Net Profit of the Bank is transferred to the Fixed Fund of the Republic. On the basis of this legal provision, an amount of EUR 181.4 million was paid out. Euro has been paid to the Fixed Fund for 2013. Dear friends, In conclusion, I would like to stress that the return of the economy to a recovery path, as well as the restoration of the credibility of the banking sector, leave no room for complacency. On the contrary, they impose the continuation of the effort with the same intensity and prudence until the consequences of the crisis are completely overturned. Already the international markets are sending the first positive signals in this direction. I am sure that we can achieve our goals and our aspirations. Thank you.

Title: Reflections on inflation targeting
text: Results of the comprehensive assessment of Cyprus banks Statement by Chrystalla Georghadji, Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus, made to journalists at the Central Bank of Cyprus 26 October 2014 Dear journalists and colleagues, Welcome to the press briefing on the results of the stress tests performed on the four systemic Cypriot banks from among 130 banks in the euro area. The four banks in question are Bank of Cyprus, Cooperative Central Bank, Hellenic Bank and RCB. First of all, I wish to thank everyone who worked on this long, arduous and very successful mission for their dedication, professionalism, diligence and great sense of responsibility. Today is a very important day for our country and, in particular, for our banking system. It is a new beginning with great expectations for the future. On 4 November 2014, an ambitious European project will be implemented: the Single Supervisory Mechanism (SSM) which, initially, will have the 130 most significant banks of the euro area under its direct control and will also be indirectly controlling another 6,000 banks. Prior to launching the SSM, the ECB had decided to carry out a comprehensive assessment, in collaboration with the national supervisory authorities, of the balance sheets and solvency of banks to ensure that the banks to be placed under direct ECB supervision are healthy, with adequate capital and able to withstand extremely adverse macroeconomic developments. The comprehensive assessment consisted of two main phases: 1) an asset quality review (AQR); and 2) the stress test exercise. The comprehensive assessment, which was part of the preparation by significant banks for their direct supervision by the ECB from 4 November 2014 onwards, had the following objectives: -enhance transparency by improving the quality of information available on the financial condition of each bank; -strengthen the banksd5 balance sheets by applying corrective measures to any problems identified by the comprehensive assessment; -boost confidence by assuring that, after taking the necessary corrective measures, the banks will be healthy and reliable. Phase 1: Asset Quality Review (AQR) Bank of Cyprus, Cooperative Central Bank and Hellenic Bank were included in this phase. The primary goal of the first phase was to assess the value of loan portfolios and their guarantees as well as the corresponding provisions, i.e. the losses resulting from the sum of the loan portfolio as at 31 December 2013, while also setting the starting point for the stress test. The exercise was carried out on the basis of a common methodology and common definitions. Its extent was unprecedented, leading to an extensive check of the financial health of the banks to be directly supervised by the ECB. Upon completion of the asset quality review, the banks had to maintain a Common Equity Tier 1 ratio of at least 8%. Out of 130 banks, 25 banks showed a deficit in the adverse scenario. Twelve of those have already covered their deficits by increasing their capital by db15 billion between January and September 2014. The results show that the capital reserves of Cyprus banks, including their capitalisations already made or announced in 2014, are more than enough to cover the capital shortfalls identified by the stress test exercise. Phase 2: Stress test exercise In addition to the three aforementioned banks, RCB also participated in this exercise. The main objective of the stress test phase was designed to simulate the capital of banks based on two three-year macroeconomic scenarios: the baseline scenario and the adverse scenario. Under the baseline scenario, the banks should maintain, over the three-year period, a minimum capital ratio (Common Equity Tier 1) equal to 8%, while in the adverse scenario it is 5.5%. This exercise was conducted in close co-operation with the European Banking Authority (EBA). The aim of the baseline scenario was to assess whether the existing capital reserves of banks are sufficient over a three-year horizon consistent with current macroeconomic forecasts. The results of the baseline scenario, calculated after taking into account the recapitalisations already made or announced in 2014, show that no Cyprus bank needs additional capital. Finally, the adverse scenario was designed to examine the strength of the Cyprus banking sector when subject to extreme macroeconomic conditions for three years. Even under these adverse macroeconomic conditions, and after taking into account the capitalisations already made or announced in 2014, the banking sector of Cyprus appears largely adequately capitalised. Measures designed to cover the small capital shortfalls indentified for Hellenic Bank have already been taken or are planned. It should be noted that the stress tests were not conducted to accurately predict future economic indicators, but rather to establish the strength of banks based on very conservative projections. Summarised results: In summary, the results of the comprehensive assessment, after taking into account recapitalisations already made in 2014, are as follows: Bank of Cyprus, Cooperative Central Bank and RCB showed capital adequacy ratios in excess of the minimum requirements in all three scenarios, i.e. the asset quality review (8%), the baseline scenario of the stress test (8%) and the adverse scenario of the stress test (5.5%). Specifically, Bank of Cyprus has a capital adequacy ratio of 11.5%, 11.6% and 5.8% respectively; Cooperative Central Bank has 13.6%, 14.1% and 9.3% respectively; and RCB has 16.7%, 15.7% and 11.6% respectively. Under the adverse scenario, Hellenic Bankd5s capital adequacy stands at 1.7% with a small capital requirement of db176 million, following the 2014 capital raising measures. It should be noted that part of this requirement (approximately db71 million) has been covered by the actions already taken. This amount consists of the following mitigating factors: conversion of further convertible capital securities (CCS1) into shares following todayd5s announcement of the bankd5s nine-month results (db23 million); acceptable allowance from the remaining convertible capital securities in issue (db46 million); and approximately db2 million revenue from the sale of its subsidiary bank in Russia. The remaining balance of db105 million is expected to be more than covered by the conversion of convertible capital securities and rights issue. Any banks showing net capital shortfalls following the comprehensive assessment have two weeks within which to submit plans on how such shortfalls will be covered. As announced previously, the Board of Directors of Hellenic Bank will carry out an increase of share capital, after taking the results of the comprehensive assessment into account. There are no additional needs for the other credit institutions after taking into account the capitalisations made in 2014. The results are particularly encouraging for the Cyprus economy because they demonstrate that the actions taken in 2014, as well as all the efforts and actions aimed at boosting the banking sector, have been more than satisfactory. The Central Bank had previously encouraged banks to strengthen their capital base and has now been vindicated for this foresight. There had been certain negative reactions and disputes at the time, but we persisted. Optimism about the future has now been restored. The results of this exercise should help boost the confidence of depositors in Cyprus banks which will in turn contribute to the efforts for economic growth. This increased confidence should also set the right conditions for lifting the remaining restrictive measures on the movement of capital overseas. It is highly important that the db1 billion available in the support programme of the Cyprus economy from international lenders, which was intended to cover the capital shortfalls of the Cyprus banking system, will not be used and will remain available as a buffer. Therefore, the national debt will be db1 billion lower than anticipated in the Memorandum of Understanding. Extensive details on the results of the exercise for each bank and additional information on the banksd5 balance sheets, have been published on the ECB website. Please note that this exercise has been carried out based on the ECB methodology for the AQR and on the EBA methodology for the stress tests. Thorough checks were performed by ECB representatives at every stage of the exercise to ensure the validity of the calculations. The complete report, with the results for all banks participating in the exercise and detailed results for each bank, are available on the ECB and EBA websites. Thank you for being here today and thank you, once again, to my colleagues who will now answer any technical questions.

Title: Dealing with crises in a globalized world: challenges and solutions
text: Restoring Confidence in Cyprus. The Outlook for the Cypriot Banking System Keynote speech by Mrs Chrystalla Georghadji, Governor of Central Bank of Cyprus, at the 10th Economist Cyprus Summit Nicosia, 4 November 2014 Introduction Honourable President, Ladies and Gentlemen, good morning. .t is my pleasure to address before such a distinguished audience the summit organised by The Economist here in Cyprus. I would like to thank the organisers for their kind invitation and for giving me the opportunity to share our experiences of what has been a challenging and unprecedented period for our banking system, but also to reaffirm our determination to fully restore confidence and financial stability. Todayd5s conference happily coincides with the launching of the Single Supervisory Mechanism (SSM): A European organ aiming (i) to ensure the safety and soundness of the European banking system and (ii) to increase financial integration and stability in Europe. The SSM is undoubtedly one of the most important steps in strengthening the Economic and Monetary Union. Indeed, it is the first established part of the EU banking union and it is to function in conjunction to the Single Resolution Mechanism. In the SSM the ultimate responsibility for specific supervisory tasks related to the financial stability of all euro area banks will henceforth lie with the European Central Bank, but national supervisors will continue to play an important role in day-to-day supervision and in preparing and implementing ECB decisions. The Central Bank of Cyprus as the national supervisor in Cyprus is well-prepared to take on this role. Developments in 2013 and 2014 It is known, during 2013 our banking sector faced its most challenging period to date. As a result of a sequence of events, including a sustained period in previous years of overexpansion in the real estate market and a very risky strategy of investing in high-yielding Greek government bonds, several Cypriot banks were left with significant imbalances. In the past 20 months, a series of corrective measures have been put into place to ensure that after the severe shocks and restructuring of the banking sector in March 2013, the foundations have been laid for the sector to be rebuilt on sound principles. In the spring of 2013, Cyprus embarked on an economic adjustment programme aimed at: (i) restoring the health of the financial sector; (ii) continuing the on-going process of fiscal consolidation; and (iii) implementing appropriate structural reforms in order to support competitiveness and return the island to a path of sustainable and balanced growth. In the banking sector, an assessment was made of the immediate priorities and shortcomings, and as a result a number of goals and milestones were set. Significant progress has been made. This includes recapitalising and restructuring the systemic credit institutions as well as strengthening the banking regulatory and supervisory regime. The largest credit institutions are proceeding with the implementation of their restructuring plans, while corporate governance practices have improved and will continue doing so. A significant milestone was achieved recently when Cyprusd5s four major banks participated in the EU-wide comprehensive assessment conducted jointly by the European Banking Authority and the European Central Bank in the context of the preparation for todayd5s launch of the SSM. One hundred and thirty banks across Europe were subjected to stress tests which were conducted at the end of an asset quality review (AQR). The AQR thoroughly reviewed and assessed the banksd5 balance sheets to establish weaknesses and existing capital deficiencies. The stress tests that followed the AQR were intended to establish whether, using a baseline and an adverse scenario, additional capital needs would arise over a three year horizon. The methodology of the stress tests applied to the four banks incorporated in Cyprus was the same as that used for all the other 126 banks throughout the Eurozone, including large banks in Italy, France and Germany. Our banks, together with staff at the Central Bank of Cyprus, worked relentlessly from the start of this year on the stress tests and the results were released last week. The starting reference date to which the series of stress scenarios were applied was 31 December 2013. This was at the end of the most turbulent period in Cyprusd5s banking history. Thus the stress tests were an additional challenge for our banks, at a very difficult time. The Bank of Cyprus, which recently underwent a db1 billion capital increase, successfully passed the tests and will not require any additional capital. With new strategic and respectable investors the bank will soon have a new Board of Directors and is proceeding with the implementation of its restructuring plans. Hellenic Bank, which did not receive any programme money and was recapitalised privately, enjoys the support of its three major shareholders. The results of the comprehensive assessment exercise have shown that the bank, under the adverse scenario, will require additional capital of db105 million. Prior to the comprehensive assessment, Hellenicd5s new shareholders had already announced that they would inject further capital to cover any expected shortfalls, to ensure that the bank can proceed smoothly with the implementation of its business plans. RCB Bank, formerly the Russian Commercial Bank of Cyprus, remains and is expected to remain well above the required thresholds. Nevertheless it is also further enhancing its shareholding with the participation of a new strategic investor, which is expected to lead to further opportunities for the bank. Finally, the Cooperative Central Bank, which was fully recapitalised with db1.5 billion from the Cyprus programme, also successfully passed the stress tests and will not require any of the additional db1 billion buffer available in the programme. The cooperative movement has undergone major reforms in the past 12 months and is expected to continue its key role of serving various communities on the island. The banking sector has certainly had its challenges, and criticisms and mistakes have been made. It is pleasing, however, to see the sector come out of this difficult juncture in a strong and healthier condition. Through the series of actions that have been taken since March 2013, the banks have been restructured and recapitalised. They are refocusing on their core banking activities with a prudent risk-based approach to lending and investing. With the successful completion of the comprehensive assessment exercise, a major burden has been lifted off the banking sector's shoulders that will allow it to concentrate on day to day operations as well as strengthen its capital base. The future of the sector looks promising and bright, and is well placed to play a leading role in Cyprus' full economic recovery. Healthy and well capitalised banks will be in a good position to provide lending to SMEs, the backbone of our economy. A further highlight is the level of foreign investment that has been drawn to our banking sector. Foreign investors helped Hellenic Bank to recapitalise thus allowing the bank to avoid the need for state support. More recently, other foreign reputable investors have recapitalised the Bank of Cyprus to the tune of db1 billion. These capital injections constitute some of the largest foreign investments seen in the history of our economy. This is a strong indication and a firm confirmation of the confidence the international community is showing in our banking sector, and a recognition that the sacrifices and recent restructuring work are beginning to bear fruit. What is now required is for domestic stakeholders to also demonstrate the same belief and commitment thus creating a ripple effect throughout the economy. With the above in mind, it is important that a solution to the foreclosure bill can be found as soon as possible so that the considerable work completed under the programme with our international lenders is not derailed. It is my firm belief that, it is not the intention of Cypriot banks to target vulnerable families, young couples and households whose circumstances have changed due to the crisis. The enactment of the foreclosure bill is, however, a necessary tool so that those who are able but unwilling to repay their debts, face the consequences should they continue to strategically default on their obligations. Every household and business, small or large, has a role to play in our economyd5s recovery. I want to take this opportunity to call on large corporate businesses to use some of the surplus funds generated in the recent boom years, to meet their repayments and cooperate with their lenders in restructuring their debts. This will allow the banks to free up capital for further lending in the economy, something that will undoubtedly be to the benefit of all. The Central Bankd5s focus will now turn to ensuring that the restructuring of loans is achieved in a viable and reasonable manner, and to reducing interest rates for the benefit of households and businesses. Concluding remarks While recent developments have demonstrated that our banks are slowly returning to a sound and strong position, important work still lies ahead. It is important that our banks continue to take positive steps and not engage in unnecessary risky activities or return to the old lending practices. The results for the four Cypriot incorporated banks which participated in the EU-wide comprehensive assessmnent, demonstrate that a turning point has been successfully achieved and the outlook for the Cypriot banking system is again very positive. The evolution of the banking union with the adoption, as of today, of the SSM, the development of the regulatory and reporting frameworks as well as the increasing scrutiny of the banksd5 capital ratios, puts the onus on banks to continue improving in all areas. Following an intensive period of structural reforms, we in Cyprus have embarked on a committed path towards financial stability and economic recovery. With a strong infrastructure, expertise in financial services, a strong legal and regulatory framework as well as a strategic geographical position, EU membership and a wide network of double tax treaties, Cyprus is and will continue to be an attractive financial centre. The Central Bank remains fully committed to the implementation of the programme agreed with our international partners and in re-establishing a thriving banking sector within a prudent and modernised governance framework. In closing, I would like to reiterate the Central Bankd5s and my personal commitment that we will continue to work to complete the mission of fully stabilising the banking sector and the economy, and to emerge even stronger from the recent crisis. Thank you.

Title: Central bank exit policies
text: Statement by Mrs Chrystalla Georghadji, Governor of the CBC, at the meeting of the Parliamentary Committee on Financial and Budgetary Affairs Projections of the Central Bank of Cyprus (CBC) within the framework of the discussion of the state budget for 2015 Nicosia, 1 December 2014 It is with appreciation, respect and a sense of responsibility that I have come to the Parliamentary Committee on Financial and Budgetary Affairs, after your kind invitation to present my views as Governor of the Central Bank during the debate of the state budget for the year 2015. I am optimistic that 2015 will be the starting point for the return of our economy to growth. This optimism is based on our experience so that the progress towards the end of the crisis has been proceeding at a faster pace and the results are more positive than initially forecasted. The maturity shown by the Cypriot people during these difficult times has certainly helped in the path to recovery. During 2013, the banking sector in our country faced the most critical period in its history. Cypriot banks faced major liquidity problems and balance sheet imbalances with negative consequences. Since then, the problems have been dealt decisively with a series of corrective measures which have repositioned the banking system on a sound footing. Systemic banks have strengthened their capital adequacy, while the banking regulatory and supervisory framework has been significantly strengthened. Larger banks have proceeded with the implementation of their restructuring plans, the implementation of corporate governance has improved and changes continue. The four major banks in Cyprus participated in the pan-European comprehensive assessment conducted jointly by the European Banking Authority (EBA) and the European Central Bank (ECB). The successful results of the exercise now allow the banking sector to focus on its normal functions and play a leading role in the process of Cyprusd5s economic recovery. The healthy and well-capitalised banks will now be able to grant viable loans to households and small businesses that are the backbone of our economy. Furthermore, the CBC will now be able to focus and address the issue of the restructuring of loans, which must be dealt with in a rational, fair and sustainable manner. This is expected to reduce non.performing loans and have positive effects on interest rates and the general economic climate for the benefit of households and businesses. In relation to economic growth, I would like to note with satisfaction the positive developments since the conclusion of the Memorandum of Understanding. The initial forecasts of our lenders for a significant recession in 2013, amounting to 8,7% did not materialise, with the outturn contained at 5,4%. During the fifth assessment of the economic programme, which took place in July 2014, the Troika adopted a very conservative baseline scenario for 2014. Both the IMF and the European Commission have recently revised this with a more positive outlook. More specifically, while the forecasts of the fifth assessment in July 2014 indicated a decline of around 4,2% for 2014, the most recent revised forecasts of the IMF and the European Commission expect a contraction of real GDP by 3,2% and 2,8%, respectively. Based on the latest available data, the CBC considers the European Commission's forecast to be more realistic. The forecasts of the Troika from the fifth assessment are incorporated in the state budget for 2015. Therefore, this budget is necessarily conservative, which would allow, in my opinion, the fastest achievement -and with positive deviations d0 of the fiscal objectives. This is also required to fully restore confidence, eliminate uncertainty, and achieve the return of economic activity to positive and sustainable levels. Thus, there needs to be continued adherence to the budgetary targets and strict implementation of the measures included in the budget for 2015. In terms of economic activity in 2015, this is in line with the expected slight recovery in domestic demand. The revised forecasts of both the IMF and the European Commission as well as of the Ministry of Finance, indicate a marginal increase in GDP of around 0,5% in real terms. We are in agreement with these estimates. In relation to the fiscal balance, the forecasts of our international lenders in the evaluation of the stimulus programme broadly followed the relatively more pessimistic forecasts for economic growth. The budget deficit as a percentage of GDP in the Memorandum of Understanding agreed in April 2013, placed this forecast at 8,3% of GDP for 2013. However, the outturn was 5,4% of GDP, i.e. about three percentage points lower than initially projected. In part, the positive divergence resulted from the relatively smaller than expected recession. Mostly, though, it came from reductions on the expenditure side, resulting from the effective implementation of the state budget. Our international lenders initially projected the budget deficit for 2014 to be 4,7% of GDP.
