However, this forecast is already outdated, as evidenced by the more updated forecasts of the IMF and the European Commission, which refer to a deficit of 4,4% and 3%, respectively. These revisions also make the fiscal forecasts for 2015 relatively more favourable, provided of course that the consistent and prudent implementation of the state budget continues. This certainly does not mean that the countryd5s vulnerable groups will be ignored. On the contrary, the further tidying up of public finances will allow essential support to needy citizens to continue in the medium and long term. Finally, I would like to refer briefly to the public debt and note that according to the recent announcement of the results of the overall evaluation of the Cypriot banks, it appears that the db1 billion included in the Troikad5s financial support programme, which was intended to cover the capital needs of the Cypriot banking system, will not be used for this purpose. Therefore, it is possible at a later stage for the Republic of Cyprus either not to borrow this amount or to use it in order to refinance the existing debt which bears a higher interest rate. There is also an important improvement in the level of public debt expected to result from the savings achieved by the better than expected fiscal results. The developments in the banking system, the fiscal sector and the economy in general constitute a positive outlook. This is recognised by the international credit rating agencies which have recently upgraded the sovereign ratings. These upgrades reflect the gradual but steady regaining of the credibility of the Cyprus financial sector and economy in general in the markets. However, by itself, this is not enough and does not constitute a final goal nor a reason for complacency. Instead, vigilance is needed since the ultimate goal is the complete restoration of confidence in the economy, ensuring sound macroeconomic conditions and sustainable development in conditions of full employment. In conclusion, I would like to reiterate the commitment of both the CBC and myself to the full consolidation of the banking system and our economy. Some battles were won but this does not in any way mean that there is room for complacency. The consolidation effort of all sectors of our economy needs to continue unabated so that our country can finally be able to leave behind the recent crisis and enter resolutely on a path of sustainable growth and full employment. The adoption and proper planning and implementation of the budget for 2015 will be an important step in this direction.

Title: Preventing deflation: the role of policy research
text: Governor's speech at the 2015 Cyprus Investors Summit organized by the Cyprus Investment Promotion Agency (CIPA) The Cypriot Banking Sector and a Promising Outlook for the Future Speech by Mrs Chrystalla Georghadji, Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus, at the 2015 Cyprus Investors Summit organized by the Cyprus Investment Promotion Agency (CIPA) Limassol, 10 February 2015 Introduction Ladies and gentlemen, It is my pleasure to address this summit before such a prominent audience. I would like to thank the Cyprus Investment Promotion Agency for their kind invitation, and for giving me the opportunity to share with you our renewed belief that Cyprus will slowly but steadily emerge stronger from the recent downturn. The Central Bank of Cyprus as well as domestic and international banks operating on the island, have expressed their commitment and determination to enhance the leading role our banking system plays in our economy. Without doubt, a solid banking sector is imperative in supporting Cyprus as a financial centre. A series of reforms have taken place following the unprecedented and challenging events our banking system and the wider economy faced during 2013. Important steps towards fully restoring confidence and stability have been taken, in cooperation with our European partners (the ECB, the IMF, and the European Commission). In November last year, a historic new journey commenced for all banks across Europe with the launch of the Single Supervisory Mechanism, known by its acronym SSM. It is a key mechanism under the European Central Bank and one of the most important steps towards a strengthened Economic and Monetary Union, aiming at ensuring safety and soundness in the European banking sector. As regards Cyprus, the four most significant banks (Bank of Cyprus, Cooperative Central Bank, Hellenic Bank and Russian Commericial Bank) are now directly supervised by the European Central Bank. In addition, less significant institutions which include smaller banks registered in Cyprus are indirectly supervised by the SSM. A new era has thus begun for both Cyprus and Europe in terms of bank supervision. Recent macroeconomic developments Before I proceed with a more detailed analysis of the developments in the banking sector, let me briefly say a few words about the progress achieved so far on the macroeconomic front. A brief overview will help set the context in which our banks are operating as well as their prospects. Initially, it should be noted that developments in the real economy have been generally better than predicted by Cyprusd5 international lenders. This indicates that the Cypriot economy and society in general, have exhibited considerable flexibility and endurance, keeping the country resilient even after the recent dramatic developments. In particular, while Troika in its fifth assessment of the Cyprus economic adjustment programme last July, predicted a real GDP decline of approximately 4.2% for 2014, the most recent revised forecasts by the IMF and the European Commission project a real GDP decline of 3.2% and 2.8%, respectively. Even better, according to the latest available data, the Central Bank of Cyprus expects a decline of around 2.5%. For 2015 the economy is expected to do better and rebound with a marginal positive growth. Secondly, the developments regarding public finances were significantly better than expected compared to past estimates by our international lenders. In its fifth assessment Troika forecasts a budget deficit of 4.7% of GDP for 2014. However, most recent estimates suggest that the budget deficit will be substantially smaller. This revision enables a relatively more optimistic fiscal outlook for 2015, provided of course that the consistent and prudent implementation of the state budget continues. Developments in the banking sector During 2013, our banking sector experienced its most challenging period to date. Several Cypriot banks were faced with an urgent need to reconsider their strategies and steps had to be taken within the context of the Memorandum of Understanding with the Troika, to refocus and restructure the sector. Unfortunately, for many years, the banking sector in Cyprus adopted poor risk and credit management practices. The sector was dominated by asset based lending and a strong focus on the real estate market, leading to an overexpansion of the banksd5 balance sheets. Although the consequences of such practices may initially be disguised and even appears successful during a growing and booming economy, eventually such recipes lead to serious imbalances. The aftermath is a high number of non-performing loans as part of the ripple effects of the global financial crisis. With falling demand, the economy in recession and prices of real estate and other assets decreasing, banks have had to reconsider their strategies. In the past two years, a series of corrective measures and reforms have taken place, aimed at strengthening the foundations of the sector following the loss in confidence and the severe shocks experienced after March 2013. Cyprus embarked on an economic adjustment programme with the Troika. In the banking sector, an assessment was made of the immediate priorities with the aim of restoring the health of our banks and the wider financial system. As already mentioned, a milestone in the restoration of confidence has recently been achieved with the successful completion of the EU-wide comprehensive assessment exercise, conducted jointly by the European Banking Authority and the European Central Bank. This was aimed at rigorously examining the balance sheets and solvency of Europed5s 130 systemic banks prior to the SSMd5s launch, which placed them under the ECBd5s direct supervision. The exercise applied the same methodology to all 130 banks tested, including the four significant banks incorporated in Cyprus. It is important to note that the starting reference date to which the series of stress scenarios were applied was 31st December 2013. This was at the end of the most turbulent year in the history of Cyprus banking, effectively presenting our banks with the additional challenge of conducting the stress test at the very bottom of our economic cycle. Despite this additional challenge and the fact that the tests applied to the four Cypriot banks were the same as those applied to the major banks of Europe, our banks delivered successful and encouraging results. It is important for the wider economy and public finances that the db1 billion buffer provided within the db10 billion Troika programme will not be needed to cover any capital shortfalls in the banking system. The improving capital position of the banks, provides the opportunity to either reduce the lending required from the programme and the national debt by db1 billion, or consider whether this may be allocated to other areas. A further positive development is the high level of foreign investment injected across our banking sector by renowned international investors and institutions. In the past 18 months, experienced foreign investors have participated with significant funds and have taken substantial positions in several banks incorporated in Cyprus. These capital injections constitute some of the largest foreign investments seen in the history of our economy. This provides encouragement and affirm indication that the confidence of the international community is returning to the Cyprus banking sector. It is pleasing to see that the recent restructuring work and reforms made in the sector and the wider economy are already delivering promising results, and the sector is coming out of this difficult juncture in a strong and healthier condition. The banks have been restructured and recapitalised and are refocusing their operations with a prudent risk-based approach to lending and investing, devoting their capital and liquidity to servicing local and international businesses wishing to invest in Cyprus. Concluding remarks Restructuring and cleaning up a bankd5s balance sheet is not easy, and market conditions remain challenging. However, this also provides opportunities. We remain fully committed to the implementation of the programme agreed with the international lenders and in re-establishing a thriving banking sector that can effectively meet the needs of businesses and households. For us this is the only way that will eventually enable the island to once again have access to adequate borrowing from the markets and return to sustained growth and prosperity. Overall, the developments so far in the banking sector, the ongoing fiscal consolidation process and the better management of the economy as a whole are creating the conditions for the islandd5s exit from the crisis. With sound infrastructure, expertise in financial services, a strong legal and regulatory framework and a wide network of double tax treaties, Cyprus is setting the stage for a sustainable recovery. This includes regaining its role as an attractive financial centre but in a more prudent and robust way. I remain positive that the Cyprus economy will come out stronger from the current crisis. Cyprus is a European Union member state; it has a strategic location between three continents, well performing industries such as tourism and shipping and is expecting further investment in the energy sector. Moreover, it maintains a strong financial services infrastructure, experience and know-how. A stronger banking sector will provide opportunities for businesses to flourish. Our banks are well capitalised and are in a strong position to provide support and to continue servicing their clients. Thank you.

Title: Supervision of the financial sector: concerns and conclusions from the crisis
text: Speech by the Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus, Mrs Chrystalla Yiorkadji, at the meeting of the House Standing Committee on Financial and Budgetary Affairs The estimates of the Central Bank of Cyprus in the context of the discussion of the state budget for 2016 Nicosia, 30 November 2015 The presence before the House Standing Committee on Financial and Budgetary Affairs for the submission of my views as Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus on the occasion of the discussion of the State Budget for the year 2016, is an exceptional honor and a top event for the Central Bank, which is given the opportunity to formulate its assessments in the process of examination and analysis of the Budget by your Committee. The optimism and forecasts that I set out last year for the course of the economy in 2015, seem to be verified, without, however, underestimating the difficulties that remain to be addressed. We are all entitled, citizens, the House of Representatives, the Government and the Central Bank, to be proud of the spirit of understanding and prudence that has been shown, without of course being complacent, because we still have a long way to go. The unprecedented and prolonged period of recession, which lasted from mid-2011 to the end of 2014, is over. The Cypriot economy is now on the path of recovery, while the prospects have so far proved to be more positive than the forecasts of the international lenders of our country. I am not, of course, unaware of the fact that significant problems persist, such as the historically high unemployment rate (14.1% at the end of September 2015, based on Eurostat data) and the amount of non-performing loans in the banking sector (around 47% or EUR 27.3 billion at the end of September 2015). However, I believe, as I will explain, that the foundations for a sustainable treatment of both these problems have now been established, with the first positive signs underlining the need for an unhindered continuation of the right course that has been mapped out. The above is reflected in the positive growth rate of GDP in the first three quarters of 2015 (growth of 1.2% was recorded compared to the corresponding nine months of the previous year), in contrast to the negative rates that were continuously recorded since the second quarter of 2011. This positive course is also reflected in many other sub-indicators, such as the Economic Climate Index, which, with the exception of some brief periods of influence by the uncertainty caused by the Greek crisis, shows a significant improvement. At the same time, macroeconomic and especially fiscal imbalances seem to have been addressed, forming a supportive framework to boost growth in the near future. At the same time, the banking sector, after a series of corrective measures that included improvements in the regulatory and supervisory framework, is now standing on a more stable and sound basis and is optimistic about the major challenges. The aforementioned positive developments also had a significant impact both on the gradual upgrades of the debt of the Republic of Cyprus by the international rating agencies and on the exit of the state to borrow from the international markets. The latest ratings of Fitch (B) and Moody's (B1), as well as the issuance of ten-year government bonds in international markets at the end of October 2015, show that the country has now entered a path of recovery and restoration of its credibility. There is, however, still a long way to go before the country's credibility is fully restored and our bonds are upgraded to the investment grade of rating agencies. That is why the effort to consolidate the economy and improve the rate of growth must not, under any circumstances, be relaxed. After all, economic growth is still at a lower level than what is required by a substantial and complete reversal of high unemployment rates and non-performing loans. Based on the most recent developments and based on the fact that the Cypriot economy has gone through a period of significant reforms in both the private and public sectors, increasing its competitiveness and adaptability, I expect that GDP growth of 1.5% or more will be recorded in 2015 and beyond 2% for 2016. The growth will come, mainly, from exports but also from the investments that have already begun to be implemented. There is also a need to strengthen lending from the banking sector to households and especially to businesses and productive sectors of the economy. Needless to say, of course, that lending must be done on the basis of accepted banking practices in order to be sustainable and not lead to adventures for the economy and the country, as has happened in the past. It is for this reason that, as far as the banking system is concerned in particular, the CBC has taken and will continue to take the appropriate measures so that the banking sector can now focus on the usual functions it has to perform. We are all aware of the enormous problems we have had to manage, but also of the dozens of structural changes and corrective measures that we have had to promote - many times in cooperation with the House of Representatives since they were legislative measures - in order to lay the foundations for our banks so that they can successfully fulfil their role as lenders to the economy and blood donors of development. This year, for the first time in almost three years of shrinking lending, we can see the reversal of this downward trend. Specifically, new business loans recorded an increase of 3.1% year-on-year in the period January-September 2015, while new housing loans increased significantly, albeit from a very low base. We consider that the CBC's decision to reduce the maximum deposit rate by one percentage point in February 2015 had a significant contribution to the effort for cheaper financing of the real economy. According to data collected by the CBC, lending rates benefited, as a result of this decision, from a corresponding reduction of about 100 basis points (i.e. 1%). This has led to a slight increase in the demand for new loans, although demand in general remains subdued. In addition, the reduction in lending rates has also improved the ability to repay loans  old and new. In general, there are many battles won by our financial system. The great battle was successfully fought in 2014, when the systemic banks of Cyprus were sufficiently recapitalised, resulting, among other things, in their successful participation in the pan-European comprehensive assessment exercise. During 2015, I consider the most important ones of managing the emerging risks in relation to developments in Greece, as well as the complete abolition of restrictions on the export of capital, without causing any negative consequences. Also positive are the indications for the capital adequacy assessments that are in their final stage and concern 2015. It is noted, however, that we should not rest on our laurels, as our banks will be continuously evaluated by the Single Supervisory Mechanism, which, as is well known, has undertaken since November 2014 the direct supervision of our 4 systemic banks and the indirect supervision of our other banks. Regarding the key issue of non-performing loans, I believe that Parliament, the Government and the Central Bank have contributed to the formation of a framework that creates the right conditions and provides healthy incentives to borrowers and lenders to find mutually beneficial solutions. More specifically, the strategy implemented is based on three pillars: 1. strengthening the framework for the regulation and supervision of banks 2. reforming the legal framework for insolvency, and 3. enacting legislation on the sale of loans As a result of the above, there is currently an operational and institutional framework for the management of Non-Performing Loans (NPLs). It is necessary, of course, to constantly monitor the implementation of the new framework in order to correct any shortcomings or weaknesses that may become apparent in practice. As far as the developments in loan restructuring are concerned, there is clear progress as 14.0 billion of loans have been restructured by the end of September 2015, of which, however, I note that loans amounting to 10.5 billion have been restructured. are still included in NPLs, as a result, to a certain extent, of the definition of non-performing loans. In particular, according to the definition of non-performing loans, as defined by the European Banking Authority and applied in all Countries of the European Union, a loan remains as non-performing for at least 12 months after it has been restructured, even if the client pays normally and without delays, in accordance with the new repayment plan. At the same time, the pace of restructuring shows a large increase compared to last year (restructurings have increased by 58% in the third quarter of 2015 compared to the third quarter of 2014). Restructuring, however, is not only a question of quantity, but also of quality. The aim is to further improve their pace and sustainability. At the moment, we are taking note of the fact that the course in NPLs has finally been reversed. This development is a milestone after 2 years of increasing trend and reflects the efforts of all parties involved. It is noted that international experience shows that the size of NPLs peaks up to 2 years after a crisis and a substantial reduction becomes possible only after 3-5 years have passed and, above all, after there is an economic recovery. Positive growth rates are the key to addressing this serious issue. In relation to the budget deficit and the budget, the forecasts of our international lenders generally followed more pessimistic than our own forecasts for the rate of economic growth. Specifically, regarding 2015, in July our international lenders estimated that GDP will grow by 0.5% in 2015 and the budget deficit will stand at 0.9% of GDP. Based on this forecast, the Budget for 2016 has also been drawn up. However, this forecast is already outdated, as shown by the latest revised forecasts of the European Commission, which refer to an increase of 1.2% of GDP for 2015 and a deficit of 0.7%. So far, the evolution of the 2015 budget data for the general government follows last year's path. Even if we take into account the lower receipts in September 2015, due in part by postponing the payment of certain taxes towards the end of the year (e.g. property taxes), the European Commission's forecast of a deficit of 0.7% of GDP for the whole year is considered high. I would also like to refer briefly to the public debt and note that, according to the developments over time in the fiscal and banking part of the Support Programme, it appears that a significant part of the total financial assistance will be a financing buffer. As a result, a significant improvement in the level of public debt resulting from the maintenance and increase of the savings achieved is expected. This does not mean, however, that the level of public debt has fallen to the desired level and, therefore, the effort of fiscal discipline must not be relaxed under any circumstances. In conclusion, I would like to stress that the continuation of the consolidation processes and the commitment to policy objectives, both in relation to the economy and the financial system, will help not only to successfully address the remaining challenges, to strengthen the recovery in the short and long term, but also to ensure its sustainability. I would like to assure you that the CBC, the Board of Directors, the staff and I personally as Governor, will continue with zeal the hard work to achieve the goals we have set. Goals that will lead to the stabilization and increase of confidence in the banking system, which can and should play an important role in the course of economic growth and lead our country to better days.

Title: Annual Report of the Central Bank of Cyprus for 2009
text: Governord5s speech at the 6th Nicosia Economic Congress -State of Play of the Banking Sector in Cyprus Nicosia, 26 May 2016 Distinguished audience, Ladies and gentlemen, I am honoured to have been invited to address this important event, especially at a time when the debate on how to stimulate growth in the economy is intensifying. In my capacity as Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus, I wish to convey a message of confidence, regarding the current state of the banking industry and its future prospects. More specifically, I would like to focus on the positive signs of the gradual recovery of our banking system as well as the, albeit slow, improvement in non-performing loans (NPLs). I will also refer to the significant developments that are taking place to shape the overall debt resolution framework. The banking sector in Cyprus has gone through significant changes in the last few years as a consequence of the financial crisis. Bond holders and uninsured depositors of the two largest banks at the time had to absorb a part of the losses suffered by the banks. Capital controls were imposed for two years but were subsequently lifted without any adverse consequences. The major banks were recapitalised either through state aid or by substantial foreign investment. At the same time, the real estate bubble that preceded the economic crisis as well as the crisis itself created an enormous stock of NPLd5s. The authorities, including the Central Bank of Cyprus, responded positively and have successfully implemented the much needed reforms under the economic adjustment programme agreed by Cyprus with its Troika partners. This enabled Cyprus to complete the adjustment programme within the agreed three year period. On a more general issue and as a response to th e global financial crisis that erupted in 2008, authorities around the world have strengthened the regulatory and supervisory framework, reflecting the lessons learned from this crisis. New rules have been introduced on: governance of financial institutions, the quantity and quality of capital required, the liquidity requirements and other issues. All these necessary changes are reflected in the various amendments to EU directives and in the issuance of new regulations. A major breakthrough has been the issuance of the EUd5s Bank Resolution and Recovery Directive, which was designed to break the link between stresses in the banking sector and the sovereign and vice versa. The EU has also adopted a common definition of non-performing exposures for all EU member states. More regulations are in the pipeline, such as the proposal for the revised standardised approach by the Basel Committee, which will make the calculation of capital requirements more risk sensitive. In November 2014, the supervision of our banking system came under the responsibility of the Single Supervisory Mechanism (SSM), the supervisory arm of the European Central Bank (ECB). Supervision for the significant institutions, covering more than 90% of our banking system assets, is now performed by joint supervisory teams consisting of ECB and Central Bank of Cyprus staff, which adhere to SSM rules, regulations and practices. Cypriot banks are now in the same arena as their European counterparts and are assessed on an equal footing. For the less significant institutions, supervision is conducted by the Central Bank in close cooperation with the SSM. Moving on, I would like to map specific elements of our banking system. Deposits and Liquidity of our banks Despite the full lifting of capital controls in April 2015, total bank deposits continued to stabilise and at the end of April 2016, registered an increase of db2 billion compared to the end of 2013, reaching db49,1 billion. In addition, reliance on Emergency Liquidity Assistance (ELA) has been reduced to db3,3 billion as at the end of March 2016, from db3,8 billion at the end of 2015 and significantly down from its peak of db11,2 billion in April 2013. The above positive trends have also been reflected in the liquidity buffers of domestic banks, which at the end of March 2016 were about 5 percent higher than at the end of 2014. Capital Adequacy Ratios and Risk Weighted Assets The common equity Tier 1 capital ratio (i.e. common equity tier 1 capital to total risk exposure amount) of locally active banks continued to improve, reaching 14,5 percent at the end of December 2015 compared to 10,4 percent in December 2013. During the same time (2013 d0 2015), risk weighted assets have been reduced by approximately db4 billion and provisions for bad debts increased by db6,6 billion. Loans and New Lending Total outstanding lending by the locally active banks declined between the beginning of 2015 and late March 2016 by approximately db3,6 billion due to deleveraging, higher level of repayments than new lending and loan restructurings. Nevertheless, positive signs are evident in new lending, with the aggregate amount of new loans to local residents increasing by db1,5 billion in 2015. This trend continued in the first months of 2016. Banksd5 Portfolio composition, Non-Performing Exposures and Provisions coverage As already mentioned, non-performing exposures have reached very high levels. However, the increasing trends observed in the recent past have stopped and we are now observing a stabilisation, while indications are that the trend will be reverted soon. As at the end of February 2016, non-performing loans amounted to db26,8 billion, down from db27,3 billion as at the end of 2014. Within this figure, an amount of db10,9 billion relates to exposures that have been restructured but are still under observance and will only be classified as performing once they exhibit capital repayments for at least 12 months. In addition, the pace of NPL restructuring has accelerated in recent quarters, with the outstanding balance of total restructured exposures reaching db14,2 billion at the end of February 2016 compared with db12,9 billion at the end of 2014. It is important to mention that the average cure rate (i.e. no arrears since restructuring) of fixed term loans restructured from 1 January 2014 onwards has improved to 76 percent and it is considered encouraging. As reflected in the Arrears Management Directive of the Central Bank of Cyprus, the correct strategy is to first try to agree on a restructuring solution with a non-performing borrower, before other options are explored. Despite the improvement noted above, the sheer size of NPLs relative to Cyprusd5 GDP makes it the biggest problem facing our banking system. It is for this reason that all involved stakeholders have to be decisive in using all tools available to tackle the problem. Addressing banksd5 high NPLs remains essential in order to revive lending and increase the prospects for economic growth. The legal framework for foreclosure and insolvency has been improved and relevant institutions and processes were set up and started to operate. Banks have taken substantial steps to improve their internal management of loans in arrears in order to further increase the pace of NPL restructuring. For this purpose, the banks have created centralised arrears management units. I would also like to make a special mention regarding the so-called d2strategic defaultersd3. From an ongoing study at the CBC, which will be published soon, it is concluded that the main reason for the increase in the NPLs in Cyprus is the unprecedented economic crisis, which led to a dramatic decrease in income. Nevertheless, it seems that a small but non-negligible portion of households was (or still is) not servicing its loans despite the fact that they could do so with a reasonably manageable degree of difficulty. This alludes to possible strategic default behaviour by a proportion of borrowers. Understanding the financial capacity of borrowers is key to designing effective prudential policies and for further fine-tuning loan restructuring strategies. This highlights the importance of strengthening banksd5 internal arrears management mechanisms and fully utilizing the tools provided by the new debt restructuring framework. Restructuring Targets Close monitoring is critical to swiftly identify operational bottlenecks and policy deficiencies, enhance transparency and take corrective measures. To this end, the Central Bank of Cyprus has set four specific bank-by-bank quarterly targets for NPL restructuring since June 2015 and began publishing the aggregate targets and their achievement in September 2015. Quarterly restructuring targets incentivize banks to further increase the volume and quality of their NPL restructurings. The targets set by the Central Bank relate to the following four indicators: 1. Proposed sustainable solutions 2. Concluded sustainable solutions 3. Successful restructurings, and 4. Early arrears management To monitor these targets, banks are required to submit reports to the Central Bank. The Central Bank of Cyprus revises up the banksd5 targets when it considers that these targets are not sufficiently ambitious. Preliminary results for 2016Q1 show that for all the banks that are subject to these restructuring targets, there is a small over-performance with respect to the first two indicators, while a small under-performance was observed for the other two indicators. Notwithstanding the small deviations at the aggregate level, specific banks have significantly underperformed on the set targets and the CBC has identified supervisory priorities and bank-specific actions to address deficiencies. Moving on to the last part of this presentation, I would like to refer to recent developments regarding the broader framework for managing NPLs. A law was adopted in November 2015 allowing banks to sell individual loans or segments of their loan portfolio, while preserving the safeguards for small borrowers. Importantly, given the high concentration of distressed assets, the law allows large loans (above db1 million) to be sold with limited obligations imposed on the selling bank or the purchaser. In the case of smaller loans, the law does not significantly affect incentives for restructuring or materially increase moral hazard concerns (i.e. that borrowers would stop servicing their loans in order to buy them back at a discount). A draft law on asset securitisation, with the aim of facilitating bank deleveraging and, eventually, unlocking additional sources of funding for the economy, is under preparation. Implementation of the new insolvency and foreclosure frameworks has begun and should be accelerated in order to have a stronger impact on NPL reduction. Progress has been made in several areas, for example: The new Insolvency Service is operational and has received a number of applications for the new procedures. The first group of insolvency professionals, assisting debtors developing restructuring plans, has been authorised, and A new IT system for facilitating processing of insolvency applications and communication with the courts is being developed. However, more needs to be done to operationalise the insolvency framework, including: Court rules for the new corporate reorganisation procedure. Review of the Civil Procedure and other related laws should be accelerated to ensure that courts are in a position to effectively and timely implement the new legal framework, and Reforms that facilitate the transfer of title deeds need to be finalised to improve the functioning of the property market and the debt restructuring framework. With respect to this, it is mentioned that a new law was adopted last September to facilitate title transfers for legacy cases relating to buyers of property from property developers. The framework for new sales of property is being reviewed to enable the swift transfer of titles in transactions not covered by the earlier legislation (non-legacy cases) and work is being done to ensure the issuance of title deeds without delay. As a closing remark, I would like to once again stress that our banking system has been through an enormous storm but has now stabilised and it is moving in the right direction. However, we need to remain vigilant to ensure that the path to recovery continues. We need to take the lessons learned from this recent crisis. Therefore, we must stand firm in implementing all the necessary laws and measures in order to address the major problem facing our banking system, i.e. the non-performing loans. I want to emphasize, however, that international experience shows that economic recovery is the most important way. Anyway, the horizon over which the problem of non. performing loans will start to be resolved, is estimated to be 3 to 5 years. I feel confident that with intensive efforts from all involved parties we will succeed.

Title: The role of central banks and social dialogue in light of the financial crisis
text: Address by the Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus, Mrs Chrystallas Yiorkadji, on breast cancer Central Bank of Cyprus, 3 October 2016 The month of October has been established globally as a "month of prevention and information on breast cancer", the most common form of women's cancer that can be cured, if detected at an early stage, thus making the need for early diagnosis even more urgent. Breast cancer is a painful experience for every woman. Like any disease, it challenges first and foremost any certainty. That we are not invulnerable. The measure of time is lost, "forever" acquires a new definition. Willingly or not, the moment we cross the threshold, our truths are redefined. So are the limits of our individual or collective existence. It sounds trivial, but it is the truth that all of us believe that some things only happen to others. By the time we realize that this is not the case. Until the moment we realize that it is impossible to go back in time, when there are no answers to "if it would be better if...". I have lived, like most, women who have gone through this experience. I am convinced, however, that the threat, the fear of any particular reality, can have a revealing power. Both for the person who suffers and for those around him. I dare ask, can a cancer make our lives better? Spontaneously we might say 'of course not'. And yet, many women who have overcome breast cancer have proven, with confidence and pride, that yes, their lives have changed for the better, in many areas, through a journey of rare moments of the soul. Millions of people die every day. Normally, from illnesses, accidents, violence. And yet, those who know, know that the craving for life overwhelms the existence even in the most difficult moments of a disease. That is why, in a timely manner, information, action, treatment, rehabilitation is needed. We need to have courage, faith, solidarity. That is why we are here today, declaring our presence in the collective effort to strengthen the Europa Donna Cyprus Association for the very important and undoubted contribution in the field of awareness and proper information about breast cancer. Thank you. Good luck. Note: The greeting, on behalf of the Governor of the CBC, was read by the Bank's spokesperson, Aliki Stylianou.

Title: Cyprus: economy and businesses, 50 years, 1960-2010
text: Speech by the Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus, Mrs Chrystalla Yiorkadji, at the Meeting of the House Standing Committee on Institutions, Merit and the Commissioner for Administration The functioning of the institution of the Central Bank of Cyprus Nicosia, 9 November 2016 Mr President of the Committee on Institutions, Merit and the Commissioner for Administration, ladies and gentlemen, Members, It is with a sense of responsibility and deep appreciation that I come before you today at your invitation to discuss the issue of the operation of the Central Bank of Cyprus. It is a great honour for me to preside over one of the three independent institutions laid down in the Constitution and the only one that the Treaty establishing the European Union provides for such independence: financial, functional, institutional and personal independence of the members of the decision-making bodies. I am sure that you are well aware of the institution and its responsibilities, but I considered it useful to make a brief introduction/briefing on the historical development, the current situation and the future orientations of the Central Bank of Cyprus, so that there is a uniform background for information, before proceeding to the discussion on the issues that you consider to concern you and are of interest to you. A. Legal Framework for the Operation of the CBC The Central Bank of Cyprus was established under Articles 118 and 121 of the Constitution of the Republic of Cyprus and in accordance with the Central Bank of Cyprus Law of 1963 (Law 48 of 1963), which was replaced by Law 138(I)/2002 ("Law"). The Central Bank of Cyprus is institutionally independent, autonomous and legally integrated into the Eurosystem. The Central Bank of Cyprus is a legal entity under public law but differs from other persons governed by public law in terms of establishment, organization and management. According to Article 8 of the Law, the organs of the Central Bank are the Board of Directors, the Governor and the Deputy Governor. The duties, responsibilities and responsibilities of each body are explicitly defined in the Constitution of the Republic of Cyprus and in the Law. It is noted that the Board of Directors of the Bank initially consisted of the Governor, the Deputy Governor and five Advisors, who were appointed by the Council of Ministers. With the Amending Laws 86(I)/2013 and 103(I)/2013, amendments were made, including, based on article 12, both Executive Directors now participate in the Board of Directors. The Governor, however, is an independent official and is appointed by the President of the Republic on the basis of Article 118 of the Constitution. In contrast to those applicable to other legal entities under public law, the Governor is not only a member of the Council, which he presides over, but is also a self-existent body of the Bank and under the Constitution and the Law exercises on his own powers and duties that are assigned exclusively to himself. Independence of the Central Bank In 1995, the predecessor of the European Central Bank, the European Monetary Institute drew up a list of the characteristics of the independence of the central banks which formed the basis for the evaluation of national laws, in particular those of the national central banks, with a view to the adoption of the common currency. The independence of central banks includes various types of independence, functional, institutional, personal and financial independence. These aspects have been analysed in opinions issued from time to time by the European Central Bank on draft legislation of the Member States, in particular on draft provisions on the functioning and responsibilities of the respective national central bank. The main positions of the European Central Bank are also recorded in the convergence reports The independence of central banks is not an end in itself but a necessary means of achieving an end that must be clearly defined and take precedence over all other purposes. This is the content of functional independence and in this regard for the Central Bank of Cyprus is Article 5 of its Law which defines as its primary objective the safeguarding of price stability. Subsection (2) of the same article provides that without prejudice to the primary objective and subject to the fulfilment of its obligations as part of the European System of Central Banks, the Central Bank of Cyprus shall support the general economic policy of the State. The principle of institutional independence is explicitly set out in Article 130 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union and is reiterated with regard to the Central Bank of Cyprus in Article 7 of its Law. The national central banks, the European Central Bank and the members of their decision-making bodies, in the exercise of their powers and the performance of their duties, shall neither seek nor take instructions from institutions or bodies of the European Union, the governments of Member States or other bodies. In turn, the institutions and bodies of the European Union and the governments of the Member States undertake to respect this principle and not to seek to influence the members of the decision-making bodies of the national central banks and the European Central Bank. The personal independence of the members of the decision-making bodies is an additional guarantee of the independence of the central banks. There are rules on term of office and dismissal which should apply not only to Governors, but also to other members of the decision-making bodies of the national central banks involved in the performance of tasks related to the European System of Central Banks. Even when a national central bank enjoys full operational, institutional and personal independence, its independence may be jeopardised if it does not have sufficient financial resources to ensure its autonomy in the performance of its mission. The main individual aspects of financial independence concern adequate own funds, autonomy in budget setting, application of accounting rules and audit of financial statements by external auditors, strict framework for any audit by a state authority, profit distribution and provisioning, as well as autonomy in personnel matters. The provisions of Articles 56 to 62 of the Law are relevant to the above and ensure some of the aspects of financial independence, in particular the formation of a reserve and the withholding of profits, as well as the preparation and approval of the annual budget of the Central Bank of Cyprus by the Board of Directors of the Central Bank. Executive Directors  Proposals for Laws of the House of Representatives that amended the governance of the Bank Law 138(I) of 2002 was amended by Law 86(I) of 2013, which provided, inter alia, for the following: (1) a change in the composition of the Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Cyprus, i.e. it increased the number of Advisors from five to seven more than the Governor and the Deputy Governor and provided that two of the Directors will be Executive, while the remaining five will be non-Executive Directors. (2) the remuneration and other terms of service of the Executive Directors, as well as the remuneration of the non-Executive Directors shall be determined by the Council of Ministers at the time of the appointment of the Directors. The Executive Directors will be full-time. (3) The Council will delegate specific tasks to the Executive Directors, who, in turn, will assist the Governor in the administration, supervision and control of the operations of the Central Bank of Cyprus. (4) the composition of the Staff Committee of the Central Bank of Cyprus is enlarged with the addition of the two Executive Directors and the The quorum required for meetings of the Staff Committee shall be increased from three members to four members. History of the Resolution Authority In addition to the above, the Central Bank of Cyprus also acts as the Resolution Authority. Briefly, I mention how the various legislations defining the role and responsibilities of the Resolution Authority have been formulated. 22/3/2013: The Resolution of Credit and Other Institutions Law of 2013 (17(I)/2013) The above law designated the Central Bank of Cyprus as resolution authority. 30/8/2013: The Resolution of Credit and Other Institutions (Amendment No. 2) Law of 2013 (38(I)/2013) The above Law provided that the Resolution Authority consisted of the Central Bank of Cyprus, the Minister of Finance and the President of the Cyprus Securities and Exchange Commission. 30/6/2014: The Resolution of Credit and Other Institutions (Amendment) Law of 2014 (90(I)/2014) The above Law redefined the Central Bank as the Resolution Authority. Furthermore, it provided that the Resolution Authority establishes the Resolution Committee as its deciding executive body, with the main responsibility for the implementation of the provisions of the Law. The Resolution Committee consisted of the Chairman, who is the Respective Governor, and the respective appointed Executive Directors of the Bank, pursuant to article 13 of the Central Bank of Cyprus Laws of 2002 to 2014. 18/3/2016: The Resolution of Credit Institutions and Investment Companies Law of 2016 (22(I)/2016) The above Law defines the Central Bank as the Resolution Authority. The Law abolishes the Resolution Committee and provides that the Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Cyprus is responsible for the exercise of the responsibilities and powers of the Resolution Authority. B. Supervisory role and responsibilities of the Central Bank of Cyprus One of the main responsibilities of the Central Bank of Cyprus is the supervision of credit institutions. Since November 2014, the institution of the Single Supervisory Mechanism, the new system of consolidated banking supervision, which includes the European Central Bank and the National Competent Authorities of the euro area countries, i.e. the Central Bank of Cyprus, has been operational in the context of greater European harmonisation  banking union. The Single Supervisory Mechanism promotes the approach of the single rulebook to the prudential supervision of credit institutions, with a view to enhancing the integrity of the euro area banking system. To ensure effective supervision, credit institutions are classified as 'significant' or 'less significant'. The European Central Bank, through the Single Supervisory Mechanism, directly supervises significant credit institutions, with the assistance of the National Competent Authorities. A credit institution is considered significant if certain conditions are met, which primarily concern the size of its assets or its size in the country where it is established. Currently, 129 groups of credit institutions are designated as significant credit institutions, including Cyprus Bank of Cyprus, Hellenic Bank, Cooperative Central Bank and RCB Bank. In addition, the subsidiaries of Greek banks operating in Cyprus, namely Alpha Bank, Eurobank, Piraeus Bank and National Bank of Greece (Cyprus) have also been designated as significant credit institutions due to their parent company. The National Competent Authorities continue to exercise direct supervision of less significant institutions, around 3,500 entities at European level, under the supervision of the European Central Bank. The European Central Bank may also undertake, under certain conditions, the direct supervision of less significant credit institutions. In addition, the European Central Bank is responsible for horizontal supervisory functions such as the licensing and revocation of banking licences. It is noted that within the scope of the supervisory responsibilities that have remained with the Central Bank of Cyprus, without the involvement of the European Central Bank, are the fight against money laundering and the prudential supervision of branches of foreign credit institutions from third countries operating in Cyprus. I now come to the series of legislation/Directives that the Central Bank of Cyprus, in the context of its supervisory and regulatory role, has issued, the main ones of which are mentioned below: Regulatory and Regulatory framework Instructions of the Central Bank of Cyprus The Procedures for Granting and Reviewing Credit Facilities (Amendment) Directive of 2016 The Directive was originally issued in December 2013, as part of addressing the consequences of the crisis, in order to (a) define the minimum practices with which Licensed Credit Institutions must comply during the process of evaluating new or even reviewing existing credit facilities, (b) to determine the minimum supporting documents that Licensed Credit Institutions must receive during the process of evaluation or revision of credit facilities, (c) to require the immediate incorporation by the Licensed Credit Institutions of these minimum practices in their internal instructions, credit policy and internal procedures. This Directive was revised in March 2016, with the aim of providing more discretionary options to Licensed Credit Institutions and to simplify and make the process of assessing new requests for grants less complex and time-consuming. This was followed by a new amendment in September 2016. The Definition of Operation of a System or Mechanism for the Exchange, Collection and Provision of Data Directive of 2015 The purpose of the Directive is to define the terms, conditions and procedures for the operation of systems or mechanisms for the exchange of data and the use of such data by the Central Bank of Cyprus in the exercise of its responsibilities, and by the Licensed Credit Institutions operating in the Republic, for the evaluation of the creditworthiness of customers or potential customers. The Assessment of the Competence and Suitability of Members of the Board of Directors and Directors of Licensed Credit Institutions Directive of 2014 The purpose of the Directive is to define- (a) the policy and procedures for the evaluation and reassessment of the competence and suitability of the evaluated persons; (b) the criteria for assessing the competence and suitability of the assessees. (c) the measures applicable in cases where members or directors of Licensed Credit Institutions have been found to be no longer competent, or Suitable. (d) criteria which make members of an administrative body independent (criteria of independence). The Discretionary Options provided by Regulation 575/2013 Directive of 2014 It defines the discretions provided by Regulation 575/2013. The Governance and Management Arrangements Directive of 2014 The purpose of the Directive is to: (a) the definition of requirements relating to the governance structures of credit institutions. (b) the definition of requirements relating to the roles and responsibilities of management bodies and top management. (c) the definition of requirements relating to the development, implementation and effective control of the regulatory compliance, risk management and internal control frameworks. The Loan Impairment and Provisioning Procedures (Amendment) Directive of 2016 The Directive was adopted around mid-2013, as part of the effort to improve the regulatory framework, and was revised in December 2014, February 2015 and May 2016. The purpose of the Directive is to: (a) to ensure the prudent application of International Financial Reporting Standards for the financial statements generated by the Licensed Credit Institutions, and (b) the definition of procedures for the identification, evaluation and measurement of the impairment of credit facilities as well as the disclosures of the policies and methods of valuation and the analysis of the loan portfolio of licensed credit institutions. The Arrears Management Directive of 2015 Code of Conduct for the handling of Borrowers facing Financial Difficulties The purpose of the Directive is the implementation by the Licensed Credit Institutions of effective and efficient strategies, policies, structures, procedures and mechanisms for the management of arrears and the achievement of fair and sustainable solutions for restructuring the lending of borrowers facing financial difficulties, with the ultimate goal of addressing the financial difficulties caused by the economic crisis. The Directive, together with the Code of Conduct, was first adopted in September 2013 and revised in February 2014. It was then reissued, after being significantly simplified, in April 2015. Legal framework Legislation governing Credit Acquiring Companies Published November 27, 2015. The aim is to regulate the sale of loans by licensed credit institutions and to ensure the protection of borrowers regarding the sale of credits up to 1 million. At the same time, the Central Bank of Cyprus has issued the Notification Procedure Directive of 2016, which sets out the procedure for informing borrowers from licensed credit institutions about credits for sale. In addition to the above, the CBC has contributed substantially to the preparation of the insolvency framework that includes the following Laws: 1. The Insolvency of Natural Persons (Personal Repayment Plans and Debt Relief Order) Law of 2015. 2. The Bankruptcy (Amendment) Law of 2015. 3. The Companies (Amendment) Law of 2015, regarding the liquidations of companies. 4. The Companies (Amendment) Law of 2015, regarding the mechanism for the restructuring of corporate debt. 5. The Insolvency Practitioners Law of 2015 and related Regulations. C. Reorganisation of the Central Bank of Cyprus In December 2014, the Governing Council of the Central Bank of Cyprus decided to commission, through an international tender procedure, a study on the reorganisation of the Central Bank of Cyprus. From the procedure, the house of Roland Berger Gmbh was chosen from among seven international consulting firms. The firm began conducting the study in May 2015 and prepared it, dividing it into four central axes. Governance, Standard Practices and Procedures, Organizational Structure and Human Resources Issues. The findings and suggestions of the consulting firm's final report, submitted at the end of July 2015, were examined in principle by the Board of Directors in early September 2015, which decided that the findings of the study would form the basis for the reorganization. The staff were informed of these developments in early November 2015. At the same time, the decision to establish an Office for the Management of the Reorganization Project as well as the terms of reference of the Office were notified to the employees. This was followed by a presentation by the Board of Directors to the staff of the main findings and proposals, as well as the planning of the Project Management Office regarding the next steps in relation to the implementation of the reorganization. As Governor, I assured the staff that nothing will be initiated or implemented in the context of the reorganization that will weaken or disrupt labor positions or bypass existing labor arrangements or contractual obligations of the Bank, without first having the necessary consultations with all parties involved. In December 2015, the Project Management Office submitted to the Board of Directors the first official progress report and the Board of Directors of the Bank approved, in principle, the organizational chart with 4 Directorates and 17 Sectors / Departments, as well as the new roles and responsibilities undertaken by each of the new organizational Sectors. On March 1, 2016, as planned, the new organizational chart and the new roles and responsibilities of the Directorates and Sectors were implemented and the heads of the Departments were appointed. At the same time, it was decided that the agency's recommendations on governance issues of the Central Bank of Cyprus should be further elaborated and more widely analyzed by the International Monetary Fund, which by the nature of its activities it provides technical assistance and advice due to its many years of expertise and friction in central bank governance issues. I will refer to the views and suggestions of the International Monetary Fund on governance issues in a moment, below. In May 2016, the Project Management Office submitted to the Governor/Board of Directors a report on the Bank's Staff Development System, which was based, among other things, on the findings/proposals of the consulting firm Roland Berger. At the same time, the Project Management Office began working on the study and analysis of the needs for numerical and qualitative staffing of the Central Bank of Cyprus, on the establishment and staffing of the organizational units and on the recording and detailed description of tasks for all jobs. After the presentation of the report of the Project Management Office to the Board of Directors and in connection with the general study of the Berger Roland, it was decided to conduct a supplementary competition for the preparation of a specialized study on key issues related to Human Resources. In addition, the terms of reference of the specialized study included, among other things, the preparation of an actuarial study on total labor costs under different payroll scenarios over a decade. After the relevant notice was published in the official newspapers of the European Union and the Republic for the preparation of the relevant study, the Central Bank awarded the contract to Promontory, who already submitted the final draft of his study, recently, at the end of October 2016. The findings and proposals of Promontory, together with the changes already underway in terms of organizational structure and, most importantly, the proposed changes of the International Monetary Fund in matters of governance, will be put, as required, by the Central Bank of Cyprus to the European Central Bank for its opinion, before their final formation and before they are made for any necessary constitutional / legislative changes. Unfortunately, despite the strong remarks and demarches about the understaffing of the Central Bank of Cyprus, especially on specialized issues such as, for example, legal advisors and experts on forensic data analysis, the Central Bank of Cyprus was and remains unable to fill vacant positions with permanent staff due to the chronic impossibility for legitimate convergence of the Personnel Committee, whose involvement is a prerequisite under the Law for all personnel issues. As you know, due to the existence of a vacancy in the Personnel Committee due to the resignation of an Executive Director in April 2015, the Personnel Committee cannot be constituted by all the persons expressly provided for by law and, therefore, cannot meet legally to deal with the matters falling within its competence, since the Law explicitly states that the Personnel Committee participates, among others, both Executive Directors. In practice, this means that the Central Bank of Cyprus is unable to recruit staff, promote, exercise disciplinary proceedings, review decisions overturned in court, dismiss or suspend employees. It is with regret that I note that this necessary simple amendment of the Law, with a provision which, as we have seen, exists in all the Laws of legal entities under public law and which was necessary for the immediate regulation of the issue, was rejected by the Plenary Session of the Parliament. The result? To make limited recruitments, exceptionally under contract, that do not serve the permanent needs of the Central Bank of Cyprus. I now come back to the issue of the technical assistance that we requested and received from the International Monetary Fund, in relation to the issues of governance and restructuring of the Central Bank of Cyprus. The Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Cyprus studied, in a number of its meetings, with great attention the relevant alternative recommendations of the International Monetary Fund and, after extensive discussions, came up with the preferred solution which it will promote for implementation. In addition, the Board of Directors also defined an indicative roadmap that can be summarized as follows: (a) final formulation of the text by the external legal advisors of the Central Bank of Cyprus, which is expected to be completed within a few days. (b) sending the text to the European Central Bank for an opinion. (c) whether or not to differentiate the text on the basis of any comments from the European Central Bank. (d) sending the text to the Ministry of Finance for the formulation of a relevant legislative proposal. (e) legislative technical control by the Legal Service of the State. (f) adoption by the Council of Ministers, and (g) discussion of the bill in the Parliamentary Committee on Finance and then in the Plenary session of the House for a vote. For a comprehensive and comprehensive briefing of your Committee, I would like to note that the External Legal Advisor of the Central Bank of Cyprus, indicated that the Board of Directors has, of course, the possibility to adopt the option of its preference, clarifying, however, at the same time, that in order to implement any of the options that have been put before the Board of Directors, an amendment to the Constitution will be required and more specifically to Articles 118.2, 119.1 and 119.3. I would like to take this opportunity and before I close, I would like to publicly thank the Board of Directors of the Central Bank of Cyprus for the excellent cooperation we have had in recent years, in the titanic joint effort we are making to strengthen confidence in the banking system, following the events that accumulated and manifested themselves in a dramatic way in 2013. But nothing could be achieved

Title: Central bank policy challenges in the crisis
text: Address by the Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus, Mrs Chrystalla Yiorkadji, on "Osteoporosis and Musculoskeletal Disorders" Central Bank of Cyprus, 10 November 2016 Referring to the etymological meaning of the word osteoporosis, it comes from the "porous bone", that is, it is characterized by susceptible or fragile bones. Reference to its existence exists 4000 years ago in Egypt, despite the fact that the disease was recognized only in 1824 (Patlak & Teitelbaum, 2001). Osteoporosis is of particular concern to the female population although data from various studies show that women underestimate its severity and consequences, do not know that hip fractures and impotence are directly related to it, as well as a large percentage are unaware that osteoporosis can lead to death (National Osteoporosis Foundation and Gallup Organisation, 1991). Musculoskeletal disorders present equally serious disorders, which are caused by the space and type of work at a cost not only to employees but also to employers. It is a fact that when we refer to our health we often think about diet, exercise d0 or lack of it, or the last conversation we had with our doctor. We overlook the conditions in which many of us spend most of our time - and that is none other than our workplace. Musculoskeletal disorders include any damage or disorder of the joints or other tissues that lead to disability with an impact on the reduction of performance at work and there are many times when they require leaving work. In addition to the definitions, there is little mention of the pain, the chronic pain they suffer and the loneliness of the people who are subjected to them by these diseases. Most are in an unspoken understanding of silence about how they feel. Some will say that this is the way things are, simply, leaving it to happen. We live in a constant noise, in a world where everything happens quickly, where there is no time, almost never. All this makes it difficult for us to communicate. At the same time, however, things change faster than before because there is information: How we face difficulties, how we are informed about the diseases that exist, how we overturn mentalities, how we dehumanize pain. Fortunately, in recent years we have been exposing the issue of pain even though for many years no one has been talking about it. Consistently, perhaps not at the pace we would like, we focus not only on providing medical care but also on providing support to people suffering from chronic pain. It is important to send the message that the distance that separates us from these people does not exist. We can create an environment where in difficult times, in the pain of ourselves and our fellow human beings, we will all have a hand to hold us. There is a lot of power in what we can all do together. As I get older, I realize that our freedom is extremely fragile, essentially it exists while we are healthy. Anything that can happen to any of us. And while there is always the temptation of pessimism, it is up to us to drive it away, through the trilogy of information, communication, knowledge. That is why we must praise the work and efforts of all those who promote the knowledge that there is help, as is done today by the Association against Osteoporosis and Musculoskeletal Disorders. Although the world is complex, it turns out that it only takes a group of people to mobilize public opinion and raise awareness, promoting the solidarity that we all know exists among us with our suffering fellow human beings. I congratulate the organisers of today's event and wholeheartedly wish you the best of luck. Note: The Greeting on behalf of the Governor of the CBC was read by the spokesperson Aliki Stylianou.

Title: Towards a new architecture for financial stability in Europe
text: Speech by the Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus, Mrs Chrystalla Yiorkadji, at the meeting of the House Standing Committee on Financial and Budgetary Affairs The estimates of the Central Bank of Cyprus in the context of the discussion of the state budget for 2017 Presentation by Chrystalla Yiorkadji, Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus, to the Parliamentary Committee on Financial and Budgetary Affairs Nicosia, 24 November 2016 Mr President, ladies and gentlemen, Thank you for the invitation to submit my views as Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus on the occasion of the discussion of the State Budget for the year 2017. It is an honor and a responsibility. The optimism and forecasts that I presented last year for 2016 not only came true, but eventually emerged even more positive, while for 2017 a continuation of the recovery of the economy observed in the last two years is expected. As regards the banking system, efforts to strengthen it even stronger will be further strengthened. The time we leave behind marked the successful exit of Cyprus from the economic adjustment program, in which our country had entered in March 2013 based on the Memorandum of Understanding agreed with the international lenders of our country. The implementation of the programme was difficult, but in the end, as the current course of the economy demonstrates, it is necessary. In fact, the Cypriot economy exited the programme in March 2016, using only 7.3 billion. approximately the available financial envelope of 10 billion. While significant problems remain, such as the high level of non-performing loans (49%), high public debt (109.6%) and unemployment (12.1%), the outlook is encouraging both for the banking sector, which is now on a much healthier basis, and for the fiscal situation, which is also supported by a return to growth and the continued reduction in unemployment. More specifically, economic activity in Cyprus showed an increase of 2.7% in real terms in the first half of 2016, compared to 0.8% in the corresponding period of 2015. Exports of services (especially tourism) and domestic demand (both investment and private consumption) have been the main drivers of growth. I would like at this point to point out that private consumption growth has continued its steady positive path amid an increase in loan restructuring, suggesting that efforts to curb non-performing borrowing are not expected to have a significant negative impact on Gross Domestic Product (GDP). For the whole of 2016, and according to the published forecasts of the Central Bank of Cyprus for June 2016, real GDP is expected to grow by 2.7%. Given the recent publication of the preliminary estimate for the third quarter of 2016 for an increase of 2.9%, and taking into account the excellent performance of tourism that continues in the fourth quarter, it is expected that in the next round of forecasts of the Central Bank of Cyprus in December 2016, the GDP growth rate for 2016 will be revised slightly upwards. Real GDP is expected to continue to grow at around the same level in 2017 and 2018, mainly reflecting strong private consumption, investment and to a lesser extent net exports. The dynamism of the economy is projected to be further strengthened, benefiting from the improvements in competitiveness that have occurred in recent years. The aforementioned positive developments related to GDP, although with some time lag, inevitably had a positive effect on the labor market, with unemployment recording continuous declines from the high rate of 16.1% recorded in its peak year, 2014. Specifically, the unemployment rate decreased, based on the Labour Force Survey, to 12.1% in the second quarter of 2016, compared to 14.1% in the previous quarter and 14.6% in the corresponding quarter of 2015. On the price front, inflation is negative for the third year in a row. In particular, in the first ten months of the year, harmonised inflation hovered at -1.4%. Excluding energy, the negative performance of inflation is limited to -0.5%. Negative inflation is due to increased competition in aviation, the spill-over effects of very low oil prices and the downward adjustments imposed on wages. In general, negative inflation contributed positively to the strengthening of real-world incomes and the competitiveness of the Cypriot economy, although its further maintenance would not be desirable, due to deflationary side effects. We expect inflation to start to return to positive levels in 2017, mainly due to the strengthening of economic activity, a small expected increase in wages and developments in external factors, such as oil prices, which, based on the projections' working assumptions, are expected to increase. The 2017 Budget is the first to be prepared since the exit of the Republic of Cyprus from the economic adjustment program last March. The macroeconomic projections included are considered prudent both for 2016, taking into account the available data, and for subsequent years, especially taking into account the significant investments by both the public and private sectors, which are expected to contribute significantly to the economic growth rate in the medium term. The path of the fiscal balance is projected to show a continued improvement from -0.3% in 2016 to 0.7% in 2019, while the primary balance (fiscal balance excluding interest payments) also records an improvement and is associated with larger surpluses from 2.3% in 2016 to 3.4% in 2019. On the positive side, the fact that, during the period of the economic programme, the Republic of Cyprus achieved a significant financial correction is also recorded. In particular, the budgetary results achieved in relation to the objectives of the programme demonstrate the commitment towards the formulation and implementation of a prudent fiscal policy. In terms of public debt, this appears to peak as a percentage of GDP around 109% in 2015 and then de-escalate to reach 96% of GDP in 2019. If some non-recurring revenues are included, public debt will de-escalate to a greater extent. Turning now to developments in the financial sector, I would like to note first of all with satisfaction that our banks have managed to successfully respond to the stricter supervisory guidelines and structural reforms of the last three main years, correcting fundamental weaknesses in the financial system, which has been key to significantly improving credibility and confidence in the sector. In principle, in 2014, the recapitalised banking sector successfully passed the European Central Bank's rigorous stress tests, which led to a significant improvement in the credibility of the banking system. In addition, there was a rapid stabilisation of deposit flows after 2013, which allowed, in April 2015, the full lifting of all restrictions on the movement of capital imposed. The recording of inputs deposits, especially from residents of Cyprus, recorded since 2015, suggesting, gradually, a return of depositors' confidence in the banking system. At the same time, and despite the observed deleveraging of loans, there is an increase, albeit limited, in the granting of new loans. In particular, lending to the domestic private sector has started to show signs of a slight recovery since 2015, as a result of the granting of new loans by banks. Nevertheless, new lending remains limited, mainly due to the ongoing efforts of both the banking sector and the private sector to deleverage their balance sheets. The improved robustness of the Cyprus economy and the state of the banking system in particular is also evident from the significant decrease in the country's government bond yields, the upgrade by international rating agencies, the significant reduction of ELA and the significant investment interest as it results from the participation of foreign individuals in banking and other sectors. As regards the level of non-performing loans, this continues to be the main problem afflicting the banking sector, despite the progress made in recent months. The banking institutions, however, have now completed the creation and staffing of the special units for the management of non-performing loans and have developed their policies and internal procedures to be able to deal with the problem to the greatest possible extent. The number of restructurings has increased and there is a substantial trend towards more sustainable restructuring in 2016. There is also an increasing trend in the amounts collected from non-performing loans. This, together with other actions by banking institutions, has led to a gradual reduction in non-performing loans, mainly in recent months. I note that non-performing lending for the domestic operations of banking institutions decreased to 24.5 billion. by the end of August 2016, compared to 27.8 billion. which had reached 26.9 billion at the end of January 2015. at the end of 2015. But there is still a way to go and a lot of work to be done to get the problem solved and there is no room for relaxing the effort. It is necessary to continue and strengthen the relevant handling, by all parties involved, in order for the problem to be managed. As is well known, non-performing lending acts as a burden on banks' balance sheets and reduces their capacity to internally strengthen their capital base. At the same time, they act, in general, and as a burden on the country's economy and it is for this reason that every effort must be made by everyone towards solving the problem. The issue of non-performing loans at euro area level is also of concern to the Single Supervisory Mechanism, which has set up a special group with members from euro area countries with high levels of non-performing loans, to examine the problem and draw up a plan to address it. In the first phase, the group has prepared draft guidelines to banks on how to handle non-performing loans in both management and provisioning. Also, the Single Supervisory Mechanism is expected to ask, in 2017, each bank with high non-performing loans to draw up a plan to reduce them to acceptable levels, the implementation of which it will monitor on an ongoing basis. In relation to the liquidity of banking institutions, we see a significant improvement with deposits increasing and emergency liquidity (ELA) decreasing significantly and with a view to its repayment early in 2017. Negative interest rates of the European Central Bank, despite their contribution to the stimulation of the euro area economy, and non-performing lending, negatively affect the profitability of banking institutions with all the associated risks to their capital adequacy which, despite this, remains, for the time being, at satisfactory levels.
