Mr President, honourable members of the House Standing Committee on Financial and Budgetary Affairs, the best way to tackle the two main problems of the economy, namely unemployment and non-performing loans, is structural reforms and growth, through more investment. In conclusion, I would like once again to assure you that the Central Bank of Cyprus and I personally as Governor, will continue, quietly but with absolute dedication, to play the role that belongs to us, both for our banking system and for the economy of the country in general in terms of what falls within our own responsibilities as the Central Bank of Cyprus and as a member of the Eurosystem. Our efforts so far have been vindicated by the results so far. The road we have been able to travel since the outbreak of the crisis has been very important. But just as long and arduous is the road that still lies ahead of us. The final elimination of the consequences of the crisis and the return of our banking system to conditions of full restoration of its credibility and its role as the main financier of economic activity and investments in our country, continue to be our ultimate goal. Thank you for your attention. I am at your disposal for any questions.

Title: Bank of Cyprus Chronology 1899-2009
text: Introductory statement by the Governor of the CBC at the meeting of the House Standing Committee on Institutions, Merit and The Commissioner Administration "The functioning of the institutions of the financial system (In particular: The management of Laiki Bank's assets)" Ex officio examination by decision of the House Standing Committee on Institutions, Merit and the Commissioner for Administration Nicosia, 8 February 2017 Allow me first to begin with a brief overview of the history of the operation of the Resolution Authority and the resolution of Laiki Bank. By the Resolution of Credit and Other Institutions Law adopted by the House of Representatives on 22 March 2013, the Central Bank of Cyprus (CBC) was designated as resolution authority. I recall that this Law was based on the proposal for a Directive of the European Union on the recovery and resolution of credit institutions and was prepared in cooperation and at the suggestion of the Troika (EU / ECB / IMF) within the framework of the financial assistance program to Cyprus for the reorganization and consolidation of the banking sector. This Law conferred the power on the Central Bank of Cyprus, with the agreement of the Minister of Finance, to take and apply resolution measures to credit institutions. With an amendment to the Law passed by the House of Representatives in August 2013, a three-member collegiate body consisting of the Central Bank, the Minister of Finance and the President of the Hellenic Capital Market Commission was appointed as the Resolution Authority. With a new amendment to the Law published on 30 June 2014, the Central Bank of Cyprus was reappointed as resolution authority. Finally, in March 2016, a new law on the resolution of credit institutions and investment companies was adopted, which transposed the European Union Directive on the recovery and resolution of credit institutions. This Law, which before its adoption was, as required by European rules, consulted with the European Central Bank, again designated the CBC as resolution authority. I understand that the issue of the CBC's independence as resolution authority has been raised, bearing in mind that the CBC also acts as the supervisor of credit institutions at the same time. At this point I would like to note that Directive 2014/59/EU on the recovery and resolution of credit institutions, known by the acronym BRRD, gives discretion to Member States to designate the resolution authority, which may be the national central bank, the competent ministry or other public administrative authority. Regardless of the above, and as I have stated in the past, the Resolution Authority has no objection to any legislative arrangements and changes in the way it operates, always within the framework of the European acquis, to strengthen its independence, including the delegation of resolution tasks and responsibilities to any other existing or new authority. I have also expressed the above position in a letter to the Minister of Finance dated October 21, 2015. However, I note that, in at least 23 Member States of the European Union, the Central Bank and/or the National Supervisory Authority has been designated as the National Resolution Authority since it is considered to have the necessary experience and know-how to carry out the difficult task of reorganising credit institutions. Having, however, in mind that there must be a clear separation of supervisory and resolution functions, as provided for by the relevant European Directive, the CBC took from the first moment the necessary measures for the organic separation of the two functions by establishing, as provided for in the Law, a separate Resolution Unit with a direct reference line to the Governor. The Resolution Authority shall take resolution measures only if it is established, inter alia, that the institution is failing or likely to fail and takes the following four resolution measures provided for in the Resolution Law: (i) Sale of works; (ii) Transfer of assets, rights or liabilities to a bridge institution; (iii) Transfer of assets and rights to an asset management company; (iv) Bail-in rescue. Regarding the resolution of Laiki Bank, I would like to remind you that the bank was placed under resolution, in accordance with the political decision taken at the Eurogroup on 25/3/2013 with the implementation of the measure of sale of business. As a result, the operations, the insured deposits, the extraordinary liquidity (ELA) liabilities and the vast majority of the bank's assets were transferred to the Bank of Cyprus, which as a consideration, and on the basis of an independent assessment carried out by KPMG London of the transferred net assets, issued and granted to Laiki Bank 18.1% of its share capital. This shareholding of Laiki Bank in the share capital of the Bank of Cyprus decreased to 9.6% following the increase of the latter's share capital in December 2014. According to KPMG's valuation report, the fair value of the shares held by Laiki Bank in the Bank of Cyprus amounted to 381m on 29/3/2013. Despite the continuous steady improvement of the Bank of Cyprus' financial position with the increase in customer deposits and the repayment of emergency liquidity, its share price remains at relatively low levels, with the result that the current market capitalization of the shares held by Laiki Bank decreased to 132m. approximately. The Special Administrator of Laiki Bank, with the approval and instructions of the Resolution Authority, appointed in November 2016 the international investment banks HSBC and Deutsche Bank to advise on the strategic options for the sale of the shares and the preparation of a relevant roadmap. The Resolution Authority is closely studying the issue, with the aim of maximising the proceeds from the sale of shares to the benefit of uninsured creditors. Regarding the criticism made about the delay in the sale of the assets held by Laiki Bank, which consist of investments in subsidiary banks in Greece, Malta, Serbia, Romania and Ukraine, I would like to point out the following: In the first year of the resolution of Laiki Bank, efforts had focused on stabilising the financial position of the subsidiaries and restoring the confidence of customers and depositors, which had been disrupted by the fact that their main shareholder/owner had been placed in resolution and, consequently, was unable to provide the required capital and liquidity support in case of need. However, some attempts had been made to sell individual assets (Marfin Bank Ukraine and AEDAK Greece  a subsidiary fund management company), which ultimately did not come to fruition. At the beginning of 2014, the Special Manager of Laiki Bank, on the instructions of the then tripartite Resolution Authority, proceeded to a tender for the recruitment of investment advisors for the provision of advisory services in relation to the sale of all assets. Five offers were received from international investment houses, of which only one concerned the provision of services for the sale of all assets. This was followed by lengthy negotiations with this bidder, which resulted in an agreement in principle in mid-September 2014. At the last minute, before the signing of the contract, the selected firm questioned the debt of Laiki Bank and the agreement was wrecked. On 6/4/2015, Mr. Chris Pavlou was appointed as the new Special Administrator, replacing Mrs. Antoniadou. Mr. Pavlou on 6/5/2015 assigned, upon his recommendation and with the approval of the Resolution Authority, to the Investment Bank of Greece (IBG) the provision of services for the sale of Laiki's assets with the process continuing to this day with the following important developments: Agreements for the sale of Marfin Bank Romania (30/12/2015), Marfin Bank Serbia (30/9/16) and Marfin Bank Ukraine (14/11/16) have been signed and the procedures for the completion of the terms and conditions arising from these agreements as well as the receipt of approvals from the supervisory and other authorities for the payment of the price and the transfer of the shares held by Laiki Bank to the buyers are progressing with several difficulties. Regarding laiki's subsidiary bank in Russia, Rosprombank, there was an unexpected development with the revocation of its operating license by the Central Bank of Russia on 13/9/2016 while negotiations with an interested buyer for its sale were at a very advanced stage. With regard to the subsidiary bank in Malta, Lombard Bank Malta, a court order secured by a "mowed" depositor blocked the shares of Laiki Bank and prohibited their sale. Following an application submitted by Laiki, the commitment was limited to 1/3 of the shares held by Laiki, resulting in the resumption of the sale process from the beginning of the year. However, difficulties are faced due to the refusal of the Executive Management of the subsidiary to cooperate in initiating the bidding process for the sale of the shares held by Laiki. Regarding IBG Greece, in early December 2016, the CBC proceeded with the announcement of a tender for the appointment of an international investment house for the provision of advisory services for the sale of Laiki's investment in this bank. Only one bid was submitted and it was decided to cancel the tender. The Resolution Authority is studying the next steps in relation to this asset. What I mentioned above, shows that the process of successfully selling the remaining assets of Laiki is not an easy task at all. The difficulties are great and largely come from external factors, such as the financial situation of the subsidiaries, the inability to effectively control their operations and provide support from Laiki, the difficult economic and political situation of their operating countries and the institutional framework of their operation, which requires obtaining approvals and compliance with the laws of each country separately to achieve the sale. All this negatively affects the interest of investors and investment advisors. Indicatively mentioned is the case of Marfin Bank Romania, for which a contract of sale was signed in December 2015 and, although 14 months have passed and all the necessary actions have been taken on behalf of Laiki, not all the required approvals have yet been received by the foreign supervisory authorities for the completion of the sale. At this point, allow me to point out a contradiction in the complaints expressed by various sides in relation to the management of Laiki Bank's assets: on the one hand, there is criticism of a delay in the sale of Laiki's assets, resulting in a decrease in value, and on the other hand, it is requested that the sale of the three main assets should not proceed, that is, investments in Bank of Cyprus, IBG and Lombard Bank Malta, predicting that there will be an increase in their value in the distant future. With regard to the proposal of SYKALA for the transfer of the management of the assets of Laiki Bank to the creditors of the bank, I recall that the Resolution Authority had taken a positive position and this position has been repeatedly expressed, both in writing and orally, to the House of Representatives and, in particular, to the Committees on Finance and Institutions that had dealt with the issue, always, of course, by adopting legislation that does not conflict with the acquis communautaire governing the recovery and resolution of credit institutions. As you know, in the context of the discussions taking place in your Committee regarding the management of Laiki Bank's assets, the Ministry of Finance was invited to address the Attorney General and raise the question of whether it is legally feasible to transfer the management of Laiki Bank's assets to its creditors. In his reply, the Attorney General expressed the opinion that any such action is not legally feasible under the existing legal framework and any legislative regulation to achieve this purpose is contrary to the provisions of the relevant European Directive. Following this development, the Resolution Authority, based on what is required by law and the relevant decrees issued in March 2013 under the Law on the resolution of Laiki Bank, which I recall provide for the sale of operations and assets, proceeds with the procedures for the sale of the bank's assets. I am at your disposal to answer any questions put by Members of the Commission.

Title: Economic governance in the euro area: lessons from the Greek crisis
text: Governor's Address at the Central Bank of Cyprus Seminar for Law Students and Young Graduates Central Bank of Cyprus, 17 February 2017 Welcome! If my colleagues and associates of the Central Bank should forgive me, I address myself first of all to the participants from the universities... groups of law students and their professors. Welcome to the seminar for students and young law graduates organized for the first time by the Central Bank of Cyprus. A seminar based on a mutual teaching method... in other words you have come here to be trained but also to train. Therefore, after the "welcome" I must say in advance a thank you for the knowledge and reflection you come to contribute, each group to the others, as well as to the Central Bank and its associates. You know, for all of us who serve the institution of the Central Bank... officials, employees, external collaborators... your contribution is very important. I will not say anything new saying that the Central Bank has been at the center of developments in the last 4 to 5 years. Developments in the financial sector, both in terms of context and in terms of the implementation of the framework, have been rapid... and I am talking about both Cyprus and the European Union as a whole. In these developments, legal science has a central role. On the one hand, the lawyer is actively involved in the formation of the framework and its implementation. The organizers of the seminar, the lawyers of the internal legal service of the Central Bank, can tell you: I do not know if they would prefer to sit at their desks, receive the questions one by one and give a legal opinion, remotely. I can assure you that the reality of recent years is far from that. The central bank's legal advisers, both internal and external, are responsible for both the framework and its implementation. They are present at the meetings of technocrats, they bring ideas and solutions to the discussions, they dawn over the draft legislation, decrees and conventions. On the other hand, the financial crisis is causing waves of court cases: appeals, lawsuits, criminal cases, arbitrations. Some colleagues within the Central Bank and our external lawyers devote perhaps most of their time to these cases. Decisions on the merits of the disputes have not yet been issued... let our lawyers correct me if I'm wrong... there have been decisions that are interesting from the point of view of procedure, but we have not reached the heart of the financial crisis. There have, however, been some important judgments of the Court of Justice of the European Union in relation to developments in financial institutions. I am referring to the preliminary rulings on Slovenia and Ireland and to the actions brought by Cypriot depositors against the European Commission and the European Central Bank. What has not been adequately covered so far ... and this is exactly where you, the academic community, have a role to play... is the systematization and analysis of the above. Taking a distance from the developments... with the sobriety, objectivity and critical thinking that must distinguish the researcher, the student, the professor... you are called upon to cultivate the theory of banking and financial law and to give a comprehensive theoretical background both to the drafting of new legislation, as well as to the implementer of the framework and ultimately to the judge. I won't keep you any longer, you have a busy schedule for today and for tomorrow. -To say a big thank you to all the employees and associates of the Central Bank who contribute to this seminar. They are also employees from Sectors and Services of the Central Bank outside the Legal Service, some of whom are here and I urge university teams to get in touch with them, to benefit from their knowledge and experience. -... and to wish two things: firstly, that this seminar will be the first annual seminar of the Central Bank for students and young law graduates and, secondly, that the members of the participating groups, students and professors, will remain close to the issues of the Central Bank, that we will see other collaborations emerge after the seminar.

Title: Introductory remarks on the role of statistics in central bank communication
text: Governor's speech at the High Level Conference organised by the National Bank of Belgium on d2Bank Restructuringd3 High Level Conference organised by the National Bank of Belgium on d2Bank Restructuringd3 Speech by the Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus, Mrs Chrystalla Georghadji Belgium, 23-24 February 2017 Distinguished guests, dear participants, 1. Introduction Let me begin by thanking my dear friend Jan Smets for his kind invitation to speak at this high level conference on the very interesting topic of d2Bank Restructuringd3. It is an honour to address such a prominent audience and to share our experiences and lessons from the financial crisis in Cyprus and in particular of the banking crisis in March 2013, which led to a wide restructuring of the banking sector. During the last decade, the world has witnessed a financial crisis of an unprecedented nature, in terms of duration and impact, on the global economy. To preserve and restore confidence in the banking system, state authorities channelled considerable public funds to credit institutions to prevent systemic failures, protect depositors and maintain financial stability. In the EU, substantial state aid was granted in the form of capital and guarantees to restore the solvency and liquidity of banks. This varied from 5% of GDP in Belgium and Spain to 20% of GDP in Cyprus and Ireland. The consequences of such interventions were increased fiscal deficits and a threat to the sustainability of public debt. International standard setters such as the Basle Committee and the Financial Stability Board responded by issuing a series of new standards aimed at strengthening preventive measures and ensuring that, should the worst happen, banks can be resolved or liquidated without use of taxpayersd5 funds and with a minimum impact on the real economy. The Financial Stability Board Key Attributes of Effective Resolution Regimes for Financial Institutions and the European Commissiond5s Proposal for the Recovery and Resolution Directive served as the basis of the Resolution Law, enacted in Cyprus in March 2013, used to restructure Cyprusd5 two largest banks, as one of the conditions for obtaining an EU-IMF financial assistance programme for Cyprus. In the next part of my presentation, I will briefly describe the internal and external causes of the banking crisis in Cyprus as part of the financial crisis which peaked in March 2013. I will then outline the efforts by the Central Bank and other policy makers in Cyprus to address those causes and mitigate their impact on financial stability and the real economy. I will conclude with remarks on the restructuring tools currently available to regulatory authorities in the EU, drawing from the lessons learned and the European Commissiond5s recently submitted risk reduction proposals. 2. The Cyprus crisis and the role of public authorities in bank restructuring For many years, banks in Cyprus operated in a growing economy with a flourishing real estate sector. This, unfortunately, led to banks adopting risk and credit management practices dominated by asset based lending. The consequences of such practices can be disguised in periods of an expanding economy, even appearing as successful as long as property prices continue to rise and demand remains at strong levels. However, in periods of economic recession, practices such as this may lead to a significant increase in arrears and non-performing loans and, as a consequence, a rapid impairment of the capital position of banks. Hence, securing what may appear to be adequate collateral, should never supersede the basic principle governing any lending transaction: the borrowerd5s ability to fully repay their debt from future cash flows. In addition, the two largest Cypriot banks pursued aggressive expansion overseas since early 2000 by extending their banking presence in Greece, followed by a wider expansion in South East Europe, Ukraine and Russia. These expansions added greatly to the size of their balance sheets, which exceeded 400% of the countryd5s GDP, and raised questions about their ability to manage such ambitious strategies. As Greeced5s sovereign debt crisis deepened, the Cypriot banks suffered a higher level of bad debts from their operations in Greece than their domestic business. The banks also experienced a massive flight of deposits from their operations in Greece of nearly db10billion between 2008 and 2012, forcing them to transfer funds from Cyprus to Greece in order to meet their liquidity requirements. The largest losses, however, resulted from the write-down of their large Greek sovereign bond holdings following the Greek debt restructuring programme in late 2011 early 2012, which cost the two largest Cypriot banks nearly 25% of Cyprusd5 GDP. In 2011, most of the international rating agencies downgraded the Cyprus governmentd5s long-term debt rating to below investment grade for a number of reasons. In May 2011, the government of Cyprus lost access to international markets, while a year later the two largest Cypriot banks, unable to find private funds for their recapitalisation, requested state aid. By early July 2012, the Government had injected db1,8billion into one of its systemic banks and was faced with additional requests for capital injection from the other major systemic bank. A few days before, in June 2012, the Government had formally applied to the Eurogroup and the IMF for financial assistance. The agreement reached between Cyprus and its lenders in March 2013 provided that Cyprus would embark on an economic adjustment programme aimed inter-alia at restoring the health of its financial sector. By using the Resolution Law that was passed a few days before the resolution action, the two largest Cypriot banks were resolved and merged with a full write down of shareholders and bond holders as well as a bail-in of uninsured depositors, including pension funds and small businesses. The total amount of deposits that suffered a d4haircutd5 either to absorb losses in one of the banks or recapitalise the other bank before the merger by conversion of deposits into equity, amounted to approximately db8billion or almost 50% of the countryd5s GDP. Cyprus was the first country in the EU d0 and still the only one d0 in which the bail-in of depositors was used to absorb losses and recapitalise its banks. A third systemic bank was recapitalised with the injection by the state of initially db1.5billion raised from the db10billion EU/IMF financial assistance programme (Cyprus actually utilised db7,25billion out of the db10billion). The Eurogroup agreement also provided for the immediate sale of the Cypriot bank branches in Greece to protect financial stability in both countries. The resolution actions on the two largest Cypriot banks, which controlled more than 40% of the domestic retail banking market, was a massive shock for confidence in banks. In light of the emergency situation, and to avoid the collapse of the banking system, the Government adopted capital controls, both internally and externally, i.e. it imposed limits on deposit withdrawals and also it limited the transfer of funds, so as to protect the liquidity of banks. The resolution of the two systemic banks and the introduction of restrictive measures in banking transactions had a disruptive effect on the real economy intensifying the ongoing recession. Economic activity decreased significantly during the period 2012-2014 which, in turn, led to the deterioration of the financial position of borrowers and the consequent sharp increase in non-performing loans. Since then, and following a series of economic reforms and the restructuring of credit institutions, public confidence in banks has gradually been restored. The capital controls were gradually lifted and eventually abolished, less than two years after they were introduced. Public finances were substantially improved and the economy returned to growth in 2015. In March 2016, Cyprus exited the financial adjustment programme with a positive GDP growth and sustainable public finances. In parallel, the Central Bank of Cyprus worked to improve the regulatory and supervisory legal framework and introduced changes to provide banks with debt restructuring tools to deal effectively with the problem of NPLs. Stricter requirements on loan origination as well as on bank governance issues were introduced. Robust foreclosure and arrear management frameworks were adopted to ensure viable restructurings of loans. Finally, a bill is currently being discussed that will provide the legal and taxation framework for loan securitisation. Dealing with NPLs remains the top priority and challenge of both the Cypriot authorities and credit institutions. 3. Lessons learned and policy issues going forward Experience in Cyprus shows that bailing-in of uninsured retail depositors and SMEs can have a big impact on the real economy, financial stability and society in general. The BRRD has acknowledged the importance of protecting these groups of depositors, first by giving priority to their claims compared to other uninsured creditors in the event of liquidation and, second, by excluding them from the bail-inable liabilities that banks are required to maintain to ensure their resolvability, a requirement known as MREL (Minimum Requirements for own funds and Eligible Liabilities). The flexibility by which resolution authorities will approach their task of determining the amount and setup of MREL as well as the period that banks will have to comply with these requirements, will effectively reshape the structure, not only of individual banks within the EU, but also the EU banking sector as a whole. Banks that pursue a traditional deposit-funded model or are still recovering from the crisis with none or limited access to capital markets will be the ones that will struggle to comply. Some of these banks may be forced to change their business model or, if the cost of compliance threatens their viability, to merge with larger banks that are able to meet MREL requirements without a burden in terms of time and cost. Another group of institutions that may be affected by MREL are the relatively small institutions which, in the event of failure, would be subject to insolvency proceedings. These banks may benefit in the short term from not having to meet an MREL requirement, at least not as stringent as that applicable to significant banks. But in the long-run, they will be at a disadvantage in attracting uninsured depositors and creditors that are exempted from bail-in or with claims that rank higher than MREL eligible liabilities. As such, I expect that a number of these banks will find it difficult to operate in the long run and will eventually be acquired by larger banks. The use of public funds in bank restructuring is also an issue that needs to be addressed, particularly in cases of systemic crises. We all agree with the principle that shareholders and creditors are the first to bear the costs of a bank failure, without the need to resort to the use of public funds. However, one needs to assess the feasibility and credibility of resolution actions in significant banks in the event of systemic banking crises. Some argue that if a bailout had occurred in Cyprus, the real economy and banking sector would have been in a better shape than they currently are and the banking sector would have been able to recover quicker. However, there is the counter argument that a bailout rather than a bail-in would have resulted in greater austerity, Greece is an example. Although these questions will most definitely be the subject of future academic studies, my suggestion would be to consider giving Member States the discretionary power to step in, in extraordinary cases of systemic banking crises where resolution measures might have a severe adverse impact on financial stability and the real economy. Moreover, as I mentioned above, the ability to apply a moratorium on the transfer of funds and the withdrawal of deposits was essential for the successful implementation of the resolution measures both before and after the resolution action under the Treaty of the Functioning of the European Union. Member States reserve the right to adopt capital controls in case of systemic crises for safeguarding public order and public security. Nevertheless, supervisors and resolution authorities should also have the discretionary power to suspend payments and deposit withdrawals to prepare for the implementation of resolution action and stabilise the bank following the resolution action. The recent European Commission proposals are moving in the right direction by introducing moratorium powers for both supervisors and resolution authorities. Limiting the moratorium prior to resolution for a short period of time of no more than five working days may be appropriate. However, from our experience, a moratorium of payments following resolution action may need to last longer. Bank restructurings as part of an open bank bail-in need careful and thorough preparation so as to identify promptly and accurately the priority of liabilities, good and bad assets and ensure that adequate systems are in place that safeguard the continuation of provision of critical services after resolution. Furthermore, the rationale of resolution action should be communicated to all those affected and the public at large in a timely manner so as to maintain confidence in the bank. A final issue which needs close attention is litigation that one should expect to be initiated by persons affected by the resolution measures. The Central Bank of Cyprus and the Republic of Cyprus are faced with hundreds of law suits in local courts and international arbitration tribunals from shareholders, bondholders and depositors of the two banks that were placed in resolution in March 2013. In this regard, resolution authorities should ensure that their decisions and actions are legally sound and are thus able to stand up to challenges in the courts. On the other hand, Treaties for the protection of investments in member states should be reassessed in light of the new EU regulatory framework for financial services and the powers given to regulatory authorities over financial institutions and credit institutions in particular. 4. Concluding remarks Concluding, I would like to stress the overriding principle that prevention is better than cure. In this regard, it is imperative that banks operate with sound policies and practices in line with a robust regulatory framework and have in place feasible and credible recovery plans whose implementation would promptly restore solvency and liquidity. In addition, supervisors should have the necessary early intervention powers to restructure banks in a credible way so as to prevent the worst from happening. Thank you for your attention.

Title: Discussion of Central banking in Latin America: changes, achievements, challenges by Klaus Schmidt-Hebbel
text: Presentation by the Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus, Mrs Chrystalla Yiorkadji, at the press conference on the The Bank's Annual Report for the year 2016 Nicosia, 26 May 2017 Distinguished guests, friends, representatives of the Mass Media, dear colleagues, I warmly welcome you to today's press conference for the presentation of the Annual Report of the Central Bank of Cyprus for 2016. Your presence here is an honour for the Central Bank. I will refer, first of all, to the latest developments for the economy and then to the Bank's financial results, which is the main purpose of this press conference. The country's economy showed further improvement in 2016 and credibility towards the banking sector strengthened. March 2016 marked the completion and exit of Cyprus from the three-year economic adjustment programme agreed by the European Commission, the European Central Bank and the International Monetary Fund. 2016, therefore, was admittedly a very important year for our country. In the banking sector, reforms to the regulatory and regulatory framework continued. At the same time, the improvement of banks' capital adequacy and liquidity has significantly helped to strengthen the trust of both local and foreign depositors in our banks. On the basis of the economic adjustment programme, important measures were implemented, which concern fiscal policy, the restructuring and consolidation of the banking sector, as well as the structure of the Cypriot economy. The ratings made by our international lenders under the program were positive, prescribing a promising course for the economy and the Cypriot banking system. However, we still have a long way to go, with many challenges still to exist. 2016 is the second year of remarkable positive growth rate of gross domestic product (GDP) after three years of contraction. This path is expected to continue in the future, provided of course that we remain committed, without any setbacks, to consolidation policies. The budgetary situation has improved, while progress on the restructuring of non-performing loans has been significant but unfortunately unsatisfactory. As a result of the positive developments, Cyprus' access to the markets for financing and the cost of financing have improved significantly, which allowed the continuation of the issuance of government securities on international markets in 2016, despite the fact that Cypriot bonds are still classified in non-investment grade by the rating agencies. Specifically, the issuance of a 7-year bond worth 1 billion. with an interest rate of 3.75% in July 2016 it was the first after the end of the economic adjustment program (March 2016) and after three issues in the period 2014-2015, from which 2.75 billion was raised. More specifically, in terms of economic activity, positive growth rates of 1.7% and 2.8% were recorded in 2015 and 2016, respectively, despite the difficult external environment and the prolonged economic recession that preceded it. The recovery in 2016 was broadly based by almost all sectors of production, with the exception of the financial and insurance services sector due to the sector's ongoing deleveraging efforts. For 2017, leading indicators point to the continuation of economic growth. Specifically, the Conjunctural Index, arrivals and revenues from tourism, the retail trade turnover index and the expenses of credit card holders recorded significant increases in the first months of 2017. For the coming years, further growth of the Cypriot economy is expected at levels around 3%, with growth based on the positive course of investments already launched in the fields of tourism, construction and other business activities, as well as in the export of services. In view of the encouraging macroeconomic developments, the labour market is expected to show further improvement. After peaking unemployment at 17.6% of the labour force in the first quarter of 2015, the unemployment rate fell to 12.9% in the fourth quarter of 2016. A further reduction in unemployment is expected for the coming years, in line with the ongoing economic recovery, the reduction of foreign workers, as well as the flexibility shown by the labour market in relation to wages. The improvement in public finances continued in 2016. The general government fiscal balance as a percentage of GDP recorded a surplus of 0.4% in 2016, compared to a deficit of 1.2% in 2015, a year that included the amount (175 million) of the strengthening of the capital base of the Cooperative Central Bank. [Excluding this amount, the government deficit in 2015 would be reduced to 0.2% of GDP.] Domestic inflation based on the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices remained negative in 2016, reaching -1.2% compared to -1.5% in 2015. It is noted that the negative levels of inflation in Cyprus over the last two years have been more related to exogenous factors, structural changes and reduction of domestic production costs and not to phenomena of self-sustaining vicious circle of price and consumption reductions. Since December 2016, the situation has reversed, with inflation recording successive positive growth rates reaching 1.5% in March 2017, mainly reflecting the significant increases in energy and unprocessed food prices. With regard to the level of inflation desired, I would like to recall that the European Central Bank's objective is inflation below, but close to, 2% over the medium term. In 2016, the domestic financial sector remained on a path of gradual recovery, albeit at a slow pace, amid positive developments for the Cypriot economy. A limiting factor in this process remains the very high level of non-performing loans, which continues to be the biggest challenge for the full recovery of the sector and the domestic economy in general. In this context, while the intensification of restructuring and the continuous and gradual reduction recorded since February 2015 to the existing levels of non-performing loans are assessed positively, but many efforts are still needed by all stakeholders to reach satisfactory levels. I will refer to the efforts of the CBC in more detail below. I note that, from December 2014 to December 2016, non-performing loans have decreased by 3.5 billion. approximately. Total non-performing loans as at 31 December 2016 amounted to 23.8 billion. compared to 27.3 billion as at 31 December 2014. I am always referring to the work on the ground of the entire banking sector. A positive development is also the gradual increase observed both in the demand for and supply of new loans from banking institutions to domestic households and businesses, mainly as a result of the improvement in domestic macroeconomic conditions and the maintenance of historically low lending rates. On the other hand, deleveraging existing loans to the domestic private sector continues at a steady pace. At the same time, the significant recording of deposit inflows, especially by residents of Cyprus and specifically by domestic non-financial corporations, indicates a gradual increase in depositor confidence in the Cypriot banking system. The annual growth rate of deposits of the domestic private sector excluding Special Purpose Entities reached 6.8% in March 2017 compared to 2.8% in March 2016. More generally, as regards the financial sector, the measures that started to be taken since 2013 to strengthen the supervisory and regulatory framework in order to lay the foundations for a healthy and stable banking sector, both in the medium and long term, continued and during 2016. Indicatively, I would like to mention the new Directive "on the Procedures for the Granting and Revision of Credit Facilities of 2016" to replace the existing Directive of 2013. The purpose of the revised Directive is to simplify the procedures for granting and reviewing loans, while maintaining best credit policy practices. The Directive emphasizes the pre-contractual information of borrowers, the implementation of transparent procedures regarding the credit policy of banks and the assessment of borrowers' ability to repay, on which banks must now rely for loans and not on collateral and / or guarantors, as was done in the past. I also mention the amendment of the "Loan Impairment and Provisioning Procedures Directive of 2014 to 2015", the adoption by the House of Representatives of the "Leasing Law of 2016", as well as many other measures that are mentioned in greater detail in the Annual Report. At the euro area level, the Single Supervisory Mechanism has already completed two years of life in November 2016. Over these two years, important steps have been taken to improve the prudential supervision of credit institutions. However, despite the positive developments, the banking sector of Cyprus continues to be under the threat of the most important problem it faces, which is, as I mentioned above, non-performing loans. A problem that is not only a consequence of the economic crisis, but is primarily rooted in the bad banking practices of the past. Despite the notable decrease in non-performing loans observed, mainly during 2016, I consider their reduction to manageable levels to be a primary objective, as their current high level is a limiting factor in banks' ability to support economic growth through the granting of new lending. I would like to make it clear here that the main responsibility for solving this problem lies with the banks themselves. However, as the large amount of non-performing loans raises supervisory concerns and risks, the Central Bank is taking various measures aimed at assisting banks in their efforts to effectively address it. For example, targets are set every three months for the pace of restructuring, supervisory measures are imposed, if necessary, in case of non-compliance with the targets and suggestions are made to the state for mainly legislative measures to better address the issue. Moreover, in our estimation, another important reason for the unsatisfactory reduction of non-performing loans so far is the fact that the new legislative framework (concerning Foreclosures, the Insolvency Framework, the Sale of Loans) has become largely unenforceable or less effective, due to the large number of variations that were added to the original texts. The Central Bank is already working on proposals to amend the legislation on the points that it considers to prevent the implementation of their provisions, which it will submit to the Ministry of Finance with a view to their promotion to the House of Representatives. Another important development, at European level, is the undertaking of initiatives by the European Central Bank in the field of non-performing loans, since this problem is not only Cypriot but also exists in other Member States of the euro area, to a smaller extent, of course, with the exception of Greece. Specifically, the European Central Bank set up in 2016 a committee composed of representatives of the national supervisory authorities (including the Central Bank of Cyprus) and the European Central Bank itself, with the aim of taking initiatives, within the framework of their powers and responsibilities, to accelerate the resolution of the problem of high non-performing loans. As a first step, it was the publication, in the form of a draft, of guidelines to credit institutions on the management of non-performing loans, which set out best practices and recommendations on strategy, governance and procedures, tools for restructuring distressed credit facilities and the assessment of collateral. The guidelines have, this year, been issued in their final form and have been published on the European Central Bank's website. At the same time, the European Central Bank, through the Single Supervisory Mechanism, has asked the banks under its direct supervision, i.e. the significant banks (as we know in Cyprus there are four), to submit, and have already done so, their plans to address the problem of non-performing loans. These plans are now being assessed by the single supervisory teams, with the aim of finalising them in 2017. It is expected that the Single Supervisory Mechanism will then closely monitor the implementation of these plans and intervene supervisoryly where diversions occur. Next, I would also like to refer briefly to the economic environment in the euro area, where both developments in the growth rate of gross domestic product and inflation allow us to be more optimistic than before about the economic prospects of the monetary union to which, as a country, we belong. In particular, the European Central Bank recently proceeded with an upward revision of the forecasts for growth and inflation in the Eurozone. The European Central Bank estimates that the real growth rate of the euro area will stand at 1.7% in 2017, 1.6% in 2018 and 1.5% in 2019. It also forecasts inflation of 1.6% for 2017, 1.5% for 2018 and 1.7% for 2019. On unemployment, the European Central Bank considers that it will continue its downward trend and the unemployment rate is expected to fall to 9.4% this year, to 9.1% in 2018 and to 8.7% in 2019. Based on these and other more detailed and individual data, the President of the European Central Bank, Mr. Mario Draghi, recently stated that the cyclical recovery is constantly strengthening, while downside risks are reduced, noting that the economy is moving in the direction of balancing. As he explained, until recently growth was fragile and uneven, while now it is strong and expanded. As regards inflation, it noted that the criteria for assessing the situation remain unchanged and pointed out that there is still insufficient and satisfactory evidence to deviate from the current policy of monetary easing. He also reiterated that interest rates will remain at current or even lower levels for a long period of time. I would now like to refer, briefly, to the audited financial results of the Central Bank of Cyprus in 2016. The Central Bank for the year 2016 reported reduced profits of 74.2m, compared to 2015 where it recorded a profit of 116m. The decrease is mainly due to the decrease in interest income and, in particular, to the decrease in interest received from the provision of emergency liquidity (ELA). The balance sheet of the Central Bank continues its upward trend and as at December 31, 2016 it stood at 13.8 billion. compared to 31 December 2015 when it was 12.0 billion. This increase results, mainly, from the overall increase in banks' deposits with the Central Bank, which at 31 December 2016 amounted to 9.0 billion. from 7.2 billion on 31 December 2015. As provided by the Central Bank of Cyprus Laws, 80% of the Net Profit of the Bank is transferred to the Fixed Fund of the Republic. Based on this legal provision, an amount of 59.4 million. Euro has already been paid to the Fixed Fund of the Republic. Dear friends, In conclusion, I would like to stress that in 2016, the significant problems, such as the high unemployment rate, the high public sector (107.8% of GDP) and private debt (around 350% of GDP), as well as non-performing loans continued to a large extent to exist and burden the Cypriot economy and, by extension, the citizens. Let's not forget, also, that the debtworthiness of the bonds of the Republic of Cyprus is still rated at a non-investment grade. I am sure, however, that with a strict commitment to a prudent economic policy, together with the prudence and patience of our people, they will yield even better results. Thank you.

Title: Strengthening economic governance in the euro area
text: Welcome address by Mrs Chrystalla Georghadji, Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus on the occasion of the opening of the Cyprus contemporary art exhibition European Central Bank, Frankfurt am Main, 20 September 2017 Your Excellency Ambassador Hadjichrysanthou Dear President Draghi Dear participating artists, Colleagues, ladies and gentlemen, I am delighted to see you all gathered here this evening. While I am often asked to give my views on banking and the economy, I rarely have the opportunity to share my thoughts about art. So I feel honoured to be here today to support this fantastic initiative which embraces the cultural diversity and richness of Europe. The fact that Cypriot works of art are being exhibited at the ECB makes me particularly proud; opening the door to a countryd5s art scene encourages us to broaden our knowledge of its culture and history. By hosting the Cyprus exhibition in its new building, the ECB has made it possible to bring contemporary Cypriot art to a wider audience. The Central Bank of Cyprus, despite its small size, also seeks to encourage and support the arts and culture in Cyprus, promoting their potential at every opportunity. Our central bank has one of the largest and most diverse art collections in Cyprus. The richness of the artwork on display today is testament to the evolution of the Cypriot art scene. Located at the crossroads of three continents -Europe, Asia and Africa d0 Cyprusd5 unique geographic and strategic position has played an important role in its turbulent past and, consequently, on the remarkable development of its artwork, bringing together the vibrant history and cultural heritage of the Middle East and Europe. The contribution of Cypriot artists to Europed5s rich history and present-day life has received international recognition, reinforced by the designation of the city of Paphos, on the western part of the island, as Europed5s Capital of Culture in 2017. Cyprusd5 capital, Nicosia, where the past meets new trends and history is blended with modern art forms, is a vivid example of how the island is constantly reinventing itself, while holding on to core traditions. Over the last decade, a young creative community has emerged and the artwork on display today shows how the Cyprus art scene has flourished with talented artists producing bold work and building bridges between the past and present. Today, Cyprus boasts a plethora of exhibition spaces and galleries which have produced a vibrant art scene that supports the ambitions of artists from various disciplines and enriches community life across the island. This exhibition -showcasing 14 artists from different generations and including some fine examples of art from the Central Bank of Cyprus collection -covers a variety of artistic media, providing a snapshot of the work of contemporary Cypriot artists and giving an insight into the diverse and exciting artistic creations coming from the island. On behalf of the Central Bank of Cyprus, I would like to warmly thank all the participants, and especially the artists themselves, for their commitment and involvement. I am happy to see so many of you here with us tonight. My sincere thanks also go to Mario Draghi and the ECBd5s Art Committee for this wonderful project. The ECB is to be commended for strengthening cultural ties in Europe through its generous support of the arts. I would also like to express my gratitude to the Art Committee of the Central Bank of Cyprus for its invaluable cooperation at all stages. Finally, I would like to say a special thank you to the exhibitiond5s curator, Britta von Campenhausen, for all her hard work and generous support in making this exhibition possible. I wish you all an enjoyable evening.

Title: The timeless significance of today's decisions
text: The evolution of the Cyprus banking system: a reform story and its challenges Keynote speech by the Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus, Chrystalla Georghadji, at the event organised by the Representation of the European Commission in Cyprus and the Central Bank of Cyprus on the d2Achievements and Challenges of the Banking Sector in Cyprus: the European Perspectived3 Nicosia, 30 October 2017 Good morning ladies and gentlemen. Itd5s a pleasure for me to address this event. My speech today will focus on the high levels of non d0 performing loans (NPLs), which unquestionably affect both the financial sector and the real economy. Although significant reforms have taken place, the current level of NPLs still presents a major challenge. I will begin by explaining the drivers behind the high level of NPLs in Cyprus. I will then briefly highlight the impact of these NPLs on banks, the economy and financial stability. Following that, I will explain our NPL resolution strategy, what we have achieved so far and the lessons learned. Lastly, I will present the way forward and in particular our expectations about the key enablers and challenges in the NPL resolution process. Gross NPLs for all banks operating in Cyprus, and which relate to households and non-financial corporations, currently stand at db21,9 billion or 44% of total loans and 120% of GDP. Net NPLs amount to db11,7 billion, which corresponds to 65% of GDP. Around half of the NPLs relate to terminated accounts (denounced loans). The main factors driving the surge in NPLs in Cyprus before the 2013 crisis were the following: Dominance of asset-based lending practices. Lending decisions were largely based on collateral coverage, rather than underlying repayment ability. Very lengthy foreclosure and legal resolution procedures. As a result, lenders had little incentive to take legal action and, instead, preferred to enter bilateral negotiations with the borrower, often resulting in the borrower pledging further collateral or receiving a restructuring. At the same time, there were no consequences for borrowers who failed to repay their loans in the short to medium term. This encouraged a culture of delays in repayment and enhanced moral hazard. Weak provisioning methodologies. Significant under provisioning prevailed due to the delay in the recognition of losses, as fully collateralised loans were not considered impaired. Widespread use of forbearance measures to deal with problematic loans and avoidance of loss recognition. In particular, extensive forbearance and loan modifications with additional collateral were carried out, despite evidence about the inability of borrowers to service their debt. Reluctance of the co-operative sector to pursue aggressive collection and work-out strategies on overdue loans.This was due to the perceived social function of the co-ops. However, this facilitated the development of a non-payment culture. Credit boom from 2005 onwards. Overexpansion of real estate market. This occurred during the period 2004 -2008 and was followed by a significant correction in real estate prices. High level of indebtedness among households and non-financial corporations. This resulted in weak repayment ability when the economy began deteriorating in 2008. Significant exposures to the real estate development sector. Poor risk management practices by banks. Following the Eurogroup decision in March 2013 on Cyprusd5 financial assistance programme and the unprecedented measures implemented to resolve and recapitalise the two largest banks, including a bail-in of uninsured depositors, the asset quality of banks deteriorated rapidly. Specifically, NPLs to legal entities and private individuals in the period June -December 2013 increased by 24% (from db21 billion in June 2013 to db26 billion in December 2013) and the respective NPLs increased from 31% in June 2013 to 42% in December 2013. This surge in NPLs was driven by the resulting negative macroeconomic developments following the resolution of the two systemic banks and the bail-in of db7,8 billion of uninsured deposits, which included the working capital of non-financial corporations and household deposits. What is the impact of NPLs on banks, the economy and financial stability? NPLs have a negative impact on banksd5 profitability by requiring an increase in impairment provisions and by increasing the costs of managing distressed loans. At the same time, NPLs consume more capital due to the implied higher risk weights. In this regard, NPLs are a significant threat to bank viability and solvency. Similarly, banks with high NPLs are more vulnerable to future shocks. High NPLs increase the risk perceived by creditors and Investors and weakens access to capital and funding, both from wholesale and customer deposits, and increases the risk premium that is translated into higher funding costs. Inevitably, the increasing cost of risk and the capital constraints, lead to higher lending rates and tighter credit standards and, therefore, to less available credit. The Cyprus banking system has faced all of the above. The doubts about the banksd5 solvency and viability resulted in a crisis of confidence, whereby deposit outflows threatened financial stability. As a result, besides the recapitalisation measures, capital controls were imposed from 2013 to 2015 in order to safeguard financial stability. Cyprusd5s NPL resolution strategy. As a result of the financial crisis of 2013, the Government requested financial assistance through the EFSF/ESM, and the IMF. The key objectives of the programme were the structural reforms and the fiscal adjustment measures aimed at restoring the macroeconomic imbalances and creating conditions for sustainable growth, full employment and the restoration of market confidence. The banking sector was the third main area of focus of the programme. The NPLs and their drivers that I mentioned earlier were not the only reason for the unprecedented banking crisis in Cyprus. The crystallisation of sizeable losses as a result of the Greek economic crisis and later from the purchase of Greek government bonds by our banks were also catalytic. As a result, a number of unprecedented resolution, recapitalisation and restructuring measures were implemented, aimed at addressing the challenges facing the banking system. In addition, decisive steps were taken to strengthen the supervisory and regulatory framework in order to lay the foundations for a healthy, more resilient and stable banking sector in the medium and long term. For example, the regulatory framework was amended in the areas of internal and corporate governance. The Cyprus authorities, in cooperation with our international partners under the financial assistance programme, have taken comprehensive action for NPL resolution. This has involved the early identification of all impediments and the creation of a comprehensive strategy, giving due consideration to the micro-prudential, macro-prudential and social aspects. In view of the limited fiscal space, the NPL resolution strategy has focused on a private sector approach under three pillars: Strengthened regulation and supervision of banks Reform of the legal framework Creation of a market for distressed assets. Strengthened regulation and supervision of banks Under the first pillar of strengthening regulation and supervision of banks, the first step was an asset quality exercise to ensure appropriate recapitalisation followed by numerous actions in the regulatory and supervisory context as well as market transparency. The regulatory framework was reinforced through new directives in the areas of NPL recognition, provisioning, loan origination and arrears management. At the same time, the supervision of banks was strengthened through enhanced supervisory reporting on arrears management, specific attention to the banksd5 arrears management capabilities and restructuring activity, using internal and external expertise, and the introduction of restructuring targets. Additionally, the establishment and utilisation of a credit register has proved very useful to banks in their NPL management. In September 2013, the Central Bank of Cyprus issued a revised directive on NPLs with regard to the identification of and reporting on NPLs, including definitions of NPLs and forbearance consistent with the European Banking Authorityd5s (EBA) definitions ahead of their implementation across the European Union in September 2014. The directive was later replaced by the EBA Implementing Technical Standards (ITS). In addition, a new directive on loan impairment and provisioning procedures was issued in 2014, aiming to ensure the prudent application of the relevant International Financial Reporting Standards. Specifically, banks are required to have in place adequate provisioning policies and procedures, including collateral valuation, based on conservative assumptions. In this regard, banks are required to identify and monitor an extensive list of trigger events ensuring that all credit facilities requiring provision are correctly and timely identified, and adequate provisions are recognized. Moreover, in the case of a collective impairment process, appropriate probabilities of default and loss given default should be used. In addition to the above, a new directive on loan origination processes and processes of reviewing existing loans was issued in December 2013, prescribing how lending origination and renewal should be assessed, and requiring banks to consider affordability as the primary criterion in their lending decisions. Lastly, the existing loan to value ratio at origination was maintained as a macro-prudential measure and supplemented by a debt service to income ratio to promote prudent borrowing and lending behaviour. A key step in this long journey of regulatory and supervisory reforms was the directive on arrears management, originally issued in 2013 and revised in 2015 to reflect experience from its application. It requires banks to apply efficient and effective strategies, policies, structures, procedures and mechanisms for the management of arrears and the attainment of fair and sustainable restructuring of credit facilities of borrowers with financial difficulties. In order to be able to closely monitor banksd5 restructuring progress, both in terms of volume and quality, banks complete and submit to the Central Bank of Cyprus on a monthly basis detailed templates. In particular, among other things, banks are completing migration matrices and provide information on NPL and restructuring flows, type of restructuring solutions and their performance, cash collection rates, cure rates, default rates and key performance indicators on restructurings and foreclosures. During 2014, on-site inspections to review the quality of restructuring solutions were conducted by our supervisory teams. Another important step was the establishment of a credit register, which is an important tool for off-site and on-site supervision. At the same time, it facilitates more effective management of credit and other related risks from the banks. The credit register has been operational since September 2014. However, the development of the credit register for supervisory, financial stability and statistical purposes is still ongoing. In September 2015, the Central Bank of Cyprus implemented a loan restructuring target framework in an effort to further incentivise banks to increase the volume and improve the quality of restructurings for loans presenting arrears of over 90 days, but also to take proactive action for the loans presenting arrears of over 30 days and to prevent them from becoming non-performing. Each quarter the Central Bank of Cyprus agrees with banks specific targets for the various phases of the restructuring process for two quarters ahead. In case of failure to achieve any of the targets, banks are required to provide detailed explanations and take corrective measures. The Central Bank of Cyprus publishes these targets, on an aggregate basis, together with the past performance of the banks and an explanation for any possible discrepancy between targets and actual performance. If need be, targets are revised. The introduction of the loan restructuring target framework has managed to push banks to increase the pace and sustainability of their restructuring activity However, our analysis reveals that the sustainability of some restructurings depends on the ability to realise the collateral held within the timeframe agreed, which is challenging. Despite the various constraints, banks continue to take measures to improve their restructuring performance. Notwithstanding the above, given the current improvement of the real economy, as indicated by the positive growth rates in real GDP, the CBC is considering revising the current targets by setting targets and key performance indicators for the level of NPLs rather than for the restructuring activity. Reform of the legal framework The second pillar of our strategy was a reform of the legal framework. Under this initiative, the Cyprus authorities have modernised the personal and corporate insolvency framework to make it more efficient and give to borrowers and lenders the right incentives to restructure. Equally important has been the establishment of a new foreclosure framework so as to minimize the time and cost of recovery from assets pledged as collateral. Another supportive initiative was the suspension of tax on real estate transfers agreed under debt restructuring, so as to accelerate foreclosure through encouraging voluntary debt for asset swaps. We also established a voluntary mediation process for restructuring solutions under the Financial Ombudsman. Last but not least, an important area of focus is the efficiency of the judicial system, where efforts are ongoing in enhancing capacity, specialisation and speed. Market for distressed assets The third pillar of our strategy relates to reducing barriers to entry and encouraging a market for distressed assets. A law enabling the sale of loans was enacted while a draft securitisation law is being prepared so as to facilitate the issuance of securities by securitization vehicles. What have we achieved? In a systemic NPL crisis such as the one Cyprus experienced, neither the banks nor the operational environment are ready to deal with NPLs. Initially, our banks were reluctant to admit the lack of capabilities and the need to utilise external expertise. However, since 2013 the banks have gone through complex changes to shift attention from lending to collecting. They have set up centralised and independent arrears management units, including call centres with proactive customer contact strategies to manage early arrears. Supervisory push was catalytic in this process. The extent of the operational changes that were necessary in developing internal NPL management capabilities was unprecedented and have started to produce results. Equally important, but more difficult to achieve, has been the cultural change. Moving away from extend and pretend restructuring such as interest only and grace periods to sustainable restructuring solutions has been a lengthy and challenging process. Staff training, the introduction of restructuring toolkits and performance management systems as well as the introduction of the supervisory loan restructuring target framework supported this process. In 2016 there was a gradually increasing use of sustainable restructuring solutions, such as debt for asset swaps, write offs, split and freeze and interest rate reduction. The reform of the legal framework, although lengthy and not yet fully tested, has succeeded in targeting strategic defaulters, encouraging a repayment culture and incentivising borrowers to negotiate a restructuring. In 2015 the Cyprus economy returned to modest economic growth after three years of contraction, reflecting the progress in implementing the economic adjustment programme. The stock of NPLs in households and non-financial corporates peaked in 2014Q4 at db28 billion and has been gradually declining ever since. It is currently at db21,9 billion. Added to this has been the increase in provisions and write-offs. However, we still have a long way ahead of us before NPLs are no longer a threat to the banks, the economy and financial stability. In our NPL resolution journey we have learned that: NPL resolution is a lengthy process Strong supervisory focus is necessary Structural changes implemented need time to reap fruit, and Coordination among all other stakeholders is essential. The last part of my remarks will focus on the way forward and in particular our expectations about the key enablers and challenges in the NPL resolution process. Cyprus is faced with an extraordinary level of NPLs across all sectors and addressing this will take time. There is no magic bullet. NPLs can decrease through a combination of actions, namely restructuring of viable borrowers and liquidation of the collateral/assets of non-viable borrowers, generous concessions from banks and write -offs, sales of NPLs as well as natural cure. However, the accomplishment of our NPL resolution goal is highly dependent on progress in a number of other areas. Specifically: Economic recovery is important as it will facilitate an improvement in debt servicing capacity and will reduce the probability of default. However, economic recovery on its own will not suffice. Given the magnitude of the problem, further intensification of sustainable restructuring activity for viable borrowers, along with the effective implementation of the refined insolvency and foreclosure frameworks and streamlining of the judicial system will be key drivers. Last but not least, a strong supervisory and regulatory focus with due consideration of the macro-prudential aspect of NPLs rather than focusing solely on NPLs as a micro-supervisory problem should be a key enabler in this process. Supervisory emphasis on sustainable restructuring, liquidation, write offs and disposition of foreclosed assets as well as on the appropriateness of provisioning and collateral valuation practices is warranted. In this regard, the Central Bank of Cyprus welcomes and supports the SSM guidance to banks on NPLs that was published for consultation in September 2016 and the European Council conclusions on the action plan to tackle NPLs in Europe. The journey to NPL resolution is not and will not be easy. The systemic nature of the NPL problem in Cyprus requires a coordinated strategy and completion of the reform agenda.

Title: Cyprus economy: challenges and prospects
text: Address by the Governor of the CBC at the Conference of the Cyprus Economists' Association on Finance Illiteracy Central Bank of Cyprus, 4 November 2017 Ladies and Gentlemen, have a nice day, I am very pleased to welcome you to today's event of the Cyprus Economists Association to discuss an issue that I consider extremely important, Financial Illiteracy. Dr.. Lewis Mandell, one of the pioneers in research on this subject in the United States of America, since the late 1990s has defined financial literacy or literacy as "the ability to use the knowledge and related skills to effectively manage the financial resources of an individual, whose ultimate goal is his financial security, for the rest of his life." Financial illiteracy, therefore, is defined as the absence of the above knowledge and skills. As economists, you study the importance of education for the economy, the need to link between education and work, as well as the prospects that an integrated planning for education can open up for the country, that is, for the country to develop competitive advantages within the global economy. To this subject of study, in our view, the capital of financial literacy should be added. The working hypothesis is that adequate training of consumers, self-employed and potential investors in economic and financial matters, that is, the financial literacy of all those who are not professionals in the financial sector, not only improves their own well-being, but is also an essential factor in the proper and rational functioning of the economy. It is not excluded that through the relevant research it will emerge that financial literacy is a factor of sustainable development of the financial sector itself, that is, that financial institutions develop better and create competitive advantages for the country as the level of financial literacy for the entire population increases. On the contrary, the lack of knowledge in financial matters sometimes leads to excessive risk-taking, with the possible consequence of exacerbating economic crises and then making it difficult to deal with them. The events we have experienced in recent years in Cyprus have highlighted the problem. Individual studies on the subject, such as that of the CUT that will be discussed today, confirm the problem scientifically. Ignorance in financial matters, when it leads to wrong choices and decisions, is a threat to the well-being of citizens. Having in mind the above, and with the aim of contributing to the fight against financial illiteracy and its consequences in Cyprus, the Central Bank of Cyprus is currently conducting a pancyprian sample survey, which aims to measure the level of financial literacy of Cypriots. The ongoing research, which is carried out in collaboration with the CUT and the University of Durham, is part of a broader research framework around the world, on the basis of a questionnaire and criteria set by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). Taking advantage of the findings of the survey, which are expected at the beginning of next year, we will seek as the Central Bank of Cyprus to contribute to the formulation of a national strategy for a more effective treatment of domestic financial illiteracy. This strategy, which will ultimately contribute to financial stability, should rather include targeted financial information campaigns but also interventions of a more permanent nature, such as the introduction of a relevant subject in secondary education. The intention of the Central Bank of Cyprus is to cooperate on the issue with public and private bodies and to mobilize the resources that will be required. In this context, we intend to explore the possibilities of financing this national strategy through the European Structural and Investment Funds. With these thoughts, I would like to wish good luck to today's event, which is the trigger for a series of events of the Cyprus Economists Association to address financial illiteracy and to reiterate that the Central Bank of Cyprus and I personally support in practice the effort for a more informed Cypriot society on economic and financial issues. Developing citizens' skills to better manage their finances is key to the well-being of all. Thank you.
