text: Speech by the Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus at the second Euro-Arab Summit Europe-Arab world relations: problems and prospects through the current situation Athens, 10 November 2017 I would first like to thank the organisers for the invitation to participate in this great Euro-Arab summit. It is an honor to be among distinguished speakers from leading institutions and organizations in the fields of politics, research and entrepreneurship. I confess that I am not an expert on either the Arab world or the Arab world's relations with the European Union (EU). However, coming from Cyprus, an ancient island at the crossroads of Europe, Africa and Asia, with strong historical ties with most countries in the region, I hope that my comments will contribute to a constructive debate towards strengthening Euro-Arab cooperation. One could say that the EU's close relations with the Arab world were dictated by geography. Spain is just 14 km from Morocco, while the second closest country is Cyprus, on the southeastern edge of the EU, 104 km from the coast of Syria. So close that, according to archaeologists, the first people in Cyprus may have come from Palestine. Let us not forget that the name of the continent where we are located also comes, according to Greek mythology, from Europe, princess of Phoenicia, today's Lebanon. The figure of this mythical princess today adorns the banknotes of the common European currency, although it is difficult to trace her at first glance. So, from antiquity to the present day, geography, history, economy and culture connect Europe with the countries of the Arab world. Euro-Arab relations have evolved through strategic, economic and political cooperation at many levels. But there was no shortage of clashes and misunderstandings between the neighbors. We are tragically reminded of the common fate of Europe and the Arab world by the deadly terrorist attacks in France, Egypt, Belgium, Tunisia, Germany, Spain and, more recently, in Somalia. These attacks also show the common challenges ahead of us: to eradicate poverty, injustice, oppression  conditions that create fertile ground for the birth of terrorists  and to win the ideological and moral battle so that the preachers of fanaticism can no longer poison the souls and minds of young people. Security, stability, the strengthening of democracy, economic and social progress are permanent objectives. We should certainly bear in mind that Europe and, even more so, the Arab world are not homogeneous geographical entities. Both regions consist of many different states with different historical experiences, different languages, cultures, religions and ethnicities. That is why we must find ways of achieving the maximum possible consensus despite the difficulties that this diversity inevitably creates. Let us not forget that the ties that unite us are strong enough to support an even closer relationship in the short and long term. Against this background, the EU is shaping and adapting its policies towards the Arab world accordingly. Today the relationship between the two mainly includes two dimensions: an economic one (trade, economy, energy) and a policy on security, stability and migration. As a central banker I will focus for a moment on economic relations between the EU and the Arab world. Perhaps the darkest period in these relations was the period of colonialism, when European colonial powers exploited the natural resources and labor of peoples in western Asia and North Africa, delaying their healthy development. [1] At the same time colonial policies have caused conflicts, in particular the long conflict between Israel and the Palestinians, a conflict that the EU is now trying to resolve, together with other partners, by participating in the Middle East Quartet. The diachronic importance of economic relations between Europe and the Arab world is shown by two products that marked the evolution of humanity: papyrus and oil. Papyrus: the plant used by the ancient Egyptians to make paper for writing, was adopted by the Greeks and then used by the Roman Empire for the production of books that spread knowledge, as well as for correspondence and legal documents, until the replacement of papyrus by other materials. Oil: the fuel that allowed rapid industrialization and development in the 20th century, high production and consumption of energy, rise in living standards. But a fuel that we must replace (to the maximum extent possible), since its excessive use became an incentive for wars, a source of unbalanced economic growth for the countries that produce it, and a source of pollution and climate change for our planet. The EU has been and continues to be the Arab world's main trading partner with around half of total Arab trade. This strong trade relationship between the EU and the Arab world contrasts with the weak intra-Arab trade of no more than 15%. This is the first feature of Euro-Arab relations. We have, as I said before, two heterogeneous groups of states: the first, the EU, is the most economically and politically united/integrated group of states in the world, with intra-Community trade of more than 70% of total trade. And the second group, the Arab states, which is perhaps the least economically integrated region in the world, with intra-Arab trade being below 15% of their total trade. [2] At the same time, various other asymmetries characterise trade between the EU and the Arab world. In recent years, the Arab world has been a stable buyer of a significant proportion of the exported goods of the EU-28, with the percentage hovering around 11%, in contrast to EU imports from Arab countries that are on a downward path, with the percentage falling to 6% in 2016. [3] With the only exceptions being Iraq and Libya, the Arab countries had a trade deficit vis-a-vis the EU last year. EU imports from the Arab countries are dominated by petroleum products, but they have been on a downward trend in recent years. Over the past decade, more than 50% of oil imports into the EU have come from the Arab world[4], while recent figures[5] show that this figure is falling sharply, as Russia has become the EU's main supplier at 30%. The decline in Arab oil exports to the EU can also be viewed positively (as I mentioned before), as an opportunity to reduce dependence on oil. Along with trade in goods, services between the EU and the Arab world are also important, with rates ranging from 5% to 6% of the EU's exported and imported services. [6] If to the above, one adds the millions of Arabs living in the EU, the relationship between the EU and the Arab world becomes even stronger than the data on trade between them suggest. With such a high degree of dependence and interaction, it is not surprising that strengthening cooperation with the Arab world is a timeless and proclaimed objective of the EU. In 1995, with the launch of the Barcelona Process, the improvement of relations with the Arab world was put back as a one of the main objectives of the Union. This aim was initially based on the need to strengthen security and stability in the region, especially in the Mediterranean, but then the whole effort was simultaneously extended towards the promotion of democracy and human rights, as well as economic and social development. This has never been an easy task, but despite the continuing old and new difficulties that arise from time to time, the EU has not ceased to fight for these objectives. In particular, policies to promote democracy and stability in the Arab world are a cornerstone of the EU's policy towards these countries. Let us not forget that the EU itself was created after the Second World War with the primary objective of ensuring peace in a part of the European continent, which has since been significantly enlarged. The economic integration of the Member States is not only an instrument for the economic prosperity of the peoples of Europe but also a strong incentive to ensure political stability and peace. Unfortunately, in recent years, the effort to consolidate democracy and political and economic stability in the Arab world faces new and greater challenges: the political instability in the Middle East and North Africa and in particular the terrorist activity of ISIS in these regions and its strikes in Europe itself, are a permanent source of insecurity and threat to the EU's policies towards the Arab world. In this context, the EU has readjusted its policy and message to Arab countries and has taken many steps towards a more effective European impact on arab world stakeholders  including governments and civil society  with the main aim of countering extremist propaganda and radical Islamic fundamentalism. [7] I am not competent to analyse the new EU strategy towards the Arab world. I would just like to mention that the continuous updating of the EU's policies towards the Arab world, the refugee and migration issue and much more, should be done with the maximum possible consensus among European countries, but also with the maximum possible consensus and understanding with the Arab world. In particular, the issue of migration and refugee flows to Europe but also to politically stable countries of the Arab world, is one of the biggest issues that concerns both sides today. Europe, like the international community in general, has a moral obligation to support the countries that bear the greatest burden of refugee flows, such as Greece on the Side of Europe and Jordan and Lebanon in the Arab world. I would now like, as Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus, to focus a little more on the relations of my own country (which has been a member of the EU since 2004) with the Arab world. Cyprus, like Greece, which is currently hosting this Euro-Arab summit, has vital interests in the Arab world. Cyprus and Greece are geographically located at the crossroads of Europe, Africa and the Middle East and have excellent relations with both Israel and most Arab countries. The prospects for further strengthening relations, particularly in the fields of energy, services, investment and tourism, are particularly positive. As far as Cyprus is concerned in particular, I would like to remind you that the country is in the process of finding and exploring hydrocarbons in its Exclusive Economic Zone. A remarkable natural gas field has already been identified, and discussions and agreements have already taken place between Cyprus and countries of the Arab world, which concern bilateral  and multilateral in some cases  cooperation in the energy sector. At the same time, Cyprus has recovered spectacularly from the crisis that hit the country in 2013, resulting in the restoration of the confidence of entrepreneurs from all over the world to invest in the country. The Cypriot government has established specific incentives to attract foreign direct investment, which already attracts a significant number of foreign investors. Of course, Cyprus has always offered excellent opportunities to investors, especially from the Arab world, not only because of the excellent services and the attractive tax system offered by the island or the well-trained staff active in the market but also because Cyprus, like Greece, is a bridge between Europe and the Arab world. Already, a large number of Arab companies are using the strategic position of Cyprus as a platform for their activities towards the European market. It is therefore not surprising that Arabs and Cypriots continue to maintain a strong relationship that extends to a wider range of activities that cover the economic and social life of our countries. In conclusion, I would like to stress, without losing sight of the importance of the specific figures mentioned above, that we can certainly greatly expand the size of our economic relations. At both national and EU level, strengthening what connects us to the Arab world is a necessity, which above all serves security, stability and prosperity in European society itself. Title: Perspectives on the ongoing crisis
text: Speech by the Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus, Mrs Chrystalla Yiorkadji, at the meeting of the House Standing Committee on Financial and Budgetary Affairs for the 2018 Budget Nicosia, 28 November 2017 Mr President, ladies and gentlemen, Thank you for the invitation to submit my views as Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus on the occasion of the discussion of the State Budget for the year 2018. My presence here is both a duty and a responsibility. Today, the large macroeconomic imbalances that accumulated before the crisis that the country experienced, are gradually and steadily decreasing. Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth has accelerated for three consecutive years and, at the same time, although with some time lag, unemployment is falling. Over the same period, public finances have improved, and the current account deficit has also been significantly reduced in part as a result of improved competitiveness. In the financial sector, banks' liquidity has improved, while the ELA has been fully repaid by the Bank of Cyprus in January 2017. The credibility of the banking sector is increasingly being restored and this fact is reflected in the net inflow of deposits from both residents and non-residents of Cyprus. The significant progress made on structural reforms, along with all the above, has also led to a series of upgrades to the country's credit rating, which is now only one step below the investment grade. As a result, the country returned to the markets on increasingly favorable terms. It is noted that the yield on the ten-year Cypriot bond is currently close to 1.6% compared to 8.4% at the end of 2013. Despite the positive developments, significant problems and challenges remain, such as the particularly high debt of the private (339%) and public sector (104% of GDP), but also the high level of non-performing loans (45%) despite the decrease by 5.5 billion. or 20% since the end of 2014. High debt and non-performing loans make the economy more vulnerable to potential adverse internal or external shocks. Allow me now to list in more detail the progress made to date. After almost four years of recession, and despite the unfavorable external environment, GDP recorded positive growth rates of 2% and 3% in 2015 and 2016, respectively. According to the most recent data for the first nine months of 2017, economic growth recorded a further improvement, reaching 3.8% year-on-year and with seasonally adjusted data. It is important to note that growth is recorded in most economic sectors, but mainly in the sectors of Wholesale and Retail Trade, Hotels and Restaurants (tourism), Construction as well as Professional, Scientific and Technical Activities. The exception is the financial and insurance sector and this arises as a consequence of the ongoing deleveraging of loans. This cannot be considered as a totally negative element since the deleveraging of loans helps to reduce high private debt. Based on the forecasts of the Central Bank of Cyprus, as published in the Economic Bulletin of June 2017, GDP for the whole of 2017 was expected to reach 3.1%. Domestic demand (private consumption and investment) and to a lesser extent net exports of goods and services were expected to make a significant contribution. However, based on recent economic developments, such as the results of the first half of the year and the excellent tourist year, the macroeconomic forecasts are revised upwards in the context of the current round of forecasts of the Central Bank of Cyprus that will end in December 2017 and it is now expected that GDP this year will grow at rates close to 4%. It should be noted that the International Monetary Fund, in its latest forecasts for the Cypriot economy (October 2017), refers to real GDP growth of 3.4% in 2017, to 2.4% in 2019 and to 2.2% in 2022, while according to the most recent forecasts of the European Commission (November 2017), economic growth is expected to reach 3.5% in 2017, and decline in 2018 and 2019, while remaining strong at 2.9% and 2.7%, respectively. In line with positive macroeconomic developments, the labour market is expected to make a further correction. According to data from the Labour Force Survey, unemployment as a percentage of the labor force in the second quarter of 2017 decreased to 10.6% compared to the first quarter of 2015 when it then peaked at 17.6%. At the same time, the data on registered unemployment show a further decline in the third quarter of 2017. Employment continues to perform positively, recording an annual increase of 2.8% for the whole of 2016 and 3.1% for the first half of 2017. In terms of forecasts, the unemployment rate is expected to decline further, reaching single digits in 2018, mainly due to the ongoing recovery in employment and the flexibility shown by the Cypriot labour market in relation to wages during the crisis. As regards prices, since December 2016, inflation in Cyprus has returned to positive levels, after three consecutive years of annual negative rates. More specifically, in the first ten months of 2017, harmonised domestic inflation reached 0.8%, compared to a decrease of 1.4% in the corresponding period of 2016. An important fact is also the continuous upward trend recorded by core inflation, i.e. inflation that does not include energy and food prices, which stood at 0.4% in the first ten months of 2017 from -0.9% in the corresponding period of last year. The upward trend of both harmonised domestic inflation and core inflation is largely due to the strengthening of the domestic economic environment and the recovery in service prices, especially in tourism services due to the high demand observed in the sector. In addition, the increase in overall inflation is partly due to the increase in energy prices, as a consequence of increased oil prices. Domestic inflation is expected to continue to move at even higher levels in 2018, mainly due to a further strengthening of economic activity, but also to a small expected increase in wages. In addition, a boost to rising prices may also come from a possible further rise in the price of oil. I would remind you that the European Central Bank's objective is price stability, which is defined as achieving inflation below, but close to, 2%. With regard to public finances, and especially in relation to the Budget for the year 2018, I would like to note the following: This Budget is the second to be submitted after the exit of the Republic of Cyprus from the economic adjustment program and presents a positive picture for the future, with the implementation of small budget surpluses and with an emphasis on development expenditure. The macroeconomic projections, on which positive fiscal developments are based, are considered reasonable for 2017, based on the available data. For the following years, the budget forecasts seem to be characterised by a more conservative character for reasons that are rather precautionary, especially if we take into account the significant investments by both the public and private sectors, which are expected to contribute significantly to the rate of economic growth in the medium term. Cyprus' fiscal performance, both in the fiscal and primary balance (which is the fiscal balance excluding the payment of interest), is one of the best in the entire European Union, as a result of the significant financial correction that has been maintained for a number of years through the economic adjustment programme. Public debt, which peaked at 107.5% in 2015, remains high. According to the submitted Budget, public debt is expected to decline, reaching 82% of GDP in 2020. An important role in this reduction, in addition to the high primary surpluses, is also played by the prepayment of part of the old debt to the Central Bank of Cyprus by 0.6 billion. in 2017, a development that contributes to reducing the cost of the borrowing rate. Despite the positive results, there must be no complacency that leads to reckless increases in state spending, as we must take advantage of the current period of recovery to improve public finances and at the same time institutionalise insurance safeguards to maintain them on a safe basis. Turning now to the developments in the country's banking sector, it should be noted first of all that the macroeconomic conditions we are experiencing are also supported by the gradual improvement of the sizes of the domestic financial sector, despite the challenges that the sector is facing. Characteristically, from the beginning of the year until today, total deposit inflows of 1.0 billion have been recorded. The continuation of deposit inflows, mainly by residents of Cyprus, reflects the gradual recovery of depositor confidence, as well as the restoration of the stability of the Cypriot banking system. At the same time, there is a steady upward trend in the provision of new loans, supported by historically low domestic interest rates, robust macroeconomic conditions and, by extension, increased demand. Nevertheless, the increase in new borrowing is covered by the continued deleveraging of existing loans, resulting in an annual growth rate of total loans in September 2017 recording a decrease of 1.8%. This trend is expected to continue in the next period, since the amount of total private borrowing (residents and non-residents of Cyprus) in relation to the size of the economy, expressed as a percentage of GDP, is still very high (376% at the end of 2016). It should be noted, however, that households and domestic non-financial institutions have overall recorded a small positive growth rate of total borrowing since the second half of 2017. In addition to the above concerning lending, I would also like to note the further strengthening of the balance sheets of banking institutions, either through improved capital ratios or through increased provisions. This improvement is a necessary condition for maintaining and strengthening the confidence of depositors and investors in general. The improvement in banks' financial position, as well as the positive horizon, are also recorded by international rating agencies, which, however, also record the challenges that banks face. I would also remind you on the positive side of the full repayment of the ELA by the Bank of Cyprus and the independence of the funding of banks by the European Central Bank, which demonstrates the return of all our credit institutions to healthier and more desirable forms of raising funding. Despite all the positives that occur, the size of the problematic portfolio of banking institutions, combined with the supervisory regulations and requirements, outline the huge challenges that our banking sector still has to face in the coming years. The level of non-performing loans (NPLs) continues to be the main problem afflicting the banking sector, despite the progress made in recent years. Specifically, from the end of 2016 until July 2017, there was a decrease of 1.5 billion. I should also mention that the major banking institutions (4) that are directly supervised by the European Central Bank have submitted their strategy to both the Central Bank of Cyprus and the European Central Bank on the amount and manner of the reduction of non-performing loans for the next three years. These strategies are elaborated and analysed by supervisors and discussed with banks. Upon completion of this process, it is expected that the supervisor will proceed with suggestions / claims to the banks and possibly, to target setting. The Central Bank is awaiting the results of this analysis in order to proceed, in consultation with the European Central Bank, to its own formulation of the target setting framework. Despite the decline in non-performing lending, the pace of decline shows a downward trend, with the number of restructurings having decreased in recent months. This is an indication that the portfolio of non-performing loans, which has not been restructured so far, cannot be addressed through restructuring alone. An important reason for this is the amount of terminated non-performing loans (i.e. loans that have been transferred to the banks' legal department for measures) reach around 50% of all remaining non-performing loans. To tackle the problem, banking institutions need to move forward with more radical and decisive solutions. I stress that the responsibility for finding solutions that radically addresses the problem lies with the banks themselves, without of course this meaning that the Central Bank of Cyprus remains uninvolved. The Central Bank of Cyprus is in constant contact with the banks but also with the European Central Bank to find effective solutions to deal with the problem, and I must say that this effort has been intensified as it is recognized that the time delay in solving the problem is to the detriment of all those involved with potentially negative consequences for the economy. I understand that there is also the social/humanitarian aspect of the issue concerning the primary residence, to which we will have to show the appropriate sensitivity, but there are also several cases that are not related to the primary residence or cases where the primary residence is put forward as an excuse for not repaying the debt. International credit rating agencies refer to the improvement in the financial position of our banking institutions compared to previous years, but also refer to the fact that their financial position, as reflected today, still remains weak due to the weight of non-performing loans. With regard to supervisory arrangements and requirements, I mention the introduction of a new international accounting standard from 2018 (IFRS9), according to which banks should also make significant provisions for performing loans. In addition, capital requirements are constantly increasing, creating pressures for new capital enhancements. In conclusion: Our economy has achieved a lot in recent years, which we must preserve with great care, because there are still many problems and challenges that remain. At the same time, we are in the run-up to the elections. It is, of course, legitimate for economic issues to be at the heart of the election debates. This is how it happens in any democratic, free society. This, however, must be done in a way that does not undermine what we have all achieved together, people, institutions, government and opposition to date, but also does not underestimate our future obligations and responsibilities. The sacrifices of the Cypriot people have been very great in recent years and woe betide us if we do not all stand up to these sacrifices.

Title: Policy challenges in the euro area
text: Address by the Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus at the green public procurement awards ceremony Nicosia, 15 December 2017 Honourable Ministers of Agriculture, Rural Development and environment, and education and culture, dear co-organizers and guests, I welcome you to the Central Bank of Cyprus, which is hosting for the second time the award ceremony for green public procurement as well as for products with the European Ecolabel. I feel very happy and honored because together I welcome the students who are awarded today for their activities on the European Ecolabel. When one hears the term 'green public procurement' for the first time, one might wonder what makes a public contract green, and why we want public procurement to be green. Green public procurement includes environmental criteria in the tendering procedure and in the evaluation of tenders, so that the public sector selects goods, services and projects with less negative effects on the environment and our health. The public sector is the most important buyer-consumer in the countries of the European Union (with a percentage of around 15-19% of the gross domestic product). It can thus not only set a good example, but contribute practically to the transition to a sustainable, circular economy. Green public procurement incentivises and opportunities for the production of new products, environmentally friendly, and for green jobs. In Cyprus, green public procurement and green products are of particular importance. I would like to give you at least 7 reasons for this: Because unemployment casts a shadow over the future, with 1 in 4 young people without employment. Our young people need quality, green jobs in their homeland and the homeland needs young people to progress. We need green public procurement, because with green contracts we save money, accounting for costs over the lifetime of the product. Economy and ecology go hand in hand. An example is the recent tender of the Municipality of Nicosia for street lighting with LED luminaires, which have a higher market price but operate with less energy, for more years, resulting in a 50% reduction in lighting costs. The LED bulbs you see here are even greener since they take some of the energy from photovoltaics. Public contracts and products must be green, because Cyprus is one of the worst EU countries in waste production and it is a crucial need to reduce solid waste. Green public procurement is vital because air pollution kills 650 people a year in Cyprus (in the EU-28, more than 400,000), according to a study by the European Environment Agency. In our cities, the main source of pollutants is vehicles that burn petrol or diesel, while the implementation of sustainable transport policy is delayed. I hope that the directive proposed by the European Commission on the promotion of the purchase of clean vehicles by the public sector will help. We want green public procurement, because organic farming gives bright prospects to Cypriot agriculture. By choosing organic products, the public sector helps to make these prospects a reality. We need to green public procurement, because our forests are at risk: from drought, man-made fires, and some not-so-green public contracts for construction. And why climate change is not a science fiction scenario, it's already here. The desertification of Cyprus seems to have begun, extreme weather events in our neighborhood and elsewhere. Alone on a small island on the edge of the Mediterranean we cannot influence the large countries that are destroying the planet; along with those who honour the Paris Agreement, perhaps we can. Certainly, however, public bodies can and must limit their own broadcasts. Let me repeat two messages sent on 12 December by the French President: 'To save the climate, every player in society needs to be committed every day.' "Ennemble, nous allons gagner la bataille" (Together we can win the battle). With these thoughts, I congratulate those who will be awarded today, especially the students, and I wish even better environmental performance in the future.

Title: Annual Report of the Central Bank of Cyprus for the year 2011
text: Address by the Governor of the CBC, Mr. Chrystallas Yiorkadji at the event of the Cyprus University of Technology on the subject of Financial Illiteracy CUT, Limassol, 13 February 2018, 7 p.m. Ladies and Gentlemen, I am particularly pleased with the invitation to address today's event organized by the Department of Commerce, Finance and Shipping of the School of Management and Economics of the Cyprus University of Technology on the very important topic, Financial Illiteracy. An issue that concerns all of us and especially the Central Bank of Cyprus which has taken initiatives in the promotion of knowledge and skills in financial matters, mainly through collaborations with public and private bodies. Today's event takes place on the occasion of the publication of a position for the elaboration of a doctoral dissertation on Financial Literacy at the University of CUT with a scholarship from the Cyprus Cooperative Bank. We congratulate this initiative, which is commendable, and we look forward to others to come. These actions will only bring benefits to the Cypriot society because they will be the basis for targeted actions so that the citizen acquires the necessary skills for the effective management of his financial resources, which will ensure financial security. As economists we study the importance of education for the economy, the need to link between education and work, as well as the prospects that an integrated planning for education can lead the country to gain competitive advantages within the global economy. To this subject of study, in our view, the chapter on financial literacy should be added. The working hypothesis is that adequate training of consumers, self-employed and potential investors in economic and financial matters, that is, the financial literacy of all those who are not professionals in the financial sector, not only improves their own well-being, but is also an essential factor in the proper functioning of the economy, creating competitive advantages for the country. On the contrary, the lack of knowledge in financial matters sometimes leads to excessive risk-taking, with the possible consequence of exacerbating economic crises and then making it difficult to deal with them. Everyone will agree that ignorance in financial matters, when it leads to wrong choices and decisions, is a threat to the well-being of citizens. Having in mind the above, the Central Bank of Cyprus is currently conducting a pancyprian sample survey, which aims to measure the level of financial knowledge of Cypriots. The ongoing research, which is carried out in collaboration with the CUT and the University of Durham, is part of a broader research framework around the world, on the basis of a questionnaire and criteria set by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). Utilizing the findings of the survey, we will seek, as the Central Bank of Cyprus, to contribute to the formulation of a national strategy for a more effective treatment of domestic financial illiteracy. With these thoughts, I would like to congratulate, once again, the Cyprus University of Technology, which has pioneered the promotion of Financial Literacy, as well as the Cyprus Cooperative Bank that will finance this doctoral position for the next three years. Thank you. Note: The speech on behalf of the Governor of the CBC was read by the spokesperson of the CBC, Mrs. Aliki Stylianou.

Title: Assumption of duties
text: Address by the Governor of the CBC, Mr. Chrystallas Yiorkadji at the second event organized by the CBC and the Cyprus Economists Association on "The Financial System of Cyprus: Challenges and Prospects" Central Bank of Cyprus Amphitheater, 10 March 2018, at 10:00 a.m. Ladies and Gentlemen, I am particularly pleased with today's event, which is being organised for the second time by the Central Bank of Cyprus and the Cyprus Economists Association, as part of the information campaign to tackle financial illiteracy in Cyprus. An issue that, as I have said on other occasions, concerns all of us and especially the Central Bank of Cyprus, which has taken initiatives in the promotion of knowledge and skills in financial matters, mainly through collaborations with public and private bodies. Today, we will have the opportunity to listen globally to what has been done in the financial system of Cyprus in recent years, mainly after the economic crisis of March 2013 and I especially thank the speakers who accepted our invitation. The challenges and prospects are there and we are all experiencing them. In this context, it is easy to target institutions and personalities. It is certainly not as easy to take responsibility for each of us and try to solve the problems. I can assure you that this is what we here at the Central Bank are doing: we are trying to delve deeper into the problems, to reflect and to find solutions. Many problems have arisen and continue to exist after the economic crisis of 2013, but as we have said many times, there has also been significant progress. The Central Bank of Cyprus will continue to monitor the situation closely and take the necessary measures so that confidence in the system is not compromised. At the same time, at the level of the euro area, the Single Supervisory Mechanism has taken important steps towards improving the prudential supervision of credit institutions. Because there is, not unjustly, a big discussion about Non-Performing Loans, I would very soon like to mention that their reduction, in the last three years, was not the targeted one. The Central Bank considers that their further reduction to manageable levels continues to be a primary objective. International experience has shown that the immediate recognition of non-performing loans and the decisive adoption of measures to address them brings significant benefits as it contributes to the proper functioning and shielding of the financial system and the recovery of the real economy. We should be correct and beneficial when making an evaluation or criticism. Our aim should be to make progress and correct the wrong haves, not just to be liked. I believe that after what our country has gone through, we must have this attitude and protect the citizens. That is why we attach great importance to financial literacy. The lack of knowledge in financial matters sometimes leads to excessive risk-taking, exacerbating economic crises and then making it difficult to deal with them. Ignorance in financial matters, when it leads to wrong choices and decisions, is a threat to the well-being of citizens. With this, I welcome you, once again, to today's event. Thank you.

Title: Greetings at ETYK
text: CBC Governor's Welcome Address at the Annual General Meeting of the Association of Cyprus Banks Nicosia, 19 June 2018 Honourable Members of the Board of Directors of the Association of Cyprus Banks, dear friends, It is my pleasure and honour to be with you today at the Annual General Meeting of the Association of Cyprus Banks, founded in 1969 as the coordinating body of its member banks. The role of the Association was subsequently upgraded and today it is the representative of the banking sector in Cyprus and an essential partner in shaping policy on banking issues, without disrupting the relationship between the supervisor and supervised entities. The role of the Association in expressing the views of the banking sector and in coordinating its members was particularly important during the financial crisis in 2013. The Association has helped and still continues to help the CBC with recommendations in formulating policy to address the serious challenges faced by the banking sector. Despite the improvement seen in the banking sector since 2013, there are still important issues that need to be addressed and which the Association can help resolve. First, as we have said on many occasions, we have to tackle the very serious problem of non-performing facilities (NPFs) which, despite the significant decline in the last two years, still continue to severely affect the banking sector. The current level of NPFs constricts the performance of banks as it reduces their profitability, while consuming a significant amount of bank capital and resources (personnel and systems) that could be used for core banking activities. As a result, the contribution of the banking sector to the recovery of the economy through new lending is limited. Thus, accelerating the reduction of NPFs continues to be a primary objective, which requires the cooperation of all stakeholders. Finding ways to deal with the problem is certainly the responsibility of the members of the Association. However, the CBC will, as it has done so thus far, continue to work closely with the banks to provide guidance and any assistance. Another major challenge for our banks is to restore profitability through a viable business model. Around 80% of Cyprus banks' income comes from net interest income. Additionally, as I have already mentioned, the high levels of NPFs are an obstacle to the profitability of banks, as there are serious doubts about the realisation of interest income, despite such income being included in their financial statements. Furthermore, low interest rates, which are expected to continue in the medium term, and the low returns on low-risk investments (e.g. government bonds), as well as the supervisory requirements and regulations, which increase both the capital and operating costs of banks, combined with the competitive environment for new financing, are the main challenges for new lending. These challenges impact on the setting of interest rates and the measurement of risk, which in turn affect the profitability and asset quality of credit institutions. Another significant challenge are the prudential regulations and requirements, such as the introduction in January of this year of the new International Financial Reporting Standard (IFRS9) for making provisions, the introduction of the minimum required eligible liabilities and various other requirements, which are expected to burden the banks and make the need for close cooperation between the Central Bank and the Association even more imperative. I would like to thank the Association for the honour in inviting me to speak today. I wish it every success in its endeavours to ensure the well-being and progress of the banking sector.

Title: Banks and Development
text: Address by the Governor of the CBC, Mr. Chrystallas Yiorkadji at the 2nd Economic and Social Policy Forum on "The problem of Financial Illiteracy and the policies required to address it" Central Bank of Cyprus, Nicosia, 2 November 2018 Ladies and Gentlemen, It is with great pleasure that today I address the forum organized by the Department of Commerce, Finance and Shipping of the Cyprus University of Technology in collaboration with the Central Bank of Cyprus on the important issue of financial illiteracy and the policies needed to address it. An issue that concerns all citizens and institutions of the country, but especially the Central Bank of Cyprus. That is why we attach due importance to the problem and have in practice taken initiatives to promote financial literacy, in the sense of information on financial matters, mainly through collaborations with public and private bodies. Today's Forum focuses mainly on actions and the creation of a framework of guidelines that will help the state and institutional organizations to set priorities and formulate policies to address financial illiteracy. I congratulate all those involved in organising this forum, and I look forward to other similar actions to be organised in the future. These actions offer significant benefits to the Cypriot society since they are the basis for targeted efforts in order to create the appropriate conditions through which the public will have the opportunity to be equipped with the appropriate knowledge for more rational management of its financial resources. A more efficient and responsible management that leads to greater financial stability and security. As the Central Bank, we attach great importance to education and information on the economy and financial issues, because the problems that financial illiteracy causes to the economy and society at large are unfortunately not negligible. The interconnection between financial education and work can help our country to gain competitive advantages and a better position in the European Union, the Eurozone, but also within the global economy in general. In this context, the role of financial literacy is therefore very important. On the contrary, the lack of knowledge in financial matters leads in many cases to the assumption of excessive risk and the possible creation of economic crises that are difficult and at a very heavy cost to deal with. Insufficient knowledge in financial matters, therefore, leads to wrong choices and unsustainable, financially, decisions, with very negative consequences for everyone. Taking into account these realities, the Central Bank of Cyprus has conducted, as announced, a pancyprian sample survey, for the quantitative recording of the financial knowledge of Cypriots, the results of which will be made public shortly. The survey, which was carried out in collaboration with the Cyprus University of Technology (CUT) and the University of Durham, is part of a broader research framework around the world, on the basis of a questionnaire and criteria set by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). Utilizing the findings of the survey, we will seek, as the Central Bank of Cyprus, to contribute to the formulation of a national strategy for effective treatment of domestic financial illiteracy. With these thoughts, I would like to congratulate, once again, all the participants in the actions to enhance financial literacy in our country, and especially the Cyprus University of Technology, which plays a leading role, in cooperation with us, in the whole effort, as well as to wish the best possible utilization, with the always full support of the CBC, of what has been done so far in this direction. Thank you.

Title: Challenges and prospects of the Cypriot economy
text: Address by the Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus at the green public procurement awards ceremony Central Bank of Cyprus Amphitheatre, 23 November 2018 Dear Minister of Agriculture, Rural Development and Environment, dear Government Representative on behalf of the President of the Republic, dear representative of the Minister of Education and Culture, dear co-organizers and guests. I welcome you to the Central Bank of Cyprus, which is hosting the green public procurement awards ceremony for the third time. I feel great joy and honor for the students who are awarded today in the framework of the environmental action "Think, Act, Change and you. We say no to plastic bags." What is a "green public procurement"? They are contracts that include environmental criteria in the tendering procedure and in the evaluation of tenders, so that the public sector chooses goods, services and projects with less negative effects on the environment and our health. It can thus not only set a good example, but also make a practical contribution to the transition to a sustainable, circular economy. Green public procurement provides incentives and opportunities to produce new, environmentally friendly products, creating "green" jobs. Regarding the effort to reduce environmental pollution from plastic bags, Cyprus has implemented the relevant legislation since July 1, 2018. The use of plastics and especially plastic bags is not only a major environmental problem and a risk to public health, but also constitutes a deadly threat to the fauna of the marine environment. Plastic bags are considered one of the deadliest marine litters as ecosystems change. Indicative are the data that show that plastic bags make up 1/3 of marine litter. At least 269,000 tons, that is, five trillion plastics, swim in the world ocean, while 8 million new tons enter annually. Their division into much smaller pieces, microplastics, makes their removal from the marine environment almost impossible. While plastic bag, it takes a second to produce, 20 minutes on average to be used, it nevertheless causes infection for more than 450 to 500 years that it takes until it decomposes. There are many examples. The case of a sperm whale, which washed up dead. Her death was caused by starvation, since her stomach was filled with plastic bags and plastic packaging of everyday products because she could not metabolize them. So these were petrified, leading her to death. 66% of sperm whales have plastic residues in their stomachs, while other marine mammals, such as cinderellas, are also threatened. There are also many turtles, which drowned, swallowing waste, plastic bags or lines that solidified in their stomachs leading them to starvation. Another sad example is the dramatic reduction in the life expectancy of the seal, which chooses the Shores of the Mediterranean in order to reproduce, has been caused by plastic bags. As I have said, this is a very serious risk to the marine ecosystem, but also to public health, and we still do not know exactly the consequences, as this is a phenomenon of the last fifty years. As the United Nations has admitted, in case the situation is not reversed, the Mediterranean is expected to turn into a "soup made of plastic", which, through the ingestion of microplastics by fish, but also plankton, with all that this entails. What we can, for sure, do is limit our own use of plastic bags. With these thoughts, I congratulate those who are awarded today, separately the students, and I wish even better environmental performance in the future.

Title: Towards a European banking union
text: Speech by the Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus, Mrs Chrystalla Yiorkadji, at the meeting of the House Standing Committee on Financial and Budgetary Affairs for the 2019 Budget Nicosia, 3 December 2018 Mr President, ladies and gentlemen, First of all, I thank you for the invitation to submit my views as Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus on the occasion of the discussion of the State Budget for the year 2019. It is a duty, an honour and a responsibility to be before you today. The Cypriot economy since 2015 shows continuous positive growth rates, preceded by almost four years of recession. In fact, in 2016, GDP recorded the highest growth rate since 2008 and stood at 4.8%. According to the latest seasonally adjusted data for the first nine months of 2018, economic growth reached around 3.8% year-on-year. GDP growth is mainly due to investment and the path of private consumption. Large private investment, with a significant share of financing through foreign capital, has already begun and is planned to be completed in the coming years. Projects such as renewable electricity production infrastructure, residential, commercial and mixed developments, marinas, luxury hotels and the casino underline the dynamics and credibility of the Cypriot economy and enhance its positive prospects. The strengthening of confidence in the Cypriot economy is also reflected in the recent upgrade of the country's credit rating to investment grade by three rating agencies. From a sectoral point of view, development is broad-based. The exception is the financial and insurance sector as a consequence of the ongoing deleveraging of loans. This, however, cannot be considered as a completely negative element, since the deleveraging of loans reduces at the same time the high private debt. The private debt ratio is particularly high in Cyprus compared to other countries, so its reduction is undoubtedly an important factor that will help households and businesses to rationalize their balance sheets and move with greater financial security and certainty in the future. In connection with the positive macroeconomic developments and according to data from the Labour Force Survey, unemployment in the second quarter of 2018 decreased to 7.3% compared to the first quarter of 2015, when unemployment peaked at 17.6%. In fact, the registered unemployed, for whom data are available until last October, continue to decline significantly, reaching the levels of 2009. At the same time, employment continues to perform positively, recording an annual increase of 3.8% for the whole of 2017 and 4.3% for the first half of 2018, further demonstrating the dynamics of the economy. Based on the forecasts of the CBC's technocrats, as published in the Economic Bulletin of June 2018, high growth rates of the Cypriot economy are expected for the period 2018-2021, due to the positive course of domestic demand. In the context of the current round of forecasts of the CBC, which will be completed in a few days, both the most recent data and the improvement of expectations regarding the investment prospects opening up in various sectors, confirm the positive assessments for the course of the Cypriot economy. In 2018, GDP is expected to grow by around 4%, while in the coming years it is expected to slow down slightly, while continuing to record high growth rates. With regard to public finances, and especially in relation to the Budget for the year 2019, I would like to note the following: This Budget is the third to be submitted after the exit of the Republic of Cyprus from the economic adjustment program and presents a positive picture for the future, with the implementation of strong budget surpluses. The macroeconomic projections, on which positive fiscal developments are based, are assessed as realistic for both 2018 and subsequent years. In general, the fiscal performance of Cyprus, both in fiscal and primary balance (which is the fiscal balance excluding the payment of interest), appears prudent, as a result of the implementation of the state budget in relation to increased revenues due to the growth of economic activity. According to the Ministry of Finance, the supplementary budget for 2018 is not expected to affect the fiscal target set for the year in question. The course of revenues due to GDP growth but also the collection of non-recurring revenues in view of the arrears plan, strengthen the expected fiscal results. However, positive developments in terms of revenues must not lead to complacency and reckless increases in government spending. Public debt, which peaked at 108% in 2015, is still very high. According to the submitted Budget, the public debt is expected to continue its downward trend, reaching 84.6% of GDP in 2021, despite the burden due to the special issuance of government bonds for the Cyprus Cooperative Bank in the context of the completion of the transaction for the sale of part of its assets. Strong economic growth rates, as well as high primary surpluses, which absolutely must be maintained, play an important role in this reduction. I would like to stress at this point that the positive course of budgetary and GDP must in no way cause complacency and derail efforts to maintain prudent fiscal policies and implement the structural reforms that are under way. Sustaining these efforts should, in addition to further supporting the growth rate, shield our economy from imponderables and should therefore be a high political priority. Turning now to the developments in the banking sector, I would like to remind you that in my speech last year in parliament, I referred to the challenges of Cypriot banking institutions in relation to the treatment of Non-Performing Loans (NPLs). And I had stressed the importance that international rating agencies give to the issue in question and the intensification of the effort that needed to be made. I also referred to the introduction of the new Ifrs9 International Accounting Standard. And indeed, the main developments that took place in the Cypriot banking sector during 2018, concerned the above issues. Starting from the new IFRS9 International Accounting Standard, which has been in force since 1 January 2018, I would like to mention the increased provisions that banks must now create for their entire loan portfolio, given that for loans of increased risk, provisions should be created that take into account the total expected losses of a loan until its maturity. The introduction of the standard in question is expected to reduce the time delay in the recognition of losses by banks in their portfolios, avoiding to the extent possible the large surprises in capital deficits observed during the financial crisis at both European and international level. In relation to the treatment of NPLs, 2018 could be characterized as a landmark year towards the deleveraging of banks' balance sheets by NPLs through sales. Also, 2018 was a year of significant consolidation of the Cypriot banking sector with the absorption of specific assets and liabilities of the Cyprus Cooperative Bank by Hellenic Bank, and the operations of USB by Astrobank. In addition, I note the changes in the relevant legislative framework for the resolution of NPLs and the upcoming government plan Estia, which provides for the subsidy of part of the loan installment by the state and banks for specific borrowers. The deleveraging of banks' balance sheets with NPL sales began in June 2018 with Hellenic Bank completing the sale of NPLs of 144m. to the company B2Kapital. Then, in September 2018, this was followed by the absorption of specific assets (other than NPLs) and liabilities of the Cyprus Cooperative Bank by Hellenic Bank, with the result that the NPLs of the Cooperative (amounting to approximately 6.8bn) remained on its balance sheet, its banking license was withdrawn and KEDIPES (Cyprus Asset Management Company Ltd) was created. In addition, at this stage, the Bank of Cyprus is waiting for supervisory approval to complete the process of selling NPLs of 2.8bn. The above transactions remove NPLs from banking institutions, improving the quality of their assets while enhancing the confidence of investors and depositors. Despite the progress that is being made and which will bring the share of NPLs below 30%, we are still a long way from European levels of an average of 3.6%. NPLs, which are no longer on bank balance sheets, remain, however, in the real economy and are measured against private debt, which is kept at particularly high levels, continuing to be a problem and a risk to household budgets, but also a deterrent to the private sector taking over new business activities. It should be noted that credit acquiring companies are governed by the Purchase and Sale of Credit Facilities and Related Matters Law and the Central Bank is in charge of licensing and supervising these companies in order to ensure financial stability. Regarding the government policy concerning the support by the state of targeted categories of citizens, I must note that the Central Bank is not negative. Nevertheless, it is my position that this policy should be expressed through the drawing up of projects the characteristics of which should serve a specific objective but without the creation of a moral hazard, which may in future entail costs greater than the planned benefit. With regard to the legislative framework concerning the ESTIA scheme, I must note that the Central Bank has a number of reservations which focus mainly on the possible creation of moral hazard which can potentially be expressed through deliberate defaults by borrowers servicing their loans who either expect any future assistance from the state or consider that this plan is unfair as it subsidises strategic defaulters. The position of the Central Bank was and is that any plan prepared must assist the whole effort made by all the institutions and bodies of the State to create the appropriate culture for the repayment of obligations and not to increase the risk of the opposite results. Regarding the challenges that our banking institutions face and are expected to face in 2019 and beyond, these focus on the following issues: (1) in their business model and in particular in their reduced interest income due to their high NPLs and forecasts, but also in the environment of low interest rates in general. I note here that particular attention should be paid to the measurement and management of credit risk due to the effort of banking institutions for new lending in a highly competitive environment, but also to the possible future increase in interest rates due to the expected gradual tightening of monetary policy. (2) the management of NPLs and the requirements of the Single Supervisory Mechanism for the provisions to be created and in particular for NPLs that have delays in repayment for a long period of time. For example, the European Council's Action Plan of July 2017 on the management of NPLs, the relevant ECB framework issued in March 2018, and the European Banking Authority's Guidelines of October 2018. (3) the upcoming regulatory changes at European level regarding the maintenance of funds (MREL, Minimum Requirement for own funds and Eligible Liabilities) for absorbing losses in those cases where banking institutions fail and enter into resolution. (4) the upcoming regulatory changes at European level regarding the maintenance of provisions for NPLs that are expected to be created in the future, to avoid weaknesses in the European regulatory framework that appeared to have existed during the recent financial and banking crisis, and (5) the challenges that Hellenic Bank has to face at an operational level for the successful integration of the work absorbed by the Cooperative. Turning now to a separate issue, namely the scourge of money laundering or money laundering and the bad reputation that Cyprus has unfortunately acquired as a country that facilitates the concealment of funds arising from illegal activities, I would like to take this opportunity to mention the following to you. The CBC has intensified its actions in recent years to combat this phenomenon, cooperating with the other competent authorities of the Republic of Cyprus. These actions focus on the effective implementation of the relevant law (Law 188(I) of 2007 as subsequently amended) by all institutions supervised by the CBC (credit institutions, payment and electronic money institutions, etc.). Cyprus will be judged by the international community for the effective implementation of the legal framework which is of course based on European law. The evaluation process of Cyprus in relation to this issue has already begun by the Moneyval Committee of the Council of Europe on the basis of the evaluation standards of the transnational Financial Action Task Force. The CBC does everything possible to respond to the assessment and takes all the measures that need to be implemented if it is very knowledgeable in the international arena, taking care of all those factors that must be included in the regulatory framework in order to avoid negative criticisms. A poor rating result will have multiple implications since both the various investors and trading partners and the international correspondent banks take seriously into account the risks of money laundering identified by such ratings. This means that weaknesses in the control and practices of the banks of the past are no longer acceptable. I am convinced that the banking sector has taken serious steps in recent years in cultivating that culture that rejects illegal access to the banking products and services offered. This is in line with the profile of Cyprus as an international financial centre as long as the level of services offered remains high, with advantages for attracting legitimate investments. Finally, I should mention that a relevant issue is the granting of citizenship to foreigners, something for which Cyprus also receives serious criticism. The CBC supports the establishment of a framework for the evaluation of applications that will prevent persons with negative information against them from attempting to acquire Cypriot citizenship. Another separate issue that concerns the CBC is the possible impact on the Cypriot economy of the expected exit of the United Kingdom (UK) from the European Union (EU) in March 2019. These effects, at first sight, are not expected to have an overall significant impact on Cyprus' GDP, although individual sectors may be affected either in positive or in a small negative but manageable degree. For example, the sector that could be affected to some extent is that of tourism (through the devaluation of sterling against the euro), while the rest of the trade sectors, including imports of goods, are expected to be less affected. In general, any negative effects of export sectors, such as tourism, are expected to be largely offset by positive effects from cheaper imports from the UK. At the same time, it should be noted that the expected exit of the UK from the EU may also present opportunities, as the full participation of Cyprus in the EU and the Eurozone, its English-based legal system, the low taxation, the geostrategic position and the high professional training of Cypriot human resources, may attract companies based in the UK and wish to continue to maintain access to the European economic area. Therefore, both the private sector and the public sector should be vigilant in order to take advantage both in the short and medium term of any potential opportunities for the Cypriot economy from the expected evolution of BREXIT. Summing up my position today, I would say that I am generally optimistic about the future of the Cyprus economy. I base my optimism on the substantial and measurable progress that has been made since 2013, both in the banking sector and in public finances, but also in the real economy. The efforts of all the competent authorities have borne considerable fruit and the economic sacrifices of our people are being vindicated day by day, more and more. Woe betide us if we allow this positive course to be reversed. Woe betide us if we deviate from our goals. As the Central Bank, we assure that on our part we will do our best, within the framework of our responsibilities, to keep Cyprus and its people on the path of sustainable growth, full employment and prosperity for all citizens.

Title: Cyprus as an international business centre post EFSF
text: Address by the Governor of the CBC, Mrs. Chrystalla Yiorkadji at the event of the Cyprus Economists' Association on "The delays in Cyprus in the administration of justice, the socio-economic consequences and the upcoming changes" March 28, 2019, CBC Amphitheatre, 5.30 p.m. Dear friends, I feel today the same intense emotion as the one I felt on April 10, 2014, the day I took office as Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus, realizing the expectations that existed for financial stability and an exit from the problems of the economy. I have always acted with respect to the Constitution and the Laws of the Republic of Cyprus but also to the citizens of this place. It is with the same respect that I have served with regard to the requirements arising from the Statute of the System of Central Banks and of the European Central Bank. This is what I am submitting today, thanking the State for entrusting me to this high office, with the President of the Republic expressing myself. I assure you that I have made every effort to carry out my duties and to address the difficulties that Cyprus has experienced as a result of the extremely difficult economic conditions. I would like to express my gratitude to the Cyprus Economists Association for today's event and all of you who are here today, because no one is indifferent to praise, especially when they are expressed with a lot of love. The theme of today's event is of particular importance because the image of the administration of justice in Cyprus is far from satisfactory. Despite efforts to improve, Cyprus has one of the highest and in some matters the highest times for processing cases and the administration of justice, be it administrative cases or civil/commercial cases. Tons of ink has been spilled on this issue and it is no exaggeration that this long delay in the administration of justice verges on denial of justice. But I would like to believe that something is changing, since we recognise and discuss these weaknesses and ways of improving the situation. The European Union's Justice Scoreboard, published in 2018 and for the judicial year 2016, ranks Cyprus, compared to the other 27 member states, among the last countries of the European Union. In terms of dispute resolution and justice time up to the low availability of electronic means. In some cases, Cyprus does not even have statistics. Today, the timing of a case is directly combined with the development and economic dimension of the functioning of justice. Because in European and international ratings available to potential investors, the functioning of the Judiciary is an important factor, which they will take into account in their decision on whether or not to invest in a country. The delay in the administration of Justice is a deterrent for a prospective investor and this is because  as lawyers explain  many years of judicial wandering reduces the indicator of legal certainty. Every investor wants to know how long it takes for a litigation to complete. If it takes many years to issue a critical decision, then it becomes impossible to plan investment, and investment interest can be lost. Based on the same data, the average required in the European Union to have a finality in a case is 8 months. It is indicative that in France the settlement of an administrative dispute takes place within 313 days at the latest, in Spain in 317 days, with the total of all the countries of the European Union being on average at 271 days. In Cyprus it takes more than 2,500 days. In the Doing Business index for 2019, Cyprus needs 1,100 days to resolve commercial cases, a very high time of administration of justice. All these and other very interesting things, will be presented to us today by our speakers and I would like to conclude with the comment that the ethos and fortitude of judges is crucial to ensuring the independence of the Judiciary, the administration of which requires "virtue and boldness". Thank you.

Title: 1st Central Bank of Cyprus Annual Conference:The Role of Monetary Policy in Tackling Inflationary Pressures
text: 1st Central Bank of Cyprus Annual Conference: The Role of Monetary Policy in Tackling Inflationary Pressures Limassol, 4 October 2023 Governors Welcome Address Dear Vice President of the ECB, Mr de Guindos, dear Luis, it is with great honour and pleasure that we welcome you to our conference today. Your presence, as the esteemed Vice President of the European Central Bank, highlights the importance of our discussions, and we look forward to your valuable insights. I also extend a warm welcome to our esteemed speakers and express my gratitude for their participation and useful contributions. To all our distinguished guests, your presence is deeply appreciated. Today's conference, on "The Role of Monetary Policy in Tackling Inflationary Pressures," marks the commencement of a series of Annual Conferences hosted by the Central Bank of Cyprus. These conferences will address contemporary economic issues and challenges. We aim to foster fruitful discussions and a collaborative environment for shared research and learning. One of the most pressing challenges in our current economic landscape has been high inflation. Why is it so crucial to bring inflation down? The consequences of not acting and leaving inflation untamed would be dire. Inflation affects all of us, every individual, every family, every business and consequently the economy itself. When left unchecked, inflation erodes the purchasing power of our income. Imagine a world where the cost of basic necessities, such as food, housing, and healthcare, increases by 10% or 15% or even more every year. A number of Eurozone countries witnessed such levels of inflation last year. Households would suffer this cost, and the lower income households suffer the most. Without an appropriate monetary policy response, we also risk entering a vicious inflationary cycle. If prices rise without control, people and businesses would expect higher prices in the future. This expectation usually leads to increased demand for higher wages, which drives up the costs for businesses. Businesses could then pass on these costs to consumers with further price increases. Monetary policy aims to keep such inflation expectations unchanged or anchored, otherwise a self-perpetuating cycle of rising prices could ensue, the well-known wage-price spiral. Moreover, unchecked inflation can lead to economic uncertainty. Businesses, when uncertain of future costs and profits, tend to postpone decisions to invest in such a risky economic environment. This could stifle innovation, job creation and economic growth. For the average citizen also, long-term planning becomes a challenge. How does one save for a child's education or one's retirement when the future value of money could be so uncertain? Furthermore, without tightening monetary policies, disparities between the wealthier and the more vulnerable segments of society are likely to widen in an inflationary environment. Those with assets, like property or stocks, might see the value of such assets rise with inflation. In contrast, those relying solely on fixed incomes or wages, could find themselves struggling to keep up with rising costs. History has shown that periods of high inflation, for the reasons just explained, tend to create social unrest. In contrast, price stability maintains social cohesion and stability. So, the societal wellbeing is a crucial outcome of price stability. Under the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) and the Statute of the European System of Central Banks and the European Central Bank (Statute of the ESCB), price stability is the primary objective of the ECB. Price stability ensures that individuals and businesses can maintain the value of their income and wealth, and plan for the future with confidence. This not only helps the economy to grow, but also pave the way for job creation and prosperity. This brings me to another pivotal point: the symbiotic relationship between price stability and financial stability. The pursuit of price stability through monetary policy, and of financial stability through macroprudential policy, are to a large extend complementary. The primary objective of the ECB is price stability, namely a two per cent inflation rate over the medium term. However, monetary policy needs to take financial stability and the stance of macroprudential policy into account. Monetary policy and macroprudential policy operate through common transmission channels, meaning that the scope for interaction between the two policy spheres is wide. For example, the Central Bank of Cyprus, acting proactively, has recently increased the countercyclical buffer to 1% of risk weighted assets for all licensed banks incorporated in Cyprus. The Countercyclical Buffer can work concurrently with monetary policy as it increases the resilience of the banking sector. During periods of stress, when losses materialise, the Central Bank can release this buffer so that the banking sector can support the supply of credit to the economy, thus mitigating the impact of the downturn of the financial cycle. It is worth noting that the Central Bank of Cyprus is one of the five countries in the eurozone that have enacted a positive, cycle neutral countercyclical buffer. The bottom line is that a stable price environment can foster economic growth and financial stability, while a stable financial system can make it easier for central banks to achieve their price stability objectives. Turning now to another important question, is the ECB monetary policy setting bringing price stability? The recent data on inflation affirms that monetary policy transmission is effective and having an impact on inflation. In addition, the ECB has managed to keep inflation expectations anchored, as most measures of longer-term inflation expectations currently stand at around 2 per cent, which is the inflation target rate. As I mentioned earlier, this is important in order to avoid a wage-price spiral. Although inflation has been reduced relative to 2022, its still above the 2% target, but some of the transmission of monetary policy decisions that have been made, still remains in progress. Based on the recent ECB macroeconomic projections of September, a continued inflation correction in the euro area is anticipated, with inflation decreasing from 8.4% in 2022, to 5.6% in 2023, and further decreasing to 3.2% in 2024 and 2.1% in 2025. As regards the inflation outlook in Cyprus, according to the latest CBC projections, also of September 2023, a significant reduction in the inflation rate is expected from 8.1% in 2022 to 3.9% in 2023. This downward trend is anticipated to continue, with inflation decreasing to 2.7% in 2024 and 2.0% in 2025. According to the same projections, the Cyprus economy will continue to exhibit resilience, with the GDP growth rate expected to reach 2,4%, 2.7% and 3.1%, in each year from 2023 to 2025. Unemployment in Cyprus is expected to decrease to 6.3% in 2023 compared to 6.8% in 2022. In the years 2024-25 unemployment is expected at 5.9% and 5.6%, respectively. Despite the lower inflation readings that I just mentioned, material uncertainty continues to persist for the eurozone. For instance, the recent spike in energy prices could transmit to the rest of the economy again, and have an upward pressure on prices. Furthermore, the elevated wages and profit margins observed in the euro area last year, need to be monitored closely, even though they are currently expected to normalize. Also the liquidity conditions in the euro area banking system can play an important role in the transmission of monetary policy and therefore inflation. Let me conclude by noting that addressing successfully the current challenges would lower inflation, secure the benefits I referred to earlier, and set the stage for new opportunities in our economies. For instance, an economic environment characterized by stable price and financial conditions, can support the much-needed efforts and investments related to structural reforms. These reforms can be directed to preserve and enhance the competitiveness of our economies, through a transition to a more technologically advanced environment. This can be beneficial to all stakeholders of the economy and all members of society. Thank you for your attention, and I look forward to the fruitful discussions that this conference will undoubtedly foster.

Title: Speech by Constantinos Herodotou, Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus, at the ICPAC Mediterranean Finance Summit
text: Speech by Constantinos Herodotou, Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus, at the ICPAC Mediterranean Finance Summit Parklane, Limassol 5 May 2022 Central Bank Challenges in a world of growing uncertainties: The conduct of monetary policy and the evolution of traditional banking Dear guests, dear co-speakers, it is a pleasure to have the opportunity to speak to you here today. These days our thoughts are with those affected by the tragic events of the Russian invasion in Ukraine. Beyond the human loss, Russia's war against Ukraine has disrupted further the global supply chains and in effect growth and inflation patterns around the world and the euro area economy. Europe faces both supply disruptions and surging prices for commodities and raw materials, problems exacerbated by the regions dependency on Russian oil and gas. How the euro area economy performs will greatly depend on the magnitude and time length of the conflict, the side effects of current sanctions on the euro area and on possible further measures. I will first describe the current economic developments in the euro area as regards growth and inflation outlook and the ECBs monetary policy stance and challenges under the prevailing uncertain geopolitical situation. As the supply disruptions from the acute phase of the pandemic were easing, the war and the consequent sanctions imposed on Russia are causing a new negative shock that is weakening the pace of the post pandemic recovery, creating new supply-side bottlenecks and increasing inflationary pressures for longer. Overall, the war in Ukraine has a strong effect on economic sentiment and increased considerably the risks to the economic growth outlook which are now skewed to the downside. According to the April IMF forecasts, euro area GDP growth in 2022 is revised down to 2,8 per cent, from the previous projection for growth of 3,9%. A 1.1 percentage points reduction in expected GDP growth.
