Title: The euro and enlargement: challenges ahead
text: Speech by the Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus, Mr. Konstantinos Herodotos, at the parliamentary session Committee on Financial and Budgetary Affairs for the 2020 Budget Nicosia, 28 November 2019 Mr President, ladies and gentlemen, Thank you for the invitation to submit my views as Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus on the occasion of the discussion of the State Budget for the year 2020. It is the duty of the Central Bank to make an objective assessment of the current economic developments in our country and, of course, today's debate on the state budget for 2020 falls within the scope of this task. Domestic economic developments The Cypriot economy continues to record strong growth rates, albeit slowing down. Growth stood at 4.1% in 2018, slightly lower than 4.4% in the previous year. In the first half of 2019, growth reached 3.3% compared to 1.2% in the euro area (seasonally adjusted data), which ranks Cyprus among the fastest growing economies of the currency bloc. GDP growth in the first quarter of 2019 is mainly due to the path of domestic demand. Large private investments, with a significant proportion of financing through foreign capital, are in the process of being implemented. The increase in private consumption (3.7% increase and 2.4 percentage points contribution to GDP growth), which reflects the increase in household disposable income, mainly due to the increase in employment (3.2%) and to a lesser extent the increase in wages (1.2%), also contributes significantly. At the same time, historically low interest rates prevailing in the euro area have supported the path of both investment and private consumption. Although the GDP growth rate exceeds the potential, due to the fact that growth is due to specific sectors and factors, the usual signs of strong economic activity are not reflected in all indicators of the domestic economy. For example, the balance of payments, as a result of strong activity in the construction sector, recorded some deterioration, while unemployment is falling significantly. On the contrary, inflation remains subdued. In the labour market in particular, and according to data from the Labour Force Survey, unemployment in the third quarter of 2019 decreased to 6.7% compared to 7.8% in the corresponding quarter of last year and 7.3% in the euro area. It should be noted that the significant increase in the influx of foreign workers shows that the domestic labor market, at least in specific sectors, such as construction and hotels, shows signs of saturation. Despite the positive developments in economic activity, the improvement in the labour market and the increases in wages, harmonised inflation in Cyprus continued to remain at positive, albeit subdued levels during the first ten months of the year. The phenomenon of prolonged subdued inflation, especially in 2019, is more pronounced in Cyprus than in the euro area due to the reduction of the consumption tax on petroleum products since December 18, 2018 but also the less dependence of the Cypriot economy on other than oil energy sources (eg throttle), whose prices increased (strengthening inflation in the euro area but not in Cyprus) during the period in question. The macroeconomic forecasts included in the state budget are broadly consistent with those of the CBC and are therefore assessed as realistic. Economic growth is projected to slow from 2018 to around 3.0% in 2019 and a little lower in 2020-22. It is noted that the corresponding provisions for the euro area are at significantly lower levels, namely slightly above 1%. The expected growth rate in Cyprus reflects the decelerating path of domestic demand. Private consumption is expected to slow down due to the acceleration in loan repayments, which, among other things, reflects the ongoing efforts to reduce the level of NPLs and the introduction of contribution rates to the GHS. The projected slowdown in investment is due to a gradual completion of investment projects. Inflation is expected to move to higher positive levels in 2020 than in 2019, mainly due to the continuation of the positive path of economic activity but also to the expected further growth of wages. Despite the positive path of economic activity and the continuation of robust economic growth, specific downside risks remain, which can slow growth to a greater extent than projected. Factors such as external geopolitical developments (Brexit, trade wars, etc.), the high domestic public and private debt, the Cyprus Investment Program, the historically low interest rates in relation to the challenges faced by the banking sector, are potential risks and continue to make the Cypriot economy vulnerable to shocks. Budgetary developments  Budget 2020 The fiscal policy strategy over time must have as its main objective the sustainable and prudent management of public finances while strengthening the productive potential of the economy. At the same time, the state budget must respect the relevant obligations arising from the participation of Cyprus in the Economic and Monetary Union of the European Union[1] and thus compliance with specific rules, including the "budget balancing rule" and the correction of deviations when they arise. Based on the estimates of the CBC technocrats, the State Budget for the year 2020 seems to be moving in the above contexts. In addition, the European Commission approved the preliminary draft budget of Cyprus, which it considers to be "in compliance with the Stability and Growth Pact for 2020". Following the surpluses of the last four years[2], the budget forecasts a surplus budget balance of 2.7% of GDP, while the primary surplus is projected at 5.1% of GDP. It is important to maintain relatively strong budget surpluses so that: (a) the public debt to be reduced in accordance with the state's targets, i.e. to approximately 80% of GDP by 2020; (b) to maintain credibility in the management of public finances; (c) be able to support important development projects, and (d) there is the fiscal capacity to support the economy in the event of a recession or in shocks that may be brought about by external geopolitical developments. The positive picture of the future of public finances, in particular the path of fiscal revenues, is influenced by the forecasts for the growth rate of the economy and the collection of non-recurring revenues[3]. Positive developments in terms of revenues should not lead to reckless permanent increases on the expenditure side, as well as possible implementation of downside risks, either from the external environment or from the internally, may affect the projected path of public debt and the ability of the state to support the economy. In addition, the modernization of the state through the implementation of structural reforms is an important parameter for achieving the goal of rational and efficient management of public finances. Developments in the banking sector Regarding the developments in the banking sector in 2019, banks continue their efforts to clean up their balance sheets from Non-Performing Loans (NPLs) and at the same time continue to supply the real economy with new lending. Specifically, new debt increased by 2.5bn in the first nine months of 2019 compared to 2.3bn in the corresponding period of the previous year. In relation to Non-Performing Loans, progress in recent years has been noticeable, given that from the end of 2014 until mid-2019, the share of NPLs in the banking sector decreased from 56% to 32%, while in absolute numbers the decrease was over 19 billion (from 28 billion to 8.9 billion). Despite this, Cyprus still maintains the highest NPL rates in Europe, after Greece (more than 40%), while the European average hovers around 3%. In addition, a large part (46%) of NPLs in Cyprus have delays of more than 5 years, while the corresponding European percentage amounts to 17%. It should also be noted that, while addressing NPLs with instruments such as the sale of loans helps to correct banks' balance sheets, these remain part of the private debt of the non-financial sector (which, excluding Special Purpose Vehicles, reaches 215% of GDP in 2018 compared to 135% in the euro area) and therefore remain a burden on the real economy. Therefore, the organic reduction of NPLs remains a significant challenge for the Cyprus economy and households, the Cypriot authorities and the banking sector in general. The CBC expects credit institutions to intensify efforts to fully clean up their balance sheets, taking advantage of the ongoing economic growth and the rise of the real estate market. However, I would also like to refer at this point to the Estia plan in relation to the effort to reduce NPLs. According to information from the CBC, the applications so far have been much lower than the potential borrowers of the Scheme. More specifically, according to data collected by banks and credit acquiring companies with a reference date of March 31, 2019, the total of potential borrowers who were probably entitled to join the Estia scheme was more than 13,800 with a total loan value of around 2.7 billion. According to the latest data (mid-November 2019), the applications so far were around 1050 of which many were not sufficiently completed, and corresponded to a value of around 260m. In recent weeks the number of applications has increased, but these numbers are much lower than the potential borrowers of the Scheme. Based on the disappointing findings so far, banks should consider how to deal with those who may be left out of Estia. We will await the banks' proposal through their three-year plan for the management of NPLs and their handling of this loan portfolio in particular. I would like to point out that the three-year plan is drawn up exclusively by the management of the banks. At this point, I would like to stress the huge importance of a stable legal framework governing out-of-court auctions alongside the existence of an effective insolvency framework in order to achieve the objective of reducing NPLs. It must be ensured that those who strategically choose not to meet their obligations are faced with an effective legal framework. The justice system also needs to be modernised in such a way that decisions are taken within a short period of time. Only in this way will the payment culture be strengthened and foreign investments in Cyprus will be attracted. I would like to point out that the Central Bank requires the banks to apply fairly and correctly the Arrears Management Directive as well as the Code of Conduct contained therein. This requirement was reaffirmed through the circular we sent to the banks (dated 21/11/2019) through which banks are also invited to submit to the Central Bank information on how they have handled complaints they have received since 1 January 2018. In this circular, the Central Bank draws the attention of the banks to the following: - offer sustainable restructuring in order to achieve a reduction in lending balances in the medium and long term. - apply a fair and sustainable pricing policy. - take all appropriate measures to ensure that the charges they impose on NPLs are within the current legal framework in relation to (a) compound interest, (b) the calculation of the daily rate and (c) interest on late payments. My view remains that where it turns out that banks have behaved outside certain frameworks then they should have to bear the consequences of their operations. It is also on the basis of this finding that about 3 months ago I took the initiative to design a mechanism for examining complaints from cooperative borrowers. The technocrats of the CBC and I personally are in contact with the ECB and we are discussing at length the mechanism that we have designed. We have received some initial comments from the ECB but in addition to the detailed description of the mechanism proposed by us, it is requested that the relevant bill be sent to them. The results of these contacts will be announced at the end of the consultations. I also wish today to refer to another important issue concerning our country's ongoing efforts to combat money laundering. We have been reading with concern lately the reports in the international and domestic media about the alleged involvement of our country in cases of money laundering. The petitions concern both legal entities established in Cyprus, as well as providers of administrative services and banking institutions. As the CBC, we note with dissatisfaction that the way in which some reports are presented does not reflect the very serious and concrete actions that have been taken in recent years to combat this phenomenon. The results of these actions have been recognized by both international organizations and correspondent banks of international standing, the confidence of which is regained by the CBC, our economy and Cypriot banking institutions. The CBC works seamlessly with the aim of further strengthening the regulatory framework, its effective implementation and informing the important centers abroad about the progress we are making. We have given a clear message to the banks about what we expect, namely the correct and faithful implementation of our law and instructions, but without adversely affecting legal transactions. These messages have been given both orally and in a circular last September, calling on banks to implement customer-friendly procedures with respect and dignity, while paying due attention to the effective implementation of the current framework on an individual basis and without exaggeration, improving the processing time of their procedures. We recognise the progress made by the banking sector in improving regulatory compliance, which allows its operations to grow on the basis of a healthy clientele. Next week, the Moneyval Committee of the Council of Europe will deal, among other things, with the 5th evaluation of Cyprus on the basis of the standards and methodology of the transnational Financial Action Task Force. Huge efforts have been made to show the evaluators the work that is being done. It goes without saying that any recommendations that may arise will be taken seriously. The CBC will continue to work in the same direction, aiming to strengthen the reputation of our country, the economy and our banking system. At this point, I would like to make a reference to the recent publications concerning the Cyprus Investment Programme (KEP). I must clarify that the CBC and the banks were not and are not part of the naturalisation process and the control carried out in relation to naturalisations. For our part, we check the procedures applied by banks when evaluating their prospective customers and when they monitor the transactions made through the bank in order to prevent the use of our country's banking system for money laundering. Banks must follow the relevant regulations and procedures, whether the transaction is aimed at naturalization or not. The CBC carries out periodic audits of banks to verify whether they adhere to the correct internal procedures in relation to the laws and regulations of the CBC. In addition to these checks, if any incident becomes apparent, the CBC can intervene and use it as trigger for an audit of banks' procedures. The CBC looks at the general filtering mechanism of banks in relation to AML and onboarding and the relevant laws and examines whether they need improvement. In cases where anything is detected, the prescribed fines will be imposed. Monetary policy ECB It would be my omission, before I finish this speech, not to mention the supporting role that the ECB's monetary policy provides for the growth path of the euro area, including our own economy. We have to recognise that the growth and employment rates recorded would have been lower without the supportive measures we have taken and without the low interest rate environment that it has shaped with its policy in the euro area. Even inflation, which remains subdued (both in Cyprus and in the euro area), would have been even lower without the above-mentioned measures. Finally, it should be noted that the efficiency of monetary policy is further enhanced when fiscal policy is designed by European governments with a growth-friendly approach. Concluding my speech today, I would like to remind you that the future of the Cyprus economy is a matter and a responsibility of all of us. The Government, the Parliament, the CBC and the other institutions of the state. We went through and suffered a lot. Populism and sweeping problems under the carpet leads nowhere. Cyprus and our economy have made great progress in recent years. But there are still many problems. So let us ensure the progress that has been made so far. And let's take advantage of the current positive economic situation to further correct the remaining distortions from the crisis but also to create preventive "pillows" that could protect the economy from possible future shocks. Our economy and its banking system deserve even better days and we must all act accordingly. [1] The general government deficit should not exceed 3% of the Gross Domestic Product at market prices and the general government debt should not exceed or follow a sufficiently declining path towards 60% of the Gross Domestic Product at market prices. [2] With the exception of 2018 due to the impact of the agreement between CCB and Hellenic Bank. [3] Increased revenues from the construction sector affected by the Cyprus investment programme, overdue (tax) debt settlement plan, etc.

Title: The international economic crisis and its implications for the Cypriot economy
text: Address by the Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus at the Webinar on Financial Literacy April 15, 2021 I welcome you to today's webinar on financial literacy, and, in particular, the results of a sample survey by the Central Bank of Cyprus, on its level in our country. Through today's seminar, the opportunity is offered to highlight the extremely important problem of low-level financial literacy, which decisively affects personal, family and general social well-being. There is also the opportunity to be informed about a new, remarkable effort that is underway to promote the issue in Cyprus. In this effort, the Central Bank of Cyprus has an essential and coordinating role. The ultimate goal is the elaboration of a National Strategy for the promotion of financial literacy and financial literacy in Cyprus. According to a general definition, financial literacy is defined as the combination of knowledge, behavior and mentality necessary for the correct making of basic individual economic decisions and, by extension, to avoid adverse consequences and achieve personal financial well-being. Without the appropriate, basic financial knowledge, but also without rational behaviors and mentalities, citizens are prone to wrong decisions or omissions that can burden their personal or family budget or even lead them to unpleasant financial situations. As has been shown by international scientific studies[1], financial literacy is unfortunately at a significantly lower level than desired. More specifically, it has emerged that a huge proportion of the world's population has significant weaknesses in understanding basic economic and financial concepts, such as the calculation of the simple interest rate, compound interest, the effects of inflation, and the importance of portfolio diversification. As a result, many people face problems with debt, savings, investment, but also planning for the future and especially their retirement. At a conference of the Governors of the Central Banks of the Commonwealth co-organised by the Commonwealth and the Central Bank of Cyprus in October 2019 in Washington, D.C., which I had the honour to chair, we invited Professor Annamaria Lusardi, one of the leading academics in the field of financial literacy, as the main speaker. One of the main conclusions of the surveys he analyzed is that only 1/3 of the population internationally possesses this basic knowledge in relation to finance. At the same time, it is noted that this problem exists even in the most developed countries of the planet. [2] Also, according to Professor Lusardi, levels of financial literacy can significantly affect the levels of borrowing of households and businesses. More specifically, the financial behavior of borrowers in combination with incomplete skills in matters of financial literacy, leads to wrong credit decisions and / or mismanagement of available resources, resulting in over-indebtedness. Financial literacy plays a key role in how the budgets of households and businesses are managed. Concrete examples are the management of their debt, financial resources in the event of an emergency, obligations for possible future education of their children or retirement. At the same time, as has been shown in discussions even at the highest level of the European Central Bank (ECB), the training of households and partners in enterprises facilitates the effective transmission of monetary policy. For example, a better understanding of key financial concepts contributes to a more effective formulation of public expectations of the direction of inflation targeted by the ECB and thus pushes citizens to better investment or consumer decisions. It appears, therefore, that such knowledge is essential for the creation of a balanced, functional and well-organised economic model. It is also important to take into account the fact that continuous developments and new trends in the economic and financial sector internationally, make financial literacy even more important today than in previous years. Firstly, citizens today are being asked by financial institutions and other financial institutions to choose between multiple and complex products relating to short-term borrowing, mortgage lending, investment and saving of personal resources. Such decisions presuppose, however, basic financial knowledge, as wrong choices can affect a person's financial well-being, as well as their ability to finance their future needs, such as buying a home, financing their children's education or saving for retirement. Second, the rapidly changing environment created by technological developments and the digital transformation of the global economy makes financial markets even faster, more volatile and more complex for someone who lacks basic financial literacy. At the same time, financial literacy can reduce the negative effects of future financial crises on the economy at large. Thirdly, it is a fact that citizens are now forced to take many economic decisions themselves, which in the past were taken to a greater extent, either by the organisations that employed them, by the trade unions and other organised groups, or by the governments themselves. For example, the burden of designing pension plans is now to a greater extent on the shoulders of workers than in the past. Of course, without proper knowledge of this issue at an individual level, any mistakes will have a significant negative impact on the economic well-being of citizens after their retirement. In addition to the above, it should also be noted that a particularly important source of pension income for previous generations was Social Security. However, with demographic developments and the ageing of the population, the difficulties in social insurance systems are increasing, which gives additional importance to the issue of the proper design of the individual voluntary pension plan. Longer life expectancy also goes without saying that we need more money to retire than previous generations and therefore more careful planning. As far as Cyprus is concerned, the experiences from the stock market crisis of 2000, as well as from the non-rational management of the portfolios of Cypriots before the 2013 crisis, have highlighted that a significant part of the population in our country does not seem to possess sufficient basic financial knowledge or rational behaviors in financial matters, such as investments, saving and borrowing. Moreover, the behaviour of Cypriot households in terms of saving and borrowing in the recent past underlines that there is insufficient awareness of a number of financial issues. The low levels of financial literacy in Cyprus are also confirmed by very important research that has been done in the past. The study by Andreou and Phillip (2018) highlighted the low level of financial literacy among Cypriot students, while the study by Andreou and Anyfantaki (2020) highlighted the fact that consumers' financial illiteracy negatively affects their active participation in online banking, which is now the main channel for the provision of banking services. However, no sample survey on Cyprus until then has been representative and comprehensive, in terms of the range of questions for adequate coverage of financial knowledge, behaviors and attitudes, and at the same time in terms of the level of coverage of the population. The CBC's research on financial literacy in Cyprus, which was completed in 2019, aimed to assist in the scientific assessment of the level of financial knowledge, behaviours and mentalities of Cypriots as a whole but also by category, on the basis of various demographic parameters such as age, gender, level of education and geographical area. Therefore, this survey filled the gap that existed, since it is considered to be the most representative and comprehensive in terms of the range of questions for adequate coverage of financial knowledge, behaviors and mentality, as well as the sampling coverage of the entire population. The survey confirms the problem while at the same time, through its more extensive coverage, it demonstrates both the areas in which Cypriots are lagging behind, as well as the population groups that should be our priority as a society to promote financial literacy. The CBC, in the context of corporate social responsibility, actively participated in an initiative of the Association of Banks and Junior Achievement Cyprus that co-organize training seminars in primary education ("Economics for success") and only recently in Gymnasiums. Also noted are the three economic and social policy forums on the subject of financial literacy organized by Dr. Panagiotis Andreou of CUT, two of which were held with the support of the CBC and the third online. The above efforts, although remarkable, are of limited scope and / or duration and have not been designed in the context of a broader targeted plan or strategy that covers all categories of the population. Finally, there are series of relevant training lectures or seminars organized by the Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports and Youth (YPAN), the Cyprus Securities and Exchange Commission, the CUT, the Cyprus Youth Board (ONEK), the Cyprus Association of Financial Analysts (CFA Institute Cyprus), the Association of Economists of Cyprus, and the recent introduction of a financial education course at the University of Cyprus. As I said before, the Central Bank has been a key supporter of various efforts made in the past. It is for this reason that the Central Bank welcomes with great satisfaction the establishment of the Ad-Hoc Committee for the formulation of a National Strategy for the promotion of Financial Literacy and Financial Education in Cyprus. This Committee operates under the auspices of the CBC and consists of executives from the Central Bank of Cyprus, the Ministry of Finance, the Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports and Youth, the Cyprus Securities and Exchange Commission, the University of Cyprus and the Cyprus University of Technology. The Ad-Hoc Committee is also accompanied by a group of renowned international experts, who, as scientific collaborators, are expected to enrich the Commission's work with best practices based on academic research and experiences from other countries. An important role in the design of the Strategy will be played by the results of the CBC survey that will be presented today. As we will see next, the results of the survey show that levels of financial literacy are lower in certain groups of the population. In particular, young people have a lower financial literacy score than the total population. Financial literacy still seems to be directly correlated with the level of education. In addition, it seems to be related to the type of secondary education that the survey participants held. The results that I have just mentioned, and which will be analysed later, give the Commission an important indication in relation to the groups of the population to which priority should be given through a structured and targeted policy. In closing, I would like to mention that as Governor of the CBC, I intend to support the Commission in every way in this effort to contribute decisively to the strengthening of financial knowledge in our country. The Committee will formulate and propose to the State a remarkable, I believe, National Strategy, which if methodically, organized, systematically and consistently begins to be implemented, will substantially help to address the problem of financial illiteracy that we face as a society. Title: The international financial turmoil and the economy
text: Introduction by the Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus, Mr Constantinos Herodotou, in the Cyprus Economic Society seminar 21 October 2021 d4The Significance of being Financially Literate and National Strategies for achieving itd5 Introduction I would like to thank the Cyprus Economic Society for offering me the opportunity to introduce todayd5s seminar, which I believe timely addresses an extremely important economic and social theme. The issue of promoting financial literacy and the role of National Strategies to achieve it are of course, relevant not only to Cyprus but also globally. Dr Chiara Monticone, a senior policy analyst of the OECD and a practitioner in the field of financial literacy with global expertise and Professor Dennis Philip, who teaches Finance at Durham University Business School, an acclaimed academic in financial literacy and close collaborator of the Central Bank of Cyprus, will have, I am sure, excellent contributions on the subject. According to a definition associated with the OECD, financial literacy is the ability of an individual to combine appropriate knowledge and skills, rational behaviour and attitudes necessary to make sound economic and financial decisions and ultimately achieve individual financial wellbeing. As more individuals operate prudently and comprehend the workings and functioning of the financial system, including how to use its services and products appropriately and efficiently, the broader economic system and society, as a whole, benefit. Therefore, financial literacy can be seen as a key element for a well-functioning economic system and thus as a prerequisite for sustainable economic growth and financial wellbeing of individuals. The establishment of the Ad-Hoc Committee to prepare the National Strategy for Financial Literacy in Cyprus Recognising the seriousness of the issue, state authorities around the globe have taken actions in order to enhance financial literacy among the wider population. A typical response to the challenge, is the establishment of a National Strategy for financial literacy in which a number of public and private stakeholders are involved. Up until recently, no such organised effort had been initiated in the case of Cyprus. Even though a number of initiatives have been undertaken by various stakeholders, these significant and valuable efforts have been limited in scope and without the necessary coordination for a truly effective impact on society as a whole. To this end, following an invitation by the Parliamentary Committee of Education and Culture, an Ad-Hoc Committee for the formulation of a National Strategy for the Promotion of Financial Literacy and Financial Education in Cyprus was established in December 2020. The Committee consists of members from the Central Bank of Cyprus (CBC), which also has the coordinating role, the Ministry of Finance, the Ministry of Education, the Cyprus Securities and Exchange Commission, Dr Panayiotis Andreou (Cyprus University of Technology) and Dr Andreas Milidonis (University of Cyprus). The Committee receives administrative and analytical support from the CBC. The ongoing work of the Committee The ongoing work of the Committee is noteworthy. It includes an evaluation of the scientific bibliography on financial literacy, as well as a review and assessment of international initiatives for the promotion of financial literacy. The Committee, with the help of CBC staff, has also conducted an in depth econometric analysis of the results of the CBCd5s sampling survey in order to representatively assess the level of financial literacy in Cyprus, as well as to identify the groups that are in greater and urgent need of financial education. For instance, people who studied financial subjects at high school scored higher in the survey than those who focused on classical studies with 5.2 out of 7, compared to 4.5 out of 7 in knowledge questions; 5 out of 7 being the minimum score for adequate knowledge as set by the OECD. The CBC had carried out a sampling survey in 2018 to better identify the extent of the financial literacy problem, covering all groups of the population at a national level. This [1] survey followed another similar survey, which focused on university students, namely, a survey by Andreou and Phillips (2018) which showed that the low level of financial literacy among university students appears to be a major problem in our society. The CBC survey, which as I mentioned covers all segments of the population, is instrumental in deriving useful results on financial literacy in Cyprus. For instance, it confirmed the rather worrisome result that financial knowledge amongst young persons of age 18-29 years in general is rather low. In particular, they score 4.4 out of 7 compared to 5.3 out of 7 for the 40-49 age group. Econometric evidence also shows they are 3.2 times less likely to achieve the minimum score of 5 out 7 in knowledge questions than the 40-49 age group. According to the international literature, it is crucial for policymakers to intervene and ensure that financial literacy is taught as a course in the school curriculum early on when children are active, keen learners and more willing to get educated about new concepts. Therefore, schools as an environment conducive to learning, play an essential, if not the most important role, in the formulation of a National Strategy in order to address the problem of financial illiteracy early on in an individuald5s life. Further to the analysis undertaken by CBC staff in support of the work of the Committee, online meetings and regular contacts have taken place between the Committee and a team of distinguished scientific collaborators, who have specialised and international expertise in the field. Namely, Dr Adele Atkinson (Atkinson Financial Research and Policy, formerly from the OECD), Dr Maria Demertzis (Deputy Director at Bruegel), Prof. Michalis Haliassos (Goethe University Frankfurt), Prof. Alexandros Michaelides (Imperial College London), and Prof. Dennis Philip (University of Durham) whom I have already mentioned. In addition to its foreign-based scientific collaborators, the Committee has also reached out to other countries and international institutions in order to learn from their own experiences. The Central Bank of Austria and the Central Bank of Portugal have already been approached within the framework of close technical collaboration that the CBC agreed with certain national central banks Governors of the euro area, soon after I took over as Governor here in Cyprus. As envisaged, the Committee is currently in the process of drafting the National Strategy proposal aiming towards the promotion of financial literacy for the population as a whole, as well as for specific target groups. The initial draft is expected to be ready towards the end of the year, while the Committee is expected to submit the complete proposal to the Council of Ministers for endorsement soon thereafter. Objectives and challenges ahead Any big change in society requires bold decisions. There may be obstacles to overcome in order for the National Strategy in Cyprus to be fully implemented and it will take some time before we see the anticipated impact on society. These hindrances may be related to conflicting views of some stakeholders which should be carefully and appropriately addressed. Another important factor which might generate difficulties, is the securement of credible and long-term sources of funding since the estimated cost for such an endeavour is envisaged to be high. Active participation in this endeavour by the State and local authorities, academic institutions, private, non-profit and public organisations is crucial for its success. Official endorsement is thus of paramount importance. The participation of private and not-for-profit stakeholders in the National Strategyd5s implementation will be further supported by the development of a code of conduct and prior agreement to specific protocols. A code of conduct is envisaged to provide a uniform framework for the contribution of stakeholders in order to achieve the common objectives set. Public awareness on financial literacy through tailored campaigns is equally important, as it will facilitate the receptivity and usefulness of a National Strategy for financial education. Last but not least, a challenge lying ahead is the proper governance structure for the body that will undertake the implementation of the National Strategy on financial literacy. [2] International organisations such as the World Bank have clearly opined that national strategies should be initiated, developed, and monitored by a credible and unbiased authority with financial education expertise and appropriate flexibility and resources. In many cases it is deemed that Central Banks can play such a role. Concluding remarks At this point, I would like to emphasise once again my personal interest and my commitment to assist the Committee's role in achieving its goals. Enhancing the populationd5s financial literacy is an ambitious but needed goal. Through the CBCd5s actions over the past years and its coordinating role in the Committee, we have shown that we consider the issue of utmost importance. Moreover, in line with recommendations by international bodies such as the World Bank, I would also like to express the willingness of the CBC to have a leading role in the implementation stage of the National Strategy. I am positive that both the State and the private stakeholders share my belief that investing in financial literacy undoubtedly means investing in a sound financial future for our country and its people. It is now time for Cyprus to take the bold step in this direction. I would like to wish you all a fruitful seminar and discussion. [1] Panayiotis C. Andreou & Dennis Philip, 2018. "Financial knowledge among university students and implications for personal debt and fraudulent investments,"Cyprus Economic Policy Review, University of Cyprus, Economics Research Centre, vol. 12(2), pages 3-23, December. [2] Financial Education Programs and Strategies Approaches and Available Resources, January 2014,

Title: Concerns about the international economic crisis and the Cypriot economy
text: Speech by the Governor of the CBC, Mr. Konstantinos Herodotos, at the 12th Limassol Economic Forum Sustainable and green growth is also important for the Eurosystem  Great risks to the economy from the effects of climate change if measures and policies are not taken in a timely manner The Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus (CBC) Mr. Konstantinos Herodotou focused on the need to accelerate actions by all parties, i.e. public and private bodies, to achieve sustainable development and limit the long-term disruption of economies and the effects of climate change on the economy and the financial system during his speech at the 12th Limassol Economic Forum. It also focused on the related challenges for the banking system, as well as the role of the Eurosystem. Especially: Mr. Herodotou noted, regarding climate change, that it is no exaggeration that we are the last generation that can act to limit it and referred to the multiple effects of climate change with special reference to the countries of the European South, as one of the most prone regions of the EU. He found it encouraging that since the Paris Agreement in 2015, political priorities have been geared towards sustainability with ambitious targets and corresponding legislative initiatives. According to the conclusions of the stress test conducted by the European Central Bank (ECB) on the effects of climate change on businesses, banks and the entire economy to which Mr. Herodotou referred, the economic cost of climate change is significantly higher in the absence of timely and effective adaptation plans. In this regard, he said that, under a scenario where no policies are taken to address climate change, the losses in GDP are twice as high compared to a scenario of an unorganized transition that limits the increase in temperature even with a delay in the implementation of relevant policies and actions. Mr. Herodotou then referred to the European Union (EU) as a pioneer in this field and cited as an example the EU's "European Green Deal" and the sustainable finance strategy. In this context, he said that the EU's target of a 55% reduction in pollutant emissions by 2035 (compared to the level of pollutants in 1990) cannot be achieved unless "green" and "sustainable" investments are significantly increased in order to fill the relevant funding gap. In this regard, he highlighted the importance of further involvement of the private sector including its contribution to innovative, digital solutions, which can contribute to sustainable and inclusive growth since "green" and "digital" agendas are basically interlinked. Mr. Herodotou then referred in detail to the key role of the Eurosystem regarding climate change and environmental risks. Central Banks, he said, are on high alert as climate-related risks affect their ability to safeguard price stability as well as financial stability. It stated that for the above reasons, the Eurosystem - i.e. the ECB together with the National Central Banks of the euro area , committed, during the recent review of the monetary policy strategy, to integrate further climate change considerations into the Eurosystem's monetary policy framework, as well as into the operational frameworks including the relevant risk management frameworks. Among other things, they decided to assess, as of 2022, the resilience of the Eurosystem's balance sheet to climate risks. As supervisor, he said that banks must immediately start preparations for the risks that could arise from climate change, such as the economic impact of natural disasters affecting critical sectors of the economy, as well as the risks of the transition to a low-carbon economy, which is likely to cause large economic price fluctuations. In this regard, he noted, supervisors are already urging banks to manage all relevant risks, and a stress test on climate-related risks for banks under the direct supervision of the ECB will be conducted in 2022. Mr. Herodotou also referred to the impact of climate change on businesses and banks where, according to the conclusions of the relevant ECB stress test, it is predicted, under the adverse scenario, that the chances of default for companies in the euro area will increase by up to 7% on average by 2050 and their profitability will decrease by much more. The spillover effects on euro area banks would also be evident, as this would lead to an increase in the probability of default of their entire loan portfolios by around 7%, with the corresponding prices for the portfolios of banks located in the most vulnerable areas increasing by much more. As an important prerequisite for the management of climate-related risks, the Governor of the CBC highlighted a number of actions that need to be taken in order to make the best possible risk management, such as the need to improve the capabilities and models for analysing monitoring models, the development of appropriate forecasting scenarios with a very long-term reference horizon and the nature of these risks, as well as a better understanding of the different channels of risk transmission in the economy and the financial system. In conclusion, he noted the following: (a) The 'green' and 'digital' agendas to be linked and supported as much as possible. b) Our efforts need to be stepped up, as analyses show that the economic and social consequences of climate change will be profound. (c) Stakeholders should keep in mind their 'starting point' in order to instil in their plans the appropriate degree of detail and ambition. October 22, 2021

Title: What the current crisis teaches us about the future of financial system supervision
text: Speech by the Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus, Mr. Konstantinos Herodotos, at the parliamentary session Committee on Financial and Budgetary Affairs for the 2022 Budget Nicosia, 6 December 2021 Madam President of the Commission, ladies and gentlemen, Thank you for the invitation to present my views as Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus on the occasion of the discussion of the State Budget for the year 2022. Today's discussion is taking place under relatively better conditions than last year, due to the mitigation of the effects of the pandemic and the strong recovery prospects already recorded, although the risk of repercussions from the new pandemic wave that is underway is real. It is the duty of all of us to rationally assess the situation that is emerging and with a full sense of responsibility for the general state of the economy and households to continue to draw up the appropriate planning for the fastest possible recovery and greater elimination of the consequences of the pandemic. The state's budgets under discussion are within the broader framework of this planning and offer the opportunity for an in-depth discussion of all relevant issues. Domestic macroeconomic developments After the large decrease in real GDP by 5.2% in 2020, caused by the effects of the pandemic, real GDP increased by 5.2% in the first nine months of 2021 compared to a decrease of 5.6% in the same period of 2020. Growth was broad-based, although domestic demand was the main driver of recovery. In particular, private consumption increased by 3% in the first nine months of the year, mainly as a result of an increase in employment and earnings. At the same time, public spending increased significantly, by 11.2% in the first nine months of the year, as a result of support measures to mitigate the effects of the crisis. There has also been a recovery in investment, with the main focus being intense building activity in housing and infrastructure projects in the fields of tourism, energy and education. In relation to foreign demand, the increasing vaccination coverage in Cyprus and the rest of the European Union led to an easing of travel restrictive measures in early summer, resulting in a significant strengthening of the tourism sector. Revenues from tourism increased significantly between January and August 2021 by 126% compared to the same period in 2020, recording a more positive course than expected. However, they remained at around 42% of 2019 levels. The effects of the pandemic are also reflected in the labour market data, albeit to a relatively limited extent so far due to the effectiveness of the state's financial measures to support workers and enhance the liquidity of businesses. According to the available data of the Labour Force Survey, unemployment in the 3rd quarter of 2021 amounted to 6,6%% compared to 8,2% in the corresponding quarter of last year. Regarding prices, based on the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP), they recorded, on average, an annual increase of 1,8% during the first ten months of 2021 compared to an annual decrease of 1,1% in the corresponding period of 2020. In general, this development is mainly due to the increases in energy prices due mainly to the significant increase in the price of oil as well as the upward impact of the base, i.e. comparison, of electricity prices in the first ten months of the year with the corresponding period of last year. Other factors related to the pandemic, such as, for example, increases in the prices of products and goods due to disruptions or shortages in the supply chain and significant increases in transport costs have also contributed to the rise in specific production prices, such as construction costs, which are not directly reflected in the consumer price indices. Indirectly, however, and gradually, these increases contribute to the increase of specific components of the HICP, such as, for example, in the prices of industrial products excluding energy and services during the period under review. Inflation is expected to continue its upward path in 2022, owing to the ongoing upward impact of the above-mentioned factors related to supply and demand conditions amid the pandemic as well as the projected ongoing recovery in domestic economic activity. As regards the macroeconomic projections, the overall GDP growth for the whole of 2021 has been revised upwards compared to the June 2021 forecast, as the economic climate has improved significantly, while the tourism sector recorded a more positive than expected path. Real GDP reached pre-pandemic levels in the third quarter of 2021. The recovery is expected to continue in the fourth quarter of 2021 as well as in the coming years due to the ongoing support foreseen by both domestic and foreign demand and the boost that EU funding through the Recovery and Resilience Fund is expected to provide. However, the unpredictable course of the pandemic, in view of the various mutations of the virus, as well as the ongoing problems in supply chains (supply bottlenecks) are downside risks to the outlook for the economy. At the same time, it is worth noting that based on the latest data and compared to the CBC's June 2021 forecast, the economic growth in 2021 and thereafter is expected to be at higher levels, due to the greater vaccination coverage of the population compared to before the summer, the great adaptability (adaptation effects) on the part of households and businesses that has been observed since the beginning of the pandemic as well as the significant support to the financial support to the financial activity expected from the above-mentioned EU funding. The macroeconomic forecasts included in the government budget are broadly in line with those of the CBC that are expected to be published at the end of December 2021, due to the Confidentiality Rules of the Eurosystem that allow publication of national forecasts only after the announcement of the forecasts for the euro area by the European Central Bank (ECB). It is noted that the CBC's updated forecasts are somewhat more optimistic at the end of the forecast horizon due to the assumptions of work in relation to the macroeconomic impact of the financing from the Recovery and Resilience Fund. For 2021, the forecast for the extent of the recovery is in line with the available data and the ongoing positive growth rates from 2022 onwards reflect support from domestic and foreign demand. Despite the expected economic recovery, the existence of downside risks related mainly to the future evolution of the pandemic should not be overlooked. Budgetary developments d0 Budget 2022 Fiscal policy has adapted to the new needs and realities of the crisis. In 2020 and 2021, the state supported the economy and workers with exceptional fiscal impact measures of about 3.5% of GDP per year. As a result, the deficit for 2020 amounted to 5.7% of GDP, while for 2021 it is expected to be smaller, but beyond 3% of GDP. With the ongoing economic recovery, the impact on public finances is positive, which is expected to continue in 2022. At the same time, it is necessary to adapt fiscal policy objectives, from limiting the negative effects of the crisis to supporting sustainable growth and a more resilient economy. The current economic conditions lead to projections for a budget deficit of 1.1% of GDP in 2022, however, this is a significant improvement on the deficit beyond the 3% estimated for this year, mainly due to the expected withdrawal of the exceptional measures to support the economy to address the negative consequences of the pandemic. The activation of the general escape clause by the European Union ensures the necessary flexibility to address possible negative effects of the pandemic in 2022 with measures that are timely, temporary and targeted. The European Commission considers that, on the basis of its own forecasts and the information contained in the preliminary draft budget of Cyprus, the fiscal stance is expected to support growth, in line with the Council's recommendations of 18 July 2021 on the stability programme. At the same time, the state should begin to adapt to the return within the European Union's fiscal rules from 2023, either existing or revised, as prudent management of public finances is also key to assessing the country's creditworthiness. Public Debt is expected to remain sustainable and, following last year's significant increase, to continue its downward trend in the coming years. As I have stressed several times, it is important to avoid any derailment of fiscal indicators, beyond the impact due to the pandemic, so as to avoid the risks of not maintaining the country's investment grade. At the same time, the crisis has created the opportunity for a transition towards a more competitive and sustainable economy. The recovery plans of our economy, and in particular the absorption of the funds of the European Recovery and Resilience Facility, enable the realization and support of development projects that focus on the dual objective of digital and green growth. In addition, the modernization of the state through the implementation of structural reforms is an important parameter for achieving the goal of rational and efficient management of public finances. Overall, the CBC believes that the policy options to be adopted through the State Budget can and should help in the transition towards a more competitive, more resilient and sustainable economy. The outlook is auspicious given the positive, additional contribution of the European Resilience and Recovery Facility. Developments in the banking sector In 2021, the banking sector was faced with the challenges it had inherited from the previous banking crisis but also with the additional challenges created as a result of the pandemic. As is generally known, with the actions of the CBC and in cooperation with the Ministry of Finance, the moratorium on loan repayment for a period of nine months was issued where a large part of the borrowers (both households and businesses) who maintained performing loans were included below it and the installments of their credit facilities were frozen. The nine-month period ended at the end of December 2020. In particular, if we take into account the fact that these loans amounted to around db11.8 billion, it is easily understood that the challenge to deal with new restructuring requests in 2021 and the treatment of a possible new wave of non-performing loans (NPLs) was evident and unprecedented. On the part of the CBC, we had repeatedly drawn the attention of the banks with letters from the Governor and meetings of the Governor with the management of the banks, as to the need for their operational readiness regarding the possible incremental flow of applications for restructuring, as well as to the need to accelerate the time and procedures of restructuring to avoid the increase in non-performing loans but also to allow viable businesses to continue their work properly. At the same time, the CBC recommended to the banks that restructurings be completed quickly and with full transparency to borrowers. From the data on the credit facilities that were restructured, a significant increase in restructurings for the first half of 2021 has been observed, as a result of the above interventions, compared to the corresponding half of 2020. Specifically, the credit facilities that were restructured in the first half of this year amounted to db1.4 billion compared to db0.27 billion in the corresponding period of last year, with the percentage of increase amounting to more than 400%. In addition, the CBC developed the appropriate tools for collecting data and monitoring the progress of loans that their repayment should restart in 2021 due to the expiration of the payment moratorium. The results so far are positive given that the percentage of new loans from those that were included under the moratorium and which have become NPLs is just below 3%. This is indicative that the CBC's actions towards the banks for the need for their operational readiness to deal with the increased volume of restructurings brought the desired result. However, given the fact that the pandemic continues to afflict societies and consequently the economies of most countries, we should be cautious and be in a state of preparedness. In addition to any new NPLs, the existence of existing NPLs continues to be a burden on the balance sheets of our banking institutions, despite the progress made and the reduction of NPLs to levels around db4.6 billion at the end of August 2021 (and still close to db4 billion if we take into account the latest announcement of the Bank of Cyprus for the sale of NPLs of approximately db0.6 million). The NPL ratio stands at 17% at the level of the banking system, and, despite its large decrease, is still significantly higher than the EU average (around 2%). At this point I would like to note that the reduction in NPLs has been recorded in an individual number of banking institutions, while most banking institutions have not shown significant progress and should therefore accelerate their efforts to reduce the risk on their balance sheets. We should also not overlook the fact that a large part of the reduction in NPLs was absorbed by the credit acquiring companies (SPDs), which are governed by the Law on the purchase and sale of credit facilities and related matters. The implementation of the Code of Conduct for the Handling of Borrowers facing Financial Difficulties as well as the implementation of the CBC Directive taking into account the principle of proportionality should be applied by the SPDs, following a request by the CBC. Also, there is an obligation from the SPDs to evaluate, at least on a biannual basis, their Arrears Management Strategy (which includes provisions for the Code) and submit their revised Strategy to the CBC. In addition, the low profitability of banks due to the current environment and competition from payment institutions create the need to increase their efficiency, while the adjustment of their business model is necessary. In this context, there is also the need for investment in digitalization, which in the short term costs while the benefits are presented gradually but substantially in the long term. On the basis of the above challenges, we cannot rule out a possible further consolidation of our banking sector. Finally, I would like to mention the risks that the banking sector and the country's economy in general may face due to climate change. These risks certainly do not only concern our banking sector but perhaps most sectors of our economy and are not only a Cypriot, but a global phenomenon. The risks mentioned are divided into two broad categories: a) the increased costs that are likely to arise from the policies that may be implemented for a shift towards the green economy ,(such as for example corporate taxation for high emission of pollutants, replacement of environmentally friendly equipment, unprofitable economically unprofitable production units) and b) the negative effects of possible natural disasters, such as fires, drought and floods. Therefore, credit institutions and businesses should prepare fit to be able to recognise and measure their exposure to climate change and environmental risks and, on the basis thereof, to take concrete and targeted decisions in a timely manner. This risk may sound unprecedented and unprecedented, but the transition towards an environmentally friendly economy is the only option to ensure the sustainability of economic growth. Rapprochement between the business world and banks The Governor of the CBC, realizing the need for more effective interactive communication between the business world, economic operators and banks, organized a meeting on September 6, 2021 in which representatives of these groups participated. During this meeting, issues related to the proper functioning of the financial sector and the enhancement of the performance of the procedures applied to banking services were discussed, always with respect to laws and European regulations, for the benefit of both businesses and the banks themselves. As a result of the aforementioned meeting, a list of 10 actions was drawn up, which was communicated in writing to all participants in that meeting on 10 September. The CBC continues its actions to elaborate all agreed actions, in the belief that this important step will facilitate the constructive dialogue that must be conducted between banks and businesses in order not to create unnecessary obstacles to business development. It is emphasized that a necessary condition for the optimization of efficiency and the services offered is the practical contribution of banks and service providers and other professional bodies in the implementation of the aforementioned actions as well as their willingness to modernize. Monetary policy of the ECB As regards the ECB's monetary policy, the challenges continued in 2021. The maintenance of the highly expansionary and flexible monetary policy by the ECB, through the decisions of its Governing Council of which the Governor of the CBC and the other Governors of the National Banks of the euro area countries are a member, continued to offer favourable financing conditions to all its member states, including Cyprus, and contributed in a substantial way to mitigating the economic impact of the pandemic. In particular, the Eurosystem has continued since March 2020 to conduct net asset purchases under the Pandemic Emergency Purchase Programme (PEPP), the total amount of which is expected to reach db1,850 trillion by the end of March 2022. At the same time, monthly net asset purchases under the Asset Purchase Programme (APP) continue in order to enhance the impact of policy rates on the real economy. At the same time, the third series of targeted longer-term refinancing operations (TLTROs III) continues to support the provision of bank loans to firms and households as it remains an attractive source of funding for banks. The Central Bank of Cyprus continues to implement the ECB's policy, including both the APP programme and the PEPP, by purchasing Cyprus government bonds. The implementation of bond purchase programmes, which continued in 2021, contributes to risk reduction by containing government bond yields and the cost of servicing public debt. As in 2020, so in 2021, the CBC conducted significant purchases of Cypriot government bonds both under the emergency PEPP and the public sector purchase programme, public sector purchase programme d0 PSPP (under the APP). Indicatively, I would like to mention that on 30 November 2021, the CBC's balance sheet contained monetary policy portfolios totalling db8.6 billion, of which approximately db5.6 billion. euro related to positions in Cypriot government bonds, resulting in a reduction in the cost of Cypriot government bonds Noteworthy for 2021 is the review of the ECB's monetary policy strategy last July, for the first time in 18 years. Under the new strategy, the medium-term inflation target is symmetrical at 2%. This means that the negative and positive deviations of inflation from the target are equally undesirable and that in a transitional period inflation may be moderately above target. Financial literacy In relation to the problem of financial illiteracy in Cyprus, which has both social and economic implications, it is important to stress that basic financial knowledge contributes to economic prosperity both on an individual and social level. The application of this knowledge in practice helps households to avoid problems such as, for example, over-indebtedness and overconsumption, lack of savings for unexpected events, inadequate pension, etc. As early as 2018, the CBC conducted a sample survey to ascertain the level of financial illiteracy in Cyprus, on the basis of a questionnaire by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). It is also noted that the state has set in 2021 the national strategy for financial literacy as one of the actions in the Recovery and Resilience Plan, so it is encouraging that both the CBC and the state share the same concern about the future of financial literacy in our country. To this end, the ad-hoc Committee ("Committee") for the establishment of a National Strategy for the promotion of Financial Literacy and the strengthening of Financial Education in Cyprus was established in December 2020, following a recommendation by the House Standing Committee on Education and Culture. The ad-hoc Committee consists of members from the CBC which has a leading and coordinating role, the Ministry of Finance, the Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports and Youth, the Hellenic Capital Market Commission and two academics in their personal capacity. At this point I would like to highlight my personal interest and commitment to full support for the work of the ad hoc Committee. Today I am pleased to report that the ad-hoc Committee has taken important steps for the design of the National Strategy on the basis of the aforementioned holistic survey conducted by the CBC in 2018 for the first time on a Pancyprian basis. The results of this Survey were made public in April 2021 and are available on the CBC's website. The aim of the Committee is to submit a Report to the Council of Ministers on the National Strategy soon. The exhibition will include an evaluation of the international literature on the subject, an analysis of the results of the aforementioned research conducted by the CBC on the level of financial literacy in Cyprus, as well as proposals for the most important strategic goals that will be set, in order to promote financial literacy in our country as soon as possible. Epilogue Summing up what I mentioned, I am convinced that Cyprus has so far managed to limit, as far as possible, the huge economic consequences of the pandemic thanks to the timely implementation of measures, both at European and domestic level since the beginning of the pandemic. The concerted effort of all of us has paid off and is reflected in the strong growth performance recorded this year despite the difficult and uncertain endemic circumstances. It is of course extremely important to continue the effort so that we can successfully face the remaining challenges that lie ahead of us and to be able to completely eliminate the consequences of the pandemic. It remains the CBC's long-standing position that targeted policy-making, adoption of new technology and coordination are fundamental to fully address the consequences of Covid-19, but also for our smooth transition to a path of sustainable development.

Title: Annual Report of the Central Bank of Cyprus for 2008
text: Fintech Evolution in the Banking System and Managing Consequent risks Nicosia, 8 December 2021 The pandemic has highlighted the importance that technology plays in allowing the financial system to continue, as smoothly as possible with its operations. Global Fintech investment continued its remarkable growth, rising from 87 billion in H2d520 to 98 billion in H1d521. Global Fintech deal volume also hit a new record of 2,456 during H1d521. Data also shows that consumers worldwide are adopting Fintech services much more quickly than anticipated. In 2017 it was predicted that 52% of consumers worldwide would have adopted Fintech services by 2019, but the estimate proved to be too conservative as the actual figure overshot it by 12 points. This overshooting happened before the pandemic. Although data is not yet available, the recent health crisis must have accelerated further this figure. The growth in the Fintech market is also obvious from the number of Fintech startups. As of November 2021, there were 10,755 Fintech startups in the Americas, making it the region with the most Fintech startups globally. In comparison, there were 9,323 such startups in Europe, the Middle East, and Africa and 6,268 in the Asia Pacific region. Cyprus is no exception to this global trend. There are currently 14 authorised electronic money institutions and 10 authorised payment institutions while there are 43 pending applications (32 EMIs and 11 PIs). Compare this with the 12 local and foreign authorised banks and subsidiaries in our country. However, as with all revolutions, these global developments come with costs and risks. The number of cyber incidents reported to the ECB Banking Supervision in 2020 increased by 54% compared to 2019. Banks are specifically targeted. Banks underwent almost 26% of cybercrimes in 2019. These included compromised credit cards, leaked credentials and malicious banking applications. Banking landscape and future change The euro area banking sector is undergoing a transformation, with higher competition from non-bank financial intermediaries and Fintech institutions. The euro aread5s financial [1] structure has seen a movement from strong bank dominance towards a more balanced composition . The development of non-bank lending diversifies the sources of finance available to businesses, providing competition to the banking sector. As a result, Credit institutions need to adapt to the unfolding competitive landscape. The ongoing digitalisation of society at large, coupled with the changes in the way people work and conduct their purchases because of the pandemic, force the banking sector to adapt to a new way of conducting business. In addition, the low profitability challenge that European banks face, exacerbates the need to adjust and acts as a catalyst for the already strong competition banks are experiencing from Fintech and the non-bank financial intermediation firms. Fintech institutions operate on a very different business model compared to traditional banks and as such, they have a competitive advantage in terms of cost structure and overheads. Their cost advantage and speed of operational and business decision making is evident by their rapid expansion and their proven ability to grow their user base quickly. However, although Fintech bring obvious benefits to users, up until recently we havend5t seen large defections of customers from traditional banks to these new players. The confidence to the incumbent banking structure together with the value that people place on their existing bank relationships provide the opportunity for an adjustment period for incumbents. Having said that, generational differences matter. Consumers aged 25 to 40, also known as generation Y, have had the biggest effect on digitization of financial [2] services . Generation Y account for almost 50% of mobile banking users. Based on this trend, banks can expect Generation Z (ages up to 24 years) to be even more engaged in digital banking and technology driven solutions. In contrast, generation X, the baby boomers, still see value in live communication and visiting physical bank branches. These younger consumers look for alternative ways of processing their financial transactions that are simpler and faster. The banking system needs to adapt. Incumbent banks that work with dated technologies and overextended branch networks are likely to lose their competitive edge. Technological innovation is the way to increase efficiency as a result of new competitors entering the market and new generations being more reliant on technology. Since the global financial crisis, the euro area banking sector has been going through a gradual restructuring process, which involves the search for new business models, the [3] adjustment to the revised regulatory regime, consolidation and the resolution of non-performing assets . In fact in 2020 the number of completed mergers and acquisitions in the banking euro area increased even though this type of M&A had been decreasing since 2010. In an effort to further contain costs and consolidate the banking sector, the number of euro area banks and branches has continuously declined by approximately 30% since [4] 2008 . Incumbent banks must restructure and improve on technology and efficiency simultaneously with the entry of new competition also from Bigtech. Technology giants are entering financial services as their next related business. Global technology giants have built extraordinary market advantages: large and engaged customer network; huge data enabling robust and increasingly precise understanding of individual customers, experience in scaling innovative technologies and because of their size, access to low cost of capital. BigTech players have already gained a foothold in financial services in select domains such as payments and in some cases lending and insurance. However, digitalisation also poses significant financial and operational risks, both in the banking sector and in the Fintech / BigTech companies, themselves. [5] The Financial Stability Board has recognised a number of operational risks, including: 1. Operational risks of third-party reliance that are transferred to banks. Usage of services, such as cloud computing, increase the interdependence of banks to third-party providers and consequently increase operational risk. Therefore, the banking system is becoming increasingly more vulnerable to operational incidents at third-party service providers. 2. The reliance of banks on digital platforms for the marketing and distribution of financial services is creating new forms of reputational interdependencies within the EUd5s banking and payments sector. 3. Furthermore, excessive reliance on automation and IT might increase the challenges for Know Your Customer (KYC) procedures and offer new scope for money.laundering. 4. Cyber risk can be further exacerbated in the case of unsupervised parallel payment systems and rising interconnectedness between application interfaces (such as smart phone payments). Further financial risks include: 1. the robustness of Fintech companies which has not been tested yet fully. In fact, the Financial Stability Board has noticed several high-profile failures among Fintech platforms such as the Lending Club in the US and Trust Buddy in Sweden; 2. also, the evolution of BigTech companies and the risk of becoming too-big-to-fail can be another source of systemic financial risk. A malfunction at a systemically important BigTech company, could bring down key services across multiple banks and countries. The above risks translate directly to financial stability threats. The transmission of any of the above risks to one institution could be immediate to other institutions or sectors as a whole. These systemic risks should be tackled by authorities. Macroprudential authorities should coordinate their actions in order to mitigate these risks and seek ways to balance the protection of customersd5 interests and financial institution risks with specific policy objectives, a level-playing field being one of them. The initiatives taken by the European Commission, such as the digital finance package, that captures d0 among others -the proposal for digital operational resilience act [6] (DORA ), and the revision of the second Payment Services Directive, are steps towards mitigating the identified risks. The increasing number of Cyber-attacks in Europe indicates that a lot more needs to be done. The growth of the Fintech sector has raised the need for regulators to adjust their role within the perimeter of prudential regulation. Extending the perimeter of bank regulation to all financial service providers could possibly constrain financial innovation. But keeping the new entrants completely out of the perimeter will tilt the playing field in their favour and leave consumers unprotected. A balance must be found to allow the regulatory perimeter to cover all activities that have systemic risk potential, while allowing for innovation. Finally, Data protection is important in order to safeguard confidence in the banking sector. As a result, Cyber security should be further enhanced and prioritised and Cyber-risk incidents need to be included in financial institutionsd5 business continuity and disaster recovery plans and be tested frequently. Given the cross-border activities of Fintech and BigTech, authorities across jurisdictions should cooperate in regulating them. THANK YOU. [1] Financial Integration and Structure in the Euro Area: [2] 4 Challenges for the financial industry and the best tech solutions to fight them, Rocky Osborn, November 2020. [3] Financial Stability Review, November 2021: [4] EU structural financial indicators: end of 2020: [5] Financial Stability Implications from the FinTech, Financial Stability Board, 27 June 2017. [6] DORA is a European attempt to streamline the third-party risk management process across financial institutions, by ensuring that an organization can continue to guarantee the continuity and quality of its services in the face of operational disruptions in information and communication technologies.

Title: Assuming responsibilities
text: Taking up office Address by Panikos Demetriades, Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus, after taking office Nicosia, 7 May 2012 First of all, I would like to thank the President of the Republic of Cyprus, Mr. Demetris Christofias, for the trust he has shown in me, with the assignment of the important post of Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus (CBC), especially today when the Cypriot economy is going through difficult days and when our domestic banks operating in Greece are facing challenges. I would also like to state in advance my will to cooperate with the Ministry of Finance, the political forces of the country, as well as with the economic and social partners of our country, always guided by the good of the economy and the well-understood public interest, and within the framework of respect for the independence of the CBC and the relevant provisions and provisions of the relevant legislation. It is well known to all of us that the current economic and financial conditions d0 and especially the state of the banking system both in Cyprus and in the other Member States of the European Union d0 are not the best. I would, however, like to give a signal of optimism. I believe that the current problems and obstacles are not insurmountable. With hard work, with good cooperation with all stakeholders as well as with responsibility, honesty and delicate handling - both inside and outside Cyprus - today's difficulties will be overcome. The role of a Central Bank in an economy is always important. The role of the CBC under the current circumstances becomes even more important. The Bank can and has a duty to play its part in resolving the current economic crisis.
