Our goal must be to restore stability to our financial system as soon as possible, through the recovery of investor confidence in our banking system and the Cypriot economy in general, utilizing all the tools at our disposal as a Central Bank. I believe that the strengthening of both the institution and the role of the CBC are basic prerequisites for the exit of the economy from the crisis. In this effort, the contribution of all the Bank's staff is significant. Each of us has his own role to play in the effort to overcome our country the difficulties it is going through today. With professionalism, honesty, responsibility, hard work, proper cooperation, mutual respect, respect for the opposite point of view, sobriety but also determination and with the best use of the Bank's human resources, I am sure that this effort will bring the desired result. I personally pledge that I will run the Central Bank based on the principles of good administration and the principles of governance appropriate to a Central Bank, meritocracy, optimal use of staff where everyone performs best, respect for the work and personality of each employee (or colleague). I expect that you, too, will work with me with the main aim of being worthy of the trust with which the Bank surrounds you, so that together we can achieve the objectives arising from the institutional responsibilities of the CBC. We need to do everything in our power to overcome today's difficulties. Failure is not an option. Because it will not only be a failure for us, but it will be tantamount to a failure for the whole of Cyprus. I would now like to thank Mr Orphanides for the rich work he has done at the Central Bank during his term of office. I have no doubt that the infrastructure that currently exists in the CBC in terms of monetary policy and Cyprus' participation in the Eurosystem, to which he joined during his term of office, owes a great deal to Mr Orphanides. The same can be said of the Bank's research orientation, which is an important background for its policy-making. I should also add that Mr. Orphanides, in his own way, has contributed greatly to the image we have outside Cyprus as an institution and as a country. Let me conclude my speech with my best wishes for all the best in his future career. I have no doubt that Mr. Orphanides has a lot to offer as a researcher and technocrat economist. I am also sure that the experiences he gained during his tenure will be useful to him in his future career.

Title: The euro conversion rate of the Cyprus pound
text: Address to ETYK Address by Mr. Panicos Demetriades, Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus, at the 44th Ordinary Pancyprian Congress of etyk Nicosia, 12 May 2012 It is with great honor that I accepted your invitation to address the forty-fourth Ordinary Pancyprian Congress of etyk, a trade union organization with a rich work in the timeless defense of workers' rights in the wider banking sector of Cyprus. I thank you very much for giving me the first opportunity since the day I took office as Governor of the CBC, to publicly and briefly express some of my assessments regarding the situation and the challenges that the Cypriot economy is currently facing. I assume my duties as Governor of the CBC at an admittedly difficult time for the economy of our country and the euro area as a whole. We have before us specific problems that need to be addressed immediately, problems that arose both from the international financial crisis that began in autumn 2008, and from its transformation into a debt crisis in many of the member countries of the euro area. Cyprus was inevitably affected by these unpleasant economic developments and especially by the consequences of the fiscal crisis that hit the Greek economy. An economy that is directly and variously linked to the economy of Cyprus and in particular to our banking sector. The consequences of the write-down of the Greek debt have created unprecedented challenges in this sector, on which the return of the Cypriot economy to conditions of healthy and sustainable growth directly depends. The manipulations carried out by both the CBC and the Ministry of Finance focus on the recapitalisation of the banking sector as soon as possible and the regaining of its role as a locomotive of growth and progress for Cypriot businesses and households. In parallel with the efforts to address the challenges in the banking sector, the efforts made by the Ministry of Finance regarding the consolidation of the country's fiscal situation, which was reversed mainly due to the international economic crisis and the recession that was consequently caused to the Cypriot economy, should be supported. Both in Cyprus and in the euro area in general, it is now understood that the austerity policy alone is not enough to restore the finances of any country on a healthy basis, especially when the rest of the EU countries follow the same policy. Above all, it needs development. Ending the upward trend in unemployment, widening employment. While respecting the Fiscal Framework agreed by the leaders of the euro area is an important step towards regaining fiscal balances, the further recession that austerity measures alone reproduce, unfortunately reinforces the vicious circle between the reduction of economic activity and the widening of budget deficits. This requires the enrichment or combination of the existing Financial Framework with a strong framework of development measures. With a strong net of protection of employment and the standard of living of citizens that will put an end to the further landslide of the state's revenues and the consequent further growth of deficits. For example, the reduction in unproductive public expenditure must necessarily be accompanied by an expansion of both the size and the quality and effectiveness of development spending. The country's productivity should also be boosted by investing in human resources and modern technology. With the primary goal for our country, the restoration of growth rates in the pre-crisis years. For the above reasons, I would like at this point to note with particular satisfaction the positions expressed by the PRESIDENT of the ECB after the last meeting of the ECB's Board of Directors in Barcelona (5 May 2012). Specifically, Mr. Draghi stressed that "there is a need for a development framework" and that "there is absolutely no contradiction between a growth framework and a fiscal framework." He also added that "growth is sustainable in the long term if it is based on a number of parameters, one of which is fiscal stability" and that "we should put growth at the center of the agenda". This position clearly seems to be gaining ground among European leaders. European Commission Vice-President Olli Rehn also expressed supportive positions towards growth, who on May 5th stressed that "while fiscal consolidation is inevitable and structural reforms are the key to growth in the medium term, active fiscal policy to promote growth is equally necessary". "We need," he added, "stability but we also need growth." In particular, Mr Rehn argued that "fiscal consolidation, while necessary, must be done in a growth-friendly and differentiated manner in order to strike a balance between the necessary fiscal consolidation and the growth concerns that exist". He further noted that we need "more European cross-border and COMMUNITY investment in infrastructure projects  in energy, transport, innovation, research and communications", adding that "in the last year the European Commission has proposed the creation of special bonds ("project bonds") for infrastructure investments, which are a new tool for unlocking private financing. We proposed, Olli Rehn continued, "the use of the EU budget and the European Investment Bank for limited risk sharing with private investors", adding also that the possibility of "reprogramming the Structural Funds as has recently been done with Greece" is being considered. This he said "can be done effectively through guarantee funds for small and medium-sized enterprises in order to address the difficult financing conditions they often face". Finally, he stressed that the European Investment Bank is a strong EU institution to support growth and jobs, which is why its capital needs need to be addressed. Green growth, he concluded, is also an important objective of the strategy for growth and jobs. I hope that the above development strategies and the new possibilities opened up in the EU through the new tools proposed by Olli Rehn will be carefully examined and exploited by our country as well. Both the tools for promoting new infrastructure projects, mainly with European funding through the reprogramming of the Structural Funds, and the release of resources to small and medium-sized enterprises, can be essential steps towards overcoming the current recession. In conclusion, I would like to assure you that both the CBC and I, as governor, will work methodically and in close cooperation with the Government, the Ministry of Finance and all the social and political actors of the country so that we can properly face the difficult challenges that lie before us. We owe it to our country, we owe it mainly to future generations. I am optimistic that with hard work, with good cooperation with all stakeholders, methodicalness, honesty and delicate handling, both inside and outside Cyprus, today's difficulties will be overcome.

Title: Comment on "What have economists learned about monetary policy over the past 50 years?"
text: Banking and Development Speech by Panicos Demetriades, Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus, at the public debate on "The Cyprus Economy Today and Tomorrow" organized by the Nicosia Chamber of Commerce and Industry Nicosia, 13 June 2012 It is with great pleasure that I accepted the invitation to participate in this public debate on the present and future of the Cypriot economy. Today I would like to briefly set out some of my views on the role of the banking sector in economic growth. The banking sector is a key part of the wider financial system and the main donor of a country's economy. The fact that in all the advanced economies of the world there are highly developed banking systems while in the underdeveloped countries these systems are still at an early stage, cannot be considered accidental. Overall, a healthy, stable and reliable banking sector that plays a key role in financial intermediation is essential for a country's economic growth and financial stability. From the simplest to the most complex banking system, there are a number of services on offer, which by extension are the raison d'etre of financial intermediation in the economy. Each banking sector offers services related to the avoidance and diversification of the risk created during the investment process, acts as a system for the effective allocation of the available resources of the economy to its various sectors, is a means of assessing and controlling the course of completion of investment projects, provides incentives for savings and facilitates the exchange of goods and services in the economy. It is also interesting that while the form of the financial system internationally and by extension of financial intermediation has changed  where internationally the financial markets now hold an upgraded role  in most countries of the world the process of saving on the one hand and investing on the other continues to pass through the concept of the banking system, thus giving it one of the most important roles in an economy. The relationship between banks and the development of the economy has been and remains to be one of the most popular topics in growth economics over the last two decades at least. It is also a topic that I have dealt with as an academic-researcher since the beginning of my academic career, that is, since 1990. Regardless of whether the development of the financial system provokes or simply follows economic growth, most of the scientific community supports the existence of a positive relationship between these two. Also, the view that it is the development of (a healthy) financial system that gives a boost to the economy and not the other way around seems to be the prevailing one. A critical analysis of this issue, guided by the academic literature, leads to the very important conclusion that the combination of loose prudential regulation and supervision with incomplete corporate governance in private banks, can have disastrous consequences for the rest of the economy. It has also been observed that the lack of transparency in conditions of lax supervision and/or regulation and weak corporate governance has the potential to even lead to the "looting" of banks (through e.g. lending to affiliated persons). With the experiences we have had recently, particularly since the financial crisis that erupted in the US in 2007 and later lay down in other developed countries, economic growth is no longer the same as the size of the financial system but with the quality of its regulation and supervision. Recent research has shown that when the financial system is under strict supervision, the growth rate of the economy can be up to 2% higher per year compared to a regime of lax supervision. It has also been observed that the quality of supervision determines whether financial reforms increase or decrease the growth rate of the real economy. For example, measures that lead to increased competition in the banking system  which, at first sight, sound good  may lead to a decrease in the growth rate of up to 0.4% per year, when supervision of the system is lax. The recent global financial crisis and its ensuing consequences have been food for serious reflection in many countries, while special committees have been set up to study the facts, draw conclusions and formulate recommendations to the competent authorities. For example, in the UK the final report of the Independent Commission on the Banking System(1), published in September 2011, includes modern economic policy lessons on hot banking issues that transcend the country's national borders. The five-member committee, led by renowned Oxford professor Sir John Vickers, aimed to propose reforms that would create a more stable and competitive banking system that could cope with future financial crises without transferring risks from banks to public finances. A banking sector that will be effective and efficient in providing basic banking services, such as deposit protection, the smooth functioning of payment systems, the efficient channelling of savings to productive investments and the management of financial risks. The report stresses the importance of taking measures at national level that support and strengthen international initiatives, such as Basel III and various European Union (EU) initiatives. It also recognises that international initiatives alone are not sufficient to ensure the stability of a large banking system of an international nature, such as that of the United Kingdom. The measures proposed by the Vickers Commission are intended to increase banks' ability to absorb losses, to facilitate the resolution of banking problems when they arise and to limit banks' incentives to take excessive risks. The first conclusion drawn in the report is that it is not right for a taxpayer to bear the risks arising from the banking system. In the same position are small depositors, who do not have the incentives or the ability to recognize, monitor and evaluate banking risks. These risks must be borne by the owners of the bank, whose funds must be able to absorb any losses. The most important suggestion of the report is the creation of a ring-fence between activities that have a retail character and those that have a wholesale or investment character. The activities that will be integrated within the ring will be those that are vital and as such need to be protected by the state, such as basic banking services to households and small and medium-sized enterprises (i.e. the taking of deposits and the provision of loans and other loans) and payment services or those that facilitate mediation between savers and borrowers with customers outside the financial system of the European Economic Zone. Other activities, such as the financing of large enterprises, will be allowed to join up to a certain limit. The size of the UK banking system is 6 trillion, which is about 4 times the country's Gross National Product (GDP). The report suggests that a sixth to a third of this size could be included in the protective ring. In other words, it suggests that the size of the system enjoying state coverage should be limited to 67%133% of the UK's GDP. The report makes suggestions that will ensure the effectiveness of the protective ring, such as the independent management of retail activities by staffing the boards with independent members, the adequacy of capital, liquidity, etc. The Cameron government has already announced that the recommendations of the Vickers Commission are acceptable and that it will seek to make the necessary arrangements in the legislative framework before the end of the current parliament's term. Another major weakness that the financial crisis has shown is that public authorities are not sufficiently equipped to they are facing failing banks operating in today's global markets. In the EU in particular, the need for more effective financial crisis management regulation at national level has become clear, as well as the need for arrangements that are more appropriate to deal with cross-border bank failures. During the crisis there were several failures of banks of major importance (e.g. Fortis, Anglo Irish Bank, Dexia), which revealed serious shortcomings in the existing arrangements. Given the absence of mechanisms to organise an orderly winding-up, EU Member States had no choice but to rescue their banking sector. In order to preserve basic financial services for households and businesses, governments were forced to inject public money into banks and provide guarantees on an unprecedented scale. Specifically, from October 2008 to October 2011, the European Commission approved state aid measures to financial institutions amounting to 4.5 trillion. (which corresponds to 37% of the EU's GNP) (2). This prevented massive bank failure and financial upheaval, but burdened taxpayers with the deterioration of public finances and failed to resolve the issue of how to deal with large cross-border banks in financial difficulties. In light of the above, there is a pressing need for decisive reforms to strengthen the banking system in the EU and avoid future errors and bailouts with taxpayers' money. Internal Market Commissioner Michel Barnier said recently, "the financial crisis has cost taxpayers a lot of money" and "we need to equip public authorities so that they can deal adequately with future banking crises. Otherwise, citizens will once again have to foot the bill, while the rescued banks will continue to act as before, as long as they know that they will be rescued again" (European Commission, 2012). With the aim of moving away from the current situation where the fate of fiscal institutions is excessively linked to that of banks, the European Commission adopted on 6 June 2012 proposals for EU-wide rules for the recovery and resolution of credit institutions, which should ensure that in the future the authorities have the means to intervene decisively before the problems arise and at a sufficiently early stage of the process, in case of problems. Moreover, if a bank's financial situation deteriorates so much that it cannot be corrected, the proposal ensures that the bank's critical functions can be bailed out, while the costs of restructuring and resolution of failed banks will be borne by their owners and creditors and not by taxpayers. The proposed tools in the new framework are divided into powers of "preparation and prevention", "early intervention" and "resolution", while the intervention of the authorities becomes more and more penetrating as the situation worsens. Banks and authorities will need to prepare timely plans to address possible scenarios for banks themselves to cope with the pressures themselves and overcome difficulties on their own. If, nevertheless, a bank encounters problems, the authorities must act immediately. Among the possible intrusive measures are the replacement of bank CEOs or the convening of shareholders to persuade them to adopt extraordinary measures, or, in extreme cases, the sale of a failing bank to a viable competitor. To be effective, resolution tools will require some funding. If market financing is not possible and in order to avoid the financing of resolution actions by the state, additional funding will be made available from resolution funds, which will receive contributions from banks depending on their liabilities and risk profiles. The funds will be used exclusively to support smooth reorganisation and resolution, and in no case to bail out banks. National resolution funds will cooperate, in particular to provide funding for the resolution of cross-border banks. To make the best use of resources, the European Commission's proposal also builds on the funding already available in the 27 deposit guarantee schemes, which will provide funding, alongside resolution funds, to protect private depositors. Cyprus has inevitably been affected by the international financial crisis and its transformation into a debt crisis in many of the euro area member countries, particularly by the negative consequences of the fiscal crisis that hit the Greek economy. An economy that is directly and in various ways linked to that of Cyprus and in particular to our banking sector. The consequences of the impairment of Greek government bonds have created unprecedented challenges in this sector, on which the return of the Cypriot economy to conditions of healthy and sustainable growth directly depends. Moreover, banks are facing, primarily due to the protracted recession in Greece but also to a lesser extent due to the negative macroeconomic developments in Cyprus, the increased difficulty of households and firms in servicing their debt obligations normally. The manipulations carried out by both the Central Bank of Cyprus (CBC) and the Ministry of Finance focus on the recapitalization of the banking sector as soon as possible, which will achieve a significant strengthening of their robustness and the transparency that is expected to contribute to the gradual restoration of market confidence. In addition to meeting banks' current capital needs, there are other parameters that need to be reviewed or improved. First of all, the banking sector over time has been the largest component of the wider financial system of our country and the main means of financial intermediation. It is a fact, however, that the banking sector is very large compared to the size of the Cypriot economy. Specifically, at the end of December 2011, the consolidated assets of all banks operating in Cyprus, including cooperative credit institutions, amounted to about 8 times the country's GDP, while that of domestic banks, including cooperative credit institutions, amounted to approximately 5.5 times the GDP of Cyprus. It is accepted that the significant growth of the banking sector in recent years is the result of the strategy of promoting Cyprus as an international centre for financial services, especially after its entry into the European Union in 2004. This strategy has been very successful, and this sector plays an important role both in domestic employment and in the economic development of the country. This growth, however, creates very significant systemic risks that oblige the state, under the current circumstances, to support large domestic banks in the event that they face significant financial difficulties. In view of the above, I am of the opinion that maintaining a healthy and dynamic banking sector with a manageable size so that there is no risk of destabilization of the entire financial system and the economy of Cyprus and of not burdening public finances in case of problems in individual banking institutions, should be the issue. It is for this reason that the CBC in the coming months will examine in depth, with the help of experts, both the issue of the optimal size of our banking system and the issue of its optimal structure. At the same time, regarding the microeconomic aspect of the banking system and the safeguarding of financial stability, we will seek on the one hand organizational improvements within the CBC itself aimed at strengthening the supervisory framework and on the other hand strengthening the financial risk management framework in the banks themselves. We intend to learn from the mistakes of the past and make the necessary improvements to make sure that such mistakes are not repeated. Indicatively, the CBC will proceed to an in-depth investigation of the circumstances that led to the current unsatisfactory financial situation of the two large Cypriot banks with the help of independent and well-known professional experts so that the findings / conclusions are highly reliable. Better management of banking risks naturally requires improvements to be made to the corporate governance of commercial banks which, among other things, include the upgrading of the boards of directors of banking institutions, which must be staffed by independent executives with excellent training and recognised prestige and honesty. A well-staffed board must include people with a deep understanding of the multidimensional nature of the financial risks that banks face today. It must also include people with experience and knowledge of banking and audit procedures, but also people with deep knowledge on issues of international economy, as well as small and medium-sized enterprises, since the latter are the backbone of the Cypriot economy. It is also important to mention that the whole effort made by the competent authorities to gradually improve the situation in the banking sector and to strengthen the confidence of investors and depositors is expected to have a positive impact on the financing costs of households and businesses in the medium term. In particular, as far as businesses are concerned, a possible reduction in the cost of borrowing in the domestic market will certainly have beneficial effects on corporate activity and profitability and consequently on the development of the real economy of the country. However, I would also like to highlight a positive element in relation to our credit system. Unlike commercial banks, cooperatives credit institutions (MFA), with their own business practices focused on the domestic economy and the separate supervisory regime, seem to have suffered, so far at least, fewer negative consequences from the crisis. This shows that diversity in a country's banking business model enhances the resilience of the system and reduces the build-up of systemic risk. Examples of other countries such as the Netherlands (Rabobank) and the United Kingdom (Building Societies) reinforce this finding. It is also important to add that academic analyses such as that of LSE Professor Emeritus Charles Goodhart, who is considered perhaps the best economist in the world on such matters, do not justify the view that in developed countries a central bank should supervise all credit institutions (Goodhart, 2000). It is for this reason that the view, which is supported, among other things, by the International Monetary Fund that there should be a single supervisory authority for all credit institutions operating in our country, does not agree with me. The most important thing is not which authority supervises the MFA but how good the supervision is. I therefore believe that the aim must be to continuously improve the effectiveness of the supervision of the cooperative credit sector, as well as that of commercial banks, as well as to strengthen cooperation between all the competent supervisory authorities in Cyprus. As regards the first, the regulatory framework for this sector is fully harmonized with the relevant EU Directives, while the directives, regulations and guidelines governing the operation of commercial banks and issued by the CBC are subsequently adopted by the Office for the Development and Supervision of Co-operative Societies for MFA. There is certainly always room for improvement in any supervisory and regulatory framework. I also note that there is already a good basis for cooperation between all the competent supervisory authorities of the Financial System of Cyprus, in accordance with both Memoranda of Understanding that are in force in matters of prudential supervision (between the competent supervisory authorities) and ensuring financial stability (between the competent supervisory authorities and the Ministry of Finance). At this point, I would like to stress that it is very important today that any structural reforms promoted by international bodies and organisations in the name of the development perspective are evidence-based, otherwise the policies imposed are very likely to have, once again, disappointing results. In conclusion, I would like to address a message of cautious optimism that, despite the very important challenges before us, with hard work, with good cooperation between the stakeholders, methodicalness, honesty and delicate handling, both inside and outside Cyprus, today's difficulties will be overcome. With the necessary corrective actions on the part of the competent authorities and the banks themselves, we aim to gradually restore the soundness of the banking sector and the confidence of the markets in it so that it can effectively perform its key intermediary role and contribute to the return of the Cypriot economy to a path of sustainable economic growth. ------------------------------------------------ FOOTNOTES: (1) Independent Commission on Banking (ICB). (2) See European Commission. BIBLIOGRAPHY: European Commission (2012) Press Release: New Crisis Management Measures to Avoid Future Bank Bailouts, 6 June. Goodhart, Charles A.E. (2000) "The organisational structure of banking supervision", Special Paper 127, LSE Financial Markets Group, October.

Title: Euro, Our Currency
text: Challenges and prospects of the Cypriot economy Speech by Panicos Demetriades, Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus, at the CUT event entitled: "Challenges and prospects of the Cypriot economy" Limassol, 28 June 2012 Import First of all, I would like to thank the Cyprus University of Technology (CUT), the Association "Friends of CUT" as well as the Limassol Chamber of Commerce and Industry (LCCI) for inviting me to attend today's event on the "challenges and prospects of the Cypriot economy". At this difficult time for the economy of our country, this invitation gives me the opportunity to share with you some of my thoughts and concerns about the current economic developments and the future development prospects of our country. Which of course depend directly on the way the greatest challenges that the country faces at the moment, namely the need to clean up its banking system, improve the fiscal situation and effectively address the erosion that has been observed over time in the competitiveness of our country. The international financial crisis that erupted in 2008 and the recession that followed also decisively affected Cyprus, contributing substantially to the creation of the aforementioned challenges. GDP growth rates decreased significantly compared to the pre-crisis years and this led to the deterioration of the country's fiscal situation. Subsequently, the debt crisis that erupted in the euro area and especially in the Greek economy added new serious problems to the already deteriorating economic situation in Cyprus. The strong economic ties between Cyprus and Greece and especially between the banking sectors of the two countries in combination with the decision of European leaders of October 2011 to write down Greek debt caused great losses to Cypriot banks, bringing them face to face with unprecedented challenges. Also, the ongoing recession and the uncertainty that characterize the Greek economy raise serious concerns about further damage to our banking system, in addition to the aforementioned direct effects of the impairment of Greek bonds. Banking system More specifically, and as far as our banking system is concerned, the extent of the losses already caused by the aforementioned developments have inevitably led our country to apply for assistance from the European Financial Stability Facility (EFSF). This decision has been triggered by the need to recapitalise Cypriot banks that were unable to secure sufficient private capital by the deadline set by the European Banking Authority of June 2012. The application for assistance from this mechanism should not be treated as a negative development. This mechanism is designed to provide support and guidance to countries applying for assistance so that they can best overcome the difficulties they face under the circumstances. For this reason, the Central Bank of Cyprus (CBC) expresses its support for the decision of the Cypriot government to request financial support from the HFSF. In these difficult economic times, when public finances are already under intense pressure, it is vital to restore the ability of the banking system to promote economic growth as soon as possible. In particular, with regard to Cyprus and the problem faced by its banking sector, the support mechanism will provide the necessary assistance and guidance to identify and evaluate accurately and with the help of independent firms any problems that have occurred in the banks' portfolios, with the ultimate goal of resolution and the further smooth operation of the system. I mention, indicatively, without necessarily adopting it, since our own assessment is still pending, the estimate of fitch, that banks need an amount corresponding to around 33% of our country's GDP (around 6 billion to recapitalize them and to address the expected future losses in their portfolios (this amount includes 1.8 billion for Laiki Bank). We expect that financial support from our European partners will help to ensure that these objectives are achieved in a timely and methodical manner, while ensuring the stability of our financial system and the economy in general. However, at this point I would like to further analyze my thoughts on the future course of the financial system of Cyprus and the EU in general, the needs for changes in the existing operating framework at European level, as well as to explain also the strategy that as a CBC at national level we plan to take with the aim of the complete consolidation and restructuring of the sector. Starting with developments in the EU regarding the future of the Union's financial sector, the need for more effective financial crisis management regulation at national and European level has become clear, as well as the need for regulations that are more appropriate to deal with cross-border bank failures. The need to create a banking union in the euro area with uniform supervision for at least systemic banks is, I believe, beyond necessary. The same opinion is shared by the European Central Bank (ECB). More specifically, ECB President Mario Draghi supported the European Commission's proposal to create a banking union in the Eurozone. Speaking in the European Parliament on May 31st, in his capacity as head of the European Systemic Risk Board, Mr Draghi argued that the form the Eurozone has had in the past decade has proved to be no longer viable unless new steps are taken to consolidate. To this end, he called on political leaders to clarify their vision of the euro, and to do so quickly, otherwise they risk a disaster, as the ECB cannot fill the political vacuum. It also argued that a banking union should be centrally supervised and have a common deposit guarantee mechanism and a clearing mechanism for failing banks. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) was also in favour of the creation of a banking union. However, I would also like to make a brief reference to the measures that we as the CBC are taking at national level towards the immediate consolidation of our banking system. In addition to meeting banks' current capital needs, there are other parameters that need to be reviewed or improved. First of all, the banking sector is very large compared to the size of the Cypriot economy. Specifically, at the end of December 2011, the consolidated assets of all banks operating in Cyprus, including cooperative credit institutions, amounted, as reflected in Chart 1, to about 8 times the country's GDP, while that of domestic banks, including cooperative credit institutions, amounted to about 5.5 times the GDP of Cyprus. The CBC in the coming months will examine in depth, with the help of experts  and now with the help of the IMF  both the issue of the optimal size of our banking system and the issue of its optimal structure. It is also necessary to take all appropriate measures in order to limit the possible future negative effects stemming from the presence of Cypriot banks in other countries. That is why, as the CBC, we will proceed in parallel with the goal of de-dependence of the Cypriot banking sector from the Greek economy through the victimization of the branches of Cypriot banks operating in Greece. Our goal is for this process to be completed by the end of 2012. Public finances In addition to the consolidation of the banking sector, the second biggest challenge facing the Cypriot economy is the consolidation of public finances. However, I would like to make it clear from the outset that Cyprus' public finances, despite the deterioration they have shown mainly due to the crisis, are in a better position than the euro area average. In particular, Cyprus' public debt stood at 71.6% of GDP for 2011, lower than that of the euro area, which stands at 87.2%, but also lower than that of strong Member States, such as Germany with the relative percentage being amounts to 81.2% of GDP for 2011. In addition, the aforementioned percentage of Cyprus is lower than the relative percentages of Greece, Ireland and Portugal (165.3%, 108.2% and 107.8% of GDP, respectively) and marginally higher than the relative share of Spain (68.5%) (see Chart 2). It is also noted that, based on data from eurostat and the European Commission's spring forecast for 2012, the projected increase in gross government debt over the period 2011-2013 as a percentage of GDP is expected to reach 6.5% for Cyprus, lower than the relative rates of Spain, Ireland and Portugal (18.5%, 12% and 9.3% respectively) (see Chart 3). However, any fiscal imbalances of our country are prudent, based on our commitments to the EU, to be immediately reduced with the ultimate goal of fully balanced budgets and compliance with the Fiscal Framework, to which as a eurozone country we are committed. Of course, support for growth should play an essential role in the country's return to fiscal stability. In order for growth to become a reality, it is necessary, first of all, to correct budgetary imbalances and, in general, to respect the financial framework, through a strategy that is perfectly friendly and compatible with development. Of course, the emphasis should always be on reducing the current expenditure of the state while productive expenditure should be maintained and strengthened with the aim of strengthening the country's GDP and creating new jobs. I would like to remind you at this point that the problem of large budget deficits that is observed in many countries of the euro area is not - with the possible exception of Greece - the cause of the economic crisis but the result. This is also pointed out in an article in the Financial Times yesterday by Paul Krugman and Richard Layard (2012), who recall that the cause of the crisis was none other than excessive lending to and from the private sector, including banks with excessive loan dependency. When the real estate bubble burst on both sides of the Atlantic, this excessive borrowing proved unsustainable, leading to a major recession which in turn caused a deterioration in the countries' fiscal situation. Therefore, the solution to this problem must focus on the root cause (limitation of excessive lending - consolidation of the banking system) and not on the large reduction in government expenditure or the imposition of significant tax increases on ordinary citizens. The above finding applies, in general, to Cyprus as well. Reducing, therefore, the current expenditure of the state should not necessarily include significant reductions in salaries or pensions and other austerity measures harmful to the development. These measures, what they usually achieve - as has been shown in the case of Greece - is to reinforce the vicious circle created between the decline in economic activity and the deterioration of the budgetary situation and the portfolio of credit institutions. The reduction in the current expenditure of the state can and must therefore come from the gradual reduction of the number of civil servants and the suppression of bureaucracy, the strengthening of productivity and the proper functioning of the state machine, the improvement of the evaluation system of civil servants and the improvement of efficiency in the use of public sector resources, better targeting of social policy programmes, further consolidation of meritocracy and reform of the pension system. However, I would also like to make a special reference to the role that the higher education of our country can play both in strengthening the real GDP of the country and in improving the fiscal situation. I know very well, also as a former member of the CUT's Dept. that the level of higher education in Cyprus is not at all inferior to that of the best European universities. Our universities, both public and private, are staffed by a well-trained academic and administrative staff, and the study programs offered largely meet the requirements of today's era. However, the quality of higher education in our country should, I believe, be seen as one of the comparative advantages of the country and draw up a similar policy, aiming at attracting foreign students as much as possible. The framework, for example, in which public universities operate could perhaps be liberalised so that it would also be able to offer undergraduate programmes in English. This development could contribute, through the increase of foreign students, a significant amount to the public coffers while at the same time it could increase the size of the market for foreign students for both private and public universities, providing them with the opportunity to increase their revenues and productivity. In short, with this strategy, the country's public universities will not only lighten public coffers but will potentially also be able to make a substantial contribution to development in a direct way. Competitiveness- structural change-growth The growth prospects of our economy should also be strengthened by strengthening competitiveness, the erosion of which is the third biggest challenge facing the country. In order to become more competitive, Cyprus must define and reassess international developments and adapt at any time to the current international economic environment. Our main goal should be to increase the country's productivity through a series of structural changes but also to contain the rate of earnings growth, not necessarily with significant wage reductions that affect overall demand and create conditions of uncertainty and recession, but mainly through the creation of a more flexible but also fairer system of payment of the ATA. Also, the recent recommendations of the European Commission for Cyprus constitute a good basis, a general framework for negotiation with the Troika with the aim of further structural reform of the Cypriot economy. At this point, however, I would like to make special reference to the European Commission's report on the harmonisation of the supervision of cooperative credit institutions (MFA) with the standards applicable to commercial banks. I would like to point out something that as the CBC we will also explain to the European Commission: this proposal has in fact long been adopted and has largely been implemented in practice. The supervision exercised over the MFA by the Co-operative Society Supervision and Development Service is effective and ensures the robustness, proper operation and development of the MFA on the same basic criteria as the supervision of the CBC in commercial banks. I would also like to add that the creation of a banking union in the euro area with uniform supervision for the systemically large banks, which as I have already said, the CBC supports, probably, as far as Cyprus is concerned, will also include some large MFA (perhaps only one), if these are considered as systemically important either for Cyprus or for the euro area itself. Although significant progress has been made in the field of the above suggestions, which is also welcomed by the European Commission itself, however, further effort is needed to upgrade the position of Cyprus in the competitiveness table. The ongoing current account deficits, which are partly a result of the country's low competitiveness in recent years, potentially expose Cyprus to increased risks. The financing of the current account deficit, which has now exceeded 10% in the three-year period 2009-2011, compared to the average of 3% observed from 1995 to 2004, did not pose a problem in the past due to the large inflow of foreign direct investment. At this point, however, I must point out that the enlargement observed in the current account balance may in fact not mean a correspondingly large reduction in the country's competitiveness. This is because in small countries such as Cyprus, the presence of foreign companies can significantly distort the overall picture, since income flows do not necessarily reflect economic transactions related to competitiveness. Therefore, the real trend of our country's competitiveness is likely to be better reflected in the balance of goods and services than in the overall current account balance. Specifically, the deficit in the balance of goods and services, although widened compared to the past, nevertheless its degree of expansion (to 5.1% in the three-year period 2009-2011 from 3.2% in the three-year period 2004-2006) is much less than the corresponding overall widening of the current account deficit (to 10.3% in the three-year period 2009-2011 from 6% in the three-year period 2004-2006). This suggests that the decline in the country's competitiveness, although real, is not of the magnitude implied by the expansion in the current account balance. But regardless of this fact, as I have mentioned before, there is certainly a need to improve the competitiveness of Cyprus through a series of structural measures aimed at increasing the country's productivity and substantially improving the efficiency of the development model on which our country is based. Among other things, measures focused on upgrading the business environment, accelerating the process of transition to the Knowledge Economy, strengthening the entrepreneurship of small and medium-sized enterprises, the proper functioning of the public sector by providing quality services to the citizen and businesses and the strengthening of the country as a financial center could be helpful. We also need more effective policies for small and medium-sized enterprises, including and facilitating their access to foreign markets, and making better use of both existing and new European programmes. It would be good to support and substantially encourage those companies that present innovative programmes and services. In other words, to help increase productivity by investing in the knowledge society, new technologies and innovation. Of course, as far as research and innovation are concerned, our university institutions such as cut are already playing a significant positive role. Which is a modern pioneering University capable of offering high-level education and research in disciplines with great economic, technical and scientific performance. With its commitment to applied research, the Cyprus University of Technology aspires to become an important helper of the state and our society in addressing contemporary challenges in all areas of science, technology and knowledge served in it. I am sure that cut can play an even greater positive role in enhancing the productivity of our country and growth, through securing resources from European programs that support academic research and new technologies. Also, I am sure that cut can play a very positive role in enhancing the productivity of small and medium-sized enterprises, through the relationships it can and should develop with the commercial and industrial world not only of Limassol but also of the whole of Cyprus. In addition to the aforementioned structural changes, Cyprus' development prospects can also benefit from financial assistance for investments through the 130 billion package. to which the leaders of Germany, France, Italy and Spain agreed in an effort to revive economic growth in Europe. The relevant measures, which are already being worked on in Brussels, include an increase in the funds of the European Investment Bank, the reorientation of unspent resources from the EU's regional aid funds and the introduction of development bonds to cofinance large public investment projects. However, before concluding my speech, I would like to point out that the existence of significant natural gas deposits in the Cyprus Exclusive Economic Zone is a new important promising development, which with proper handling by the state will substantially enhance the long-term development of the country, significantly increasing the standard of living of the Cypriot people. In particular, the exploitation of natural gas presupposes the construction of pipelines from the deposit in the country, liquefaction facilities, port extensions, internal network and infrastructure for transportation, etc. These projects are multi-billion investments in construction, energy, infrastructure and technology. These investments can lead to an upward economic cycle with multiplier benefits to the country's GDP. A very important role will certainly be played by the banking sector in Cyprus, which will be called upon to finance many of these investments, which will help to bring our financial institutions to a more rapid recovery. Epilogue The Cypriot economy continues, despite the current difficulties, to be a basically robust economy. Although the international financial crisis and the debt crisis in the euro area brought to the surface various structural problems and at the same time caused huge losses to Cypriot banks, however, due to the sound basis of our country's economic data, these problems are manageable. For this reason, the inclusion of our country in the EU support mechanism should not be of particular concern. The mechanism, as I have already said, will help Cyprus in a substantial way to overcome the current problems and to return as soon as possible to a sustainable development trajectory. I would like to assure, on behalf of the CBC, that we will fight the battle in close cooperation with the Ministry of Finance and the government within the framework of our role so that any conditions placed before us do not undermine the growth prospects of our economy nor the position of Cyprus as a financial center. The broader consensus reached so far in dealing with fiscal, banking and other problems is, I believe, the best guarantee for the successful confrontation of all current and future challenges and the guarantee of long-term prosperity conditions for the entire Cypriot people. ----------------------------------------------Profile Krugman, Paul and Richard Layard, (2012) "A manifesto for economic sense", Financial Times, 27 June.
